Florida Cannabis & Hemp Research — Audited Final Report (Parts 0–12)

Last audited: 24 October 2026  |  Original reports: Run 1, Parts 0–6, and Run 2, Parts 7–12, both delivered 24 October 2026  |  Method: primary sources only for confirmations. News, law-firm blogs, trade press and AI summaries never confirm a claim; where only a secondary source exists the verdict is Unverified. This merged file supersedes the Run 2-only audited file delivered earlier on 24 October 2026 (florida-cannabis-hemp-audited-final.html); its Run 2 audit and rewrite are carried into this file unchanged, and Run 1 (Parts 0–6) is now audited and rewritten on the same basis.

Federal baseline — used as given, not re-audited

Scheduling is split. Under a final rule at 91 FR 22714 (effective 28 April 2026), FDA-approved cannabis products and state-licensed medical marijuana are in Schedule III. All other marijuana, including all adult-use, remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is NOT final. IRS 280E: Treasury has said rescheduling generally removes 280E as a bar for businesses no longer dealing in Schedule I/II substances (guidance forthcoming); adult-use activity remains fully subject to 280E. Hemp: Public Law 119-37 §781 takes legal effect 12 November 2026, but Public Law 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026 to only the provisions excluding cannabinoids that are not naturally produced or are synthesized. The full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap apply after 11 December 2026. USDA has delayed enforcement of the DEA-registered-laboratory hemp testing requirement until 31 December 2026. The federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider is in force through 11 December 2026. No federal cannabis banking law has been enacted. This report applies Schedule III and the 280E change to Florida MMTCs’ medical activity only, and treats any adult-use activity as Schedule I. No statement in either original run that contradicted this baseline was found as an assertion of law; two tensions are preserved as flags, not rewritten: (1) unamended Florida text in §381.986(4)(a)8.a. still requires the physician informed-consent form to state marijuana is Schedule I; (2) the original Part 10 reading of the 12 November 2026 tranche is narrower than the baseline wording and is flagged [VERIFY against §2019 text] — the baseline wording governs in this rewrite.

How to read the rewrite (Parts 2A and 2B): every section and all detail from both originals are kept. Only what the audits changed has been changed, in place, plus a boxed “Audit corrections applied” note at the head of each affected Part so a reader can see the correction without hunting. Where a correction note or an Audit table entry and an original passage conflict, the correction governs. Flags [VERIFY] and [UNAVAILABLE] remain only on items still unresolved after these audits, listed in full in Parts 1A and 1B. One post-report update is carried as a dated note, not backdated: Rule 64-4.214 was proposed only at 24 October 2026 and was subsequently adopted effective 2 November 2026.

PART 1A — AUDIT: RUN 1, PARTS 0–6

Method. Primary sources only for confirmations: Florida Statutes (Online Sunshine, leg.state.fl.us), Florida Administrative Code / Florida Register (flrules.org), OMMU at the Florida Department of Health (knowthefactsmmj.com), FDACS, Florida Department of Revenue, Governor's bill actions, Florida Division of Elections, Florida Supreme Court opinions, and official county/city codes. News, law-firm blogs, trade press and AI summaries never confirm a claim; where only a secondary source exists the verdict is Unverified. Verdicts: Confirmed = primary source opened; Corrected = wording must change; Removed = do not carry as current; Unverified = primary source not opened or only secondary exists. The federal baseline in the introduction was used as given and was not re-audited; no Run 1 assertion of law was found to contradict it (see the federal-baseline note at the end of this Part).

COUNT DECISION — READ FIRST (resolves the Run 1 total-licence conflict). Latest authoritative snapshot, OMMU Weekly Update, 23 October 2026 (file 102326-OMMU-Update.pdf, opened directly in the Parts 4–5 audit): 49 named MMTCs, 784 dispensing locations, 943,271 qualified patients (active ID card). Source: https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/ommu_updates/2026/102326-OMMU-Update.pdf. Arithmetic: 28 named on 28 August 2026, minus 1 (the Moton Hopkins Jr. row disappears from the October table — reason not confirmed, do not infer issuance, surrender, merger or renaming), plus 22 September 2026 licences = 49. The figure 50 (28+22) is wrong. The figure 27 is a secondary pre-order count that apparently already excluded the Moton Hopkins Jr. row. This supersedes the Parts 2–3 audit's interim decision to adopt 781 locations (25 September 2026, OMMU via CannBus) and the Part 6 headline's Herald-reported 943,271/784: both figures are now primary-confirmed at 23 October 2026, not merely secondary-reported. Dated snapshots only: 28 August 2026 — 940,116 patients / 778 locations / 28 named entities (082826-OMMU-Update.pdf); week of 2–8 October 2026 — 942,370 patients / 782 locations (100926-OMMU-Update.pdf). Week 16–22 October 2026 dispensations: 426,655,358 mg THC; 1,049 mg CBD; 148,489.350 oz smokable.

How to read this document

Research date / Accessed date: 24 October 2026 for every fact, unless a different publication or update date is stated in the fact itself.

Florida status in one line: Medical-only as of 24 October 2026. No adult-use measure is on the 2026 ballot, no adult-use licence type exists, and no adult-use implementation plan is in force.

Flags: [VERIFY] = uncertain, conflicting, or not confirmed on the official page itself in this run. [UNAVAILABLE] = not located. Proposed bills and initiatives are never described as law.

Dollar sales figures conflict across trackers (Headset vs Brightfield vs BDSA) and no official dollar series exists; no single dollar total is adopted as official.

Federal baseline (fixed context, not re-researched): state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity and remains fully applicable to adult-use; hemp PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026 but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026, after which the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply; USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026; the federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026; there is no federal cannabis banking law. Florida MMTCs are state-licensed medical operators, so Schedule III / 280E relief applies to their medical activity under this baseline. One Florida-text tension is flagged in Part 1: §381.986(4)(a)8.a. still requires the consent form to state marijuana is Schedule I.

Source reports preserved: the four underlying research files are retained at ~/workspace/research_notes/florida-cannabis-hemp-run1-20261024/ (part01.md, part23.md, part45.md, part6.md). Every fact below carries its source link and Accessed 2026-10-24 date in the source reports and in this HTML.

PART 0 — HEADLINES

0.1 Florida is medical-only in October 2026. No adult-use measure is on the 2026 ballot.

  • Medical only, no change in law as of 24 October 2026. An adult in Florida may lawfully use marijuana only as a registered medical patient buying from a licensed Medical Marijuana Treatment Center (MMTC). Secondary summary dated 16 October 2026: "an adult in Florida can use marijuana legally only as a registered medical patient who buys from a licensed medical marijuana treatment center" and "No adult-use amendment is on the 2026 general election ballot." Source: https://www.drgreenrelief.com/blog/is-recreational-marijuana-legal-in-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary).
  • 2024 Amendment 3 FAILED. It received 55.9% yes (5,934,139 votes) to 44.1% no (4,685,443 votes) on 5 November 2024, short of Florida's 60% threshold for constitutional amendments, so it did not pass. Sources: https://www.gatorsports.com/story/news/2024/11/06/recreational-marijuana-law-florida-not-pass-election/75960996007/ and https://www.gatorsports.com/story/news/politics/elections/2024/11/05/florida-marijuana-amendment-early-election-results-passage-vote/75972689007/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary, reporting Associated Press / official results; official canvass pinpoint [VERIFY] for Run 2).
  • 2026 attempt FAILED TO QUALIFY — it is not a "result" because there was no vote. Smart & Safe Florida's "Adult Personal Use of Marijuana," Serial No. 25-01, filed 14 January 2025, needed 880,062 valid signatures by 1 February 2026. The Division of Elections listed 783,592 verified signatures by the deadline — a shortfall of about 96,470. Secretary of State Cord Byrd determined on 2 February 2026 that 25-01 "failed to meet the legal requirements for placement on the 2026 General Election ballot" and that under §100.371(14)(a) "all signatures are now expired." The Department of State then posted that all 22 active initiative petitions failed for 2026. The campaign disputed the count, saying it had submitted about 1.4 million signatures, and challenged invalidation of roughly 70,000 signatures from "inactive" voters or nonresident/noncitizen circulators; as of April 2026 a federal judge upheld the stricter petition rules. Sources: https://www.tallahassee.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/10/19/florida-elections-vote-recreational-marijuana-amendment/92326407007/ ; https://gmg-wkmg-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/news/florida/2026/02/02/no-citizen-initiatives-on-2026-florida-ballot-including-marijuana-amendment-state-says/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary). Do not confuse this with a 2026 election result: no 2026 adult-use vote took place.
  • The fight has moved to 2028 — three initiatives, none qualified. The Division of Elections register (accessed via search 2026-10-24) lists for the 2028 General Election: Serial 25-01, "Adult Personal Use of Marijuana," Smart & Safe Florida, Active, 14 January 2025; Serial 26-01, same title, Floridians for Marijuana, Active, 30 September 2026; Serial 26-03, same title, Let Florida Vote IV, Pending FIEC (Financial Impact Estimating Conference), 29 September 2026. None has ballot position, and none has the 880,062 valid signatures or the 60% vote that would be needed. Source: https://constitutionalinitiatives.dos.fl.gov/?account=70115&seqnum=1 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official register, via search extract; direct register re-check is Gap G-02). Secondary detail on 26-01 (22 October 2026 reporting, not law): adults 21+, possession limit 2 ounces including no more than 5 grams concentrate, no public smoking/vaping, no child-appealing marketing/packaging, MMTCs could sell to adults, separately licensed non-vertically-integrated businesses possible, Legislature to set licensing rules before effect, home grow not legalised by the measure itself but could be authorised later by lawmakers, effective first day of the sixth month after the election. Source: https://themarijuanaherald.com/2026/10/florida-two-new-marijuana-legalization-initiatives-filed-for-2028/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary; full text of 26-01/26-03 [VERIFY]).
  • Consequence: there is NO legislative adult-use implementation plan in force, because no adult-use measure passed. Any adult-use licence type, tax, or implementation timeline in 2026 material is PROPOSED ONLY (see §1.9).

0.3 Schedule III / §280E — what it means for Florida MMTCs (fixed baseline applied, not re-researched)

  • Florida MMTCs are state-licensed medical operators under §381.986. On the fixed federal baseline, their medical activity is Schedule III activity from 28 April 2026, so §280E is generally lifted for that medical activity, while any adult-use activity — which does not lawfully exist in Florida — would remain Schedule I and fully subject to §280E.
  • Contradiction / stale-text flag (does NOT contradict the federal baseline; it shows Florida text has not caught up): §381.986(4)(a)8.a. still requires the standardised informed-consent form to include "The Federal Government's classification of marijuana as a Schedule I controlled substance." That statutory sentence is now inaccurate for state-licensed medical marijuana under the fixed baseline. Whether the Department of Health / Boards of Medicine and Osteopathic Medicine have updated the adopted consent form in rule is [VERIFY] — see Gap G-03. No Florida statute or OMMU notice amending that sentence for Schedule III was located in this run.
  • No Florida Schedule III response law was located in this run [UNAVAILABLE / VERIFY]: no Florida statute, OMMU notice, or Department of Revenue guidance stating how Florida treats Schedule III medical marijuana for state purposes was found. This is a Run 2 / Part 2 follow-up, not a finding that no such guidance exists.

0.4 Hemp — the current position in one paragraph

  • Florida hemp law is unchanged by the Legislature in 2024, 2025, or the 2026 regular session (which adjourned 13 March 2026 without enacting hemp legislation — secondary, see §1.5.9). Delta-8 and other hemp-derived cannabinoids remain lawful only inside §581.217's 0.3% total delta-9 THC framework, with a 21+ age rule for ingestion/inhalation products, child-resistant / non-child-appealing packaging, and a COA/QR-code regime enforced by FDACS stop-sale orders. The 2024 cap-and-ban bill (SB 1698) was vetoed; the 2025 Senate/House pair (SB 438 / HB 7027) died without agreement. FDACS enforcement, not new statute, is the live story: by the time of FDACS's 2025 "Operation Safe Summer" release, FDACS said it had removed over 1.3 million packages of illegal hemp products since 1 July 2023, including 197,303 packages in that operation in all 67 counties. Source: https://www.fdacs.gov/News-Events/Press-Releases/2025-Press-Releases/Commissioner-Wilton-Simpson-Announces-Over-17-000-Dangerous-7-OH-Packages-Removed-from-Florida-Stores-Following-Emergency-Ban — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official FDACS release, via search extract).
  • Federal hemp dates are imminent and Florida has no conforming statute yet: on the fixed baseline, 12 November 2026 removes federal hemp status from products with cannabinoids "not capable of being naturally produced" by the plant, and 11 December 2026 brings the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per-container cap. No official FDACS or Florida Legislature response conforming §581.217 to PL 119-37 / PL 119-103 was located in this run [UNAVAILABLE] — see §1.5.10 and Gap G-04. Florida's own 0.3% delta-9 rule does not change by itself when federal law changes; only a Florida amendment, or federal preemption/supremacy litigation, would change what is lawful in Florida, and neither was located.

PART 1 — LAWS

1.1 Legal status: medical only

Bottom line: As of 24 October 2026, Florida law authorises only (a) medical use of marijuana by qualified patients/caregivers through MMTCs under Article X, §29 and §381.986, and (b) hemp and hemp extract within §581.217. Every other acquisition, possession, use, sale, or cultivation of cannabis (as defined in §893.02(3), excluding conforming medical marijuana and hemp) is a Chapter 893 offence. There is no decriminalisation statute, no adult-use statute, and no home-grow right.

What is legal for a non-patient: - Buying and possessing hemp / hemp extract that complies with §581.217, if 21+ for ingestion/inhalation products (§581.217(7)(d)) — see §1.5. - Possessing nothing else cannabis-related: non-patient possession of cannabis is criminal at any amount (see §1.3 table). A non-patient may not lawfully buy from an MMTC, receive a transfer from a patient (transfer to anyone other than the patient or the patient's caregiver is expressly excluded from "medical use," §381.986(1)(k)4.), or grow a plant. - Being present where a patient lawfully uses is not itself made lawful possession; do not infer a "social use" defence — none is stated in §381.986.

What is NOT legal, even for patients (summary; detail in §1.3–§1.4): smoking in an enclosed indoor workplace; use in a public place (except low-THC cannabis not in smoking form); use on public transportation, in a vehicle/aircraft/motorboat, or on school grounds except under §1006.062; use at work except when permitted by the employer; transfer to a non-patient/caregiver; purchase from anyone other than an MMTC; cultivation by the patient; possession above the certified 70-day / 4-ounce smoking limits; smoking-form use by a minor except the terminal-condition + paediatric-concurrence route; use inconsistent with the physician's directions/certification; and commercially produced food items other than "edibles" as defined, or marijuana seeds, as "medical use."

1.2.1 Florida Constitution, Article X, §29 — "Medical marijuana production, possession and use" (Amendment 2, adopted 8 Nov 2016, 71.3% [VERIFY exact canvass — secondary figure commonly reported; official canvass pinpoint is Gap G-05])

  • Official link: Online Sunshine Constitution: https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=... (Constitution, Art. X) — Accessed 2026-10-24 [VERIFY — the direct Online Sunshine constitution URL was not opened in this run; the text below was confirmed against the FindLaw reproduction and the Division of Elections full text, and must be re-verified against Online Sunshine in Run 2]. Mirror checked: https://codes.findlaw.com/fl/florida-constitution1968-revision/fl-const-art-10-sect-29/ — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Plain summary: Medical use by a qualifying patient or caregiver in compliance with the section is not subject to criminal or civil liability or sanctions under Florida law; a physician issuing a certification with reasonable care is likewise protected; and a registered MMTC, its agents/employees, in compliance, is likewise protected. It defines "debilitating medical condition," "Department" (Department of Health), "identification card," "marijuana" (by reference to §893.02(3) (2014) plus low-THC cannabis as defined in §381.986(1)(b) (2014)), "Medical Marijuana Treatment Center," "physician certification," and "qualifying patient"/"caregiver" concepts, and requires the Department to regulate MMTCs, issue ID cards, and set rules. It does NOT itself create adult-use rights, a home-grow right, or employment protections.
  • Verbatim operative text — (a) Public policy:

    "(1) The medical use of marijuana by a qualifying patient or caregiver in compliance with this section is not subject to criminal or civil liability or sanctions under Florida law." "(2) A physician shall not be subject to criminal or civil liability or sanctions under Florida law solely for issuing a physician certification with reasonable care to a person diagnosed with a debilitating medical condition in compliance with this section." "(3) Actions and conduct by a Medical Marijuana Treatment Center registered with the Department, or its agents or employees, and in compliance with this section and Department regulations, shall not be subject to criminal or civil liability or sanctions under Florida law."

  • Verbatim — (b)(1) "Debilitating Medical Condition":

    "means cancer, epilepsy, glaucoma, positive status for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Crohn's disease, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, or other debilitating medical conditions of the same kind or class as or comparable to those enumerated, and for which a physician believes that the medical use of marijuana would likely outweigh the potential health risks for a patient."

  • Last amended: Not amended since adoption in 2016. The 2024 Amendment 3 proposal would have amended this section; it failed (see §0.1). The 2026/2028 proposals would amend it; none has passed.

    §381.986(1)(e) "'Edibles' means commercially produced food items made with marijuana oil, but no other form of marijuana, that are produced and dispensed by a medical marijuana treatment center." §381.986(1)(f) "'Low-THC cannabis' means a plant of the genus Cannabis, the dried flowers of which contain 0.8 percent or less of tetrahydrocannabinol and more than 10 percent of cannabidiol weight for weight; the seeds thereof; the resin extracted from any part of such plant; or any compound, manufacture, salt, derivative, mixture, or preparation of such plant or its seeds or resin that is dispensed from a medical marijuana treatment center." §381.986(1)(g) "'Marijuana' means all parts of any plant of the genus Cannabis, whether growing or not; the seeds thereof; the resin extracted from any part of the plant; and every compound, manufacture, salt, derivative, mixture, or preparation of the plant or its seeds or resin, including low-THC cannabis, which are dispensed from a medical marijuana treatment center for medical use by a qualified patient." §381.986(1)(k) "'Medical use' means the acquisition, possession, use, delivery, transfer, or administration of marijuana authorized by a physician certification. The term does not include: 1. Possession, use, or administration of marijuana that was not purchased or acquired from a medical marijuana treatment center. 2. Possession, use, or administration of marijuana in the form of commercially produced food items other than edibles or of marijuana seeds. 3. Use or administration of any form or amount of marijuana in a manner that is inconsistent with the qualified physician's directions or physician certification. 4. Transfer of marijuana to a person other than the qualified patient for whom it was authorized or the qualified patient's caregiver on behalf of the qualified patient. 5. Use or administration of marijuana in the following locations: a. On any form of public transportation, except for low-THC cannabis not in a form for smoking. b. In any public place, except for low-THC cannabis not in a form for smoking. c. In a qualified patient's place of employment, except when permitted by his or her employer. d. In a state correctional institution, as defined in s. 944.02, or a correctional institution, as defined in s. 944.241. e. On the grounds of a preschool, primary school, or secondary school, except as provided in s. 1006.062. f. In a school bus, a vehicle, an aircraft, or a motorboat, except for low-THC cannabis not in a form for smoking. 6. The smoking of marijuana in an enclosed indoor workplace as defined in s. 386.203(5)." §381.986(1)(a) "'Attractive to children' means the use of any image or words designed or likely to appeal to persons younger than 18 years of age, including, but not limited to, cartoons, toys, animals, food, or depictions of persons younger than 18 years of age; any other likeness to images, characters, or phrases that are popularly used to advertise to persons younger than 18 years of age; or any reasonable likeness to commercially available candy."

1.2.3 Chapter 893 — Florida Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act (criminal provisions)

1.2.4 §581.217 — "State hemp program" (FDACS)

  • Official link: https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0500-0599/0581/Sections/0581.217.html — Accessed 2026-10-24 (opened and read in full, 207 lines).
  • History line as printed: "History. — s. 1, ch. 2019-132; s. 5, ch. 2020-135; s. 26, ch. 2023-154; s. 2, ch. 2023-299." So the statute was last amended in 2023 (SB 1676, ch. 2023-154, plus ch. 2023-299). No 2024, 2025, or 2026 amendment to §581.217 appears in the current text. The 2023 amendments added the 21+ rule, the "attractive to children" definition, and food-safety parity (see §1.5).
  • Plain summary by subsection: (1) Program created within FDACS; "This section constitutes the state plan" for 7 U.S.C. §1639p. (2) Findings: hemp is an agricultural commodity; hemp-derived cannabinoids, including cannabidiol, "are not controlled substances or adulterants if they are in compliance with this section." (3) Definitions (quoted below). (4) FDACS shall seek USDA approval of the state plan within 30 days after adopting rules; if not approved, Commissioner + Administration Commission recommend amendments to the Legislature. (5) Cultivation licensure (unlawful without licence; fingerprints; land description + GPS; 10-year bar after felony controlled-substance conviction; falsification bar). (6) Certified seed/cultivars only. (7) Distribution/retail sale of hemp extract (COA, container, 21+, stop-sale — quoted below). (8) Land registry (3 years). (9) Monthly USDA reporting. (10) Violations / corrective action plans / 3-in-5-years → 5-year ineligibility; culpable-mental-state violations reported to Attorneys General. (11) Enforcement (FDACS + state attorneys, sheriffs, police; entry during business hours; random inspections at least annually). (12) Rulemaking duties (post-decarboxylation testing, disposal, packaging/labelling, advertising). (13) Applicability (does not authorise violating other law; pilot-project carve-out; negligent violators not subject to other state/local criminal/civil enforcement except under this section).
  • Verbatim definitions:

    §581.217(3)(e) "'Hemp' means the plant Cannabis sativa L. and any part of that plant, including the seeds thereof, and all derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids, salts, and salts of isomers thereof, whether growing or not, that has a total delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol concentration that does not exceed 0.3 percent on a dry-weight basis, with the exception of hemp extract, which may not exceed 0.3 percent total delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol on a wet-weight basis." §581.217(3)(f) "'Hemp extract' means a substance or compound intended for ingestion, containing more than trace amounts of a cannabinoid, or for inhalation which is derived from or contains hemp and which does not contain controlled substances. The term does not include synthetic cannabidiol or seeds or seed-derived ingredients that are generally recognized as safe by the United States Food and Drug Administration." §581.217(3)(a) "'Attractive to children' means manufactured in the shape of humans, cartoons, or animals; manufactured in a form that bears any reasonable resemblance to an existing candy product that is familiar to the public as a widely distributed, branded food product such that a product could be mistaken for the branded product, especially by children; or containing any color additives." §581.217(3)(g) — "Independent testing laboratory" must have no direct/indirect interest in the tested entity or in any hemp/marijuana cultivator/processor/distributor/dispenser/seller, and must be ISO/IEC 17025-accredited.

  • Verbatim — distribution/retail conditions (§581.217(7)(a)–(e)):

    "(a) Hemp extract may only be distributed and sold in the state if the product: 1. Has a certificate of analysis prepared by an independent testing laboratory that states: a. The hemp extract is the product of a batch tested by the independent testing laboratory; b. The batch contained a total delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol concentration that did not exceed 0.3 percent pursuant to the testing of a random sample of the batch; and c. The batch does not contain contaminants unsafe for human consumption [and d. the batch was processed in a facility holding a current, valid human-health/food-safety permit meeting that entity's sanitisation requirements, documented by that entity's report]; 2. Is distributed or sold in a container that includes: a. A scannable barcode or quick response code linked to the certificate of analysis …; b. The batch number; c. The Internet address of a website where batch information may be obtained; d. The expiration date; and e. The number of milligrams of each marketed cannabinoid per serving. 3. Is distributed or sold in a container that: a. Is suitable to contain products for human consumption; b. Is composed of materials designed to minimize exposure to light; c. Mitigates exposure to high temperatures; d. Is not attractive to children; and e. Is compliant with the United States Poison Prevention Packaging Act of 1970, 15 U.S.C. ss. 1471 et seq., without regard to provided exemptions." "(d) Products that are intended for human ingestion or inhalation and that contain hemp extract, including, but not limited to, snuff, chewing gum, and other smokeless products, may not be sold in this state to a person who is under 21 years of age. A person who violates this paragraph commits a misdemeanor of the second degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082 or s. 775.083. A person who commits a second or subsequent violation of this paragraph within 1 year after the initial violation commits a misdemeanor of the first degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082 or s. 775.083." "(e) Hemp extract distributed or sold in violation of this subsection is subject to s. 500.172 and penalties as provided in s. 500.121. Hemp extract products found to be mislabeled or attractive to children are subject to an immediate stop-sale order."

1.3.2 Cultivation — home grow is PROHIBITED (confirmed)

  • Patients and caregivers may NOT cultivate. §381.986(12)(d): "A qualified patient or caregiver who cultivates marijuana or who purchases or acquires marijuana from any person or entity other than a medical marijuana treatment center violates s. 893.13 and is subject to the penalties provided therein." §381.986(5)(f): the Department "may revoke the registration of a qualified patient or caregiver who cultivates marijuana or who acquires, possesses, or delivers marijuana from any person or entity other than a medical marijuana treatment center." §381.986(12)(j): an unlicensed person/entity that "cultivates, processes, distributes, sells, or dispenses marijuana, as defined in s. 29(b)(4), Art. X" likewise violates §893.13.
  • Only a licensed MMTC may cultivate, and only "within an enclosed structure and in a room separate from any other plant" (§381.986(8)(e)6.b.), using only Department-approved pesticides (after FDACS consultation) and never restricted-use pesticides (§381.986(8)(e)6.a.).
  • The 2024 Amendment 3 and the 2026/2028 proposals did NOT include a home-grow right in their operative summaries as reported; the 2028 26-01 proposal expressly leaves home grow to future legislation (see §0.1). The Smart & Safe post-2024 statement expressing interest in "expanding access … through home grow" is advocacy, not law.
  • Hemp cultivation is different: it requires an FDACS licence (§581.217(5)(a): "It is unlawful for a person to cultivate hemp in this state without a license issued by the department") — see Part 7, not a patient right.

1.3.3 Public consumption and smoking rules

  • General ban for patients: §381.986(1)(k)5. excludes from "medical use" use/administration on public transportation, in a public place, at work (unless employer permits), in a correctional institution, on preschool/primary/secondary school grounds (except §1006.062), and in a school bus/vehicle/aircraft/motorboat — in each case except for low-THC cannabis not in a form for smoking. Smoking in an enclosed indoor workplace (§386.203(5)) is separately excluded (§381.986(1)(k)6.).
  • Criminal penalty for public use by a patient: §381.986(12)(c): "A qualified patient who uses marijuana, not including low-THC cannabis, or a caregiver who administers marijuana, not including low-THC cannabis, in plain view of or in a place open to the general public; in a school bus, a vehicle, an aircraft, or a boat; or on the grounds of a school except as provided in s. 1006.062, commits a misdemeanor of the first degree."
  • Smoking as a medical route: Smoking was NOT a lawful medical route under the 2017 implementing act. It became lawful with SB 182, ch. 2019-1, signed 18 March 2019, which removed the smoking exclusion. Current law therefore allows a qualified physician to certify smoking as a route, subject to §381.986(4)(c) documentation (other routes tried, research, signed opinion that benefits outweigh risks) for non-terminal patients, and, for minors, the terminal-condition + most-effective-route + board-certified paediatrician concurrence + parental written consent regime (§381.986(4)(d)).
  • Smoking-form packaging (verbatim, §381.986(8)(e)13.): marijuana in a form for smoking must be in "a sealed receptacle with a legible and prominent warning to keep away from children and a warning that states marijuana smoke contains carcinogens and may negatively affect health. Such receptacles … must be plain, opaque, and white without depictions of the product or images other than the medical marijuana treatment center's department-approved logo and the marijuana universal symbol."
  • Private-property rule: §381.986(15)(d): "This section does not impair the ability of any party to restrict or limit smoking or vaping marijuana on his or her private property." Landlords, employers, and property owners may therefore ban it on their property; tenant/landlord detail is Part 12.
  • Public smoking/vaping bans in the PROPOSED adult-use measures are not law. The 2024/2026/2028 summaries all prohibit public smoking/vaping, but none has been enacted.

1.3.4 Allowed medical product forms, dose, potency, and supply limits

Forms allowed (from §381.986 and Rule 64ER22-8): Whole flower and ground whole flower and pre-rolled marijuana cigarettes (smoking form only); vaporisation/inhalation products; oral products (capsules, tinctures); sublingual tinctures; suppositories; topicals (creams); edibles (only as defined — commercially produced food items made with marijuana oil, no other form of marijuana, produced/dispensed by an MMTC); and marijuana delivery devices specified in the certification. A physician certifies specific routes/forms; a patient may buy only within the certified routes. MMTCs may not dispense/sell any other cannabis/alcohol/illicit-drug-related product, including tobacco/hemp wrapping papers, other than a certified delivery device (§381.986(8)(e)16.f.). Pre-rolled cigarettes may not use tobacco or hemp wrapping paper (§381.986(8)(e)10.).

Edible potency caps (verbatim, §381.986(8)(e)8.):

"Edibles may not contain more than 200 milligrams of tetrahydrocannabinol, and a single serving portion of an edible may not exceed 10 milligrams of tetrahydrocannabinol. Edibles may not have a potency variance greater than 15 percent. Marijuana products, including edibles, may not be attractive to children; be manufactured in the shape of humans, cartoons, or animals; be manufactured in a form that bears any reasonable resemblance to products available for consumption as commercially available candy; or contain any color additives." Edibles producers must hold a Chapter 500 food-establishment permit, and MMTCs may not begin processing/dispensing edibles until the Department's edible rule is effective; processing facilities must pass a Food Safety GMP inspection (e.g., GFSI or equivalent) within 12 months of licensure or stop processing (§381.986(8)(e)8.–9.).

Note the asymmetry: 2.5 oz is the 35-day dispensing cap; 4 oz is the possession cap for smoking form.

A flower THC-percentage cap [VERIFY — none was located in §381.986; do not import another state's cap].
