[AUDIT: that aggregate reading is DELETED — see Audit table, Parts 0–1.] That is the inhalation route's 70-day cap, not a separate statutory aggregate cap in the text read. Whether the MMUR enforces a cross-route aggregate is [VERIFY] — the statute caps dispensing per 70-day period and per certification, and the rule sets per-route daily/70-day amounts; the interaction (whether a patient certified for multiple routes can stack to the sum of route caps) is a registry-enforcement question, Gap G-08.

1.3.5 "Low-THC cannabis" vs "marijuana" — the distinction, precisely

  • Statutory definitions (see §1.2.2A): "Low-THC cannabis" is defined by the flower test — dried flowers ≤0.8% THC and >10% CBD, weight for weight — plus seeds/resin/derivatives dispensed from an MMTC. "Marijuana" is defined broadly to include all Cannabis genus material dispensed from an MMTC for medical use, "including low-THC cannabis." In other words, low-THC cannabis is a subset of "marijuana" for §381.986 purposes, not a separate non-marijuana category — but it carries distinct legal consequences:
  • Public-place / vehicle / transport exception: low-THC cannabis not in smoking form may be used in public places, on public transportation, and in vehicles/aircraft/motorboats where other marijuana may not (§381.986(1)(k)5.).
  • Public-use crime exception: §381.986(12)(c) criminalises public use of marijuana "not including low-THC cannabis" — so public use of low-THC (non-smoking) is not that crime.
  • Pregnancy: a physician "may not issue a physician certification, except for low-THC cannabis, to a patient who is pregnant" (§381.986(4)(a)4.).
  • MMTC obligation: every MMTC "must produce and make available for purchase at least one low-THC cannabis product" (§381.986(8)(e)7.).
  • Historical origin: low-THC was the only lawful category under the 2014 Compassionate Use Act (ch. 2014-157, cancer / seizure / severe muscle-spasm conditions); Amendment 2 (2016) and ch. 2017-232 folded it into the broader medical programme while preserving these carve-outs.
  • Do NOT confuse with hemp: Hemp (§581.217, ≤0.3% total delta-9 THC, dry weight; wet weight for extract) and low-THC cannabis (§381.986, ≤0.8% THC and >10% CBD, MMTC-dispensed) are different tests, different regulators, and different distribution channels. A product can be hemp but not low-THC cannabis (e.g., ≤0.3% THC but ≤10% CBD), and vice versa in THC terms (0.8% > 0.3%, so a low-THC product at 0.5% THC is NOT hemp). The proposed 2026 CS/HB 733 / SB 902 revision would have redefined low-THC to cover all product forms (excluding edibles) at ≤0.8% THC and >2% CBD (not 10%) — that revision DIED and is not law (see §1.9); the 10% CBD flower test above remains the current statute.
  • THC measurement difference: Hemp uses total delta-9 THC (see §1.5.2); low-THC uses the flower's THC and CBD percentages as stated, without a decarboxylation formula in the definition itself [VERIFY whether Department rule applies a THCA conversion to low-THC testing].

1.4 Medical programme

1.4.1 Qualifying conditions (verbatim, §381.986(2))

"A patient must be diagnosed with at least one of the following conditions to qualify to receive marijuana or a marijuana delivery device: (a) Cancer. (b) Epilepsy. (c) Glaucoma. (d) Positive status for human immunodeficiency virus. (e) Acquired immune deficiency syndrome. (f) Posttraumatic stress disorder. (g) Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. (h) Crohn's disease. (i) Parkinson's disease. (j) Multiple sclerosis. (k) Medical conditions of the same kind or class as or comparable to those enumerated in paragraphs (a)-(j). (l) A terminal condition diagnosed by a physician other than the qualified physician issuing the physician certification. (m) Chronic nonmalignant pain."

  • "Chronic nonmalignant pain" is defined (§381.986(1)(c)) as pain caused by, or originating from, a qualifying condition and persisting beyond its usual course. "Terminal condition" (§381.986(1)(p)) is a progressive disease/condition causing significant functional impairment, not reversible without life-sustaining procedures, that will result in death within 1 year if it runs its normal course.
  • For a (2)(k) "comparable" condition, the physician must submit supporting documentation to the applicable board within 14 days (same-kind/class opinion, efficacy documentation, benefit-vs-risk opinion, plus board-rule items); the Department forwards it to the Consortium (§381.986(4)(b)).
  • No condition list expansion by rule was located in this run [VERIFY — check OMMU/Board rules for any added conditions; none is in the statute].

1.4.2 Qualified physician and certification rules

  • Who may certify: a physician holding an active, unrestricted Florida licence under Chapter 458 (allopathic) or 459 (osteopathic) who has completed the required 2-hour course + examination (Florida Medical Association / Florida Osteopathic Medical Association; ≤$500; administered at least annually, distance-learning permitted; renewal of course certification biennially, and before each licence renewal) (§381.986(3)(a)). A qualified physician may not be employed by, or have a direct/indirect economic interest in, an MMTC or testing laboratory (§381.986(3)(b)). Medical directors have a parallel 2-hour requirement (§381.986(3)(c)).
  • Pre-certification duties (verbatim core, §381.986(4)(a)): the physician may certify only if he/she (1) conducted an examination and full history assessment — initial certification requires an in-person physical examination ("an examination conducted by a qualified physician while the physician is physically present in the same room as the patient"); (2) diagnosed a qualifying condition; (3) determined medical use would likely outweigh health risks (documented; second physician concurrence + documentation if patient <18); (4) determined/documented pregnancy status (no certification except low-THC if pregnant); (5) reviewed the PDMP history (§893.055); (6) reviewed the MMUR and confirmed no active certification from another physician; (7) registered as issuer in the MMUR, entering condition, dosage (not exceeding the Department's daily dose amount), amount/forms, delivery-device types, updating within 7 days of any change, and deactivating when no longer recommended; (8) obtained voluntary, informed written consent each time, on the Boards' standardised form (contents listed in §1.0.3 note, including the now-stale Schedule I statement).
  • Telehealth renewals — the rule, exactly: "For certification renewals, a qualified physician who has issued a certification to a patient after conducting an in-person physical examination may conduct subsequent examinations of that patient through telehealth as defined in s. 456.47" (§381.986(4)(a)1.). And §381.986(4)(g): "A qualified physician must evaluate an existing qualified patient at least once every 30 weeks before issuing a new physician certification. A qualified physician who has issued a certification to the patient after conducting an in-person physical examination as defined in subparagraph (a)1. may conduct the evaluation through telehealth." Consequences: (i) a new physician who has never examined the patient in person may NOT renew by telehealth — an in-person exam by that physician is required first (OMMU physicians FAQ, secondary reporting, Accessed 2026-10-24); (ii) telehealth as defined in §456.47 does not include email/fax (secondary reporting of OMMU FAQ); (iii) the former bar on advertising/marketing telehealth before 1 July 2023 (§381.986(4)(i)2.) is spent history.
  • Smoking-route documentation: see §1.3.3.
  • Physician discipline / pattern review: The Department monitors registration/certification for diversion/misuse and may suspend a qualified physician's MMUR registration up to 2 years for non-compliance (§381.986(4)(i)). The Boards' joint Physician Certification Pattern Review Panel tracks certifications by physician, county, and statewide and reports annually to the Governor, Senate President, and House Speaker (§381.986(4)(j)). A physician certifying without reasonable belief in a qualifying condition commits a first-degree misdemeanour (§381.986(12)(a)); receiving MMTC compensation related to a certification is subject to discipline under §456.072(1)(n) (§381.986(12)(g)).
  • 2026 change that DIED: CS/HB 733 / SB 902 would have revised Department approval of qualified physicians/medical directors — not law (see §1.9).

1.4.3 Registry ID cards, fees, caregivers

  • Cards (verbatim core, §381.986(7)(a)): "The department shall issue medical marijuana use registry identification cards for qualified patients and caregivers who are residents of this state, which must be renewed annually." Cards must be counterfeit/tamper-resistant and include name, address, date of birth; full-face passport-type colour photo taken within the prior 90 days (or DHSMV photo); patient/caregiver identification; unique numeric MMUR identifier (plus, for caregivers, the patient(s) assisted); and expiration date. Parental/guardian written consent is required before issuing a card to a minor (§381.986(7)(b)). Cards must be returned within 5 business days after revocation (§381.986(7)(e)).
  • Fee — $75: The statute authorises only "a reasonable fee" (§381.986(7)(d)) and allocates $10 of the fee to Florida A&M University's Division of Research for minority education about medical marijuana and unlawful-use impacts. The $75 amount (initial and renewal, plus $2.75 online convenience fee; $15 returned-payment fee as reported) comes from OMMU's cards page / practice, not from the statute text itself — sources: https://www.drgreenrelief.com/florida-medical-marijuana-laws/ and https://www.drgreenrelief.com/telemedicine/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary reporting of OMMU). Direct OMMU cards-page confirmation is Gap G-09. Renewal applications are accepted only within the 45 days before expiry (OMMU practice, secondary). From 27 July 2026, OMMU's FAQ (secondary reporting, 27 July 2026) states a patient cannot complete an ID-card application (initial or renewal) without a current or scheduled certification with open orders in the Registry, and a caregiver cannot complete one unless connected to a valid, active patient — the check was moved earlier in the process; the card term, $75 fee, and 45-day window did not change. Source: http://greenscreens.tv/v2/blog/florida-medical-marijuana-card-renewal-rule-2026-dispensaries/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary; direct OMMU FAQ [VERIFY]).
  • Approval email as temporary authority: Once an application is approved, the patient "instantly receive[s] an approval email which can be used to fill an order at an approved MMTC while the physical card is printed and mailed" (OMMU weekly-update background text, via https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/ommu_updates/2026/082826-OMMU-Update.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary/official PDF via search). Processing: 5 business days to process a complete application + 5 business days to print (OMMU 16 Oct 2026 update, secondary — see §0.2).
  • Caregivers (verbatim core, §381.986(6)(b)): must (1) not be a qualified physician and not be employed by / have an economic interest in an MMTC or testing lab; (2) be 21+ and a Florida resident; (3) agree in writing to assist; (4) be registered for no more than one patient (exceptions below); (5) complete the Department's caregiver certification course (≤$100, renewed biennially); (6) pass background screening (§381.986(9)) unless the patient is a close relative. A patient may designate no more than one caregiver, except: minor patients (parents/legal guardians), adults with intellectual/developmental disability preventing self-care (parents/legal guardians), hospice patients, and teaching-nursing-home research participants (§381.986(6)(c)). A caregiver may serve more than one patient only in the mirror-image exceptions (multiple minor children, multiple disabled adult children, all hospice patients where the caregiver is a hospice employee providing personal care, or all teaching-nursing-home research participants) (§381.986(6)(d)). Caregivers may not receive compensation other than actual expenses (§381.986(6)(e)). For patients under 18, only the caregiver may purchase/administer (§381.986(6)(f)). A caregiver must carry the card whenever possessing marijuana/delivery devices and present it on law-enforcement request (§381.986(6)(g)); failure/refusal to present is a second-degree misdemeanour unless registry verification shows authorisation, with a $5 clerk dismissal if a valid card is produced before/at the court appearance (§381.986(12)(e)).
  • Residency — including seasonal residents and out-of-state patients (see also §1.4.5): "Qualified patient" means "a resident of this state" added to the MMUR by a qualified physician (§381.986(1)(m)). Adults prove residency with a valid Florida driver licence or ID card; seasonal residents who cannot meet that test may provide two documents from the statutory list (deed/mortgage/lease; co-resident proof + statement; utility hookup/work order within 60 days; utility bill ≤2 months old; financial-institution mail ≤2 months old; government-agency mail ≤2 months old; or other Department-rule documentation) (§381.986(5)(b)). "Seasonal resident" means a person who temporarily resides in Florida for at least 31 consecutive days per calendar year, maintains a temporary residence, returns to the home jurisdiction at least once per calendar year, and is registered to vote or pays income tax elsewhere (§381.986(5)(b)3.). Minors prove residency with a certified birth certificate or current Florida K-12 registration record plus a qualifying parent/guardian (§381.986(5)(b)3.).

1.4.4 Supply limits — restated for the programme (cross-reference)

See §1.3.4 for the full table. Programme summary: 70-day (non-smoking) / 35-day (smoking, ≤2.5 oz) dispensing windows; 3 × 70-day / 6 × 35-day certification caps (210 days); 70-day / greater-of-4-oz possession caps; original-packaging requirement; Department exception process with 14-day deemed approval. Every dispensation must be recorded in the MMUR with date, time, quantity, form, device type, and patient/caregiver name + MMUR number (§381.986(8)(e)16.g.), and the dispensing employee's name/unique identifier (§381.986(8)(e)16.c.).

1.4.5 Out-of-state patients — no reciprocity

  • Florida does not recognise out-of-state medical cards as authority to buy from an MMTC. The statute requires Florida residency, Florida MMUR registration, a Florida qualified physician's certification, and a Florida MMUR ID card. No reciprocity provision appears in §381.986. A non-resident who is not a "seasonal resident" as defined cannot become a qualified patient at all.
  • Seasonal residents ARE the out-of-state pathway: a person meeting the 31-day / temporary-residence / return-home / vote-or-tax-elsewhere test may register (see §1.4.3) — but must still see a Florida qualified physician in person first and obtain a Florida card. An out-of-state card alone, a telehealth-only out-of-state certification, or a visiting patient's home-state authorisation does not suffice [VERIFY against OMMU FAQ — no OMMU reciprocity FAQ was opened; the conclusion rests on the absence of any reciprocity clause in §381.986].
  • Florida cards elsewhere / transport: whether other states honour a Florida card is that state's law (Part 10 topic); transporting marijuana across state lines remains a federal offence and a Florida §893.13 offence outside the MMTC system — see Part 10 in Run 2.
  • Visitors and hemp: a visitor 21+ may lawfully buy compliant hemp extract in Florida under §581.217 (no residency requirement in §581.217(7)); that does not authorise buying MMTC marijuana.

1.5 Hemp

1.5.1 THC limits, measurement, and Florida's USDA plan status

  • Plant / hemp limit: total delta-9 THC ≤0.3% on a dry-weight basis (§581.217(3)(e), verbatim in §1.2.4). Hemp extract limit: ≤0.3% total delta-9 THC on a wet-weight basis (same paragraph) — the wet-weight test is stricter in practice because it counts the finished product's total weight including liquids/carriers, not just dry plant matter.
  • How total delta-9 THC is measured in Florida practice: post-decarboxylation or other similarly reliable methods, as the Department's rules must provide (§581.217(12)(a)). In FDACS/industry practice the formula is: Total THC = delta-9 THC + (THCA × 0.877). Sources for the formula: https://brewerslaw.com/federal-thc-limit-hemp-beverages-florida-comparison/ and https://www.cannabisregulations.ai/state-legality/florida-hhc — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary; the 0.877 factor itself appears in the federal total-THC definition and in Florida hemp COA practice, but the current FAC rule text stating the factor was not opened [VERIFY — priority gap]). Do not confuse this with the new federal total-THC definition taking full effect 11 December 2026 (see §1.5.10), which is broader than delta-9 + THCA.
  • No per-serving or per-container milligram cap in current Florida law. Compliance is percentage-based (0.3%), not milligram-based. A 25 mg delta-8 gummy, a high-milligram tincture, or a THC beverage is not unlawful by milligram amount alone if its total delta-9 THC concentration is ≤0.3% (wet weight for extract) and it meets COA/packaging/age rules. Every milligram cap proposed (5 mg/serving, 50 mg/container, 10 mg/container for beverages) was in a bill that was vetoed or died — see §1.5.9. This is the single most misunderstood point in Florida hemp law.
  • USDA-approved state plan: §581.217(1) states the section "constitutes the state plan" for 7 U.S.C. §1639p, and §581.217(4) directs FDACS to seek USDA approval within 30 days after adopting rules. Florida operates a state plan (not USDA-direct licensing) — that is the structure of the statute and of FDACS's programme — but the USDA approval letter, approval date, and current USDA plan listing entry were not opened in this run [VERIFY — check USDA's approved-plans list in Run 2 / Part 7]. Do not state an approval date here.
  • Cultivation testing/disposal: FDACS rules must provide post-decarboxylation testing and disposal procedures for non-compliant plants/products (§581.217(12)(a)–(b)); licensees must complete corrective action plans for negligent violations, report periodically for at least 2 years, and are ineligible for 5 years after a third negligent corrective-action-plan violation in 5 years; violations with a culpable mental state greater than negligence must be reported to the Florida and U.S. Attorneys General (§581.217(10)). Hot hemp (>0.3%) is not "hemp" and falls back into §893.02 "cannabis" (Schedule I) unless it is conforming §381.986 marijuana — the practical consequence is criminal exposure, not merely a civil corrective plan, for knowing violations.

1.5.2 Hemp extract products — delta-8, delta-9, THCA, and others

  • Delta-8 THC: lawful in Florida if hemp-derived and within the 0.3% total delta-9 framework. The statute does not name delta-8 as prohibited; §581.217(2)(b) provides hemp-derived cannabinoids "are not controlled substances or adulterants if they are in compliance with this section," and the "hemp" definition expressly includes "derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids, salts, and salts of isomers." Because hemp naturally contains very little delta-8 (<0.1% as commonly reported), almost all commercial delta-8 is made by converting CBD — Florida law as written does not ban that conversion process as such, and FDACS has not (in the material checked) taken enforcement against delta-8 as a cannabinoid category; its enforcement has targeted packaging, labelling, child-appeal, and synthetic-cannabinoid products. Sources: https://legalclarity.org/is-delta-8-legal-in-florida-what-you-need-to-know/ ; https://www.cannabisregulations.ai/state-legality/florida-hhc — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary; the "no category ban" point is an enforcement observation, not a statutory safe harbour — [VERIFY] against FDACS enforcement releases).
  • Delta-9 THC in hemp products: lawful only at ≤0.3% total delta-9 (wet weight for extract). A hemp product above 0.3% total delta-9 is marijuana/cannabis under Chapter 893, not hemp, however it is labelled. "Hemp-derived delta-9" gummies/beverages that are compliant do so because a large product weight dilutes a multi-milligram dose below 0.3% — e.g., a 10 mg delta-9 dose in a ~3.3 g gummy is ~0.3%; the same dose in a smaller gummy may exceed it. Retailers/consumers must check the COA percentage, not just the milligram dose.
  • THCA (tetrahydrocannabinolic acid): lawful only as counted toward total THC. THCA itself is non-intoxicating until heated/decarboxylated, but Florida's total-THC formula (delta-9 + THCA×0.877) counts most of it. A "THCA flower" product testing at, say, 15% THCA is therefore ~13% total THC and is marijuana, not hemp, however it is marketed. The vetoed SB 1698 would have codified a THCA-inclusive total-THC definition for hemp extract; its veto means the statutory text still says "total delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol concentration" without spelling out the THCA conversion — the conversion lives in testing practice/rules, which is why the FAC pinpoint matters (Gap G-10). Do not advise that THCA products are "legal hemp" without a COA showing ≤0.3% total THC.
  • THC-O / THC-O-acetate and HHCO: treated as controlled substances, not hemp. FDACS has repeatedly seized them as controlled substances under §893.03(1)(c)190 (FDACS release on the Asik Wholesale / North Miami Beach seizure: 1,106 packages of THC-O products "categorized as a controlled substance under federal and state law, §893.03(1)(c)190, Fla. Stat."). Source: https://www.fdacs.gov/News-Events/Press-Releases/2023-Press-Releases/Commissioner-Wilton-Simpson-Announces-Seizure-of-Over-1-700-Illegal-Hemp-THC-O-Mushroom-Products-from-South-Florida-Business — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official). The 2025 sweep totals also count "420,000+ packages containing illegal synthetic cannabinoids" since July 2023 (see §1.5.8).
  • HHC (hexahydrocannabinol): not banned as a category in current Florida statute or, in the material checked, by FDACS rule; lawful only inside the 0.3% / COA / packaging / 21+ framework. SB 1698 would have banned HHC outright; it was vetoed. FDACS enforcement against HHC products has focused on packaging/labelling violations. Source: https://www.cannabisregulations.ai/state-legality/florida-hhc — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary). HHC's federal status after 11 December 2026 is a different question (see §1.5.10) — do not conflate state and federal treatment.
  • Delta-10, THC-P, THC-V, and other isomers/analogues: no Florida statute or rule naming them was located in this run [UNAVAILABLE for a categorical statement]. They fall, if at all, inside §581.217's broad "isomers" language only if the finished product is ≤0.3% total delta-9 and otherwise compliant, and outside it if they are synthetic / not capable of being naturally produced (federal test from November/December 2026 — see §1.5.10). Any claim that a specific analogue is "legal in Florida" without a COA and a cannabinoid-specific analysis is [VERIFY].
  • Synthetic cannabidiol: expressly excluded from "hemp extract" (§581.217(3)(f): "The term does not include synthetic cannabidiol…"). Synthetic CBD products therefore cannot use the hemp-extract pathway as written.
  • CBD (non-intoxicating): hemp-derived CBD in compliance with §581.217 is not a controlled substance or adulterant (§581.217(2)(b)). Topical CBD (creams, lotions, balms) is not "hemp extract" because it is not intended for ingestion or inhalation, so the 21+ rule does not apply to topicals as such (secondary summary of the statutory definition — Accessed 2026-10-24; the definition's "intended for ingestion … or for inhalation" language supports this reading).

1.5.3 Minimum age

  • 21+ for ingestion/inhalation hemp extract — verbatim in §1.2.4 (§581.217(7)(d)): products "intended for human ingestion or inhalation and that contain hemp extract, including, but not limited to, snuff, chewing gum, and other smokeless products, may not be sold … to a person who is under 21 years of age." First violation: second-degree misdemeanour; second/subsequent within 1 year: first-degree misdemeanour. The penalty falls on the seller. Online sellers must age-gate (secondary reporting notes uneven compliance; no Florida online age-verification statute pinpoint was opened [VERIFY]).
  • No age limit in §581.217 for: hemp seed, hemp fibre, hemp-derived topicals not intended for ingestion/inhalation, or hemp products that are not "hemp extract" as defined (e.g., seed-derived ingredients GRAS by FDA, expressly excluded from "hemp extract"). Whether a local ordinance imposes a broader age rule is a Part 3 question.

1.5.4 Packaging and anti-child-appeal rules (hemp)

  • Statutory container rules (§581.217(7)(a)2.–3., verbatim in §1.2.4): scannable barcode/QR code linked to the batch COA; batch number; website where batch information may be obtained; expiration date; milligrams of each marketed cannabinoid per serving; container suitable for human consumption, light-minimising, temperature-mitigating, not attractive to children, and compliant with the Poison Prevention Packaging Act (child-resistant) without regard to exemptions.
  • "Attractive to children" (verbatim, §581.217(3)(a)): "manufactured in the shape of humans, cartoons, or animals; manufactured in a form that bears any reasonable resemblance to an existing candy product that is familiar to the public as a widely distributed, branded food product such that a product could be mistaken for the branded product, especially by children; or containing any color additives." Rule 5K-4.034 (as amended March/November 2025, secondary) is reported to add a "cartoon" definition (character/illustration with exaggerated features, human traits, or superhuman abilities) and lists of prohibited (37) and conditionally prohibited (29) colour additives — official rule text [VERIFY].
  • Advertising: FDACS rules must include "Advertising regulations that ensure that hemp extract intended for human ingestion or inhalation is not marketed or advertised in a manner that specifically targets or is attractive to children" (§581.217(12)(d)). The November 2025 Rule 5K-4.034 amendment is reported to align the rule's "attractive to children" definition with §581.217(3)(a) across edibles, vapes, beverages, and tinctures — secondary, [VERIFY].
  • Inhalation-only labelling (reported in a 2026 FDACS inspection summary, secondary): inhalation-only hemp extract must bear "Not Intended For Ingestion, Do Not Eat" — source: https://floridafoodsafety.org/news/inspections/hallandale-queen-of-smoke-fdacs-inspection-may-2026 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary inspection write-up; rule pinpoint [VERIFY]).

1.5.5 Food permits and registrations (hemp) — summary (full inventory is Part 7)

  • Hemp extract may be sold to a Florida business only if that business is "properly permitted as required by this section" (§581.217(7)(b)).
  • The batch COA must state the batch "was processed in a facility that holds a current and valid permit issued by a human health or food safety regulatory entity" meeting that entity's sanitisation requirements, documented by that entity's report (§581.217(7)(a)1.d.).
  • Hemp extract distributed/sold in Florida is subject to Chapter 500, 502, or 580 as applicable (§581.217(7)(c)), and violations are subject to §500.172 and §500.121 penalties (§581.217(7)(e)).
  • In practice this is the FDACS hemp food establishment permit (food establishments selling/manufacturing hemp extract) — permit fees, renewal cycle, and the FDACS permit registry are Part 7 questions and are NOT stated here. The May 2026 Hallandale inspection summary (secondary) illustrates enforcement: a shop selling hemp extract without a current permit / unpaid fee drew stop-sale/stop-use orders — Accessed 2026-10-24.

1.5.6 THC drinks (hemp beverages)

  • Current law: no hemp-beverage-specific statute. A hemp beverage is a hemp extract product intended for ingestion: it must meet the same 0.3% wet-weight total delta-9 test, COA/QR/batch/expiry/mg-per-serving container rules, child-resistant / non-child-appealing packaging, and 21+ sale rule as any other ingestible hemp extract. There is no Florida requirement (in current law) that hemp beverages be sold only through liquor-licensed retailers or alcohol wholesalers, no Florida beverage milligram cap, and no Florida hemp-beverage excise tax.
  • What was proposed and died: SB 438 (2025) would have limited hemp beverages to liquor-licensed sellers (and, in some summaries, alcohol-wholesaler distribution) with a 5 mg cap; HB 7027's amended version is reported to have allowed beverages up to 5 mg THC per 6 fl oz, 10 mg per container, 100 mg per package, without a liquor-licence requirement, plus a 15% excise tax. None of this is law. The "diet weed" / THC-beverage market size figures circulating in secondary coverage (~$500 million, industry estimates) are not official figures and are not adopted here.
  • Interaction with alcohol law: whether a hemp beverage containing alcohol, or sold in a licensed alcohol premises, triggers Division of Alcoholic Beverages and Tobacco requirements is [VERIFY] — no DBPR/ABT hemp-beverage guidance was located in this run. Do not assume a hemp beverage is an "alcoholic beverage" or that it is exempt from alcohol law if it contains alcohol.

1.5.7 Enforcement and stop-sale actions

  • Statutory tools: immediate stop-sale order for mislabelled or child-attractive hemp extract (§581.217(7)(e)); §500.172 / §500.121 penalties; FDACS entry during business hours, random inspections at least annually per cultivation licensee (§581.217(11)); corrective action plans (§581.217(10)); referral of culpable-mental-state violations to Attorneys General.
  • Operation Kandy Krush (July–August 2023, FDACS's then-largest sweep): 700+ businesses in all 67 counties inspected; 83,000+ packages uncovered in that sweep (68,689 packages seized in one reporting of the operation, including high-potency THC items; figures vary by release — see conflict note below); the operation followed SB 1676 (ch. 2023-154). Sources: https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/FLDAC/bulletins/366fb90 ; https://hempgazette.com/news/kandy-krush-hemp-hg2009/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official FDACS release + secondary).
  • Cumulative totals — conflict flagged: FDACS releases state, at different dates, (a) "over 631,000 hemp products designed to target children and more than 420,000 packages containing illegal synthetic cannabinoids" since July 2023 (release on the Hollywood / High Roller Private Label LLC seizure: 186,377 packages child-targeting + 644 packages THC-O/HHCO at that site) — source: https://www.morningagclips.com/fdacs-announces-over-186000-packages-of-hemp-products-uncovered/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary reproduction of FDACS release); and (b) "over 1.3 million packages of illegal hemp products" removed since 1 July 2023, including 197,303 packages in "Operation Safe Summer" in all 67 counties (2025 FDACS release, §0.4). These are not contradictory if (b) is the later cumulative total and (a) is an earlier subtotal, but the dates/definitions (products vs packages; child-targeting vs all illegal) differ by release, so no single cumulative figure should be quoted without its release date. The 1.3 million figure is the latest cumulative figure located; the 631,000/420,000 figures are earlier and should be treated as superseded subtotals, [VERIFY] against the dated FDACS releases in Run 2.
  • 2025 enforcement posture (secondary): FDACS began strict enforcement of amended Rule 5K-4.034 on 16 June 2025, including seizures and permit suspensions/revocations, with fines up to $5,000 per violation reported (secondary; statutory basis for the $5,000 figure — §500.121 vs §381.986(13)(b) $5,000 citation vs MMTC $10,000 fines — [VERIFY] which penalty provision applies to hemp food establishments).
  • THC-O / synthetic enforcement: see §1.5.2. FDACS has also seized Amanita muscaria products alongside hemp/THC-O products in at least one Miami Beach warehouse action (1,700+ products, criminal charges for operating without a food permit and selling adulterated/misbranded food under §500.04) — that action is a food-safety action, not a hemp-cannabinoid precedent, and is noted only to avoid misreading it as one.

1.5.8 Vetoed hemp bills — what they would have done

SB 1698 (2024) — VETOED 7 June 2024 (Governor Ron DeSantis). - Passed Senate unanimously; House 64–48, late March 2024 (secondary reporting of the vote — Accessed 2026-10-24). - Would have: (i) prohibited manufacture, delivery, holding, offering for sale, distribution, or sale of hemp extracts containing delta-8 THC, among other ingredients; (ii) revised "hemp extract" to ≤0.3% total delta-9 THC, or, if sold at retail, the lesser of 0.3% total delta-9 or 5 mg per serving and 50 mg per container (wet-weight basis); (iii) redefined total delta-9 to include THCA (closing the "THCA loophole"); (iv) in industry summaries, effectively banned many synthetic/converted cannabinoids. Sources: https://www.bipc.com/desantis-vetoes-bill-that-would-have-banned-some-delta-8-thc-products ; https://mjbizdaily.com/news/florida-governor-ron-desantis-vetoes-proposed-hemp-ban/391502/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary; bill text pinpoint [VERIFY] on flsenate.gov in Run 2). - Veto message (verbatim core, via secondary reproduction): "While Senate Bill 1698's goals are commendable, the bill would, in fact, impose debilitating regulatory burdens on small businesses and almost certainly fail to achieve its purposes" and "would introduce dramatic disruption and harm to many small retail and manufacturing businesses in Florida." The Governor urged the Legislature to return in 2025 with "sensible, non-arbitrary regulation" focused on quality control, packaging, and where/how hemp products are sold. Source: https://www.wmnf.org/ron-desantis-vetoes-bill-targeting-hemp-industry/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary, News Service of Florida). - Effect of the veto: none of SB 1698's caps, delta-8 ban, or THCA definition became law. Current law remains §581.217 as amended in 2023.

SB 438 (2025, Sen. Colleen Burton) — PASSED SENATE, DIED IN HOUSE. - Senate passage: 37–0, 9 April 2025 (flsenate.gov bill page, via search extract). Died: 16 June 2025, "Died on Second Reading Calendar" (flsenate.gov related-bills table) / "died in the House" (secondary). - Would have: banned synthetic cannabinoids including delta-8; limited hemp beverages to liquor-licensed retailers (and alcohol-wholesaler distribution in some summaries); capped THC potency at 5 mg per serving (50 mg per package in summaries); imposed advertising restrictions; required testing by a certified medical cannabis laboratory. Sources: https://flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2025/438/ByVersion ; https://www.floridatrend.com/articles/2025/05/07/florida-hemp-industry-wins-another-reprieve-regulations-this-year/ ; https://www.bipc.com/updates-on-texas-and-florida-hemp-regulation — Accessed 2026-10-24. - HB 7027 (2025, House Commerce Committee, Rep. Michelle Salzman) — DIED on Second Reading Calendar, 16 June 2025. - Would have (as amended, secondary): no delta-8 ban; no liquor-licence requirement for hemp beverages; beverage dosing 5 mg per 6 fl oz / 10 mg per container / 100 mg per package; inhalables 2.5 mg THC per gram, max 5 mg per inhalable; edibles 2.5 mg per gram, 5 mg per serving, 100 mg per package; tincture provisions removed in the amended version; 2029 dosage reductions deleted; direct-to-consumer delivery permitted with out-of-state delivery permits and 21+ / address-verified delivery; plus a 15% excise tax on hemp purchases (House version only). Sources: https://hempsupporter.com/bill/protect-hemp-products-in-florida/ ; https://www.bipc.com/updates-on-texas-and-florida-hemp-regulation — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary; bill-text pinpoints [VERIFY]). - HB 1597 (2025, Rep. Trabulsy) and SB 1030 (2025, Sen. Davis) and HB 601 (2025, Rep. Cassel) — similar/compare hemp bills; all died 16 June 2025 (HB 1597: indefinitely postponed 3 May 2025, died in Housing, Agriculture & Tourism Subcommittee; SB 1030: died in Agriculture; HB 601: died in Housing, Agriculture & Tourism Subcommittee). Source: flsenate.gov SB 438 related-bills table — Accessed 2026-10-24. - Why they failed (secondary explanation, not a legislative finding): the House and Senate versions could not be reconciled — delta-8 ban vs no ban, liquor-licence requirement vs none, and the 15% excise tax were the reported sticking points. The Legislature adjourned without a hemp bill in 2025 and again enacted none in the 2026 regular session (adjourned 13 March 2026).

1.5.9 State response to the new federal hemp definition (12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026) — [UNAVAILABLE] as an official Florida response

  • No Florida statute, FDACS rule, FDACS guidance, or legislative bill conforming §581.217 to PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019 was located in this run. Searches for an FDACS statement on the federal dates returned FDACS releases on 7-OH and on cumulative hemp seizures, but no hemp-definition response. This is recorded as [UNAVAILABLE], not as proof that FDACS is silent — FDACS may issue guidance in November 2026, after this research date.
  • What the fixed baseline means if Florida does nothing (analysis, not Florida law):
  • From 12 November 2026, federal hemp status is lost for products containing cannabinoids "not capable of being naturally produced" by Cannabis sativa L. (the clearest example in Florida practice is THC-O, already treated by FDACS as a controlled substance — so the November date changes little in Florida for THC-O).
  • From 11 December 2026, the full federal total-THC definition applies and final products with >0.4 mg combined total THC (and similarly acting cannabinoids) per container lose federal hemp status, as do naturally producible cannabinoids synthesised/manufactured outside the plant (which, on a plain reading, captures most converted delta-8 and HHC). Such products would, federally, be "marijuana" under the Controlled Substances Act (CRS summary, secondary, September 2026 — via https://greenscreens.tv/v2/blog/federal-hemp-november-12-2026-what-changes-florida-dispensaries/ — Accessed 2026-10-24).
  • Florida law does not automatically follow: §581.217's 0.3% test, 21+ rule, and COA regime remain Florida law until the Florida Legislature amends them. A product that loses federal hemp status may still meet Florida's state hemp test — but it would then be federally unlawful marijuana, with federal enforcement, banking, transport, and tax consequences, and Florida law enforcement could still treat it as cannabis under §893.02 if it exceeds 0.3% or is a controlled substance under §893.03. Conversely, a product that meets the new federal 0.4 mg cap but exceeds Florida's 0.3% test is unlawful in Florida. Businesses must satisfy both regimes; neither regime's compliance alone is sufficient. This dual-compliance point must be re-checked after 11 December 2026 — it is the highest-priority Run 2 update.
  • MMTCs are not directly affected: MMTC products are §381.986 marijuana, not §581.217 hemp, and §381.986(8)(e)16.f. bars MMTCs from selling other cannabis products. The federal hemp dates do not change MMTC authorisation (secondary analysis, Accessed 2026-10-24, via the GreenScreens post above).
  • USDA DEA-lab testing delay to 31 December 2026 (fixed baseline): no Florida implementation notice was located; hemp cultivation testing in Florida continues under FDACS rules / §581.217(12)(a) in the interim [VERIFY against FDACS hemp testing guidance].

1.6 Packaging, labelling, advertising, delivery, zoning, and buffer rules — MMTCs and hemp (combined summary; full local detail is Part 3)

1.6.1 MMTC packaging and labelling (statute; rules add detail [VERIFY])

  • Poison Prevention Packaging Act compliance for all marijuana packaging (§381.986(8)(e)11.e.).
  • Label (verbatim core, §381.986(8)(e)11.f.): firmly affixed, legible label stating: (I) the marijuana/low-THC meets the testing requirements; (II) MMTC name of origin; (III) batch + harvest number and date dispensed; (IV) certifying physician's name; (V) patient's name; (VI) product name (if applicable) and dosage form, including THC and CBD concentration — "The product name may not contain wording commonly associated with products that are attractive to children or which promote the recreational use of marijuana"; (VII) recommended dose; (VIII) warning that transfer to another person is illegal; (IX) the Department's marijuana universal symbol.
  • Patient package insert in each package: clinical pharmacology; indications/use; dosage/administration; dosage forms/strengths; contraindications; warnings/precautions; adverse reactions (§381.986(8)(e)12. — the statute lists (a)–(g) in full; the insert's full content list is in the statute, not summarised away here).
  • Smoking-form receptacles: sealed, plain, opaque, white, no product depictions/images other than the MMTC's Department-approved logo and the universal symbol, plus keep-away-from-children and carcinogen warnings (§381.986(8)(e)13., verbatim in §1.3.3).
  • Edible receptacles: plain, opaque, white, no product depictions/images other than the approved logo + universal symbol; each edible individually sealed in plain, opaque wrapping marked only with the universal symbol (and marked with the symbol where practical); receptacle must list all ingredients, storage instructions, expiration date, prominent keep-away-from-children-and-pets warning, and a warning that the edible "has not been produced or inspected pursuant to federal food safety laws" (§381.986(8)(e)15.).
  • Delivery devices: Department rules must require an appearance "consistent with medical use" (§381.986(8)(e)14.); devices may not be displayed or dispensed in the waiting area (see §1.6.3 security summary) and, in secondary summaries of newer device rules, must be labelled at dispensing with MMTC name, physician name, date dispensed, and patient name — rule pinpoint [VERIFY] (secondary: https://moderncanna.com/laws-regulations/new-florida-rule-tightens-restrictions-on-cannabis-delivery-devices-what-mmtcs-and-patients-need-to-know/ — Accessed 2026-10-24).
  • Website price transparency: each MMTC must publish on its website every product (form, strain, CBD/THC content, dose unit, doses available, CBD:THC ratio), the price for a 30-day, 50-day, and 70-day supply at standard dose for each product, each delivery-device price, and any discount policies/eligibility (§381.986(8)(e)9. — note: the statute says "30-day, 50-day, and 70-day" supply prices; the "50-day" figure is as printed and is not a typographical error in this report).

1.6.2 MMTC advertising

  • Verbatim, §381.986(8)(h): "A medical marijuana treatment center may not engage in advertising that is visible to members of the public from any street, sidewalk, park, or other public place, except: 1. The dispensing location … may have a sign that is affixed to the outside or hanging in the window of the premises which identifies the dispensary by the licensee's business name, a department-approved trade name, or a department-approved logo. A medical marijuana treatment center's trade name and logo may not contain wording or images that are attractive to children or which promote recreational use of marijuana. 2. A medical marijuana treatment center may engage in Internet advertising and marketing under the following conditions: a. All advertisements must be approved by the department. b. An advertisement may not have any content that is attractive to children or which promotes the recreational use of marijuana. c. An advertisement may not be an unsolicited pop-up advertisement. d. Opt-in marketing must include an easy and permanent opt-out feature."
  • Hemp advertising: see §1.5.4 (FDACS rules must ensure hemp extract advertising does not specifically target or appeal to children, §581.217(12)(d)). No general Florida ban on hemp advertising to adults was located.

1.6.3 MMTC delivery and transport

  • Patient delivery is authorised: MMTCs "may … deliver marijuana to qualified patients 24 hours a day" (§381.986(8)(f)4., second clause), while dispensing from premises is barred between 9 p.m. and 7 a.m. ("Not dispense from its premises marijuana or a marijuana delivery device between the hours of 9 p.m. and 7 a.m., but may perform all other operations and deliver marijuana to qualified patients 24 hours a day"). OMMU's patient guidance confirms MMTCs may deliver and patients without a local MMTC may arrange delivery (secondary/official OMMU patients page extract — Accessed 2026-10-24).
  • Transport manifest (verbatim core, §381.986(8)(g)1.): every vehicle transporting marijuana must carry a manifest generated from the MMTC's seed-to-sale system stating departure date/time, originating MMTC name/address/licence number, recipient name/address, quantity/form, arrival date/estimated time, vehicle make/model/plate, and delivering employees' names/signatures; a copy goes to each recipient (signed receipt); the transporter must present the manifest + employee ID to law enforcement on request (failure/refusal: second-degree misdemeanour, §381.986(12)(h)); manifests retained ≥3 years. Vehicles must be in good working order; product locked in a separate compartment/container; transporter carries employee ID at all times; at least two persons per vehicle, at least one remaining in the vehicle during delivery; specific safety/security training for transport/delivery employees (§381.986(8)(g)2.–6.).
  • Hemp delivery: no §581.217 delivery-vehicle manifest regime exists. The failed HB 7027 would have created out-of-state delivery permits and 21+/address-verified delivery — not law. Interstate hemp shipment is a Part 10 topic.

1.6.4 Zoning and buffers — MMTCs (statute; local application is Part 3)

  • State preemption (verbatim, §381.986(11)): "Regulation of cultivation, processing, and delivery of marijuana by medical marijuana treatment centers is preempted to the state except as provided in this subsection."
  • Cultivation/processing buffer (verbatim, §381.986(11)(a)): "A medical marijuana treatment center cultivating or processing facility may not be located within 500 feet of the real property that comprises a public or private elementary school, middle school, or secondary school." (No exception procedure is stated for cultivation/processing in (11)(a) itself.)
  • Dispensing-facility local power (verbatim, §381.986(11)(b)1.–2. and (c)): a county/municipality "may, by ordinance, ban medical marijuana treatment center dispensing facilities from being located within the boundaries of that county or municipality. A county or municipality that does not ban dispensing facilities under this subparagraph may not place specific limits, by ordinance, on the number of dispensing facilities that may locate within that county or municipality." If it does not ban, it may set location criteria and permitting requirements that do not conflict with state law/Department rule, but "may not enact ordinances for permitting or for determining the location of dispensing facilities which are more restrictive than its ordinances permitting or determining the locations for pharmacies licensed under chapter 465" and "may not charge a medical marijuana treatment center a license or permit fee in an amount greater than the fee charged … to pharmacies." Dispensing-facility buffer: "may not be located within 500 feet of the real property that comprises a public or private elementary school, middle school, or secondary school unless the county or municipality approves the location through a formal proceeding open to the public at which the county or municipality determines that the location promotes the public health, safety, and general welfare of the community" (§381.986(11)(c)). Building/Fire Code compliance may still be enforced locally (§381.986(11)(d)). Facilities approved under former §381.986(8)(b) (2016) are grandfathered from this subsection's location requirements.
  • Proposed (DIED) buffer expansion: CS/HB 733 / SB 902 would have prohibited MMTC cultivating/processing/dispensing facilities within a specified distance of parks, child-care facilities, and early-learning facilities (with local approval exceptions and grandfathering for pre-existing facilities and for parks/facilities established after approval) — not law.
  • Hemp zoning: §581.217 contains no statewide hemp-retail zoning buffer and no local-ban provision comparable to §381.986(11). Local authority over hemp/CBD/smoke shops rests on general zoning, business-tax, and (for food establishments) FDACS permitting — full treatment is Part 3. Do not apply the 500-foot MMTC school buffer to hemp shops.

1.7 Seed-to-sale tracking system used

  • Statutory system (verbatim, §381.986(8)(d)): "The department shall establish, maintain, and control a computer software tracking system that traces marijuana from seed to sale and allows real-time, 24-hour access by the department to data from all medical marijuana treatment centers and marijuana testing laboratories. The tracking system must allow for integration of other seed-to-sale systems and, at a minimum, include notification of when marijuana seeds are planted, when marijuana plants are harvested and destroyed, and when marijuana is transported, sold, stolen, diverted, or lost. Each medical marijuana treatment center shall use the seed-to-sale tracking system established by the department or integrate its own seed-to-sale tracking system with the seed-to-sale tracking system established by the department. Each medical marijuana treatment center may use its own seed-to-sale system until the department establishes a seed-to-sale tracking system. The department may contract with a vendor to establish the seed-to-sale tracking system. The vendor selected by the department may not have a contractual relationship with the department to perform any services pursuant to this section other than the seed-to-sale tracking system. The vendor may not have a direct or indirect financial interest in a medical marijuana treatment center or a marijuana testing laboratory."
  • How it operates in practice (emergency rules 64ER24-1 / 64ER24-2, via Cornell LII — Accessed 2026-10-24): each MMTC operates an Internal STS Tracking System that feeds the Department through an API using Form DH5059-OMMU-11/2023 ("MMTC Seed-to-Sale Required Data Collection Document"); data retained 3 years; CSV production within 48 hours on Department request; only MMTC owners/officers/managers/employees, the MMTC's STS vendor, and the Department's STS vendor may access it (third-party website access is a disciplinary offence under Rule 64-4.210); primary/secondary technical contacts notified via Form DH5057-OMMU-11/2023 to ommu_seedtosale@flhealth.gov. Integration deadlines (by the third training session with the Department's STS vendor; extensions up to 6 months for hardware/software/technical infeasibility outside the MMTC's control) and non-compliance discipline (including suspension/revocation) are in 64ER24-1.
  • Vendor name [VERIFY]: the Department's STS vendor is not named in the statute or in the emergency-rule extracts read. Secondary sources commonly name Metrc as the vendor in other states, but no source in this run names Florida's STS vendor, and Metrc must NOT be asserted as Florida's vendor — this is a common error to avoid. The MMUR (patient/physician/dispensing registry) is a separate system from the STS inventory system, though dispensations are recorded in the MMUR and manifests are generated from the STS system. Whether the permanent Rule 64-4.221 has replaced 64ER24-1/2, and the vendor identity, are priority Run 2 checks (Gap G-11).
  • Hemp seed-to-sale: §581.217 has no seed-to-sale tracking system comparable to §381.986(8)(d). It has a land registry (GPS + legal description, 3 years, §581.217(8)), monthly USDA reporting (§581.217(9)), batch COAs (§581.217(7)(a)), and FDACS inspections. Do not describe hemp as "seed-to-sale tracked" in the MMTC sense.

1.8 Employment and drug-testing protections for patients — there are essentially none in statute

  • Verbatim — §381.986(15) (Applicability):

    "(a) This section does not limit the ability of an employer to establish, continue, or enforce a drug-free workplace program or policy." "(b) This section does not require an employer to accommodate the medical use of marijuana in any workplace or any employee working while under the influence of marijuana." "(c) This section does not create a cause of action against an employer for wrongful discharge or discrimination."

  • Plain consequence: a Florida employer may maintain a drug-free workplace, test (including pre-employment, random, and for-cause testing under §§112.0455 / 440.102 as applicable), and take adverse action — including refusal to hire and termination — based on a positive marijuana test or on medical marijuana use, even if the use was off-duty, off-site, and medically authorised, and the patient has no claim under §381.986 itself for wrongful discharge or discrimination. The statute also preserves the employer's right to restrict use at work (§381.986(1)(k)5.c. — use at work is not "medical use" unless the employer permits it) and to restrict smoking/vaping on private property (§381.986(15)(d)).
  • MMTC-employee rule (distinct): MMTCs must "Implement an alcohol and drug-free workplace policy" (§381.986(8)(f)9.) and all MMTC employees must be 21+ and pass Level 2 background screening (§381.986(8)(e)4.).
  • Nursing-home / hospice / assisted-living carve-out (not employment protection): §381.986(15)(e) does not prohibit medical use (or caregiver assistance) in a licensed nursing home, hospice, or assisted living facility "if the medical use of marijuana is not prohibited in the facility's policies" — i.e., facility policy controls.
  • Workers' compensation: "Marijuana, as defined in this section, is not reimbursable under chapter 440" (§381.986(15)(f)).
  • Case-law complication [VERIFY — do not overstate]: secondary summaries report a 2024 circuit-court decision, Giambrone v. Hillsborough County, in which a judge held the constitutional amendment requires a public employer to accommodate off-site medical use absent on-the-job impairment (EMT, random test, no impairment evidence), with Hillsborough County appealing. Source: https://legalclarity.org/florida-drug-and-alcohol-testing-laws-in-the-workplace/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary). No appellate decision was located in this run, so the trial-court ruling's reach is uncertain and it does not change the statutory text. Do not cite Giambrone as settled law.
  • Federal overlay (fixed baseline + general law, not Florida statute): federal DOT safety-sensitive testing still applies regardless of state patient status; the ADA does not protect use of a federally controlled substance (and, for medical marijuana, the Schedule III question for ADA purposes after April 2026 is [VERIFY] — the fixed baseline addresses §280E and scheduling, not ADA case law). Federal firearms consequences for patients are a Part 12 topic, not an employment topic.
  • Pending protections that DIED (see §1.9): SB 136 (2026) would have barred public employers from adverse action against qualified patients (with an impairment exception and a 5-business-day notice/contest/confirmation-test procedure); SB 1702 / HB 689 (2026) would have given employers immunity from civil liability where use occurred on-site or the employee tested positive under §112.0455 and use impaired job performance. Neither is law; the absence of both means the §381.986(15) position above stands unmodified.

1.9 Pending legislation and ballot measures — confirmed status on official sites

Status key: ENACTED = signed / chaptered; VETOED = passed Legislature, vetoed by Governor; DIED = session adjourned without passage (with last action stated); PENDING/ACTIVE (initiative) = in the Division of Elections process, not on a ballot, not law. "Died" bills may be refiled in a later session; a died bill is not law and its provisions must not be described in the present tense as requirements.

1.9.1 Adult-use — legislative bills

  • No adult-use legalisation bill enacted in 2025 or 2026 was located. The adult-use path in Florida in this period is by citizen initiative (constitutional amendment), not by ordinary legislation, because Article X, §29 is constitutional and the Legislature has not passed an adult-use statute. Any claim of a "legislative implementation plan" for adult use is therefore not applicable: there is no passed measure to implement. If a 2028 initiative passes with 60%, implementation would require (at minimum) Department of Health rulemaking/licensing under the amendment's own terms and, on the §1, ch. 2017-232 reversion note, legislative action to prevent §381.986's expiry 6 months after the amendment's effective date — that is a forward-looking risk, not a current plan.
  • Related 2026 bills that touched §381.986 but were not adult-use legalisation: CS/HB 733 / SB 902 (Department of Health omnibus — see §1.9.3); SB 136, SB 1702/HB 689 (employment — see §1.8/§1.9.3). None enacted.

1.9.5 Laws on the petition process that affect cannabis initiatives — CS/HB 1205 (2025), ENACTED

  • Signed 2 May 2025 (secondary: WKMG/AP, 2 Feb 2026, Accessed 2026-10-24; flsenate.gov bill text CS/HB 1205, Accessed 2026-10-24).
  • What it changed (from the bill text and secondary summaries — bill-text pinpoints [VERIFY] for each bullet in Run 2):
  • Only Florida residents may collect/handle initiative petitions (volunteer or paid); paid circulators must register with the Secretary of State; it is a third-degree felony to collect more than 25 signed petitions (other than one's own / immediate family's) without registering.
  • Petition forms must include the voter's address/county of legal residence, voter registration number or date of birth, Florida driver licence / ID number or last four digits of Social Security number, attestation of registered-voter status, signature + signing date; circulator forms must include a barcode/serial number and the circulator's affidavit (name, permanent address, circulator number).
  • Completed petitions must be returned within 10 days of collection (reduced from 30 days as reported).
  • Non-U.S. citizens and non-Florida residents may not collect petitions; persons with felony convictions whose rights have not been restored are barred from collecting (as reported).
  • A $1 million bond for amendment sponsors is reported in secondary summaries (Central Florida Substack, Accessed 2026-10-24) — bond requirement pinpoint [VERIFY] on the enrolled bill text; do not quote it as confirmed until verified.
  • The state may not spend public funds on political ads/messages about an initiative (secondary summary of CS/HB 1205's effect on future adult-use amendments — Accessed 2026-10-24, via Dr. Green Relief summary of the 2025 law; pinpoint [VERIFY]).
  • Higher civil/criminal penalties for petition violations, and stricter signature-matching (address must match voter-registration file, as reported).
  • Effect on cannabis initiatives (causal claim — secondary, not a legislative finding): critics (including House Minority Leader Fentrice Driskell, quoted in WKMG/AP) argue HB 1205 made qualification "all but impossible" and explain why all 22 active initiatives, including Smart & Safe's, failed for 2026; supporters (including Sen. Don Gaetz, quoted in secondary) argue it targets corruption of the process, not the process itself. The Department of State's 2026 failure determination rested on the signature count and the 1 February deadline (§100.371), with HB 1205's circulator/validity rules as the contested background. Do not state as fact that HB 1205 alone caused the 2026 failure — the verified facts are the 783,592 count vs the 880,062 threshold and the Secretary's determination; the invalidation of ~70,000 signatures and the HB 1205 litigation are disputed/contested facts.
  • Other petition-process law (not new in 2025–2026): Art. XI, §§3, 5(b) (8% + geographic distribution + 1 February deadline); §100.371(14)(a) (signature expiry on failure to obtain ballot placement); §100.371(15) (Secretary's failure determination); §15.21 (Secretary → Attorney General notification; Supreme Court advisory review); FIEC review. PART 2 — TAXES

2.1 Headline answer

Question Answer in one line
Is there a Florida cannabis excise tax today? No. No medical-marijuana excise tax and no adult-use excise tax is in current Florida law.
Is medical marijuana subject to Florida sales tax? No, as defined in §381.986 — §212.08(2)(l) exempts "Marijuana and marijuana delivery devices, as defined in s. 381.986" from Chapter 212 taxes. The current statute text as published does not add a "purchased by a qualified patient or caregiver" qualifier; that qualifier exists only in a proposed, dead 2026 bill (SB 1398, §2.7).
Is hemp subject to sales tax? Yes in general, with a food-exemption grey area for ingestibles — no hemp excise tax; ordinary Chapter 212 sales tax (6% state + county discretionary surtax where levied, capped as in §2.4) applies to taxable tangible personal property. Whether a given ingestible hemp product is exempt as a food product / dietary supplement is not settled by a hemp-specific DOR ruling found for this file — see §2.5 and Gap 2-07.
Do MMTCs pay Florida corporate income tax? Yes, if taxed as a corporation — 5.5% on Florida net income under Ch. 220, starting from adjusted federal income. There is no Florida cannabis-specific §280E decoupling statute found; Florida follows the federal result through conformity, so the Schedule III change flows through unless/until the Legislature acts or a 2026 conformity bill changes the IRC adoption date. See §2.6.
Do individuals pay Florida income tax on cannabis income? No — Florida levies no personal income tax (Art. VII, §5, Fla. Const.). This is a structural fact, not a cannabis exemption.
Is there a local cannabis tax? No cannabis-specific local tax was found. Local revenue from cannabis businesses is limited to (a) the county discretionary sales surtax on taxable (non-medical-marijuana) sales only, (b) ordinary local business taxes / business tax receipts under Ch. 205, and (c) for MMTC dispensing facilities, a local licence/permit fee capped at the pharmacy fee (§381.986(11)(b)2.). A locality may not invent a cannabis excise tax. See §§2.4, 3.5.
What tax revenue does the State actually collect from medical marijuana? Because medical marijuana itself is sales-tax-exempt and there is no excise, there is no DOR "medical marijuana sales-tax revenue" series to report. The identifiable state revenue streams are MMTC licence/renewal fees (§2.3), patient/caregiver ID-card fees (Part 1 territory, noted only for completeness), corporate income tax on MMTCs taxed as corporations (§2.6), and sales tax on non-marijuana items sold by MMTCs/hemp retailers. No official aggregate for any of those streams was located for this file — see §2.8 and Gap 2-09. Do not quote a "Florida cannabis tax revenue" total.

2.2 Medical marijuana — sales-tax exemption (verbatim law)

2.2.1 The exemption

Citation: §212.08(2)(l), Fla. Stat. — "Sales, rental, use, consumption, distribution, and storage tax; specified exemptions."

Verbatim text (current published text, as retrieved):

"(l) Marijuana and marijuana delivery devices, as defined in s. 381.986, are exempt from the taxes imposed under this chapter."

Source: https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._212.08 — Accessed 2026-10-24. The same text appears in the official Senate bill-text mirror for SB 1398 (2026), which quotes the existing paragraph before proposing to amend it: https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026/1398/BillText/Filed/HTML — Accessed 2026-10-24.

Strict construction clause — verbatim:

"(m) This subsection shall be strictly construed and enforced."

Source: §212.08(2)(m), same link — Accessed 2026-10-24. Practical consequence: the exemption should be read narrowly. It covers only "Marijuana" and "marijuana delivery devices" as defined in §381.986 — i.e. product dispensed from an MMTC for medical use by a qualified patient (see Part 1 for the full §381.986(1)(g) and (h) definitions, quoted there). It does not by its terms exempt:

  • marijuana acquired outside an MMTC (which is not "medical use" under §381.986(1)(k) in any event);
  • hemp/CBD products sold by a non-MMTC retailer (see §2.5 — different analysis, food exemption only);
  • merchandise, apparel, or other non-marijuana items sold at an MMTC;
  • a delivery device that is not a "marijuana delivery device" as defined in §381.986.

Last-amended date: [VERIFY]. The exemption paragraph was added by the 2017 implementing law (SB 8-A, Ch. 2017-232, Laws of Fla., creating the current §381.986 framework and amending §212.08). The precise last-amendment date of §212.08(2)(l) itself was not re-verified from the Online Sunshine history note in this session; Run 2 should pull the history line from https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2025/212.08 before citing a date. The substance — exemption in force on 24 Oct 2026 — is confirmed by the current text above and by the fact that SB 1398 (2026) proposed to narrow it (see §2.7), which presupposes it is current law.

2.2.2 General sales-tax rate that would otherwise apply

Citation: §212.05, Fla. Stat. (tax imposed) — the general state rate is 6% on the sale price of tangible personal property sold at retail in Florida, with the county discretionary surtax in addition where levied (see §2.4). Source for the 6% rate as applied in 2026: Florida Department of Revenue, "Sales and Use Tax" guidance and Form DR-15DSS, Discretionary Sales Surtax Information for Calendar Year 2026, as summarised in secondary sources checked 2026-10-24 (see §2.4 for the surtax-chart caveat). The 6% state rate itself is not in doubt; the county-by-county combined rate is where secondary sources conflict (see §2.4).

Consequence for patients: a qualified patient's MMTC purchase of marijuana or a marijuana delivery device bears 0% Florida sales tax and 0% discretionary surtax, because the underlying Chapter 212 tax is exempt — the surtax in §212.054 piggybacks only on transactions "subject to the state tax imposed … by this chapter" (verbatim in §2.4). A non-patient cannot lawfully buy from an MMTC at any tax rate; the exemption does not create a lawful non-patient sale.

2.2.3 What MMTCs must still collect sales tax on

Secondary tax guidance (Dimov Tax, "Florida Cannabis Sales Tax," undated page, retrieved 2026-10-24, https://dimovtax.com/florida-cannabis-sales-tax/) summarises the position consistently with the statute: exempt = marijuana / delivery devices dispensed to a qualified patient; taxable at 6% + county surtax = "everything else you sell." That guidance is secondary and is not a DOR ruling, but it follows directly from §212.08(2)(l) + §212.08(2)(m) strict construction. Items that fall outside the exemption on that reading include:

  • non-cannabis merchandise sold at a dispensary (apparel, etc.);
  • hemp or CBD products, if sold by an MMTC at all — note §381.986 restricts what an MMTC may dispense, and Part 1/Part 11 should confirm whether MMTC sale of non-MMTC hemp product is permitted; do not assume it is;
  • smoking accessories that are not "marijuana delivery devices" as defined in §381.986 — however, §381.986(1)(h) expressly provides that "delivery devices intended for the medical use of marijuana by smoking need not be dispensed from a medical marijuana treatment center in order to qualify as marijuana delivery devices," so a smoking device bought elsewhere for medical use can still fall within §212.08(2)(l). That nuance is statutory, not secondary. Source: §381.986(1)(h) text retrieved via https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._381.986 — Accessed 2026-10-24.

[VERIFY]: No DOR Technical Assistance Advisement (TAA) specifically ruling on MMTC non-marijuana merchandise or on the smoking-device point was located for this file. Run 2 should search floridarevenue.com TAAs for "381.986" / "marijuana delivery device."

2.3 Licence and renewal fees paid by MMTCs (and testing labs)

These are fees, not taxes, but they are the State's principal direct revenue from MMTCs and the task expressly requires them here. All amounts are per licence unless stated otherwise.

2.3.1 Statutory fee authority (verbatim substance)

§381.986(8) (licensure of MMTCs) authorises the Department of Health to set by rule:

"…initial application and biennial renewal fees sufficient to cover the costs of implementing and administering this section, and establishing supplemental licensure fees for payment beginning May 1, 2018, sufficient to cover the costs of administering ss. 381.989 and 1004.4351."

Source: §381.986(8) text as quoted in SB 1398 (2026) bill text, https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026/1398/BillText/Filed/HTML — Accessed 2026-10-24. Note on citation drift: in the current codification the fee-setting language sits in §381.986(8); older summaries cite it as (8)(e) or similar. Run 2 should pin the current paragraph letter from Online Sunshine. The principle — fees must be cost-recovery, set by rule, not by statute at a fixed dollar figure — is why the renewal fee changes every two-year cycle (see §2.3.3).

  • Source (secondary, but reporting an emergency rule): Florida Trend, "State sets stage for more marijuana licenses" (2022, reporting Emergency Rule 64ER22-9), https://www.floridatrend.com/article/35443/state-sets-stage-for-more-marijuana-licenses/ — Accessed 2026-10-24: "the rule also set the application fee for new licenses at $146,000, more than double the $60,830 fee established during the state's initial round of licensing more than five years ago." 2.3.3 Biennial renewal fee — formula-based, $1,340,383.11 for renewals due 1 Jan 2025–31 Dec 2026

  • Current cycle figure: $1,340,383.11 for renewal applications due between 1 January 2025 and 31 December 2026.
  • Sources (secondary, reporting the OMMU Renewal Fee Schedule): https://catalyst-bc.com/florida-cannabis-licensing-opportunities/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 ("Biennial renewal fee | $1,340,383.11 for renewal applications due January 1, 2025 to December 31, 2026 | MMTC Renewal Fee Schedule"); corroborated by https://www.cannabisindustrylawyer.com/florida-mmtc-license-transfer/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 ("the biennial renewal fee for renewals due between January 1, 2025 and December 31, 2026 is $1,340,383.11").
  • Formula (from the adopted renewal rule text as summarised in the Florida Administrative Register): renewal fee = [(FY1 actual expenditures + FY2 actual expenditures) − (MMTC initial licence application fees received during FY1 and FY2)] ÷ total number of licensed MMTCs, where FY1/FY2 are the two most recently completed state fiscal years immediately preceding the first day of the two-year calendar period during which renewals are due. Source: Florida Administrative Register extract for Rule 64-4.215, https://flrules.org/gateway/GotoLink.asp?Goto=BigDocFAW&Para=2026/5290/5290doc.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24 (rule text stating the formula and that Rule 64-4.215 takes effect / was noticed in 2026, replacing Emergency Rule 64ER25-1; the extract notes renewal applications 120–150 days before licence-period end under the new rule).
  • Prior cycle figure (superseded, for trend only): $1,223,124.42 for renewals due 1 January 2023–31 December 2024. Source: JD Supra summary of Emergency Rules 64ER22-9 / 64ER22-10 (2022), https://www.jdsupra.com/post/contentViewerEmbed.aspx?fid=5d3f4695-474f-430e-9709-f899eae88498 — Accessed 2026-10-24. Earlier press reporting rounded this to "more than $1 million" / "more than $1.3 million" in different articles — the $1,223,124.42 figure is the precise one to use for 2023–24, and it must not be conflated with the 2025–26 figure.
  • Fee for renewals due after 31 December 2026: [UNAVAILABLE] as of 24 Oct 2026. The next two-year schedule had not been published in any source opened for this file. Do not extrapolate.
  • Why the fee jumped: Governor DeSantis stated in 2022 that MMTCs "weren't paying enough," given licences reselling for tens of millions of dollars. Source: Florida Trend article above — Accessed 2026-10-24. That is a policy rationale, not a statutory formula element.

2.3.4 Performance bond / financial assurance — $5 million, reducible to $2 million

  • $5,000,000 performance bond (or irrevocable letter of credit / cash equivalent) on licensure, per §381.986(8) and Rule 64-4.217, F.A.C. (as summarised in secondary sources). Reducible to $2,000,000 once the MMTC is serving at least 1,000 qualified patients, with OMMU approval.
  • Sources: https://catalyst-bc.com/florida-cannabis-licensing-opportunities/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 ("Financial assurance | $5 million (bond, letter of credit or cash) within 10 business days of approval | Rule 64-4.217"); https://legalclarity.org/how-much-is-a-grow-license-in-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (same $5m / $2m structure). This is a bond, not a fee or tax — it is refundable/returnable on compliance and must not be added to "tax revenue."
  • [VERIFY]: Rule 64-4.217 full text was not opened in this session; confirm the 10-business-day deadline and the 1,000-patient reduction threshold from flrules.org in Run 2.

2.3.5 Certified marijuana testing laboratory fee

  • Application fee reported as $78,000 per testing facility under Rule 64-4.301, F.A.C. Source: https://catalyst-bc.com/florida-cannabis-licensing-opportunities/ — Accessed 2026-10-24. Flag as secondary-only [VERIFY] — no OMMU fee schedule for labs was opened in this session. Testing-lab fees belong in Part 4 in detail; they are noted here only because the task asks for "licence and renewal fees paid by MMTCs" and labs are the only other state-licensed cannabis actor.

2.3.6 Patient / caregiver ID-card fees (for completeness only — Part 1 territory)

  • $75 state application/renewal fee for a Medical Marijuana Use Registry ID card, plus $2.75 online convenience fee ($77.75 total online). Sources: multiple secondary guides retrieved 2026-10-24, e.g. https://legalclarity.org/how-to-renew-a-florida-medical-marijuana-card/ and https://www.drgreenrelief.com/telemedicine/. These are registry fees, not taxes, and are not MMTC fees. They are included here only so a reader does not mistake them for a cannabis tax. [VERIFY] against the current OMMU fee page in Run 2 / Part 1.

2.4 Local (county) sales taxes — discretionary surtax

2.4.1 Statutory framework (verbatim)

Citation: §212.054, Fla. Stat. — "Discretionary sales surtax; limitations, administration, and collection." §212.055, Fla. Stat. — authorising provisions for each surtax type.

Verbatim — §212.054(1):

"No general excise tax on sales shall be levied by the governing body of any county unless specifically authorized in s. 212.055. Any general excise tax on sales authorized pursuant to said section shall be administered and collected exclusively as provided in this section."

Verbatim — §212.054(2)(a) (operative piggyback rule):

"The tax imposed by the governing body of any county authorized to so levy pursuant to s. 212.055 shall be a discretionary surtax on all transactions occurring in the county which transactions are subject to the state tax imposed on sales, use, services, rentals, admissions, and other transactions by this chapter … The surtax, if levied, shall be computed as the applicable rate or rates authorized pursuant to s. 212.055 times the amount of taxable sales and taxable purchases representing such transactions."

Verbatim — §212.054(2)(b)1. ($5,000 cap):

"The sales amount above $5,000 on any item of tangible personal property shall not be subject to the surtax."

Source for all three quotes: https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._212.054 — Accessed 2026-10-24; corroborated by DOR Technical Assistance Advisements at https://floridarevenue.com/TaxLaw/Documents/TAA%2092A-078.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24.

Consequences:

  1. No county may levy a general sales excise except as authorised in §212.055. There is no §212.055 authorisation for a cannabis-specific surtax. A county therefore cannot add a "cannabis surtax" on top of the state rate.
  2. The surtax applies only where the underlying sale is subject to state sales tax. Because medical marijuana is exempt under §212.08(2)(l), no discretionary surtax applies to a medical-marijuana sale in any county, even a high-surtax county. The surtax does apply to taxable hemp products, merchandise, and other taxable sales by cannabis/hemp businesses, at the rate of the county where the sale occurs (for tangible personal property, generally the delivery county — see §212.054(2)(a) proviso that a sale "is not subject to the surtax if the property … is delivered within a county that does not impose a discretionary sales surtax").
  3. $5,000 cap: for a single item of tangible personal property, only the first $5,000 of the sales amount bears surtax. For ordinary hemp retail (items well under $5,000) the cap is irrelevant; it matters only for bulk/wholesale-size single items. Do not apply the cap to services or admissions.
  4. Rate range: DOR's calendar-year 2026 chart (Form DR-15DSS) is the authoritative county-by-county source. Secondary summaries of that chart retrieved 2026-10-24 conflict on individual counties (see §2.4.2). The range is consistently reported as 0% to 1.5% in 2026 (one secondary source says "up to 2%" — that appears to be a generic Chapter 212 maximum, not a 2026 levied rate, and is flagged below). Combined state + surtax on a taxable sale is therefore 6.0% to 7.5% in 2026 on the 0–1.5% reading [AUDIT: this is the 15-jurisdiction range only; statewide maximum returned is Hamilton County 2%/8.0% (secondary, Unverified)].

  • Property tax: MMTC/hemp business real property and tangible personal property are subject to ordinary county/municipal ad valorem tax like any business property.
