2.5 Hemp products — sales tax, no excise

2.5.1 No hemp excise tax

"Taxes: Currently, there are no excise taxes on the sale of consumable hemp products in Florida."

Source: Florida House / Senate bill analysis for HB 7029 / PCS 7029 (2025 hemp bill analysis, "Taxes" section), https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2025/7029/Analyses/h7029.BUC.PDF — Accessed 2026-10-24. The same sentence appears in the House PCS analysis, https://www.flhouse.gov/Sections/Documents/loaddoc.aspx?PublicationType=Committees&CommitteeId=3276&Session=2025&DocumentType=proposed committee substitute analyses&FileName=PCS7029.BUC.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24. That analysis is from 2025, but no 2026 law creating a hemp excise was found in this session (2026 session ended 13 March 2026 with no hemp bill enacted, per secondary hemp-beverage survey, https://csgsouth.org/policies/hemp-beverages-high-risk-or-high-reward/ — Accessed 2026-10-24, "Checked: May 2026"). Conclusion: no hemp excise in force on 24 Oct 2026.

2.5.2 Ordinary sales tax applies to taxable hemp sales

Hemp products sold at retail are tangible personal property. Unless an exemption applies, the sale bears 6% state sales tax + the county discretionary surtax (where levied, on the first $5,000 per item) under §§212.05, 212.054. Hemp retailers must register with DOR and collect/remit — see the secondary FDACS/DOR summary at https://legalclarity.org/florida-cbd-bill-what-are-the-new-regulations/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 ("Businesses must also register with the Florida Department of Revenue for sales tax purposes and maintain records for at least three years in case of audit" — secondary, but consistent with Ch. 212 dealer registration, §212.13).

2.5.3 The food-exemption grey area — ingestible hemp extract

This is the single most uncertain hemp-tax point in Florida, and it must not be stated flatly either way:

Arguments for exemption (ingestibles only):

  • §212.08(1)(a): "Food products for human consumption are exempt from the tax imposed by this chapter." §212.08(1)(b) defines "food products" as "edible commodities, whether processed, cooked, raw, canned, or in any other form, which are generally regarded as food."
  • §500.03(1)(n), Fla. Stat., provides that "hemp extract" is a food product for human ingestion subject to the Florida Food Safety Act (Ch. 500). Source: 2025 bill analysis above — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Rule 12A-1.011(2)(a)12., F.A.C., states that "dietary supplements (including herbal supplements) and meal replacements, including liquid food supplements," are tax-exempt food products. DOR applied that rule to exempt dietary-supplement shots in TAA 19A-014: https://www.floridasalestax.com/taas/taa-19a-014-food-and-drink-non-alcoholic-grocery/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 ("Because [the] shots … are dietary supplements, they constitute food products exempt from taxation" under §212.08(1)(b) and Rule 12A-1.011(2)(a)(12)).
  • Secondary tax commentary therefore argues ingestible hemp products "marketed as a dietary supplement" can claim the food exemption: https://dimovtax.com/florida-cannabis-sales-tax/ — Accessed 2026-10-24; https://www.floridasalestax.com/florida-tax-law-blog/2019/september/is-cbd-subject-to-florida-sales-tax-/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (2019, pre-dating current hemp rules, arguing CBD as "herbal supplements" but noting DOR "may take the position" non-MMTC CBD is taxable because it is not specifically exempted).

Arguments against a blanket exemption / reasons for caution:

  • No DOR TAA or rule specifically addressing hemp extract was located for this file. The TAA above is about vitamin shots, not hemp.
  • The food exemption does not help non-ingestible hemp products at all: vapes / inhalables, topicals, and smokable hemp are not "food products for human consumption" and are taxable as tangible personal property on any reading. The secondary Dimov summary agrees ("You cannot make that argument for a vape, topical or smokable").
  • Hemp beverages sit in the same grey area: a hemp drink that is a "food product" may be exempt, but a drink sold as an intoxicating product, or a product that fails FDACS hemp-extract rules, should not be assumed exempt. No DOR beverage-specific ruling was found.
  • Practical filing position [VERIFY / professional advice, not law]: a hemp retailer that treats all ingestibles as exempt without a DOR ruling bears audit risk; a retailer that taxes all ingestibles over-collects from consumers. Either position should be documented and, ideally, confirmed by a DOR TAA request. Do not present either as settled law.

2.5.4 Hemp business fees that are not taxes (cross-reference only)

FDACS hemp cultivation licences and hemp food establishment permits carry fees under §581.217 and Ch. 500 / Rule 5K-4.034. Those fees belong in Part 7 in full and are not repeated here except to state: they are regulatory fees, not sales or excise taxes, and no hemp fee revenue aggregate was located for this file (Gap 2-09).

2.6 Corporate income tax, §280E, and Florida conformity

2.6.1 Florida has no personal income tax; corporations pay 5.5%

  • Rate — verbatim substance of §220.11(2)(a): the tax is 5.5% of the taxpayer's net income for the taxable year (for taxable years beginning on or after 1 January 2022, after the temporary rate-adjustment provisions of §220.1105 expired). Sources: §220.11 as summarised at https://legalclarity.org/what-is-income-tax-in-florida-state-and-federal-rules/ — Accessed 2026-10-24; Tax Foundation 2026 state profile, http://taxfoundation.org/location/florida/page/8/?source=syndication — Accessed 2026-10-24 ("Florida has a 5.50 percent corporate income tax rate, a 6.00 percent state sales tax rate").
  • Exemption: §220.14 provides a $50,000 standard exemption (net income above $50,000 is taxed). Source: same LegalClarity summary — Accessed 2026-10-24. [VERIFY] the current §220.14 text from Online Sunshine in Run 2.
  • Who pays: corporations and entities taxed as corporations for federal purposes that conduct business, earn income, or exist in Florida (Ch. 220). An LLC taxed as a partnership / disregarded entity does not itself pay Florida corporate income tax; its income passes to owners who, as Florida residents, pay no Florida personal income tax. An LLC electing corporate treatment does pay. Source: §220.02(1) legislative intent (LLC classified as partnership "not be subject to the tax imposed by this code"), https://law.onecle.com/florida/title-xiv/220.02.html — Accessed 2026-10-24, and DOR Ch. 12C-1 guidance, https://FloridaRevenue.com/rules/Pages/Adopted/12C-1_0725.aspx — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Apportionment: multistate corporations apportion Florida net income under §220.15 (property/payroll/sales factors as currently weighted — do not state a single-factor formula without verifying the current §220.15 weighting in Run 2; older summaries cite a three-factor formula, newer law has moved toward single-sales-factor for many taxpayers, and this file does not resolve it — Gap 2-10).

2.6.2 Conformity — Florida "piggybacks" federal taxable income; no cannabis decoupling statute

  • Mechanism: Florida corporate income tax "piggybacks" federal determinations and uses adjusted federal income (§220.13) as the starting point for Florida net income. Each year the Legislature adopts the current Internal Revenue Code as of a specified date (see §220.03 for the definition of "Internal Revenue Code").
  • Source: DOR Tax Information Publication TIP #25C01-01, "Florida Corporate Income Tax Adoption of 2025 Internal Revenue Code" (2025), https://sup18bqylgpy9i9of9rc.vchorizon.xyz/taxes/tips/Documents/TIP_25C01-01.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24: "sections 60-61 of ch. 2025-208, Laws of Florida, amend the Florida Income Tax Code to adopt the IRC retroactively to January 1, 2025. This means Florida will follow the computation of federal taxable income." The same TIP notes §220.13(1)(e) modifications (bonus-depreciation addback, etc.) continue to apply — i.e. conformity is not wholesale; Florida adds back / subtracts specified items.
  • Critical finding — no §280E decoupling: No Florida statute, rule, or DOR guidance was found that decouples Florida corporate income tax from IRC §280E, or that creates a Florida-specific cannabis deduction addback/subtraction. Searches for "Florida 280E decoupling," "Florida corporate income tax cannabis," and Ch. 220 cannabis provisions returned only secondary CPA commentary stating the opposite — that Florida follows the federal result:
  • GreenGrowth CPAs, "Florida Cannabis CPA" (retrieved 2026-10-24, https://greengrowthcpas.com/industries/cannabis/florida-cannabis-accounting/): "Florida does not have its own cannabis tax rule. Its corporate income tax starts from federal taxable income, so it follows the federal result. Through 2025, that meant 280E disallowed ordinary business expenses on both returns. Effective April 28, 2026, medical cannabis sold under a state license is Schedule III, so for Florida MMTCs 280E no longer applies going forward on either return."
  • That page also states: "Treasury has said its forthcoming guidance will apply the change to the full 2026 tax year for calendar-year filers" — secondary, [VERIFY] against actual Treasury/IRS guidance; do not cite it as law.
  • What this means, step by step:
  • Through the 2025 tax year (and earlier years still open to audit): an MMTC's federal taxable income was computed with §280E disallowing ordinary and necessary business expenses (only cost of goods sold deductible), because marijuana was Schedule I. Florida adjusted federal income started from that disallowed figure, so §280E effectively applied on the Florida return too — not because Florida enacted §280E, but because Florida started from the federal number and made no cannabis adjustment in §220.13.
  • From 28 April 2026 (Schedule III for state-licensed medical marijuana): §280E by its terms applies only to Schedule I and II substances (26 U.S.C. §280E). A Florida MMTC's medical marijuana is therefore no longer subject to §280E federally on a go-forward basis, and — because Florida follows the federal computation with no cannabis decoupling — no longer subject to the §280E disallowance on the Florida return either, for the medical activity. Ordinary business expenses (payroll, rent, utilities, insurance, general administration) become deductible on both returns for that activity, subject to normal substantiation and to any future IRS/Treasury guidance on effective-date / full-year application.
  • Adult-use (if Florida ever adopts it) remains Schedule I federally: §280E would continue to apply federally to adult-use activity, and — on the same conformity logic — would continue to flow into the Florida computation for that activity, unless Florida then enacted a decoupling provision. A mixed medical/adult-use operator would need to segregate income and expenses; no Florida allocation rule for mixed operators was found (Gap 2-10).
  • Hemp businesses were never subject to §280E after the 2018 Farm Bill (hemp is not a Schedule I controlled substance), federally or in Florida. No change from Schedule III affects hemp tax treatment.
  • Caveats that must travel with this conclusion:
    • The federal Schedule III order's precise scope (state-licensed medical marijuana "in any form covered by a state medical marijuana license," FDA-approved products) and any DEA-registration condition discussed in secondary CPA commentary (e.g. https://bgm360.com/news-insights/potential-tax-impacts-of-doj-rescheduling-order/ — Accessed 2026-10-24, arguing a DEA registration may be required for §280E relief) are federal questions outside this Part's Florida-law scope and are flagged for Part 1 / federal-baseline verification. This file relies on the fixed federal baseline given in the commission, not on that secondary DEA-registration argument.
    • Whether Florida's 2026 IRC adoption act (2026 session, Ch. 2026-_) adopts the IRC as of 1 January 2026 — and therefore captures the April 2026 Schedule III change for the 2026 Florida return without further action — was not verified in this session. DOR's October 2026 proposal to amend Rule 12C-1.051 for taxable years beginning on/after 1 January 2026 (Bloomberg Tax, 2 Oct 2026, https://news.bloombergtax.com/daily-tax-report-state/florida-dor-proposes-amending-corporate-income-tax-rule-to-update-forms-for-irc-conformity — Accessed 2026-10-24) concerns forms and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, not §280E. **Run 2 must check the 2026 conformity act (flsenate.gov, 2026 session, Ch. 220) and any DOR TIP #26C01- before stating the Florida 2026 treatment as settled.** Until then, the §2.6.2 conclusion is stated as "follows the federal result under the conformity mechanism," not as "DOR has confirmed §280E relief on the 2026 Florida return."
    • No Florida DOR cannabis-specific TAA, TIP, or rule on §280E was located. If DOR issues one, it supersedes secondary CPA commentary.

2.6.3 Other business taxes that touch MMTCs/hemp businesses (ordinary, not cannabis-specific)

  • Unemployment / reemployment tax (Ch. 443): ordinary employer tax; no cannabis rate found.
  • Tangible personal property tax: ordinary county property tax on business equipment; no cannabis exemption found.
  • Federal taxes: federal corporate/partnership income tax, payroll taxes, and (for Schedule III medical, prospectively) normal deductibility — federal detail is outside this Part except for the §280E flow-through above.
  • No Florida franchise tax separate from Ch. 220 in the modern sense; Ch. 220 is cited as "Income Tax Code" / corporate income and franchise tax. Do not invent a separate franchise-tax line.

2.7 Proposed (NOT law) adult-use taxes

Rule for this section: every item here is PROPOSED and must be labelled as such. None is current law.

2.7.1 2024 Amendment 3 — failed; no excise tax in the amendment; sales-tax-only projection

  • Amendment 3 (2024) would have allowed adults 21+ to possess/purchase/use marijuana for non-medical personal consumption and allowed MMTCs and other state-licensed entities to sell it. It failed on 5 Nov 2024 with ~55.9% of the vote, short of Florida's 60% supermajority requirement for constitutional amendments (Art. XI, §5(e), Fla. Const.). Source: Tallahassee Democrat / TC Sentinel reporting retrieved 2026-10-24, https://www.tcsentinel.com/recreational-marijuana-will-not-appear-on-florida-s-november-ballot.html ("Amendment 3 drew 55.9% … but failed to clear the 60% supermajority") — Accessed 2026-10-24. Official canvass figures belong in Part 9; the 55.9% figure here is secondary-reported.
  • Tax content of Amendment 3: none — no excise tax rate was in the amendment text. The ballot summary said only "Allows consistent legislation." The Financial Impact Estimating Conference statement (on the ballot) said:

    "The amendment's financial impact primarily comes from expected sales tax collections. If legal today, sales of non-medical marijuana would be subject to sales tax and would remain so if voters approve this amendment. Based on other states' experiences, expected retail sales of non-medical marijuana would generate at least $195.6 million annually in state and local sales tax revenues once the retail market is fully operational, although the timing of this occurring is unclear." Source: ballot financial-impact statement as reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Florida_Amendment_3 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary reproduction of an official statement; Run 2 should cite the FIEC statement directly from the Florida Office of Economic and Demographic Research). A secondary analysis citing the FIEC gives a range of $195.6 million to $431.3 million per year in state and local sales-tax revenue at full operation: https://legalclarity.org/florida-amendment-3-what-you-need-to-know/ — Accessed 2026-10-24. Use the $195.6m "at least" figure as the ballot figure; the $431.3m upper end is secondary-reported FIEC range, not ballot text.

  • Why "sales tax only" matters: had Amendment 3 passed, adult-use sales would have borne ordinary 6% + surtax (because the §212.08(2)(l) exemption covers only §381.986 marijuana, and adult-use marijuana would not have been §381.986 marijuana unless the Legislature preserved the exemption — a question the amendment left to "consistent legislation"). The Legislature could then have added an excise tax by general law, but no such excise was enacted, because the amendment failed.

2.7.2 2026 adult-use initiatives — failed to qualify; no 2026 ballot tax to report

  • Smart & Safe Florida's 2026 "Adult personal use of marijuana" initiative did not qualify for the November 2026 ballot. The Division of Elections listed 783,592 verified signatures by the 1 Feb deadline against 880,062 required, and the Department of State declared all 22 active initiative petitions failed to meet requirements for the 2026 General Election ballot. Sources: https://www.tallahassee.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/10/19/florida-elections-vote-recreational-marijuana-amendment/92326407007/ — Accessed 2026-10-24; https://gmg-wkmg-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/news/florida/2026/02/02/no-citizen-initiatives-on-2026-florida-ballot-including-marijuana-amendment-state-says/ — Accessed 2026-10-24. There is therefore no 2026 adult-use election result and no 2026 adult-use tax in law.
  • A separate 2028-track petition (Serial No. 26-03, "Let Florida Vote IV," full text at https://initiativepetitions.dos.fl.gov/InitiativeForms/Fulltext/Fulltext_2603_EN.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24) does contain a taxation reservation, quoted verbatim because it is the only proposed adult-use tax language located in a filed petition text:

    "…nothing herein shall limit the right of the legislature, subject to Section 19 of Article VII of this Constitution, to exercise its authority through general law in providing for the taxation of sales of marijuana and appropriating such tax revenues to fund law enforcement, education, or as otherwise determined by the Legislature. Nothing in this section shall limit the legislature from enacting laws consistent with this section." That is a reservation of legislative taxing power, not a tax rate. It sets no percentage, base, or distribution formula. Any future adult-use tax rate would have to come from a later general law. Do not cite a "proposed Florida adult-use tax rate" — none exists in a filed, qualifying measure as of 24 Oct 2026. (Secondary articles that say a 2026 measure would "create a tax structure" or "direct tax revenue" — e.g. https://whatsonmyballot.info/blog/marijuana-legalization-ballot-2026 — Accessed 2026-10-24 — are generic and, for Florida, inaccurate as to a specific rate; they are not relied on here.)

2.8 Revenue figures — what official data does and does not exist

Revenue stream Official figure located? What to say instead
Medical-marijuana sales-tax revenue No — by design, $0, because sales are exempt. DOR does not publish a "foregone" series found for this file. Do not invent a foregone-revenue estimate. State the exemption (§2.2) and note the 2024 FIEC projection (§2.7.1) is for a hypothetical adult-use market, not medical revenue.
Medical-marijuana excise revenue No — no excise exists. $0 by absence of tax, not by collection data.
MMTC application + renewal fee revenue (aggregate) No aggregate published figure located. The per-licence figures in §2.3 are known; multiplying them by licence counts would be analyst arithmetic, not official revenue, because renewal dates are staggered biennially and new-licence application counts vary by batching cycle. Do not publish a multiplied total as "revenue." Report per-licence fees (§2.3) and licence counts from Part 4/Part 5 sources; Run 2 may request DOH/OMMU fee-collection totals via public-records request if the parent agent authorises it (not done here).
Hemp sales-tax revenue (aggregate) No hemp-specific DOR series located. Hemp sales tax, where collected, is reported in general dealer returns by NAICS / product category, not as a "hemp" line. State the tax treatment (§2.5); do not quote a hemp tax total.
Hemp fee revenue (FDACS) No aggregate located. Part 7 territory.
Corporate income tax paid by MMTCs (aggregate) No MMTC-specific DOR aggregate located (DOR does not publish taxpayer-level or industry-level corporate-tax collections for MMTCs). State the rate and conformity mechanism (§2.6); do not quote a total.
Local surtax revenue attributable to hemp/cannabis businesses No cannabis-attributable surtax series located. Surtax is distributed to counties by DOR in aggregate, not by product. State the surtax mechanism (§2.4); do not allocate a share to cannabis.

Bottom line for Part 2 revenue: Florida's medical-marijuana tax policy is exemption + fees + ordinary corporate income tax, not excise taxation. Any dossier table that shows a Florida "cannabis tax revenue" line must show fees only, with the per-licence figures and a "no aggregate published" note, or it will mislead.

PART 3 — LOCAL RULES

3.1 Authority of counties and municipalities — the "ban or pharmacy-parity" rule

3.1.1 State preemption for cultivation, processing, and delivery

Citation: §381.986(11), Fla. Stat. — "PREEMPTION."

Verbatim — §381.986(11), introductory sentence and (a):

"Regulation of cultivation, processing, and delivery of marijuana by medical marijuana treatment centers is preempted to the state except as provided in this subsection. A medical marijuana treatment center cultivating or processing facility may not be located within 500 feet of the real property that comprises a public or private elementary school, middle school, or secondary school."

Source: https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._381.986 (subsection (11), lines 2477–2479 of the retrieved text) — Accessed 2026-10-24.

What "preempted to the state" means in practice:

  • A county or city may not regulate how an MMTC cultivates, processes, or delivers marijuana (growing methods, processing standards, delivery procedures) — that is DOH/OMMU territory under §381.986(8) and Ch. 64-4, F.A.C.
  • The only local powers over MMTCs are those expressly preserved in §381.986(11)(b)–(d) (dispensing-facility location/permitting, ban option, school buffer, building/fire code enforcement). Anything beyond that — e.g. a local cap on the number of dispensaries, a local potency limit, a local cultivation ban framed as a zoning rule for cultivation/processing facilities — is preempted on the face of the statute. Note the Palm Bay 2026 ordinance recitals make exactly this point (see §3.2.6).
  • Building and fire code are expressly preserved: §381.986(11)(d): "This subsection does not prohibit any local jurisdiction from ensuring medical marijuana treatment center facilities comply with the Florida Building Code, the Florida Fire Prevention Code, or any local amendments to [those codes]." Verbatim from the same subsection — Accessed 2026-10-24.

3.1.2 The dispensing-facility rule — verbatim (the core of Part 3)

Verbatim — §381.986(11)(b)1.–2. (full operative text):

"A county or municipality may, by ordinance, ban medical marijuana treatment center dispensing facilities from being located within the boundaries of that county or municipality. A county or municipality that does not ban dispensing facilities under this subparagraph may not place specific limits, by ordinance, on the number of dispensing facilities that may locate within that county or municipality."

"A municipality may determine by ordinance the criteria for the location of, and other permitting requirements that do not conflict with state law or department rule for, medical marijuana treatment center dispensing facilities located within the boundaries of that municipality. A county may determine by ordinance the criteria for the location of, and other permitting requirements that do not conflict with state law or department rule for, all such dispensing facilities located within the unincorporated areas of that county. Except as provided in paragraph (c), a county or municipality may not enact ordinances for permitting or for determining the location of dispensing facilities which are more restrictive than its ordinances permitting or determining the locations for pharmacies licensed under chapter 465. A municipality or county may not charge a medical marijuana treatment center a license or permit fee in an amount greater than the fee charged by such municipality or county to pharmacies. A dispensing facility location approved by a municipality or county pursuant to former s. 381.986(8)(b), Florida Statutes 2016, is not subject to the location requirements of this subsection."

Source: https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._381.986 (subsection (11)(b)) — Accessed 2026-10-24.

Verbatim — §381.986(11)(c) (school buffer + local waiver):

"A medical marijuana treatment center dispensing facility may not be located within 500 feet of the real property that comprises a public or private elementary school, middle school, or secondary school unless the county or municipality approves the location through a formal proceeding open to the public at which the county or municipality determines that the location promotes the public health, safety, and general welfare of the community."

Source: same — Accessed 2026-10-24.

Plain-English decoding (each point is a direct consequence of the verbatim text, not an expansion):

  1. Two lawful choices, no middle ground on restrictiveness: a locality may (A) ban dispensing facilities entirely within its boundaries by ordinance, or (B) allow them — but if it allows them, it may not (i) cap their number by ordinance, or (ii) impose permitting/location rules more restrictive than its pharmacy rules (Ch. 465 pharmacies). A locality that tries to allow dispensaries but with pharmacy-plus-extra buffers, spacing, or caps is acting outside §381.986(11)(b). That is why many 2017 local debates were framed as "ban or pharmacy-parity" (see e.g. Palm Beach County staff report, §3.3).
  2. "Ban" means dispensing facilities only. The ban power in (b)1. is expressly limited to "dispensing facilities." It does not authorise a locality to ban an MMTC's cultivation or processing facility by ordinance — those are preempted under (11) introductory text, subject only to the 500-foot school buffer in (11)(a), which has no local waiver (contrast (11)(c) waiver for dispensing facilities). A local ordinance that purports to ban cultivation/processing should be flagged as preempted on its face, though enforcement/litigation history is Part 9 territory.
  3. County vs municipality jurisdiction: a municipality's location/permitting ordinance governs facilities within its boundaries; a county's governs facilities in unincorporated areas only. A county ban does not ban dispensaries inside an incorporated city within that county, and a city ban does not affect unincorporated areas. This county-city split explains several apparent contradictions in the table in §3.3 (e.g. a county ban coexisting with dispensaries in a city in that county).
  4. Number caps are void if imposed by an allowing locality. Historical local caps (e.g. Orlando's original "one per dispensing organisation" concept, Fort Lauderdale's "one per 40,000 residents" concept, Hillsborough's proposed caps — see §§3.3–3.4) are inconsistent with (b)1. to the extent they were enacted by a locality that did not ban dispensaries. Whether any such cap was ever litigated to invalidation, repealed, or simply never enforced is [VERIFY] jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction in Run 2; this file reports the historical proposal and flags the statutory conflict, and does not assert any current cap is in force.
  5. Fee cap: local licence/permit fee for an MMTC ≤ pharmacy fee in that jurisdiction (see §3.5).
  6. Grandfather clause: a dispensing location approved under former §381.986(8)(b) (2016) is not subject to the current (11) location requirements. That protects early (pre-SB 8-A) approvals.

Last-amended date for §381.986(11): [VERIFY]. The subsection was created in its current form by SB 8-A (2017 Special Session, Ch. 2017-232). Later amendments (e.g. 2019 smokable-flower law, Ch. 2019-1; subsequent DOH bills) may have touched §381.986 generally but the (11) text quoted above is the current published text as retrieved. Run 2 should pull the Online Sunshine history note for (11) specifically.

3.1.3 Authority over hemp / CBD / smoke shops — NO equivalent of §381.986(11)

Finding: there is no hemp equivalent of the "ban or pharmacy-parity" rule in §581.217.

  • §581.217 (State Hemp Program) creates the FDACS state hemp programme, cultivation licensing, and hemp-extract food regulation, but does not contain a local-preemption / local-ban provision parallel to §381.986(11) in any text located for this file. [VERIFY] by opening current §581.217 in full in Run 2 / Part 7 — the absence of a provision is harder to prove than its presence, and this file states it as "no such provision located," not as a certified negative.
  • Consequences of that absence (general local-government law, not hemp-specific preemption):
  • Counties and municipalities retain their general police / zoning power over retail uses, including hemp/CBD/smoke shops, subject to (a) state law (FDACS hemp-extract rules, Ch. 500 food safety, Ch. 893 controlled-substances definitions as amended for hemp), (b) their own zoning codes, and (c) the Florida Constitution's home-rule provisions (Art. VIII). They may zone a smoke shop as a retail use, require a local business tax receipt under Ch. 205 (see §3.5), and enforce building/fire codes — but they may not redefine hemp as marijuana, or ban a product that state law expressly permits, without a state-law basis. Any local hemp ban should be checked against §581.217 and Ch. 500 before being reported as valid.
  • No statewide hemp-retail licence exists to be "banned" locally in the MMTC sense: hemp food establishments are permitted by FDACS (Division of Food Safety), not by the locality. A locality cannot revoke an FDACS permit; it can only enforce its own zoning/business-tax requirements.
  • Proposed (not enacted) local restrictions: 2026 hemp bills SB 1270 / SB 1030 would have prohibited FDACS-permitted hemp businesses from being located in specified areas (near schools/daycares, per the bill summaries at https://legiscan.com/FL/text/S1270/2026 — Accessed 2026-10-24) and would have required FDACS pre-approval of advertisements. Those are proposals, not law, and they did not pass in the 2026 session. Do not cite them as current local-authority law.
  • Smoking preemption (related but distinct): §386.209 preempts regulation of smoking to the state, with narrow exceptions for school-district property and for municipal/county restriction of outdoor smoking on their own property/beaches. That preemption concerns smoking conduct, not the location of a hemp retail store, and should not be conflated with §381.986(11). Source: §386.209 as quoted in HB 143 (2012) bill text, https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2012/0143/BillText/Filed/HTML — Accessed 2026-10-24. [VERIFY] current §386.209 text in Run 2.
  • Practical summary for a hemp retailer: expect general retail zoning + FDACS permit + DOR registration + Ch. 205 business tax receipt (where the locality levies one), not an MMTC-style local ban/parity analysis. If a city claims to "ban hemp shops," ask for the ordinance citation and check it against §581.217 — no such ordinance was verified for the 15 jurisdictions in §3.3 in this session (Gap 3-05).

3.1.4 Authority over cultivation/processing facilities (MMTC) — local role is minimal

  • Cultivation/processing facilities: state-preempted except for (i) the 500-foot school buffer in §381.986(11)(a) (no local waiver), and (ii) building/fire code enforcement in (11)(d).
  • A locality therefore cannot impose a local buffer (e.g. 1,000 feet from a park/church/daycare) on a cultivation/processing facility by ordinance, and cannot require a local cultivation licence beyond building/fire permits. Historical Sarasota County Ordinance 2014-66, which zoned "cannabis farms" to agricultural districts by special exception and imposed 500-foot separations from schools/houses of worship/daycares/parks/beaches (see §3.3, Sarasota row), predates SB 8-A (2017) and is inconsistent with current (11) preemption to the extent it regulates cultivation/processing location beyond the school buffer. Its current status (repealed? amended? superseded?) is [VERIFY] — do not cite the 2014 Sarasota scheme as current law.

3.2 Local bans, moratoriums, caps, and zoning — general history

Most Florida local action on MMTCs clusters in 2016–2018:

  • 2016 (pre-Amendment 2 / low-THC era): cities/counties adopted low-THC dispensary zoning, moratoriums, or bans under the 2014 Compassionate Medical Cannabis Act framework (former §381.986). Examples: Sarasota County Ord. 2014-66; Alachua County Ord. 16-15 (9 Aug 2016); Palm Beach County moratorium Ord. 2017-009 (Dec 2016, 1-year sunset).
  • 2017 (SB 8-A, June 2017): the Legislature replaced the local framework with §381.986(11) "ban or pharmacy-parity." Localities that had imposed pharmacy-plus restrictions (extra buffers, caps, special exceptions) had to choose: repeal/amend to pharmacy parity, or ban. The Florida Association of Counties (FAC) / Florida League of Cities surveys from 2017–March 2018 are the best contemporaneous record of those choices (see §3.3 source note).
  • 2017–2018 moratoriums: many localities imposed temporary moratoriums (typically 180 days, some 210 days or 1 year) while drafting SB 8-A-compliant ordinances. A moratorium is not a ban: it pauses new applications; it does not permanently prohibit dispensaries and it expires by its terms. Examples in the FAC survey: Hillsborough Ord. 2016-20 (180 days); Pinellas Ord. 2017-05 (180 days); Polk Ord. 2017-001 (180 days); Citrus (180 days); Seminole (210 days to 1 May 2018); St. Johns (to 31 Mar 2018). All of those moratoriums have long expired; citing them as current bans would be an error.
  • Permanent bans (2017–2018, unincorporated areas and some cities): DeSoto, Flagler, Gilchrist, Hendry, Indian River (unincorporated, with grandfathering), Lake (unincorporated, eff. Nov 2017), Osceola (with grandfathering for already-permitted facilities), and others outside the 15-jurisdiction check — plus, within the 15, Collier (unincorporated, 2023, see §3.3) and Palm Bay (Brevard County city, 2026, see §3.3). Each ban must be read with its grandfather / nonconforming-use clause: existing, already-approved dispensaries typically remain as legal nonconforming uses.
  • 2023–2026 new bans: the pattern did not end in 2018. Collier County (unincorporated) prohibited dispensaries in 2023 (see §3.3); Palm Bay adopted a ban ordinance in 2026 (Ord. 2026-13, see §3.3); Deltona (Volusia County) planning board recommended a ban in 2025 (Ord. 21-20-25, recommendation only — commission adoption [VERIFY]). Run 2 should re-check every "allow" jurisdiction in §3.3 for a post-2018 ban, because a 2017 "allow" does not guarantee a 2026 "allow."

Direct answer to the task's question 3: No official statewide list, maintained by OMMU, DOH, FAC, or any state agency, of which Florida counties/municipalities ban vs allow MMTC dispensing facilities, was located for this file.

  • OMMU publishes a dispensary location list (addresses by MMTC) — that proves a dispensary exists at an address, not the legal status of the jurisdiction's ordinance, and it does not list jurisdictions with zero dispensaries or with bans.
  • The closest official-sector compilation is the Florida Association of Counties (FAC) Medical Marijuana Implementation Survey, updated March 2018 (county-attorney survey), https://faca.fl-counties.com/sites/default/files/2018-03/Medical%20Marijuana_Implentation%20County%20Attorney%20Survey_0.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24, plus the FAC "Comprehensive Ordinance Review" (Feb 2017), http://fl-counties.com/sites/default/files/2017-02/Comprehensive Ordinance Review.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24. Both are 2017–2018 snapshots, not current law. They are used below as the historical baseline, with a "current status [VERIFY]" flag on every row where a post-2018 code check was not completed in this session.
  • Method for the table below: for each of the 15 required jurisdictions, the table gives (a) the FAC 2017–18 position, (b) any later ordinance/evidence located in this session, and (c) the current-status assessment. Where the only evidence is the 2017–18 survey, the row is labelled "ALLOW (2017–18 survey) — current code [VERIFY]" and must not be quoted as a 2026 finding without re-checking the current county/city code on Municode or the county clerk's ordinance index. Where dispensaries are known to operate in the jurisdiction in 2026 (from OMMU-derived secondary lists), that is noted as practical evidence of allow, not as a code verification.

3.4 Local civil-citation ordinances for small-amount possession (instead of arrest)

State-law baseline (so the local ordinances can be understood): possession of not more than 20 grams of cannabis is a first-degree misdemeanour under §893.13(6)(b), punishable by up to 1 year in jail / $1,000 fine under §§775.082, 775.083 (see Part 1 for full penalties). No statewide decriminalisation exists. Local civil-citation ordinances do not change state law, do not legalise possession, and do not bind state officers (Florida Highway Patrol, FDLE, sheriff's deputies acting under state law in some contexts) or a local officer who elects to arrest instead. Every ordinance below is discretionary: the officer may cite instead of arresting; the ordinance does not require citation.

Verbatim-text note: full ordinance texts were opened for Miami Beach and Miami-Dade (Uniform Penal Code listing) and partially for Wilton Manors and Tampa (draft) in this session. For other jurisdictions, the table gives the reported fine schedule from secondary sources and flags the ordinance citation as [VERIFY]. Do not present a secondary-reported fine as verbatim ordinance text.

General secondary range across jurisdictions: first offence typically $75–$100 (some sources say $75–$155 including higher-fine jurisdictions); second offence $150–$250; third $300–$500 or community service / drug education (secondary, https://www.thedensonfirm.com/criminal-defense/understanding-florida-marijuana-laws-and-your-rights/ — Accessed 2026-10-24; https://legalclarity.org/possession-of-a-controlled-substance-in-florida-laws-and-penalties/ — Accessed 2026-10-24). That range is a secondary synthesis, not an ordinance, and must not be attributed to any single jurisdiction. Wilton Manors: verified $25 (Municode). All others in this row: [VERIFY] ordinance + fine.
City of Jacksonville / Duval County NO civil-citation ordinance found in force. A 2019 proposal — Council Member Garrett Dennis's "Jacksonville Civil Citation for Small Quantity Marijuana Possession Ordinance" ($100 for ≤20 grams) — was introduced and discussed with community meetings in July 2019 but is not shown as adopted in any source checked. Source: NORML, 26 July 2019, http://norml.org/blog/2019/07/26/florida-municipality-considering-marijuana-decriminalization-measure/amp/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 ("Jacksonville … could join … Council Member Garrett Dennis recently introduced … If approved, the ordinance would impose a $100 fine"). N/A — proposal only. Jacksonville is NOT listed as a civil-citation jurisdiction in this file. Secondary guides that say "Jacksonville tends to enforce state law strictly" (https://mmjhealth.com/is-weed-legal-in-miami-miami-cannabis-marijuana-laws-2025/ — Accessed 2026-10-24) are consistent with no ordinance. Run 2 should confirm no later adoption from the Jacksonville Ordinance Code index.
Leon County / Tallahassee, Lee County, Polk County, Brevard County, Collier County No civil-citation ordinance located for these jurisdictions in this session. They do not appear in the NORML 2019 or Tallahassee Democrat 2026 civil-citation lists reproduced above. N/A Treated as NO civil-citation ordinance found — [VERIFY] by code search in Run 2 before stating a negative absolutely. Absence from two secondary lists is evidence, not proof.

Common limits on every civil-citation ordinance (from the verbatim texts opened):

  • Age: Tampa/Hillsborough: 18+ only. Miami Beach original: discretionary, with exclusions below. Wilton Manors: counting rules imply adult programme; age floor not in the extract retrieved — [VERIFY].
  • Exclusions (Miami Beach verbatim pattern, widely replicated): not available if charged in conjunction with a felony, DUI, domestic-violence incident, or violent crime. Tampa: no other criminal charges from the same incident; qualified for own-recognisance release.
  • Medical possession excepted: Hillsborough County ordinance expressly excepts "lawful possession of cannabis medically prescribed by a licensed physician." (Note the ordinance's "prescribed" wording predates current certification language; the exception's scope for MMTC patients should be read with §381.986, not with the ordinance's shorthand.)
  • No effect on >20 grams, resin/concentrates as separately charged, sale/delivery, or public-consumption charges. Civil citation is a possession-only off-ramp for ≤20 grams of cannabis flower as defined in §893.13(6)(b) (which excludes resin — see Part 1 penalties).

3.5 Local licence / permit fees and buffer rules

3.5.1 MMTC local fee cap (state law, verbatim — see §3.1.2)

"A municipality or county may not charge a medical marijuana treatment center a license or permit fee in an amount greater than the fee charged by such municipality or county to pharmacies."

Source: §381.986(11)(b)2. — Accessed 2026-10-24. Practical meaning: if a city charges pharmacies $X for a local business tax receipt / certificate of use / occupational licence, it may charge an MMTC no more than $X for the equivalent local permit. It may charge less. It may not impose an MMTC-specific surcharge above the pharmacy rate.

What was NOT found: a published schedule of actual pharmacy vs MMTC local fees for any of the 15 jurisdictions. Miami-Dade's certificate-of-use system (annual renewal, inspections, revocation for ordinance violation — described in the 2016 Manatee Clerk compilation, https://records.manateeclerk.com/BoardRecords/Browse/Agendas/Board-of-County-Commissioners/2016/10/BC20161025DOC006.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24) is the only local MMTC permit system described in any detail in sources opened, and no dollar fee is stated in that compilation. Every local MMTC fee figure is therefore [VERIFY] / [UNAVAILABLE] in this file — Run 2 must pull each jurisdiction's business-tax-receipt / certificate-of-use fee schedule (typically on the city/county tax collector or business-tax web page) and compare the pharmacy vs MMTC line items. Do not estimate fees.

3.5.2 General local business tax (Ch. 205) — applies to hemp/cannabis businesses like any business

  • Municipal authority — verbatim substance of §205.042: "The governing body of an incorporated municipality may levy, by appropriate resolution or ordinance, a business tax for the privilege of engaging in or managing any business, profession, or occupation within its jurisdiction," after at least 14 days' public notice between readings, with proposed classifications and rates published. Source: §205.042 as published (2007/2013 codifications retrieved), https://flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2013/0205.042 and http://flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2007/Chapter205/All — Accessed 2026-10-24. County business tax authority is in §205.043 et seq. (same source).
  • Application: an MMTC dispensing facility, a hemp food establishment, and a smoke shop are all "businesses" for Ch. 205 purposes and, where the locality levies a business tax, must obtain a local business tax receipt (formerly "occupational licence") in addition to the state licence/permit. The Ch. 205 receipt is not a cannabis licence and does not authorise cannabis activity by itself.
  • Interaction with the MMTC fee cap: Ch. 205 gives the locality power to levy a business tax, but §381.986(11)(b)2. caps the MMTC amount at the pharmacy amount. For hemp shops, no §381.986 cap applies (they are not MMTCs), so a locality's ordinary Ch. 205 schedule applies in full — subject to any general Ch. 205 rate limits and to the locality's own classifications. No hemp-specific Ch. 205 classification was located.
  • Amounts: [UNAVAILABLE] by jurisdiction in this file (see §3.5.1). Do not quote a "typical" business-tax-receipt fee.

3.6 Business concentration — ONLY what official sources say

Constraint honoured: no ranking, clustering estimate, or "hotspot" analysis by this researcher is included. Only figures stated by an official or secondary source that itself cites OMMU are reproduced, with their dates and caveats.

3.6.1 Statewide dispensary count (OMMU-derived, secondary-reported)

  • 781 dispensing locations, 25 September 2026 (OMMU weekly/periodic report as reported by CannBus, Q3 2026 market report, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/fl_cannmir.html — Accessed 2026-10-24): "781 Dispensing locations Sep 25, 2026" and "Operator, location and patient counts are from OMMU's Sep 25, 2026 report." Operator breakdown in the same report (CannBus calculation from OMMU list): Trulieve 170, MÜV 86, Curaleaf Florida 78, Ayr Cannabis 65, Surterra Wellness 44, Green Dragon 41, Planet 13 Florida 34, FLUENT 33, Sunnyside 31, Sanctuary Cannabis 27, all other (13 MMTCs) 172 — total 781. The report also states "four companies run 399 of the 781 dispensing locations (51.1%; CannBus calc.)" and "23 MMTCs with stores" plus "22 New MMTC licenses final order Sep 11, 2026" (new licensees not yet dispensing at the report date).

  • Use the 781 figure (25 Sept 2026, OMMU via CannBus) as the latest count in this file, with the CannBus attribution attached. The OMMU dispensary list itself was not downloaded and counted independently in this session (Part 5 territory); Run 2 / Part 5 should download the OMMU list and recount, and Part 6 should reconcile any difference.

3.6.3 What official sources do say about where dispensaries are (without a county table)

  • Dispensaries operate in every region of Florida (the OMMU list includes addresses from Miami-Dade to Duval to Leon to Lee to Hillsborough — verifiable by opening the OMMU list, Part 5). That qualitative statement — statewide distribution, not concentration — is the most that can be said from official sources without a county tally.
  • Jurisdictions with bans (Collier unincorporated, Palm Bay, etc.) necessarily have zero new dispensing facilities in the banned area (subject to grandfathering), which mechanically shifts new locations to neighbouring allowing jurisdictions (e.g. Marco Island / Bonita Springs for Collier patients, per the Gulfshore article). That is a logical consequence of a ban, not a measured concentration finding, and is stated as such.

Federal baseline applied (fixed context, not re-researched). State-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity and remains fully applicable to adult-use. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026, after which the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026. No contradiction with that baseline was found in the Florida licence sources examined for this Part. Florida MMTCs are state-licensed medical operators, so on that baseline their medical activity is the Schedule III / 280E-lifted category; any future adult-use activity would remain Schedule I / fully subject to 280E. That application is stated here as an inference from the fixed baseline, not as a Florida statute.

PART 4 — LICENCE TYPES

4.0 — The one-licence model: there is no separate Florida cultivation, processing, wholesale, retail, delivery or microbusiness marijuana licence

Florida licenses one marijuana business type: the Medical Marijuana Treatment Center (MMTC). It is vertically integrated by statute. There is no separate state licence for a standalone cultivator, processor, wholesaler/distributor, retailer/dispensary, delivery-only operator, or consumption lounge for marijuana. The only independent marijuana licence/certification is the Certified Marijuana Testing Laboratory (CMTL) (see §4.2).

Verbatim, § 381.986(8)(e) (Accessed 2026-10-24):

“A licensed medical marijuana treatment center shall cultivate, process, transport, and dispense marijuana for medical use.”

And OMMU's own weekly-update wording (28 August 2026, opened directly):

“MMTCs are vertically integrated businesses, and are the only businesses authorized to cultivate, process, and dispense low-THC cannabis and medical marijuana.” — https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/ommu_updates/2026/082826-OMMU-Update.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24.

After initial licensure, each MMTC must separately receive authorisation at three stages before dispensing (same source):

“After initial licensure, each MMTC must receive authorization at three stages prior to dispensing low-THC cannabis or medical marijuana: (1) cultivation authorization, (2) processing authorization, and (3) dispensing authorization.”

These are authorisations within the single MMTC licence, not separate licence types. An MMTC may not, as a general rule, wholesale to another MMTC. Verbatim, § 381.986(8)(c):

“A medical marijuana treatment center may not make a wholesale purchase of marijuana from, or a distribution of marijuana to, another medical marijuana treatment center, unless the medical marijuana treatment center seeking to make a wholesale purchase of marijuana submits proof of harvest failure to the department.”

An MMTC also, as a general rule, may not contract out directly-related cultivation, processing or dispensing services, with one narrow statutory exception for an MMTC licensed under § 381.986(8)(a)1. contracting with a single entity for all four functions (§ 381.986(8)(e), Accessed 2026-10-24).

What an MMTC licence therefore allows, in one licence: cultivate (including low-THC cannabis), process, transport, and dispense low-THC cannabis and medical marijuana to qualified patients and caregivers at approved dispensing locations and via delivery, subject to physician certification/order limits. Dispensing is in milligrams of THC (medical marijuana) and milligrams of CBD (low-THC cannabis) — OMMU Weekly Update, 28 August 2026, Accessed 2026-10-24. Delivery devices are dispensed from MMTCs except that delivery devices for smoking need not be dispensed from an MMTC to qualify (§ 381.986(1), definition of “marijuana delivery device”).

4.1 — MMTC licences

4.1.1 — Statutory basis and who issues them

  • Issuer: Florida Department of Health, through OMMU. § 381.986(8)(a): “The department shall license medical marijuana treatment centers to ensure reasonable statewide accessibility and availability as necessary for qualified patients…” — https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._381.986 — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Constitutional basis (for cross-reference only; full treatment is in Part 1/Part 9): Fla. Const. Art. X, § 29 (Amendment 2, 2016).
  • Licence term: biennial (2-year). § 381.986(8)(b): “The department shall renew the licensure of a medical marijuana treatment center biennially if the licensee meets the requirements of this section and pays the biennial renewal fee. However, the department may not renew the license of a medical marijuana treatment center that has not begun to cultivate, process, and dispense marijuana by the date that the medical marijuana treatment center is required to renew its license.” — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • One licence per person/entity; one application per individual: § 381.986(8)(b): “An individual may not be an applicant, owner, officer, board member, or manager on more than one application for licensure as a medical marijuana treatment center. An individual or entity may not be awarded more than one license as a medical marijuana treatment center.” — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Ownership cap / cross-ownership ban: § 381.986(8)(e): “A medical marijuana treatment center, and any individual or entity who directly or indirectly owns, controls, or holds with power to vote 5 percent or more of the voting shares of a medical marijuana treatment center, may not acquire direct or indirect ownership or control of any voting shares or other form of ownership of any other medical marijuana treatment center.” — Accessed 2026-10-24. There is no separate statutory cap on number of cultivation/processing facilities or on total canopy/plant count per MMTC in § 381.986 as retrieved; the binding quantity controls are the dispensing-location rules (see §4.1.5, with the expiry caveat) and the staged authorisations. Canopy/plant-count rules, if any in rule, are [VERIFY] — none was located in § 381.986.
  • Transfer of ownership: § 381.986(8)(e) permits transfer to an individual/entity who meets the requirements of the section, with at least 60 days' written notice before the anticipated change, an application received at least 60 days before the change, department notice of errors/omissions within 30 days, a 21-day cure window for omitted information (after which the application is deemed incomplete, withdrawn, and fees forfeited), and department approval/denial within 30 days after receipt of a complete application. A publicly traded corporation/company meeting the requirements is not precluded from ownership. — https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._381.986 — Accessed 2026-10-24. Full transfer/relocation/surrender/revocation detail belongs to Run 2 Part 11; it is summarised here only to show that an MMTC licence is transferable through this statutory route, which is why secondary-market licence sales/asking prices exist (see §4.6).
  • Profit-sharing ban with landlords: § 381.986(8)(e): “A medical marijuana treatment center may not enter into any form of profit-sharing arrangement with the property owner or lessor of any of its facilities where cultivation, processing, storing, or dispensing of marijuana and marijuana delivery devices occurs.” — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Staff age/background: § 381.986(8)(e): “All employees of a medical marijuana treatment center must be 21 years of age or older and have passed a background screening pursuant to subsection (9).” — Accessed 2026-10-24.

4.1.2 — Applicant eligibility — verbatim operative requirements, § 381.986(8)(b)

“An applicant for licensure as a medical marijuana treatment center must demonstrate: 1. That, for the 5 consecutive years before submitting the application, the applicant has been registered to do business in the state. 2. Possession of a valid certificate of registration issued by the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services pursuant to s. 581.131. 3. The technical and technological ability to cultivate and produce marijuana, including, but not limited to, low-THC cannabis. 4. The ability to secure the premises, resources, and personnel necessary to operate as a medical marijuana treatment center. 5. The ability to maintain accountability of all raw materials, finished products, and any byproducts to prevent diversion or unlawful access to or possession of these substances. 6. An infrastructure reasonably located to dispense marijuana to registered qualified patients statewide or regionally as determined by the department. 7. The financial ability to maintain operations for the duration of the 2-year approval cycle, including the provision of certified financial statements to the department. 8. That all owners, officers, board members, and managers have passed a background screening pursuant to subsection (9). 9. The employment of a medical director to supervise the activities of the medical marijuana treatment center. 10. A diversity plan that promotes and ensures the involvement of minority persons and minority business enterprises, as defined in s. 288.703, or veteran business enterprises, as defined in s. 295.187, in ownership, management, and employment.” — https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._381.986 — Accessed 2026-10-24.

Notes on items 2, 8, 9, 10: - Item 2 is the nursery certificate requirement (§ 581.131, FDACS). It is why a pure retail or pure processing applicant cannot enter without a qualifying nursery history; the Pigford licence is expressly exempt from item 2 (see §4.5). - Item 8 background screening is Level 2 (fingerprint-based) under § 381.986(9) — see also proposed Rule 64-4.208, published in Florida Administrative Register Vol. 52 No. 185, 23 September 2026 (OMMU Notices page, https://knowthefactsmmj.com/notices/ — Accessed 2026-10-24). - Item 9: the medical director must hold an active, unrestricted licence as an allopathic physician (Ch. 458) or osteopathic physician (Ch. 459) and comply with § 381.986(3)(c). - Item 10 renewal proof: on renewal the applicant must show effectiveness of the diversity plan by including (a) representation of minority persons and veterans in the workforce, (b) efforts to recruit minority persons and veterans, and (c) a record of contracts with minority and veteran business enterprises (§ 381.986(8)(b)10., Accessed 2026-10-24).

Do not cite a last-amended date without checking Online Sunshine / flsenate.gov for the current-year version. The 2017 implementing law was SB 8A (2017A), and the 2017 text is at https://flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2017/0381.986 — Accessed 2026-10-24.

4.1.4 — How the number of MMTC licences grows with registered patients — the statutory formula

Verbatim, § 381.986(8)(a)4. (Accessed 2026-10-24):

“Within 6 months after the registration of 100,000 active qualified patients in the medical marijuana use registry, the department shall license four additional medical marijuana treatment centers that meet the requirements of this section. Thereafter, the department shall license four medical marijuana treatment centers within 6 months after the registration of each additional 100,000 active qualified patients in the medical marijuana use registry that meet the requirements of this section.”

There is no overall numerical cap in that paragraph — it is a floor/trigger (4 per 100,000), not a ceiling. The arithmetic consequence at October 2026 patient levels is stark, and is the source of the “state still owes licences” reporting:

  • OMMU Weekly Update, 28 August 2026 (opened directly): 940,116 qualified patients with active ID cards; total dispensing locations 778. — https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/ommu_updates/2026/082826-OMMU-Update.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Secondary reporting of the OMMU 23 October 2026 update: 943,271 patients, 784 dispensing locations — Marijuana Herald, 23 Oct 2026, https://themarijuanaherald.com/2026/10/florida-medical-marijuana-new-record/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary; the 23 Oct OMMU PDF itself was not opened directly for this Part — [VERIFY] against the OMMU PDF).
  • At ~940,000 patients, the 4-per-100,000 trigger, read literally from the first 100,000, implies on the order of 36+ “additional” licences beyond the base tranches — but the statute's base tranches (pre-2017 licensees + 10 under (8)(a)2.) and the question of whether the trigger counts from zero, from the first 100,000, or cumulatively, plus the department's actual batching practice, mean no single “licences owed” number should be quoted as a statutory fact. Secondary analyses (e.g. Suncoast NORML, https://www.suncoastnorml.org/post/florida-approves-22-new-medical-cannabis-licenses-but-the-state-may-still-owe-patients-more — Accessed 2026-10-24; MJBizDaily, https://mjbizdaily.com/news/florida-grants-22-cannabis-licenses-despite-judges-call-to-rescore/618145/ — Accessed 2026-10-24) report that OMMU “has generally not followed the statute” on timing and that the September 2026 round was “catch-up”. That characterisation is secondary and is flagged as such; the statutory duty (4 within 6 months per 100,000) and the actual issuance dates are the verifiable facts.

4.1.5 — Dispensing-location caps — original cap, regional allocation, and the expiry problem [VERIFY — read carefully]

The 2017 statute as originally enacted (SB 8A, 2017A) provided, in § 381.986(8)(a)5.:

“A medical marijuana treatment center may not establish or operate more than a statewide maximum of 25 dispensing facilities, unless the medical marijuana use registry reaches a total of 100,000 active registered qualified patients. When the medical marijuana use registry reaches 100,000 active registered qualified patients, and then upon each further instance of the total active registered qualified patients increasing by 100,000, the statewide maximum number of dispensing facilities that each licensed medical marijuana treatment center may establish and operate increases by five.” — 2017 text, https://flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2017/0381.986 — Accessed 2026-10-24; 2017A bill summary, https://FLSenate.gov/Committees/BillSummaries/2017A/html/8 — Accessed 2026-10-24.

Regional allocation was also in the original scheme: each MMTC's regional maximum = (region's share of statewide population) × its statewide maximum, rounded, using Florida Estimates of Population 2016, recalculated after each Decennial Census; an MMTC could sell an unused regional slot to another MMTC (2017A summary, same source).

Critical caveat — the cap as written cannot be the current operative cap. The 2017A Senate summary states: “These limitations on dispensing facilities expire on April 1, 2020.” (same source). And the observed market contradicts any 25+5-per-100,000 cap today: at ~940,000 patients that formula would give 25 + (9 × 5) = 70 per MMTC, yet OMMU's own 28 August 2026 table shows Trulieve at 170 locations, MÜV at 86, Curaleaf Florida at 76 (see §5.3). Therefore: do NOT present “25 + 5 per 100,000” as a current cap. The current dispensing-location rule after the 1 April 2020 expiry — whether the cap was repealed, replaced, or simply lapsed, and what, if anything, now limits locations per MMTC — is [VERIFY] against the current-year § 381.986(8)(a)5. text on Online Sunshine. For this Part, the safe statement is: no per-MMTC dispensing-location cap is evidenced in the current OMMU data; individual MMTCs operate well above the expired 2017 formula, and each new location still requires department dispensing authorisation/approval (OMMU weekly “locations approved” listings).

4.1.7 — Legal challenges

  • Florida Department of Health v. Florigrown, LLC, per curiam (all seven justices concurred on vertical integration and licence-number limits; Justice Lawson dissented only on special-privileges/special-laws — “6–1” only as shorthand for that third point) [Audit correction], 27 May 2021 (Fla.). The Florida Supreme Court rejected Florigrown's constitutional challenge to vertical integration and to the licence caps, holding Florigrown had “not demonstrated a substantial likelihood of success on the merits” and reversing the temporary injunction that had frozen licensing. Effect: the vertically integrated, capped model survived. — Secondary summaries: GrayRobinson/Cannabis Law Journal, https://journal.cannabislawreport.com/gray-robinson-the-florida-supreme-court-rejects-florigrowns-consitutional-challenge-to-the-states-vertical-licensure-system-for-medical-marijuana/ — Accessed 2026-10-24; Florida Weekly, https://www.floridaweekly.com/articles/fort-myers-arts-and-entertainment-news/fort-myers/florida-justices-reject-challenge-to-medical-marijuana-law-2/ — Accessed 2026-10-24.
