4.2 — Certified Marijuana Testing Laboratory (CMTL) licences

4.2.1 — Basis

  • Statute: § 381.988, Fla. Stat. — http://flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2020/381.988 — Accessed 2026-10-24. Definition in § 381.986(1): “‘Marijuana testing laboratory’ means a facility that collects and analyzes marijuana samples from a medical marijuana treatment center and has been certified by the department pursuant to s. 381.988.” — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • What it allows: A CMTL collects and analyses marijuana samples from MMTCs; MMTCs must test processed marijuana using a marijuana testing laboratory before dispensing, with results verified and signed by two MMTC employees (§ 381.986(8)(e)10.d. area, Accessed 2026-10-24). A CMTL is independent: it may not be owned or controlled by an MMTC (see §4.2.2).
  • No other independent marijuana licence exists. In particular, there is no standalone “processor”, “transporter” or “retailer” testing-lab-adjacent licence; testing is the sole carve-out from vertical integration.

4.2.2 — Certification requirements (from § 381.988 and the OMMU application form, as retrieved)

From the OMMU “Application for Marijuana Testing Laboratory Certification” (draft form, 3 Apr 2019, hosted on knowthefactsmmj.com — https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/DRAFT-2019-04-03-Rule-64-4.016-MTL-Application-Certification-and-Renewal.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24):

“A marijuana testing laboratory or an applicant for certification who has received written notification from the department that its application for certification or application for renewal as a marijuana testing laboratory has been found to be in compliance with the provisions of sections 381.986 and 381.988, F.S., and department rules. Notification may only be provided by the department after the following requirements have been met: (1) A marijuana testing laboratory submitted a completed application accompanied by an application fee; (2) A marijuana testing laboratory is not owned or controlled by a medical marijuana treatment center; (3) A marijuana testing laboratory submitted proof of an accreditation or a certification; (4) All owners and managers of a marijuana testing laboratory have submitted and passed a level 2 background screening pursuant to section 381.988(1)(d), Florida Statutes; and (5) A marijuana testing laboratory demonstrated to the department the capability of meeting the standards for certification.”

From § 381.988 (Accessed 2026-10-24): - DOH must adopt rules for initial certification and biennial renewal, including initial application and biennial renewal fees “sufficient to cover the costs of administering this certification program”, and must renew biennially if the lab meets the requirements and pays the fee. - Certification standards rules must cover, at minimum: security standards; minimum personnel standards; sample collection method/process standards; proficiency testing for THC potency, CBD concentration, and contaminants unsafe for human consumption as determined by rule; reporting content/format/frequency; audits and onsite inspections; quality assurance; equipment and methodology; chain of custody; and any other standard DOH deems necessary for public health/safety. FDACS and DEP assist in developing the rule. - A CMTL must adhere to §§ 381.986(8)(d), (8)(e)10.d., (8)(g) and 381.988, department rules, and representations in its initial application; it may seek a variance/waiver from application representations under § 120.542 (OMMU form, above).

Fees, current rule numbers, and the certified-lab list: [VERIFY] in part. The 2019 draft form is not a current rule; the current CMTL testing rules are in the proposed Rule 64-4.303 / 64-4.306 / 64-4.307 / 64-4.309 package (notice of correction, Florida Administrative Register Vol. 52 No. 159, 17 Aug 2026 — OMMU Notices, https://knowthefactsmmj.com/notices/ — Accessed 2026-10-24). The dollar amount of the CMTL application/renewal fee was not located in the sources opened — [UNAVAILABLE] in this Part; do not infer it from the MMTC fees. The count of certified labs is reported secondarily as 6 (CannBus Q3 2026, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/fl_cannmir.html — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary) and historically as 9 (Americanna announcement, Dec 2021, https://cannabisnewsflorida.com/current-issue/americanna-laboratories-receives-certified-marijuana-testing-laboratory-approval/ — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary). The two figures are from different years and are not directly comparable; the current OMMU CMTL directory/list was not opened directly and its current count and names are [VERIFY] (see Part 5, §5.2, item 3). Known CMTL names from secondary sources (not a verified current list): ACS Laboratory (Sun City Center), Americanna Laboratories (Jacksonville), ACT Laboratories of Florida (Davie), AccuScience (Eustis), Atlas Labs FL (Lakeland) — the latter four also appear on USDA's hemp-lab list, which is a different authorisation (see §5.2, item 9); do not conflate USDA hemp-lab registration with OMMU CMTL certification.

4.3 — Edibles, processing and other endorsements / approvals MMTCs need

There is no separate “edibles licence” or “processing licence” in Florida. Processing is inside the MMTC licence; edibles require an additional food-establishment permit plus a GMP inspection. This is the only true “endorsement-like” approval for MMTCs located in this Part.

Approval Requirement Source
FDACS food-establishment permit for edibles (per physical location) § 381.986(8)(e)8.: “A medical marijuana treatment center that produces edibles must hold a permit to operate as a food establishment pursuant to chapter 500, the Florida Food Safety Act, and must comply with all the requirements for food establishments pursuant to chapter 500 and any rules adopted thereunder.” Edibles limits in the same paragraph: ≤200 mg THC per edible package, ≤10 mg THC per single serving, potency variance ≤15%; not attractive to children; not human/cartoon/animal-shaped; not resembling commercially available candy; no colour additives. MMTCs could not begin processing/dispensing edibles until the effective date of the department's rule. https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._381.986 — Accessed 2026-10-24.
FDACS Rule Ch. 5K-11 (MMTCs and Edibles), R. 5K-11.002 (1) MMTCs producing/manufacturing edibles must be permitted as food establishments under Ch. 500 and Ch. 5K-11. (3) Before producing edibles, the MMTC must: (a) file Form FDACS-14031 (Rev. 12/19), Medical Marijuana Treatment Center Food Permit Application; (b) pay the permit fee in subsection (6); (c) list all edibles it intends to produce; (d) pass an initial FDACS inspection under Ch. 500, R. 5K-4.002 and R. 5K-4.004. (4) Renew annually (except initial inspection). (6) Fees: initial Jan–June $650 + epidemiology fee (§ 381.006(10)); initial July–Dec $325 + epidemiology fee; renewal $650 + epidemiology fee; late fee $100. (7) A permit is required per physical location/address; an MMTC may produce edibles at more than one location with a permit for each. (8) Not transferable — a new food permit is required before manufacturing at a new location or after a change in ownership. Changes/additions to food products must be notified in writing to FDACS before implementation. R. 5K-11.002 — http://flrules.elaws.us/fac/5k-11.002 and https://regulations.justia.com/states/florida/5/5k/chapter-5k-11/section-5k-11-002/ — Accessed 2026-10-24. Form FDACS-14031: http://forms.fdacs.gov/14031.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24.
Food Safety GMP inspection (processing facilities) § 381.986(8)(e)9.: “Within 12 months after licensure, a medical marijuana treatment center must demonstrate to the department that all of its processing facilities have passed a Food Safety Good Manufacturing Practices, such as Global Food Safety Initiative or equivalent, inspection by a nationally accredited certifying body. A medical marijuana treatment center must immediately stop processing at any facility which fails to pass this inspection until it demonstrates… such facility has met this requirement.” https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._381.986 — Accessed 2026-10-24.
Cultivation / processing / dispensing authorisations (staged) Three staged authorisations within the MMTC licence (see §4.0). New September 2026 licensees: cultivation request within 180 days, processing within 270 days, dispensing within 365 days (secondary; rule cited as 64-4.216 — [VERIFY]). OMMU Weekly Update 28 Aug 2026 (stages) — Accessed 2026-10-24; Vicente LLP / Catalyst BC (deadlines) — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary).
Low-THC product availability duty Each MMTC “must produce and make available for purchase at least one low-THC cannabis product” (§ 381.986(8)(e) area, Accessed 2026-10-24). This is a product duty, not a separate licence. Same source.
Preroll paper rule An MMTC producing prerolled marijuana cigarettes “may not use wrapping paper made with tobacco or hemp” (§ 381.986(8)(e)10., Accessed 2026-10-24). Same source.
No other endorsements located No separate “concentrates”, “vape”, “topical”, “delivery-only” or “wholesale” endorsement exists in § 381.986 as retrieved. Delivery is within the MMTC licence (approved locations + delivery). Any rule-level product authorisation beyond edibles/GMP/staged authorisations is [VERIFY] against Ch. 64-4. —

Hemp-side permits are NOT MMTC endorsements. FDACS hemp cultivation licences and hemp food-establishment permits (Ch. 500 / R. 5K-4.034 area; $650/year per establishment for hemp food establishments in secondary summaries) are separate hemp authorisations, covered in Run 2 Part 7 and inventoried as data sources in §5.2 below. An MMTC does not need a hemp licence to sell medical marijuana, and a hemp permit does not authorise marijuana sales.

4.4 — Adult-use licence types: PROPOSED ONLY — none enacted, none in force

Current position (Accessed 2026-10-24): Florida has NO adult-use licence type, enacted or in force. Medical-only.

  • 2024 Amendment 3 — FAILED. On 5 November 2024, Amendment 3 (Marijuana Legalization Initiative) received 5,950,589 Yes (55.90%) to 4,693,524 No (44.10%) and was defeated because citizen-initiated constitutional amendments require 60% (Art. XI, § 5(e)). It would have allowed adults 21+ to possess up to 3 oz (5 g concentrate) and would have authorised existing MMTCs to sell for personal use, with the Legislature able to license other entities. Because it failed, no adult-use licence type was created and no MMTC “conversion” occurred. — Ballotpedia (secondary compilation of certified results), https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_Amendment_3,Marijuana_Legalization_Initiative(2024) — Accessed 2026-10-24; LegalClarity summary, https://legalclarity.org/florida-amendment-3-what-you-need-to-know/ — Accessed 2026-10-24. Official Division of Elections canvass [VERIFY] for the final certified numbers before quoting them in the combined dossier.
  • 2026 adult-use initiative — DID NOT QUALIFY for the November 2026 ballot. The Department of State posted that all 22 active initiative petitions failed to meet Florida law for placement on the 2026 General Election ballot, including recreational marijuana. Smart & Safe Florida's follow-up (initiative 25-01, “Adult Personal Use of Marijuana”) is reported as dismissed on Florida Supreme Court review on 4 February 2026, with the Division of Elections listing its election year as 2028 (secondary). No 2026 adult-use vote will occur; no 2026 adult-use licences exist. — WJXT/News4JAX, 2 Feb 2026 (via CDN copy), https://gmg-wjxt-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/news/florida/2026/02/02/22-initiative-based-proposals-fail-to-meet-florida-requirements-for-placement-on-2026-ballot-department-of-state-says/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary); Catalyst BC (above, secondary, for the 4 Feb 2026 dismissal / 2028 listing); TC Sentinel, 21 Oct 2026, https://www.tcsentinel.com/recreational-marijuana-will-not-appear-on-florida-s-november-ballot.html — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary). Division of Elections initiative page itself was not opened directly — [VERIFY].
  • 2028 initiatives — PROPOSED ONLY, not law. As of September–October 2026 secondary reporting, three 2028-oriented proposals are in early initiative stages: Smart & Safe Florida's 2028 proposal (must restart ~880,000-signature collection); Floridians for Marijuana (approved 30 Sept 2026, per Cannabis Business Times); Let Florida Vote IV (pending with the Financial Impact Estimating Conference as of 29 Sept 2026). None has qualified for a ballot, none has passed, and none creates any licence type today. Their proposed licence structures (e.g. whether non-MMTC entities could be licensed, and one proposal's “reasonable, objective qualifications” / fee-limit language) are proposals only and must not be described as enacted licence types. — Cannabis Business Times, https://www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/us-states/florida/news/15836634/florida-may-have-3-options-to-legalize-adultuse-cannabis-in-2028 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary); Beard Bros, https://beardbrospharms.com/articles/floridas-next-recreational-marijuana-fight-two-new-amendments-aim-for-2028/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary).
  • No legislative adult-use implementation plan is in force, because no ballot measure passed. Any future implementing law would be needed after a successful amendment; none exists to inventory. If a future amendment passes, the federal baseline in the task brief applies: that adult-use activity would remain Schedule I and fully subject to §280E, unlike MMTC medical activity.
  • What this means for Part 4's licence table: the complete enacted marijuana licence inventory for Florida is: (1) MMTC licence, (2) CMTL certification. Plus, as a permit (not a marijuana licence): FDACS food-establishment permit for MMTC edibles. Nothing else.

4.5 — Social equity, minority and small-business provisions

Florida has no general social-equity programme, no social-equity licence category, no fee waiver/reduction programme for minority or small businesses, and no small-business / microbusiness / craft licence type in § 381.986 as retrieved. What exists is narrow and specific:

4.5.1 — The Pigford / Black Farmers Litigation licence(s)

  • Original 2017 provision. § 381.986(8)(a)2.b.: “As soon as practicable, the department shall license one applicant that is a recognized class member of Pigford v. Glickman, 185 F.R.D. 82 (D.D.C. 1999), or In Re Black Farmers Litig., 856 F. Supp. 2d 1 (D.D.C. 2011). An applicant licensed under this sub-subparagraph is exempt from the requirement of subparagraph (b)2. [the FDACS nursery-certificate requirement]. An applicant that applies for licensure under this sub-subparagraph, pays its initial application fee, is determined by the department through the application process to qualify as a recognized class member, and is not awarded a license under this sub-subparagraph may transfer its initial application fee to one subsequent opportunity to apply for licensure under subparagraph 4.” — https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._381.986 — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • 2022 cycle and 2023 expansion (HB 387, Ch. 2023-292, Laws of Florida — cited secondarily). DOH opened Pigford applications in March 2022; 12 applicants; $146,000 fee; intent to award to Terry Donnell Gwinn announced, then challenged by other applicants. HB 387 (signed June 2023) required DOH to approve licences for all qualified applicants and gave deficient applicants a 90-day cure period. Result in July 2023: two licences — Terry Donnell Gwinn and Shedrick McGriff — taking the state to 24 licensed operators at that time (secondary reporting). Gwinn's cultivation was reported at an Alachua County facility; both had to seek cultivation authorisation within two months (secondary). — Southeast AgNet, 24 July 2023, https://southeastagnet.com/2023/07/24/two-florida-black-farmers-marijuana-licenses/ — Accessed 2026-10-24; Cannabis Query summary, https://cannabisquery.com/uncategorized/florida-grants-medical-marijuana-licenses-to-black-farmers-in-landmark-bill-signed-by-governor-desantis/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary). HB 387 chapter number and effective date [VERIFY] against flsenate.gov.
  • 2024 expansion (SB 1582, Department of Health bill, signed June 2024). SB 1582 added provision for at least three further Black-farmer applicants who had been deemed ineligible, bringing the potential total of Pigford-earmarked licences to six. One of the three was reported as the family of Moton Hopkins (deceased; courts had deemed the family ineligible to receive the licence in his place). — CLTampa / News Service of Florida, https://www.cltampa.com/news/florida-lawmakers-sign-off-on-expanding-medical-marijuana-licenses-for-black-farmers-17469336 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary); MJBizDaily, 19 Mar 2024, https://mjbizdaily.com/florida-bill-aims-to-award-medical-cannabis-licenses-to-3-black-farmers/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary); MJBizDaily follow-up, https://mjbizdaily.com/news/florida-to-license-more-black-marijuana-farmers-adult-use-campaign-finances/392141/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary). Whether the three SB 1582 licences were actually issued, to whom, and when, is [VERIFY] — secondary summaries conflict in framing (“can award” vs “will award”), and Catalyst BC's summary states OMMU's MMTC list shows five licences issued to Pigford-cycle applicants from 2023 to 2025 (secondary, https://catalyst-bc.com/florida-cannabis-licensing-opportunities/ — Accessed 2026-10-24). The OMMU 28 August 2026 table itself shows three “n/a” rows — Magic Mortgage Corp., Inc.; Leola Robinson; Moton Hopkins Jr. — with 0 locations and 0 dispensations (see §5.3). Those three names are consistent with Pigford-cycle licensees not yet dispensing, but OMMU does not label them as Pigford licensees in the weekly table, so that identification is inference, not an OMMU statement — [VERIFY] against the OMMU MMTC list / DOH orders. Do not assert the three n/a rows are the SB 1582 licensees without that check.
  • Fee-transfer survival. Proposed Rule 64-4.214 “maintains a provision allowing certain applicants from the earlier Pigford/Black Farmers Litigation licensing cycle to request a transfer of their previously paid application fee” (Marijuana Herald, 12 Sept 2026, secondary, above), and Emergency Rule 64ER22-9(4) already provided that transfer mechanism via Form 6 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/florida/Fla-Admin-Code-Ann-R-64ER22-9 — Accessed 2026-10-24).

4.5.2 — Diversity plan (all applicants) and citrus preference (2017 tranche only)

  • Diversity plan: every MMTC applicant must have a diversity plan (see §4.1.2, item 10); DOH “shall identify applicants with strong diversity plans” and implement training/educational programmes to enable minority and veteran businesses to compete (§ 381.986(8)(b)). This is a scoring/identification duty, not a set-aside, quota, fee reduction, or separate licence category. Renewal requires proof of effectiveness (workforce representation, recruitment efforts, contracts record).
  • Citrus preference (2017 only): for up to two of the 10 licences under (8)(a)2., preference to applicants owning/converting a citrus canning/concentrating/processing facility (§ 381.986(8)(a)3.). This was a one-tranche preference, not an ongoing social-equity programme.
  • No veteran-specific licence, no minority set-aside beyond Pigford, no fee waiver: secondary summaries confirm “Though license-capped Florida has no social equity program designed to encourage minority participation” (MJBizDaily, above) and “There are no fee waivers or reductions for Black American entrepreneurs” except the Pigford fee-transfer provision (DocMJ summary, https://docmj.com/three-black-americans-will-get-a-florida-cannabis-business-license/ — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary). Treat those as secondary characterisations consistent with the statute text retrieved, not as statutory quotes.

4.6 — Estimated startup costs and reported licence sale prices (NON-OFFICIAL — secondary only)

No official Florida startup-cost schedule exists. The figures below are non-official estimates / asking prices from dated secondary sources and must not be presented as state figures.

Figure Value and date Source (secondary)
MMTC licence asking price, late 2021 (historical peak) “Tens of millions of dollars”; “more than $50 million eight years ago” (i.e. ~2018, per Politico via MJBizDaily) MJBizDaily, Oct 2026, https://mjbizdaily.com/news/are-florida-medical-cannabis-operators-looking-to-exit-the-2-billion-market/618258/ — Accessed 2026-10-24; MJBizDaily marketing-rules article, https://mjbizdaily.com/news/florida-moves-to-ban-celebrity-endorsements-in-mmj-marketing-revamp/617915/ — Accessed 2026-10-24.
MMTC licence asking price, September–October 2026 (post-22-licence order) ~$3 million–$4 million (420 Property listings; “about $4 million… license only”); one 420 Property listing for a September 2026 MMTC at $999,000 asking (published 6 Oct 2026, updated 15 Oct 2026); another at $2.85 million (leasehold footprint included) MJBizDaily (above, Oct 2026); 420 Property listing #2118, https://www.420property.com/listing/rare-florida-mmtc-license-with-approved-letter-from-september-of-2026-fully-vertical-unlimited-dispensary-capabilities-florida-usa-2118/ — Accessed 2026-10-24; 420 Property listing #2015, https://www.420property.com/listing/rare-florida-mmtc-license-platform-with-secured-leasehold-footprint-fully-vertical-development-ready-opportunity-florida-usa-2015/ — Accessed 2026-10-24. Asking prices are not sale prices; no completed-sale price was verified in the sources opened. The NY420Week claim that “the last bare licence traded at $9 million, down from $55 million” (22 Sept 2026, https://newyork420week.com/articles/florida-just-issued-22-cannabis-licences-worth-a-fraction-of-what-they-used-to-be — Accessed 2026-10-24) is unverified single-source secondary and conflicts with the $3–4m asking range — [VERIFY] before quoting any “traded” price.
New-operator build-out to first sale, 2026 “Up to $30 million in startup costs to build MMTCs, factories and grow facilities” (Politico via MJBizDaily) MJBizDaily marketing-rules article (above). Non-official estimate.
Generic “open a dispensary in Florida” estimate, 2026 “Several million dollars to over $10 million, depending on licensing, facility setup, security, and operational requirements” IndicaOnline, https://indicaonline.com/blog/how-to-open-a-dispensary-in-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary, marketing content — low weight).
Official costs that are fixed (for a startup budget build-up) $146,000 application (non-refundable, per cycle) + $5m bond / $2m if ≥1,000 patients (assurance, premium unpublished) + biennial renewal by formula (~$1.34m for 2025–2026 cohort, secondary) + FDACS edibles food permit $650/year per location (+ epidemiology fee) if producing edibles + nursery-certificate / 5-year entity history (sunk cost, not a fee) See §4.1.3 for official sources. Any total “startup cost” built from these plus facilities/staff/inventory is an estimate, not an official figure.

Why prices fell (secondary explanation, not a finding of this Part): MJBizDaily (Oct 2026, above) attributes the exit wave to the September 2026 bond deadline (25 Sept 2026), investor groups from 2023 no longer willing to fund projects, and post-Amendment-3-failure growth scepticism. That causal account is secondary and is noted here only to explain why asking prices and sale prices must not be conflated.

PART 5 — LICENCE DATA SOURCES

Instruction complied with: No attempt is made below to list every licence holder. This is an inventory of sources, with access/format/update/fields/limitations for each, plus the official counts that those sources themselves publish (by MMTC, from the OMMU weekly table). Where a source has no download, that is stated plainly. Where a direct download link was verified by opening it, it is given verbatim; where a link was only returned in search results, it is given as returned and marked as not directly opened where applicable.

5.1 — How to read this inventory

  • “Download” means a file (PDF/CSV/XLSX) with a stable URL that can be saved.
  • “Search / interactive, no download” means the source is a web search or dashboard; any export button is noted if one is known. Absence of a noted export button does not prove none exists — the page was not interactively tested (this research used text fetch/search only; live-browser clicking was not available to this subagent).
  • “Latest data date” is the date on the data itself (e.g. the weekly update's coverage week), not the date the page was crawled.
  • OMMU is the authoritative source for MMTC counts. Secondary aggregations (CannBus, Catalyst BC, news) are used only where OMMU's own file was not opened, and are marked secondary.

5.2 — Source-by-source inventory

5.2.1 — OMMU Weekly Updates (the master periodic source)

Weekly PDFs live under https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/ommu_updates/<YYYY>/<MMDDYY>-OMMU-Update.pdf (pattern evidenced by opened files; the index page listing all weeks was not opened directly — [VERIFY] the current index URL).
Exact direct download link + file name (verified by opening) https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/ommu_updates/2026/082826-OMMU-Update.pdf — file name 082826-OMMU-Update.pdf — opened directly and read in full for this Part — Accessed 2026-10-24. Other weekly files returned in search (not directly opened for this Part): https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/0919025-OMMU-Update.pdf (19 Sept 2025); https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/102425-OMMU-Update.pdf (24 Oct 2025); https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/ommu_updates/2026/061926-OMMU-Update.pdf (19 June 2026); https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/ommu_updates/2025/121925-OMMU-Update.pdf (19 Dec 2025, via staging mirror in search — use the knowthefactsmmj.com URL, not the staging host).

Plus: qualified patients (active ID card count), complete-application processing time (5 business days), ID-card printing time (5 business days), weekly newly approved dispensing locations (MMTC + city). 5.2.6 — Licensing actions, administrative complaints, inspections and final orders

Field Detail
Holder type MMTCs (and, via DOH generally, qualified physicians / CMTLs).
Statutory basis § 381.986(10): DOH “shall conduct announced or unannounced inspections”, “shall conduct at least a biennial inspection of each medical marijuana treatment center”, and “may impose reasonable fines not to exceed $10,000 on a medical marijuana treatment center” for listed violations (violating § 381.986 or rule; failing to maintain qualifications; endangering health/safety/security; improper disclosure; procuring approval by bribery/fraud/extortion). — https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._381.986 — Accessed 2026-10-24. Complaint portal (patients/consumers): Complaint-Portal.MQA.FLHealthSource.gov (cited in weekly PDFs).
Where actions are published — NO single OMMU enforcement list was located OMMU does not publish, in the sources opened, a searchable list of MMTC administrative complaints, fines, suspensions or revocations. Enforcement records must be found via: (a) DOAH central final-orders database — agencies must transmit final orders rendered on/after 1 July 2015 to DOAH under § 120.53 (R. 1B-32.003 — https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/florida/regulations/florida_regulations_1b-32-003 — Accessed 2026-10-24; UF LibGuide, https://guides.law.ufl.edu/floridaadminlaw/orders — Accessed 2026-10-24); DOAH case search covers cases from 1975+, searchable by agency/division/case suffix, with PDFs of filed documents in many cases; (b) DOH Agency Clerk / final orders (search DOAH's agency-orders database for “Department of Health” + MMTC name); (c) DOAH recommended orders for licence challenges (e.g. Case No. 25-1076 for the 2023 cycle, cited secondarily).
Format DOAH: interactive search + PDF orders. No CSV/XLSX. No OMMU bulk enforcement download evidenced.
Update frequency / latest data date DOAH: orders must be transmitted within 90 days of being rendered (R. 1B-32.003). No MMTC-specific enforcement count was compiled for this Part — [UNAVAILABLE] as a dataset; individual cases must be searched by MMTC name.
Limitations Searching DOAH requires knowing the MMTC legal name (not just its trade name in the weekly table) and the correct agency filter; inspection reports themselves (as opposed to final orders) are not in DOAH and were not located as a public OMMU dataset. Do not assert any MMTC has or has not been disciplined without a DOAH/DOH search for that entity.

5.2.11 — Local (county/city) business tax receipt / permit records

Field Detail
Holder type Businesses (including dispensaries and hemp/CBD/smoke shops) holding a local business tax receipt (formerly occupational licence) or local permit, where the jurisdiction publishes records.
What was verified No statewide local-receipt dataset exists, and no specific county/city MMTC/hemp receipt database was verified as a holder list in the sources opened for this Part. Local receipt records are jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction (county tax collector / city clerk / business-tax portals), generally searchable by business name/address only, and they record tax-receipt status, not state licence status. A local receipt does not prove an MMTC licence, and absence from a local portal does not prove absence of a state licence (e.g. delivery-only presence, or a facility in an unincorporated area).
Format / access Varies by jurisdiction: interactive search portals (most), PDF lists (some), in-person records (some). No bulk download standard.
Limitations / follow-up For the combined dossier, Part 3 (local rules) should name the jurisdictions checked and, for each, whether a searchable receipt portal exists. That check was not done for this Part (outside Parts 4–5 scope except as a data-source inventory) — listed as a gap (G-12). The one local record actually seen (Columbia County permit-search copy of a hemp cultivation licence, §5.2.7) shows that county permit-search systems can incidentally surface state licences filed locally, but that is not a systematic source.

5.3 — Total licence and dispensary counts by MMTC (official figures, dated)

5.3.1 — Directly opened official source: OMMU Weekly Update, 28 August 2026

Part 6 — Market Data

FLORIDA — Cannabis & Hemp Research, Run 1, PART 6 ONLY: MARKET DATA

Scope note: This file covers Part 6 only (market data) for the Florida Run 1 dossier. It does not cover Parts 0–5 or 7–12. All facts accessed 2026-10-24 unless a different publication date is stated. Federal baseline applied as fixed context (not re-researched): state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity and remains fully applicable to adult-use; there is no federal cannabis banking law. No contradiction with that baseline was found in the Part 6 sources below. Florida has no adult-use retail market, so every dollar figure in this part is either a medical-market estimate or a hemp-market estimate — never an official adult-use sales total.

How to read the numbers — the single most important caveat in this part: Florida does not publish dollar sales for medical marijuana. The Office of Medical Marijuana Use (OMMU), Florida Department of Health, publishes weekly volumes — milligrams of THC dispensed, milligrams of low-THC (CBD) cannabis dispensed, and ounces of marijuana in a form for smoking — by MMTC, plus patient and dispensing-location counts. It does not publish annual or monthly dispensing totals, dollar sales, prices, or product-type splits in those weekly reports. Every dollar figure below is therefore a secondary, modelled estimate (Headset, BDSA or Brightfield Group via trade press), and the competing estimates disagree. They are labelled as such and must not be quoted as official Florida figures.

Official source hub: OMMU weekly updates are posted at KnowTheFactsMMJ.com (the Department of Health's OMMU site). The official October 9, 2026 weekly update PDF was opened and read directly for this part (see §6.1).

6.1 Medical dispensing volumes — official OMMU weekly data

6.1.1 What OMMU reports, and what it does not

  • OMMU publishes a weekly update every Friday containing: (A) number of qualified patients with an active ID card; (B) physician information (see §6.2 — the physician count is no longer shown in 2026 reports); (C) newly approved MMTC dispensing locations; (D) weekly MMTC dispensation amounts by operator; (E) weekly total dispensation amounts. Source: OMMU Annual Report 2026 description of the Weekly Update, via KnowTheFactsMMJ.com — [STAGING URL REMOVED in Audit — replace with the live KnowTheFactsMMJ.com annual-report URL once located; do not cite the staging URL as the official hub] — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Medical marijuana is dispensed in milligrams of THC; low-THC cannabis is dispensed in milligrams of CBD; smokable marijuana is reported separately in ounces. Source: OMMU Weekly Update, 9 October 2026, p. 1 — https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/ommu_updates/2026/100926-OMMU-Update.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • OMMU does not publish annual or monthly dispensing totals in these reports, and does not publish dollar sales. Source: CannBus, Florida Cannabis Market Intelligence Report Q3 2026, §3 ("OMMU does not publish annual or monthly dispensing totals in these reports") — https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/fl_cannmir.html — Accessed 2026-10-24. Year-to-date totals quoted below are sums of weekly figures as compiled and reported by The Marijuana Herald, not totals published by OMMU itself.

Trend reading (official counts only): Patient growth has slowed sharply from the double-digit annual increases of the years after Amendment 2 (2016). Calendar 2025 growth was +3.9% (895,469 on 3 January 2025 → 930,226 on 2 January 2026, CannBus calculation). Dispensary locations grew faster than patients over the same year (+5.0% September-to-September on the Tallahassee Democrat comparison; 702 on 3 January 2025 → 781 on 25 September 2026, +11.3%, CannBus calculation). Patients are ≈ 4.9% of Florida adults on CannBus's calculation (941,616 ÷ 19.03 million adults) — derived, not official. Processing times stated in the 9 October 2026 OMMU update: 5 business days for a complete application, 5 business days for ID card printing. 6.6 Hemp market figures — official first, secondary marked

6.6.1 The headline finding: Florida's licensed hemp cultivation is tiny, and approved acres vastly exceed planted acres

Florida's hemp story in market terms is a story of collapse in field cultivation alongside a large, separately regulated retail market in hemp-derived products (delta-8, delta-9, THCA and CBD products sold through smoke shops and other retailers — regulated under § 581.217 and FDACS food-establishment rules, covered in Parts 1 and 7). No official Florida figure for hemp retail sales, hemp product sales, or the size of the hemp-derived THC retail market was located. The often-quoted claim that Florida's hemp-derived cannabinoid market is "several times larger than its legal medical cannabis market" is a secondary analyst quote (cannabis economist Beau Whitney, via MJBizDaily, September 2026), not a measured total. Source: MJBizDaily, September 2026 — https://mjbizdaily.com/news/are-florida-medical-cannabis-operators-looking-to-exit-the-2-billion-market/618258/ — Accessed 2026-10-24. Treat any hemp retail total as [UNAVAILABLE] unless Run 2 locates a measured source.

6.9 Key takeaways for Part 6

  1. Florida is a volume market without a dollar market, officially. Everything official is in milligrams and ounces: ≈ 427 million mg THC and ≈ 148,500 oz smokable in a typical October 2026 week; 18.06 billion mg THC and 6.22 million oz smokable year-to-date through 22 October 2026 (sums of weekly reports). Dollar sales (≈ $1.65B for 2025 on Headset) are modelled estimates that disagree across trackers.
  2. Growth has matured into flatness. Patients +1.8% year-on-year to a record 943,271 (23 October 2026); THC volume −0.6% year-on-year in late September; smokable flower still growing (+5.7% to +8.6% depending on the September week compared). Locations (+5.0% year-on-year) are growing faster than patients.
  3. Concentration is high and unit-dependent. Trulieve: 21.7% of locations, ≈ 26–27% of THC milligrams, ≈ 33–34% of smokable ounces. Top four by locations: ≈ 51% of locations, ≈ 58% of THC volume. No official dollar shares exist.
  4. Field hemp has effectively collapsed while hemp retail is unmeasured. Planted hemp fell from 271–300 acres (2020–2021) to 29 acres (2025); utilised floral value from $4.37M to ≈ $1.2M. No official hemp retail sales total exists to set against the medical market.
  5. Banking is thin and narrowing on paper. Two verified Florida programmes (USF Credit Union Verde; Cogent Bank) plus one remote programme (Safe Harbor); Verde's own current page no longer claims plant-touching coverage that Florida Trend reported in July 2026 — the single most important banking item to re-verify.
  6. The Florida event calendar is medical/research-led, not trade-led. FMCCE (Orlando, May), CCORC (Lake Nona, November) and Alternative Products Expo (Miami, March) are the verified B2B/research anchors; Benzinga Miami and NECANN Florida are not verified as 2026 events.

PART 7 — HEMP LICENCES

7.0 The shape of Florida hemp licensing in one paragraph

Florida does not have a single "hemp licence" that covers everything, and it does not have separate hemp processor, distributor, or retailer licences. There are exactly two FDACS authorisations that do the work, plus two ancillary registrations/agreements and one legacy pilot route:

  1. License to Cultivate Hemp (FDACS Division of Plant Industry, §581.217 + Rule 5B-57.014) — the ONLY authorisation to plant, grow and harvest hemp in Florida.
  2. Hemp Food Establishment permit (FDACS Division of Food Safety, Ch. 500 + Rules 5K-4.020 / 5K-4.034, $650/year) — the authorisation that covers extracting, manufacturing, processing, packing, holding, preparing, distributing and selling hemp extract intended for human consumption (ingestion or inhalation), at wholesale or retail. This one permit does the work that other states split across processor, distributor and retailer licences. There is no separate Florida "hemp processor licence", "hemp distributor licence" or "hemp retail licence" in statute or rule — see §7.4.
  3. Nursery registration (§581.031(21) + Rule 5B-57.014(7)) — an additional registration for nurseries propagating hemp plants for distribution, which must ALSO hold a cultivation licence.
  4. Designated Laboratory Compliance Agreement (FDACS-08121, Rev. 04/21, under Rule 5B-57.014(2)(d)) — the agreement a DEA-registered, ISO/IEC 17025-accredited lab must enter into with FDACS to conduct regulatory THC sampling/testing. This is a testing authorisation, not a licence to sell hemp.
  5. Industrial Hemp Pilot Project / Special Permit (§1004.4473 + Rule 5B-57.013) — the university pilot route (UF/IFAS, FAMU, and other eligible institutions). §581.217(13)(b) expressly provides that §581.217 "does not apply to a pilot project developed in accordance with 7 U.S.C. 5940 and s. 1004.4473". Whether FDACS still issues NEW pilot permits in 2026, as opposed to administering existing pilot sites, is [VERIFY] — see §7.5.

A business that both grows hemp AND makes/sells ingestible or inhalable hemp extract needs both authorisation 1 and authorisation 2, separately. A business that only sells hemp extract it did not grow still needs authorisation 2 for each establishment. A business that only sells non-ingestible, non-inhalable hemp products (e.g. topical CBD creams, hemp fibre, hemp seed foods that are FDA-GRAS and excluded from the "hemp extract" definition) does NOT need a hemp food establishment permit for that activity as such — but see §7.4.3 for the limits of that statement. A hemp cultivation licence does NOT authorise marijuana cultivation, and a hemp food permit does NOT authorise MMTC marijuana sales; the MMTC edibles food permit (Ch. 5K-11, Run 1 Part 4) is a different permit population under the same FDACS food-permit system and must not be merged with hemp food-permit counts.

7.2 Licence type 1 — License to Cultivate Hemp

Field Detail
What it allows Planting, watering, growing and harvesting hemp ("Cultivate" means "planting, watering, growing, or harvesting hemp", §581.217(3)(d)). It does NOT by itself authorise manufacturing, processing into, or selling hemp extract for human consumption — that needs a hemp food establishment permit (§7.3). It does NOT authorise marijuana cultivation.
Statute §581.217, Fla. Stat. Last amended 2023 (chs. 2023-154, 2023-299). History line as printed on Online Sunshine (opened directly): "History. — s. 1, ch. 2019-132; s. 5, ch. 2020-135; s. 26, ch. 2023-154; s. 2, ch. 2023-299." — https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0500-0599/0581/Sections/0581.217.html — Accessed 2026-10-24.

Code R. 5B-57.014, "State Hemp Program" — https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/florida/Fla-Admin-Code-Ann-R-5B-57-014 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (full rule opened directly, lines 1–800; Cornell LII mirror of the FAC text — the flrules.org original was not separately opened in this run, so rule history/amendment date is [VERIFY] against flrules.org).
Issuing authority FDACS Division of Plant Industry (DPI). Programme page: https://www.fdacs.gov/Divisions-Offices/Plant-Industry/Hemp-Cultivation-Licensing — Accessed 2026-10-24 (opened directly). Application portal: https://plant.fdacs.gov/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (linked from the FDACS programme page; also cited as https://www.hemp.fdacs.gov in the FDACS applicant checklist).
Core prohibition (verbatim, §581.217(5)(a)) "It is unlawful for a person to cultivate hemp in this state without a license issued by the department." Rule 5B-57.014(4) repeats: "It is unlawful for a Person to cultivate hemp in this state without a License to Cultivate Hemp issued by the Department."
Fee CONFLICT — no fee figure is adopted here [VERIFY]. The text of Rule 5B-57.014 opened in this run states no application or annual licence fee amount in the sections read (the licensee "shall be responsible for any fees or costs to conduct sampling or laboratory testing", 5B-57.014(8)(a)). Secondary sources conflict: LegalClarity (accessed via search, 2026) states "the license application itself carries no filing fee" with background-check/fingerprinting costs at the applicant's expense (reported $10–$100 depending on provider) — https://legalclarity.org/florida-hemp-license-application-and-requirements/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary); Cannabis Training University states "around $1,000 annually" / "Annual license fee: ~$1,000" — https://cannabistraininguniversity.com/jobs/hemp-license-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary). Neither figure is confirmed against an FDACS fee schedule in this run. Do NOT quote $1,000 as the FDACS fee, and do NOT quote $0 as confirmed, until the FDACS application form FDACS-08112 fee block or a DPI fee schedule is opened. Sampling/testing costs are in any event payable by the licensee.
Term / renewal 12 months from issuance. Rule 5B-57.014(5)(a) (verbatim): "A License to Cultivate Hemp expires twelve months after the date of issuance." Renewal (5)(b)–(c): on or before expiry the licensee must either renew or cease cultivation; renewal follows the application procedures in (4), except fingerprints need not be resubmitted for a person whose fingerprints were submitted for the licence being renewed. Statute §581.217(5)(c): "The department shall adopt rules establishing procedures for the issuance and annual renewal of a hemp license." This matches Run 1 Part 5's example (issued 9 Sept 2025, expiring 9 Sept 2026).
Transfer Not transferable. Rule 5B-57.014(5)(d) (verbatim): "A License to Cultivate Hemp is not transferable."
Application requirements (Rule 5B-57.014(4), opened directly) (a) Application form FDACS-08112 (12/19); (b) "A detailed description of each location intended for the cultivation of hemp, including address, legal land description, tax parcel number, and GPS coordinates" (statute §581.217(5)(d) likewise requires "the legal land description and global positioning coordinates of the area where hemp will be cultivated"); (c) "A full set of fingerprints for each Control person and the Responsible person submitted through a Livescan service provider evaluated by the [FDLE] for state and national processing to Department ORI number FL925080Z" (FDACS programme page confirms ORI FL925080Z is currently active and that fingerprinting must be conducted prior to issuance and renewal); (d) "An environmental containment plan for each Cultivation location" (silt fences / berms / fallow areas; equipment-cleaning plan; transport/movement plan ensuring propagative parts, live plants and plant material are covered and in full containment between noncontiguous locations). FDACS applicant checklist (PDF): https://ccmedia.fdacs.gov/content/download/91622/file/hemp-program-applicant-checklist.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24.
Disqualifiers (verbatim, §581.217(5)(e)) The department shall deny issuance or refuse renewal if it finds the applicant/licensee: "1. Has falsified any information contained in an application for a hemp license or hemp license renewal; or 2. Has been convicted of a felony relating to a controlled substance under state or federal law. A hemp license may not be issued for 10 years following the date of the conviction."
Seed requirement "A licensee may only use hemp seeds and cultivars certified by a certifying agency or a university conducting an industrial hemp pilot project pursuant to s. 1004.4473." (§581.217(6), verbatim). Rule 5B-57.014(6)(e): "Use only Certified hemp seed, Pilot project hemp cultivars, or Pilot project hemp seed as defined in Rule 5E-4.016, F.A.C., or nursery stock that was grown from Certified hemp seed, Pilot project hemp cultivars, or Pilot project hemp seed." Seed/cultivar and nursery-stock labels and receipts must be kept 3 years from harvest and produced on request (5B-57.014(6)(c)–(d)). No separate "hemp seed dealer licence" was verified in statute or rule in this run — the Immokalee property flyer in Part 8 claiming a "Hemp Seed Dealer license" is a broker's description, not a verified FDACS licence type, and is flagged as such in Part 8 [VERIFY].
Where hemp may be grown (Rule 5B-57.014(6)(f), verbatim, and FDACS programme page) "Only cultivate hemp on lands that are used primarily for bona fide agricultural purposes pursuant to Section 193.461, F.S., lands located within an area zoned for agricultural or industrial use, or at a nursery as defined in Section 581.011, F.S." FDACS programme page, "Land Zoning Requirements", quotes the same rule paragraph — Accessed 2026-10-24. This is the zoning test that matters for Part 8 hemp-suitable land: agricultural or industrial zoning (or a registered nursery), NOT general commercial/residential zoning.
Signage Rule 5B-57.014(6)(g): "Post signage at every Cultivation location access point which contains the following information: a contact phone number for the Responsible person and the following statement, 'Hemp is being cultivated under a license issued by the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services.'" (Phone numbers of individuals are not reproduced in this report; the rule's signage content requirement is stated, not the number itself.)
Testing (pre-harvest) Rule 5B-57.014(8)(a): "Within thirty (30) days prior to the harvest date, the Department or its agent shall collect a representative sample from each Lot to be tested for Total delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol concentration" under the Pre-Harvest Sampling Manual FDACS-08127 (Rev. 03/25). The licensee pays sampling/testing fees/costs and must be present at collection. Acceptable level = total delta-9 ≤0.3% dry weight (5B-57.014(2)(a)). Retest of the retained sample, confirmatory sampling/testing, and disposal are in 5B-57.014(8)(d)–(i) (see §7.2.1). FDACS "List of Approved Designated Laboratories for THC Testing", revised 8 September 2026 (FDACS Division of Plant Industry), is the current designated-lab list as located — the list itself was located via search return, not opened in full in this run, so lab names/counts are NOT stated here [VERIFY against the FDACS list]. Run 1 Part 5's USDA DEA-lab list for Florida (AccuScience Eustis, ACS Sun City Center, ACT Davie, Atlas Lakeland, Product Development Partners Tampa, US Pharma Miami Lakes) is a USDA list, not the FDACS designated list, and must not be substituted for it.
Harvest / movement / disposal Harvest notice ≥30 days before intended harvest (5B-57.014(9)(a)); no harvest until FDACS notifies an acceptable THC level, except the locked-storage early-harvest procedure in (9)(b). Intrastate movement between noncontiguous locations requires a fully enclosed vehicle/container, bill of lading / proof of ownership with originator licence number and lot, and stops at agricultural inspection stations (§570.15) (5B-57.014(11)(a)). Interstate movement INTO Florida of propagative parts/live plants, unprocessed and processed material is prohibited unless the stated conditions are met (soilless/sterile media + phytosanitary certificate + origin licence for live material; origin licence + acceptable-THC COA + frozen/dried transport for unprocessed; non-viable processing + origin licence + acceptable-THC COA for processed) (5B-57.014(11)(b)). Abandoned operations must destroy all material to non-viability under the Hemp Waste Disposal Manual FDACS-08115 before vacating (5B-57.014(12)).
Inspections / violations FDACS "shall conduct random inspections, at least annually, of each licensee" (§581.217(11)(d)); Rule 5B-57.014(10) random annual inspections. Negligent violations → corrective action plan, periodic reporting for at least 2 calendar years, 5-year ineligibility after a third negligent corrective-action-plan violation in 5 years (§581.217(10)(a)–(c); Rule 5B-57.014(13)). Culpable-mental-state-greater-than-negligence violations → immediate report to the Florida Attorney General and the U.S. Attorney General (§581.217(10)(d); Rule 5B-57.014(13)). After licence, FDACS also requires enrolment in Agricultural Best Management Practices (BMPs) via the Office of Agricultural Water Policy (FDACS programme page, "After You Apply" — Accessed 2026-10-24); BMP enrolment gives a presumption of compliance with water-quality standards and is required in Basin Management Action Plan areas as the alternative to water-quality monitoring.
Land registry / USDA reporting FDACS "shall maintain a registry of land on which hemp is cultivated or has been cultivated within the past 3 calendar years, including the global positioning coordinates and legal land description for each location" (§581.217(8)) and "shall submit monthly to the [USDA Secretary] a report of the locations in the state where hemp is cultivated or has been cultivated within the past 3 calendar years" with licensee contact information (§581.217(9)). This is a government land registry for enforcement/USDA reporting — it is NOT a public licensee directory (see §7.6).

7.2.1 What happens to a "hot" lot (over 0.3%)

Rule 5B-57.014(8)(d)–(i) (opened directly): on notice of an unacceptable THC level, the licensee must, within the stated windows, either (1) request retest of the retained sample (within 1 business day of notice, at licensee cost), or (2) arrange collection/destruction by a DEA-registered reverse distributor or duly authorised federal/state/local law-enforcement officer, or (3) dispose of the lot under the Hemp Waste Disposal Manual FDACS-08115 (Rev. 04/21 (FDACS-08121) / Rev. 03/25 (FDACS-08127) in the current Rule 5B-57.014 reference list), or (4) request a confirmatory sample/test (within 1 business day, to DPIHemp@FDACS.gov — an agency mailbox printed in the rule, not a personal address). If the confirmatory test also fails, the Plant Industry director (or designee) notifies the licensee, who must within 10 days arrange collection/destruction or manual disposal; if the licensee refuses or neglects to comply, FDACS may destroy the plants at the licensee's expense with no damages to the licensee. The licensee must notify FDACS within 1 business day of collection/destruction via Notice of Disposal FDACS-08116 (Rev. 04/21). Note: there is NO general "remediation" (re-testing after blending/reprocessing a hot lot back into compliance) in Rule 5B-57.014 as read — the options are retest/confirmatory test of the retained sample, or destruction/disposal. Do not import other states' remediation rules into Florida.

7.3 Licence/permit type 2 — Hemp Food Establishment permit

Field Detail
What it allows Extracting, manufacturing, processing, packing, holding, preparing, or selling hemp extract intended for human consumption (ingestion and/or inhalation), at wholesale or retail, from a permitted establishment. This is the single permit that covers what would be called "processing", "distribution" and "retail" in other states — see §7.4.
Definition (verbatim, Rule 5K-4.034(2)(f), opened directly) "'Hemp Food Establishment' means an establishment as defined in Section 500.03(1)(p), F.S., extracting, manufacturing, processing, packing, holding, preparing, or selling Hemp Extract intended for Human Consumption at wholesale or retail." "Human Consumption" (5K-4.034(2)(g)) "includes products intended for human Ingestion and/or human Inhalation but does not include topical applications." "Processor" or "Extractor" (5K-4.034(2)(k)) "means the establishment that removes the Hemp Extract oil from the Hemp plant" — a defined activity inside the food-establishment regime, NOT a separate licence type.
Statute Ch. 500 (Florida Food Safety Act), §500.12 (food permits); §581.217(7)(b)–(c), (e) (see §7.8 for verbatim distribution/retail-sale text). §581.217(7)(b) (verbatim): "Hemp extract may only be sold to a business in this state if that business is properly permitted as required by this section." §581.217(7)(c): "Hemp extract distributed or sold in this state is subject to the applicable requirements of chapter 500, chapter 502, or chapter 580."

The $5,000 figure is the Chapter 500 administrative-fine ceiling on the permit face, NOT a per-violation hemp fine schedule — do not conflate it with Run 1's MMTC $10,000 fine ceiling (§381.986(10)).
Term / renewal Annual. Permits state a "RENEW BY" date; renewal requires a renewal application and fees before expiry via https://foodpermit.fdacs.gov. FDACS wholesale page: "Each year, the food establishment owner is required to submit a renewal application and permit fees prior to the expiration of their food permit." Permits are issued only after application, successful inspection, and receipt of fees (same page).
Pre-permit requirements Waste disposal plan: Rule 5K-4.034(3) (older numbering, cited in Run 1 and in the rule's permit section as read via secondary reproductions) requires a Hemp Food Establishment to "submit to the Department a Waste disposal plan prior to manufacturing, processing, packing, holding, preparing, or selling Food constituting of or containing Hemp Extract" — the waste-disposal-plan paragraph number in the current LawServer text was not isolated in this run, so the requirement is stated as a rule requirement with its pinpoint [VERIFY] against the flrules.org current text. Approved Source: ingestion product must be manufactured by an "Approved Source" (an establishment meeting local/state/federal food-safety or health standards of its jurisdiction of origin), with valid food licence/permit and most recent inspection report producible on request (5K-4.034(4)(a)); inhalation product must be manufactured by a source permitted to manufacture for inhalation, with licence/permit and inspection report producible on request (5K-4.034(4)(b)).
Product / facility rules (Rule 5K-4.034(4)–(5), opened directly, summarised) Total delta-9 THC ≤0.3% (5K-4.034(4)(g): "Hemp Extract intended for Human Consumption shall not contain a Total delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol concentration of more than 0.3%", where "Total delta-9" = delta-9 + (0.877 x THCA) per (2)(m)); no manufacture/processing/packing/holding/preparation in a private home or living/sleeping room (4)(h); no vending-machine sale (4)(i); no Cottage Food Operations Law (§500.80) manufacture/processing/packing/holding/preparation/sale (4)(c); light-minimising, 21 C.F.R. Part 170-compliant containers (4)(e)–(f); potentially-hazardous / time-temperature-control foods stored per R. 5K-4.002 (4)(d); full contaminant limits for ingestion and inhalation (pesticides, residual solvents, metals, biologicals) in (5), including prohibited inhalation substances vitamin E acetate, 2,3-butanedione (diacetyl) and myclobutanil (5)(a), and myclobutanil prohibited at any concentration for inhalation (5)(b)46.
What the permit does NOT do It does not authorise cultivation (needs §7.2 licence); it does not authorise marijuana (MMTC) sales; it does not authorise sale of hemp extract that fails §581.217(7) (COA/QR/batch/expiry/mg-per-serving/child-resistant/non-child-appealing container rules — see §7.8); it does not authorise a hemp product to be sold through a vending machine or under the Cottage Food law.
Info link FDACS wholesale/manufactured food permit page https://www.fdacs.gov/Business-Services/Food/Food-Establishments/Wholesale-Manufactured-Food-Establishment-Permit ; renewal portal https://foodpermit.fdacs.gov ; rule https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/florida/regulations/florida_regulations_5k-4-034 — all Accessed 2026-10-24.

7.4 Licence types that do NOT exist as separate Florida hemp licences

Supposed type Florida position (with basis)
Hemp processor licence (standalone) Does not exist as a separate licence. "Processor"/"Extractor" is a defined activity inside the Hemp Food Establishment regime (Rule 5K-4.034(2)(k)), and extraction/manufacturing/processing of hemp extract for human consumption is covered by the $650/year Hemp Food Establishment permit (§7.3). Secondary summaries that say "FDACS issues two main authorizations" — cultivation licence + food establishment permit — are consistent with the rule text (LegalClarity, https://legalclarity.org/florida-hemp-license-application-and-requirements/ — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary). A cultivator who only ships raw biomass to a processor needs only the cultivation licence; the moment that cultivator extracts oil, formulates tinctures or packages edibles, the food-establishment permit applies (same source, consistent with Rule 5K-4.034(2)(f) "extracting, manufacturing, processing…").
Hemp distributor licence (standalone) Does not exist as a separate licence. "Each establishment distributing products consisting of or containing Hemp Extract intended for Human Consumption must be permitted as a Hemp Food Establishment" (Rule 5K-4.034(3)(a), verbatim). Distribution is therefore a permitted-establishment activity, not a distributor licence. §581.217(7)(b) adds the buyer-side rule: hemp extract may only be sold to a Florida business "if that business is properly permitted as required by this section".
Hemp retail licence (standalone) Does not exist as a separate licence. A retail shop selling hemp extract for ingestion/inhalation must hold a Hemp Food Establishment permit for that establishment (Rule 5K-4.034(2)(f) "selling … at wholesale or retail"; (3)(a) "distributing"). Enforcement in 2026 illustrates the point: FDACS inspections of hemp/smoke shops in Riverview (Feb 2026), Jacksonville (Apr 2026) and Live Oak (July 2026) turned on operating "without a valid food permit" / "without a Food Permit" under §500.12, with stop-sale/stop-use orders — not on a missing "retail licence" (secondary inspection write-ups, https://floridafoodsafety.org — Accessed 2026-10-24; FDACS inspection reports themselves were not opened in this run, so these are secondary enforcement illustrations, not FDACS findings quoted verbatim).
Hemp "smoke shop licence" Does not exist as a hemp-specific licence. Smoke shops fall under the general food-permit regime if they sell ingestible/inhalable hemp extract, plus general local business-tax receipts (Ch. 205, Run 1 Part 3) and general zoning. No hemp-specific smoke-shop licence was located in statute or rule.
Hemp beverage licence Does not exist. A hemp beverage is an ingestible hemp extract product: same §581.217(7) container/COA/21+ rules and same Hemp Food Establishment permit, with no beverage-specific licence, mg cap, liquor-licence requirement or excise tax in current law (Run 1 §1.5.6, unchanged). The older Rule 5K-4.034 draft language subjecting alcohol-containing hemp foods to the Beverage Law was not confirmed in the current rule text opened in this run [VERIFY] — do not assert an alcohol-law trigger for hemp beverages without DBPR/ABT guidance.
Out-of-state hemp seller / shipper licence No Florida out-of-state seller permit was located. An out-of-state manufacturer selling into Florida must still meet §581.217(7) (COA from an independent testing laboratory, QR/batch/expiry/mg-per-serving container, child-resistant/non-child-appealing packaging) and the buyer must be properly permitted (§581.217(7)(b)); whether the out-of-state seller itself must hold a Florida food permit is [VERIFY] — Run 1 §1.5.6 and secondary summaries note direct-to-consumer shipping is not expressly banned but 21+ age verification before delivery is required in practice. Do not assert either a permit requirement or an exemption for out-of-state sellers.
Hemp testing-lab licence (standalone, for extract) No standalone Florida hemp-extract testing licence. Extract COAs must come from an "Independent testing laboratory" as defined in §581.217(3)(g) (no direct/indirect interest in the tested entity or in any hemp/marijuana cultivator/processor/distributor/dispenser/seller; ISO/IEC 17025-accredited by a third-party accrediting body). For CULTIVATION, the lab must additionally be a FDACS "Designated laboratory" (DEA-registered + ISO 17025 + FDACS compliance agreement FDACS-08121) under Rule 5B-57.014(2)(d), (6)(j). These are accreditation/agreement tests, not a hemp-lab licence. They are distinct from the OMMU Certified Marijuana Testing Laboratory (CMTL) licence under §381.988 (Run 1 Part 4) — overlap in lab names does not mean identical authorisation.

7.4.1 What about non-ingestible hemp products?

  • Topicals: "Human Consumption" in Rule 5K-4.034(2)(g) "does not include topical applications". A topical CBD cream/lotion/balm is therefore NOT a "hemp extract intended for human consumption" for Rule 5K-4.034 purposes, and the 21+ rule in §581.217(7)(d) (which applies to products "intended for human ingestion or inhalation") does not apply to topicals as such (Run 1 §1.5.2, unchanged). Topicals remain subject to the Florida Drug and Cosmetic Act (older rule draft language, [VERIFY] pinpoint) and to general product-safety law. This is NOT a blanket exemption for any product labelled "topical" that is in fact intended for ingestion/inhalation.
  • Hemp seed / seed-derived ingredients / fibre: "Hemp extract" "does not include … seeds or seed-derived ingredients that are generally recognized as safe by the [FDA]" (§581.217(3)(f), verbatim). Hemp seed foods and hemp fibre products that are not "hemp extract" do not need a hemp food establishment permit for that reason alone, but may need ordinary food permits under Ch. 500 if they are food establishments, and fibre/textile products fall outside the food-permit regime entirely. Whether a given seed/fibre product needs any FDACS permit is a product-specific question [VERIFY per product].
  • Hemp flower / smokable hemp (inhalation): Smokable hemp IS hemp extract intended for inhalation if it contains more than trace cannabinoids and is derived from hemp (§581.217(3)(f)). It therefore needs the food-establishment permit at the selling establishment, the §581.217(7) container/COA regime, and the 21+ rule, plus the inhalation-specific labelling in Rule 5K-4.034 (including, as reported in a 2026 FDACS inspection summary in Run 1, "Not Intended For Ingestion, Do Not Eat" for inhalation-only product — rule pinpoint [VERIFY], carried from Run 1).

7.4.2 Local permits that are NOT hemp licences

  • County/city business tax receipts (Ch. 205): Every Florida business, including hemp businesses, generally needs a local business tax receipt from each county/city where it operates. This is a general local tax/registration, not a hemp authorisation, and amounts vary by jurisdiction (Run 1 Part 3: no dollar local fee schedule was located for any jurisdiction [UNAVAILABLE]). Do not describe a business tax receipt as a "hemp licence".
  • Zoning / land-use approval: Hemp cultivation is limited by Rule 5B-57.014(6)(f) to bona fide agricultural lands (§193.461), agricultural- or industrial-zoned lands, or registered nurseries. Hemp food establishments are subject to general local zoning for food/retail uses; no hemp-specific state zoning buffer (unlike MMTCs' 500-ft school buffers) was located in §581.217 or Rule 5K-4.034. Local hemp/CBD/smoke-shop zoning, if any, is a Part 3 matter and was not re-checked here.

7.5 Ancillary authorisations

7.5.1 Nursery registration (hemp plants for distribution)

Rule 5B-57.014(7) (verbatim substance, opened directly): "Nurseries propagating hemp plants for distribution shall: (a) Register with the Department pursuant to Section 581.031(21), F.S. (b) Hold a License to Cultivate Hemp issued by the Department. (c) Only distribute hemp plants for cultivation to Persons who are authorized to cultivate Hemp. (d) Maintain copies of hemp plant movement records or sales invoices including Department-issued license numbers for three (3) years from the date of sale or the date of movement and provide copies to the Department upon request."

So a nursery is NOT an alternative to a cultivation licence — it is an additional registration ON TOP of a cultivation licence, and it may only supply authorised cultivators. A nursery that only grows hemp for its own harvest (not for distribution as plants) is simply a cultivator; a nursery that sells hemp plants to others must do both. Nursery registration fees under §581.031 were not opened in this run [VERIFY] — do not quote a nursery fee.

7.5.2 Industrial Hemp Pilot Project permit (university route)

  • Statute: §1004.4473, "Industrial hemp pilot projects". Purpose (verbatim substance): "to cultivate, process, test, research, create, and market safe and effective commercial applications for industrial hemp in the agricultural sector in this state" for UF/IFAS, FAMU, any land-grant university with a college of agriculture, and any Florida College System institution or state university with an established agriculture, engineering or pharmacy programme. An institution must obtain its board of trustees' authorisation and register the pilot project with FDACS.
  • Rule: Fla. Admin. Code R. 5B-57.013, "Industrial Hemp Pilot Project" — https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/florida/regulations/florida_regulations_5b-57-013 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (LawServer mirror; rule text located via search, not opened in full in this run). Rule 5B-57.013(2) (via search return): "An institution or university shall not cultivate Industrial Hemp pursuant to [§1004.4473], except under an Industrial Hemp Special Permit issued by the Department's Division of Plant Industry", on submission of an Industrial Hemp Pilot Project Proposal (scope/design/objectives; varieties and seed-certification plan; etc.).
  • Current status [VERIFY]: UF/IFAS reports its pilot project was approved by the UF Board of Trustees in March 2018, permitted by FDACS-DPI in early 2019, and has "over 40 permitted sites and facilities on university-owned properties and also with qualified project partners (QPPs) across the state", plus a DEA Schedule I registration for research with low-THC cannabis — https://agronomy.ifas.ufl.edu/graduate/uf-hemp-pilot-project-research/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (university page, undated in the extract; the "over 40 sites" figure may be historical). FDACS's current Plant Industry Permits page still states: "Hemp intended for commercial products, nursery stock, or research may only be grown under a commercial Cultivation License or an Industrial Hemp Pilot Project Permit" — https://www.fdacs.gov/Agriculture-Industry/Plant-Industry-Permits — Accessed 2026-10-24. Whether FDACS issues NEW pilot permits in 2026, or only administers existing pilot sites alongside the commercial §581.217 programme (which post-dates the 2014 Farm Bill pilot authority, 7 U.S.C. §5940), was not confirmed in this run [VERIFY]. Do NOT advise a commercial grower to apply for a pilot permit — pilot permits are institution/university instruments, not a commercial shortcut. §581.217(13)(b) confirms the pilot route sits outside §581.217.

7.5.3 Designated Laboratory Compliance Agreement (cultivation testing)

Rule 5B-57.014(2)(d) (opened directly): a "Designated laboratory" is a laboratory that "(1) Holds an ISO 17025 accreditation; and (2) Is registered with [DEA] in accordance with 21 CFR 1301.13; and (3) Has entered into a compliance agreement with the Department to conduct [THC] sampling and testing" (Designated Laboratory Compliance Agreement, FDACS-08121, Rev. 04/21, incorporated by reference via flrules.org Ref-13542). Only designated labs that qualify as Independent testing laboratories under §581.217(3)(g) may be used for THC regulatory harvest sample analysis (Rule 5B-57.014(6)(j)). FDACS's "List of Approved Designated Laboratories for THC Testing" was revised 8 September 2026 (FDACS Division of Plant Industry, via search return) — the list's contents were not transcribed in this run [VERIFY against the FDACS list]. This agreement is a testing authorisation, not a licence to cultivate, process or sell hemp.

7.8 Hemp extract product rules that bear on licensing (cross-reference to Run 1 §1.5 — no change)

This section does NOT re-litigate Run 1 §1.5; it states only the rules a licensee/permit holder must satisfy to keep the authorisations in §§7.2–7.3, with verbatim statute text opened directly in this run on Online Sunshine:

  • Distribution/retail-sale gate (verbatim, §581.217(7)(a)) — hemp extract may only be distributed/sold in Florida if the product: "(1) Has a certificate of analysis prepared by an independent testing laboratory that states: a. The hemp extract is the product of a batch tested by the independent testing laboratory; b. The batch contained a total delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol concentration that did not exceed 0.3 percent pursuant to the testing of a random sample of the batch; c. The batch does not contain contaminants unsafe for human consumption; and d. The batch was processed in a facility that holds a current and valid permit issued by a human health or food safety regulatory entity … Such compliance must be documented by a report from the regulatory entity"; "(2) Is distributed or sold in a container that includes: a. A scannable barcode or quick response code linked to the [COA]; b. The batch number; c. The Internet address of a website where batch information may be obtained; d. The expiration date; and e. The number of milligrams of each marketed cannabinoid per serving"; "(3) Is distributed or sold in a container that: a. Is suitable to contain products for human consumption; b. Is composed of materials designed to minimize exposure to light; c. Mitigates exposure to high temperatures; d. Is not attractive to children; and e. Is compliant with the [Poison Prevention Packaging Act], without regard to provided exemptions."
  • Age 21+ (verbatim, §581.217(7)(d)): "Products that are intended for human ingestion or inhalation and that contain hemp extract, including, but not limited to, snuff, chewing gum, and other smokeless products, may not be sold in this state to a person who is under 21 years of age. A person who violates this paragraph commits a misdemeanor of the second degree … A person who commits a second or subsequent violation of this paragraph within 1 year after the initial violation commits a misdemeanor of the first degree…"
  • Stop-sale (verbatim, §581.217(7)(e)): "Hemp extract distributed or sold in violation of this subsection is subject to s. 500.172 and penalties as provided in s. 500.121. Hemp extract products found to be mislabeled or attractive to children are subject to an immediate stop-sale order."
  • "Attractive to children" (verbatim, §581.217(3)(a)): "manufactured in the shape of humans, cartoons, or animals; manufactured in a form that bears any reasonable resemblance to an existing candy product that is familiar to the public as a widely distributed, branded food product such that a product could be mistaken for the branded product, especially by children; or containing any color additives."
  • Cannabinoid scope (unchanged from Run 1 §1.5.2): delta-8 lawful only inside the 0.3% / COA / packaging / 21+ framework (no category ban in current Florida statute); delta-9 lawful only at ≤0.3% total delta-9 (wet weight for extract); THCA counted toward total THC via the 0.877 factor (now confirmed in rule text, §7.0); THC-O/HHCO treated as controlled substances under §893.03(1)(c)190 (FDACS seizures); HHC not category-banned in current Florida statute (SB 1698 would have banned it; vetoed); synthetic cannabidiol expressly excluded from "hemp extract" (§581.217(3)(f)). No per-serving/per-container mg cap in current Florida law — every mg cap proposed (SB 1698: 5 mg/serving, 50 mg/container; SB 438/HB 7027 variants) was vetoed or died.
  • Federal dates — NO Florida response found (still [UNAVAILABLE]): Fresh searches in this run for an FDACS statement, guidance, rule or press release on PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019 returned only law-firm and industry commentary (e.g. BD Law, GreenScreens, Duty Room, Cova — all secondary, October 2026), which consistently notes that Florida's own total-THC formula already applies today and that the federal dates do not by themselves amend §581.217. No FDACS, Legislature or Attorney General response was located. Run 1 §1.5.9's dual-compliance conclusion therefore stands: after 11 December 2026 a product must satisfy BOTH the new federal definition (including the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap and the manufactured-cannabinoid exclusions) AND Florida's 0.3% / COA / packaging / 21+ regime; compliance with one alone is not sufficient. Whether FDACS issues guidance in November–December 2026, or the 2027 Legislature (next regular session, March 2027 per Run 1 secondary reporting [VERIFY convening date]) files a conforming bill, is a post-24-October-2026 follow-up. MMTCs are not directly affected: MMTC products are §381.986 marijuana, not §581.217 hemp (Run 1 §1.5.9, unchanged).

PART 8 — CANNABIS-ZONED PROPERTIES

8.0 Method, and why this section is short

Searches run (Accessed 2026-10-24): 420 Property Florida listings index ("20 listings found" for Florida); 420 Property Florida MMTC / licence listings; LoopNet Florida cannabis dispensary searches (Tallahassee, Bradenton, Gulf Breeze, Spring Hill); Crexi/LoopNet-style general searches for Florida cannabis cultivation facilities; "Florida hemp farm property for sale acreage"; "Florida cannabis greenhouse facility for sale price 2026"; MLS / Land and Farm / residential-portal mirrors of hemp-farm listings.

What the searches actually show: Florida has NO general "cannabis-zoned" property category in the way some adult-use states do, because there is no adult-use licence and no standalone cultivation/processing/retail licence to zone for. What is publicly listed falls into three distinct buckets, and this section keeps them strictly separate — conflating them is the main error to avoid:

  1. MMTC licence-platform sales (the dominant 420 Property Florida inventory): the price is for a vertically integrated MMTC licence (statewide, cultivation through retail), sometimes bundled with a starter facility or an optional parcel. These are NOT fee-simple property sales unless the listing says the real estate is included and priced. They are included below ONLY where real estate is expressly part of the offering, and are labelled "licence (+ optional real estate)" so they are never mistaken for a property sale.
  2. Dispensary-occupied investment properties on LoopNet: fee-simple retail buildings sold as leased investments, with an MMTC tenant (Trulieve, Goldflower, Jungle Boys, Mint) under a long NNN lease. The buyer buys the building and the lease income, NOT the MMTC licence and NOT a vacant dispensary. Zoning is ordinary commercial zoning (CP, HCD, GC), not a cannabis-specific zone — the dispensary use is lawful there because the locality allows MMTC dispensing under §381.986(11) pharmacy-parity rules (Run 1 Part 3), not because the parcel carries a cannabis zone.
  3. Hemp/agricultural properties: farm land and greenhouse properties marketed for hemp (or formerly hemp) use. These are ordinary agricultural properties; their "hemp suitability" comes from agricultural/industrial zoning (Rule 5B-57.014(6)(f)) and existing greenhouse/well/irrigation infrastructure, NOT from a hemp-specific zone. A hemp cultivation licence is personal to the licensee, non-transferable (Rule 5B-57.014(5)(d)), and does NOT run with the land — a buyer of a "hemp farm" must obtain their own cultivation licence, and a seller's claim that "licenses are available for negotiation" (Immokalee, below) must not be read as a transferable licence.

Status rule applied throughout: Every listing is marked [VERIFY] unless the listing itself shows it is active and recent. Only the Clermont listing (published 16 October 2026 on 420 Property, opened directly) and the Goldflower Tallahassee listing (LoopNet, date on market 9 March 2026, opened directly) meet the "active and recent" test on the evidence in this run; all others are [VERIFY] as to current availability, even where a price is stated. Prices are asking prices (or, for Palatka, a completed-sale price), never appraised values. No listing was visited in person; zoning was taken from the listing itself, not from a county zoning map, and must be re-checked against the county/city code before any purchase — in particular the §381.986(11) 500-ft school buffers for MMTC cultivation/processing (no waiver) and dispensing (waivable by formal public proceeding) are NOT shown on any listing and must be measured for the specific parcel.

What was NOT found: No publicly listed property in Florida was found in this run that is described as zoned specifically for cannabis (e.g. a "cannabis overlay" or "marijuana zone" parcel with a street address and price) — because Florida law creates no such zone. No Crexi Florida cannabis-zoned listing with a verified street address and price was located.
