8.5 Zoning / buffer due-diligence checklist for any Part 8 property (from Run 1, unchanged)

  1. MMTC cultivation/processing: state 500-ft buffer to elementary/middle/secondary schools, NO waiver (§381.986(11), Run 1 Part 3). Measure from the parcel, not from the listing's marketing radius.
  2. MMTC dispensing: state 500-ft school buffer, waivable only by formal public proceeding (§381.986(11)). Localities that allow dispensing may not cap dispensary numbers or impose rules stricter than for Ch. 465 pharmacies, and may not charge a local fee greater than the pharmacy fee; localities that ban dispensing do so by ordinance (Run 1 Part 3 — Collier County unincorporated and City of Palm Bay were the bans most strongly evidenced; the 15-jurisdiction table in Run 1 Part 3 must be re-checked parcel-by-parcel).
  3. Hemp cultivation: agricultural or industrial zoning, or bona fide agricultural land (§193.461), or a registered nursery (Rule 5B-57.014(6)(f)). Commercial/retail zoning alone does NOT satisfy the hemp cultivation test.
  4. Hemp food establishment: general food/retail zoning + FDACS food permit for the establishment; no state hemp buffer was located.
  5. Licence does not run with land: MMTC licences are company licences subject to DOH ownership-change/transfer approval (Part 11); hemp cultivation licences are non-transferable (Rule 5B-57.014(5)(d)); hemp food permits are non-transferable per establishment. Every "licence included" claim in a property listing must be verified against the regulator, not the broker.

Scope: Part 9 only. Parts 7, 8 and 10–12 are not covered here. This Part is written to be read with Run 1, Parts 0–6. Research date / Accessed date for every fact below: 2026-10-24, unless a different publication, decision or update date is stated in the fact itself. Federal baseline used as fixed context (not re-researched): state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity and remains fully applicable to adult-use; hemp PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026 but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026, after which the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply; USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026; the federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026; there is no federal cannabis banking law. Florida MMTCs are state-licensed medical operators, so on this baseline their medical activity is the Schedule III / 280E-lifted category. No contradiction with that baseline was found in the Part 9 sources examined, subject to the one stale-text flag carried from Run 1: §381.986(4)(a)8.a. still requires the informed-consent form to state that marijuana is Schedule I. How to read flags: [VERIFY] = uncertain, conflicting, or not confirmed on the official page itself in this run. [UNAVAILABLE] = not located. Proposed initiatives and bills are NEVER described as law. No personal phone numbers or emails of individuals are reproduced; only public agency contact points are given.

9.1 Every state agency regulating cannabis and hemp

Florida does not have a single cannabis regulator. Medical marijuana is regulated principally by the Department of Health through OMMU; hemp is regulated principally by FDACS; taxation by the Department of Revenue; retail hemp enforcement at licensed tobacco/nicotine retailers by DBPR's Division of Alcoholic Beverages and Tobacco; criminal enforcement by FDLE and local law enforcement; elections and ballot measures by the Department of State's Division of Elections; and ballot-language review by the Attorney General and the Florida Supreme Court. The table gives each agency's cannabis/hemp role, its legal basis, its public website, and public contact points only. Where a contact point was not confirmed on an official page in this run, the table says so rather than inventing one.

Agency Cannabis / hemp role (with legal basis) Public website Public contact (agency only)
Florida Department of Health — Office of Medical Marijuana Use (OMMU) The medical marijuana regulator. Implements Art. X, §29 and §381.986: licenses MMTCs (cultivation, processing, transport, dispensing in one vertically integrated licence), licenses/certifies marijuana testing laboratories under §381.988, maintains the Medical Marijuana Use Registry (MMUR), qualifies physicians, issues patient/caregiver ID cards, inspects MMTCs at least biennially (§381.986(10)), imposes fines up to $10,000 per violation, publishes the weekly update (patients, locations, dispensing volumes) and the MMTC list. OMMU's own homepage states: "Licensed medical marijuana treatment centers (MMTCs) are the only businesses in Florida authorized to cultivate, process and dispense low-THC cannabis and medical marijuana." Source: https://knowthefactsmmj.com/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official). https://knowthefactsmmj.com/ Mon–Fri 8 a.m.–6 p.m. Eastern, 850-245-4657 (option 1); MedicalMarijuanaUse@FLHealth.gov; toll-free application line 800-808-9580; ID-card applications by mail to PO Box 31313, Tampa, FL 33631-3313; OMMU mailing address 4052 Bald Cypress Way, Bin M-01, Tallahassee, FL 32399. Sources: OMMU homepage and OMMU GovDelivery updates — https://knowthefactsmmj.com/ and https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/FLDOH/bulletins/3f71cca — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official).
Florida Department of Health — Boards of Medicine (Ch. 458) and Osteopathic Medicine (Ch. 459) License the physicians who may become "qualified physicians" under §381.986; a physician must hold an active, unrestricted Ch. 458 or Ch. 459 licence and complete the required 2-hour course and examination before ordering low-THC cannabis or medical marijuana (OMMU weekly updates state this requirement verbatim). The Boards also own the standardised informed-consent form whose Schedule I sentence is flagged as stale in §9.0. Whether the Boards have updated that form for Schedule III is [VERIFY] (Run 1 Gap G-03, carried forward). https://www.flhealthsource.gov/ (licence verification / FLHealthSource) — via OMMU physician pages Via OMMU contacts above; no separate cannabis-specific Board contact was confirmed in this run [VERIFY].
Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS) — State Hemp Program The hemp regulator under §581.217. Divisions involved: Division of Plant Industry (cultivation licences), Division of Food Safety (hemp food establishment permits; hemp extract for human consumption under Rule 5K-4.034), and Division of Agricultural Environmental Services (pesticide / related matters, per FDACS programme materials). FDACS also holds the interagency agreement with the Department of Health required by §381.986(10) for MMTC cooperation, and its Division of Food Safety issues the food-establishment permits MMTCs need for edibles production under Ch. 500. FDACS's hemp child-resistant-packaging resources page gives its Division of Food Safety address as 3125 Conner Boulevard, C-26, Tallahassee, FL 32399-1650, phone (850) 245-5520, and cites "Section 581.217, Florida Statutes – Rule 5K-4.034, F.A.C." Source: https://ccmedia.fdacs.gov/content/download/118770/file/hemp-extract-child-resistant-packaging-resources.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official FDACS document). https://www.fdacs.gov/ ; hemp pages via https://www.fdacs.gov/Cannabis-Hemp/Hemp-CBD-in-Florida (as cited in FDACS labelling guidance) FDACS general: 1-800-HELP-FLA (1-800-435-7352); Division of Food Safety Business Center: (850) 245-5520; food-permit portal: https://foodpermit.fdacs.gov — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official FDACS documents).
Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS) — Division of Food Safety, enforcement role Enforces §581.217 product rules: stop-sale orders for mislabelled or child-attractive hemp extract, seizure/injunction under §§500.121/500.172 for adulterated/misbranded food, and the Operation Kandy Krush / Operation Safe Summer sweeps (Run 1 Part 1 §1.5.7: over 1.3 million illegal hemp packages removed since 1 July 2023, per FDACS 2025 release). See FDACS row above See FDACS row above.
Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) — Division of Alcoholic Beverages and Tobacco (ABT) NOT a marijuana licensor and NOT the MMTC regulator — that is a common error, corrected here. DBPR's cannabis-adjacent role is retail hemp enforcement: since 1 July 2024 ABT has included hemp investigations in its targeted under-21 sales operations at licensed retail stores (gas stations, grocery stores, smoke shops). DBPR's own release states: "Since July 1, 2024, DBPR's Division of Alcoholic Beverages and Tobacco (division) has made more than 120 arrests for the sale of hemp to minors at licensed retail stores, including gas stations, grocery stores and smoke shops" and "In just 3 months, our efforts have resulted in 127 arrests" with "more than 1,100 investigations". Source: https://www2.myfloridalicense.com/historic-initiative-to-prevent-sale-of-harmful-hemp-products-to-minors/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official DBPR release). ABT also issues retail tobacco/nicotine dealer permits (§569.003), which is why smoke shops selling hemp fall within its inspection reach. A 2026 DBPR bill (HB 1341) that would have expressly authorised DBPR action against establishments violating hemp-extract laws died in subcommittee; its companion CS/SB 432 passed as ch. 2026-148 — whether ch. 2026-148 itself contains a hemp provision is [VERIFY] (see §9.2). Do not cite DBPR as the MMTC licensor. https://www.myfloridalicense.com/ Via DBPR's public site; no cannabis-specific DBPR phone/email was confirmed on an official page in this run [VERIFY].
Florida Department of Revenue (DOR) Administers sales tax (Ch. 212), including the §212.08(2)(l) medical marijuana exemption and ordinary sales tax on taxable hemp products, and corporate income tax (Ch. 220) including the 280E conformity question (Run 1 Part 2). DOR publishes post-legislative reviews: its 2019 review confirms for SB 182 (ch. 2019-1): "Medical marijuana delivery devices intended for use with smokable medical marijuana are no longer required to be purchased from a medical marijuana treatment center. As such, these devices are exempt from sales and use tax when purchased by a qualified patient from a vendor." Source: https://floridarevenue.com/TaxLaw/Documents/PLR-123272_2019%20PLR_Links.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official DOR document). No DOR cannabis-specific guidance confirming Schedule III / 280E treatment for the 2026 Florida return was located in this run [UNAVAILABLE] (Run 1 Part 2 Gap 2-12, carried forward). https://floridarevenue.com/ Taxpayer assistance is published by DOR generally; a cannabis-specific DOR contact was not confirmed on an official page in this run, so no phone/email is asserted here [VERIFY]. Secondary tax guides list 850-488-6800 for taxpayer assistance — not adopted as an official-page fact in this Part.
Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE) NOT a marijuana licensor. Its statutory cannabis roles are: (1) §943.17261 — "The Department of Law Enforcement shall develop a 4-hour online initial training course, and a 2-hour online continuing education course, which shall be made available for use by all law enforcement agencies in this state. Such training shall cover the legal parameters of marijuana-related activities governed by ss. 381.986 and 381.988 relating to criminal laws governing marijuana." Source: https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2024/0943.17261 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official statute page, via search extract; direct Online Sunshine re-open is Gap P9-03). Note the same section's history note: §1, ch. 2017-232 provides the 2017 act expires 6 months after a cannabis-related constitutional amendment is adopted, which would repeal §943.17261 as designated — see §9.2 reversion note. (2) Forensic seized-drug analysis: FDLE's Seized Drugs section "examine[s] evidence, submitted by Law Enforcement Agencies, for the presence or absence of controlled substances as referenced in Florida Statutes §893 and §877.111" using mass spectrometry, gas chromatography and infrared spectrophotometry. Source: https://www.fdle.state.fl.us/Forensics/Disciplines/Seized-Drugs — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official). (3) The "one percent procedure": after the hemp programme made it impossible for crime labs to distinguish legal hemp from illegal marijuana by appearance, "FDLE scientists validated the DEA's 'one percent procedure.' With this technique, scientists are able to determine whether or not a substance contains more than one percent THC – more than 0.3 percent is illegal." Source: https://www.fdle.state.fl.us/News/2020/December/FDLE-highlights-2020-accomplishments — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official). (4) FDLE's own medical-marijuana enforcement guidance (2019) confirms there is no reciprocity: "Medical marijuana treatment centers licensed by the Florida Department of Health (DOH) are the sole source for medical marijuana. Bringing medical or recreational marijuana from another state into Florida violates s. 893.13, F.S., and Florida has no reciprocity agreements with other states." Source: https://www.fdle.state.fl.us/getContentAsset/dc941cd4-f649-4c61-99a8-337faeef1fa0/73aabf56-e6e5-4330-95a3-5f2a270a1d2b/TM-2019-03-MedicalMarijuanaUpdates-final3-signedPkt.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official FDLE document). Day-to-day possession/cultivation enforcement is by local sheriffs and police, not FDLE alone. https://www.fdle.state.fl.us/ Via FDLE's public site; no cannabis-specific FDLE phone/email is asserted here [VERIFY].
Florida Department of State — Division of Elections Administers constitutional-initiative petitions (signature verification, ballot placement, FIEC coordination) and certifies election results, including the 2016 and 2024 cannabis amendments and the 2026/2028 initiative register. The Division's Amendments portal, opened in this run, returned the Division's address and phone but not the 2024 canvass table (see §9.0(1)). Source: https://floridaelectionwatch.gov/Amendments — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official, content-limited on open). Initiative register: https://constitutionalinitiatives.dos.fl.gov/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official register, via search extract in Run 1; direct re-open is Gap P9-04). https://dos.fl.gov/elections/ ; https://floridaelectionwatch.gov/ Room 316, R.A. Gray Building, 500 S. Bronough Street, Tallahassee, FL 32399-0250; 1-850-245-6200. Source: https://floridaelectionwatch.gov/Amendments — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official).
Florida Attorney General and Florida Supreme Court The Attorney General petitions the Supreme Court for an advisory opinion on every citizen-initiative petition that reaches the review threshold (Art. IV, §10; Art. V, §3(b)(10), Fla. Const.); the Court reviews single-subject compliance (Art. XI, §3) and ballot title/summary clarity (§101.161(1)), and — since ch. 2020-15 — facial validity under the federal constitution. The Court's cannabis opinions are in §9.3.2. The Attorney General also receives mandatory referral of intentional/reckless hemp violations under §581.217 (with the U.S. Attorney). https://www.myfloridalegal.com/ ; https://supremecourt.flcourts.gov/ Via the Courts' public sites; no individual contact is given.
Other agencies with a defined but secondary role (a) Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles and FDLE may enter interagency agreements with the Department of Health under §381.986(10) for MMTC purposes. (b) Agency for Health Care Administration: no MMTC licensing role was located in this run; do not list AHCA as a cannabis licensor. (c) Florida Department of Education / school districts: relevant only to the medical-marijuana-in-schools rules, which belong to Part 12, not this Part. (d) County/city governments: local MMTC dispensing bans and pharmacy-parity rules under §381.986(11) — see Run 1 Part 3. (e) USDA: approves Florida's hemp plan and lists it as approved (updated 17 February 2026, per Run 1 Part 5); USDA is a federal, not Florida, regulator and is listed here only to prevent confusion. — —

Regulatory-map warning. Three errors recur in secondary writing and are corrected here: (1) DBPR does not license MMTCs; (2) FDACS does not license MMTCs — it licenses hemp cultivation and permits hemp food establishments, and issues the food permits MMTCs need for edibles; (3) FDLE does not license anyone in this field — it trains officers and analyses seized drugs. The only marijuana licences in Florida are the DOH/OMMU MMTC licence and the §381.988 certified marijuana testing laboratory certification (Run 1 Part 4).

9.2 Key dates — chronological history

Date Event What happened / why it matters Source (Accessed 2026-10-24)
16 June 2014 Compassionate Use Act signed Governor Rick Scott signed SB 1030, the "Compassionate Medical Cannabis Act" (ch. 2014-157), allowing low-THC, high-CBD cannabis oil ("Charlotte's Web") for epilepsy, cancer and conditions chronically producing seizures or severe and persistent muscle spasms. House 111–7, Senate 30–9 (secondary vote tallies). Physicians could order from 1 January 2015; only oil, no smokable form. Low-THC was defined as ≤0.8% THC and >10% CBD — the definition Run 1 Part 1 carries forward. Secondary, consistently reported: https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=66e4440e-c3b2-459e-84af-2a7bc93746c1 ; https://www.gray-robinson.com/insights/post/750/Regulated-Products-E-lert-Medical-Marijuana-in-Florida-Voters-Did-Not-Approve-Amendment-2-Now-What — Accessed 2026-10-24. Chapter number ch. 2014-157 is as in Run 1 Part 1; direct session-law pinpoint [VERIFY] (Gap P9-05).
27 January 2014 (opinion) / 4 November 2014 (vote) First Amendment 2 — court approval, then voter defeat The Supreme Court approved the 2014 medical initiative for the ballot (Medical Marijuana I, see §9.3.2), but voters rejected it: 3,370,761 Yes (57.62%) / 2,478,993 No (42.38%) — a majority, but short of 60%. The 2014 defeat is why the 2016 re-run was drafted with clarifications (parental consent for minors, "debilitating" definition, no malpractice immunity). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Florida_Amendment_2 (sourced there to the Florida Secretary of State) and https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_Amendment_2,Medical_Marijuana_Legalization_Measure(2016) — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary compilations of official results; direct canvass [VERIFY], Gap P9-06).
25 March 2016 Right to Try expansion (HB 307) Governor Scott signed HB 307, expanding the Right to Try Act to allow terminally ill patients to use full-strength cannabis, and addressing implementation problems in the 2014 low-THC programme. House 99–16, Senate 28–11 (secondary). This is a bridge statute between the low-THC programme and Amendment 2; it is not itself the Amendment 2 implementing law. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Florida — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary; bill pinpoint [VERIFY], Gap P9-05).
8 November 2016 Amendment 2 adopted Voters adopted the medical marijuana amendment, adding Art. X, §29. Adopted figures: 6,518,919 Yes (71.32%) / 2,621,845 No (28.68%). The amendment took effect 3 January 2017 (as reported contemporaneously) and required the Department of Health to adopt rules by 3 July 2017 and implement by 3 October 2017. It guarantees qualified patients' medical use, creates the MMTC system, and leaves the Legislature to implement — including the explicit statement that the section does not require violation of federal law or purport to give immunity under federal law. https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_Amendment_2,Medical_Marijuana_Legalization_Measure(2016) (election results "from Florida Division of Elections") — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary compilation; direct canvass [VERIFY], Gap P9-06).
9 June 2017 (passed) / 23 June 2017 (signed) Implementing law — SB 8-A, ch. 2017-232 After the regular session ended 8 May 2017 in impasse over Amendment 2 implementation, Governor Scott called a special session 7–9 June 2017; the Legislature passed SB 8-A on 9 June 2017 and the Governor signed it 23 June 2017. The Act rewrote §381.986: vertically integrated MMTCs, 10 additional licences (to 17 total at the time, including the Pigford licence and citrus preferences), the patient-based licence formula (4 per 100,000 patients — see Run 1 Part 4 for the exact trigger text), the 25 + 5-per-100,000 dispensing-location provision (whose later expiry is flagged in Run 1 Part 4), the sales-tax exemption now in §212.08(2)(l), local-government rules now in §381.986(11), and — controversially — a ban on smoking as a medical route, plus the rule that MMTCs are not subject to Ch. 465/499 licensure. The Florida Bar's account states: "On June 9, 2017, the Florida Legislature passed Senate Bill 8-A, the Medical Use of Marijuana Act, which was signed into law by Gov. Scott on June 23, 2017." Source: https://www.floridabar.org/the-florida-bar-journal/floridas-medical-marijuana-industry-remains-hazy/ — Accessed 2026-10-24. Reversion note (material to any future adult-use amendment): §1, ch. 2017-232 provides that if Art. X, §29 "is amended or a constitutional amendment related to cannabis or marijuana is adopted, this act shall expire 6 months after the effective date of such amendment" and §381.986 would revert to the pre-2017 text. This is printed in the current §381.986 history note (Run 1 Part 1). It is not current law today, but it means a future adult-use amendment would, without legislative action, sunset the current implementing act — there is therefore no standing "legislative implementation plan" for adult use to report, only this tripwire. Florida Bar article above; MPP signing notice https://blog.mpp.org/medical-marijuana/florida-medical-marijuana-regulations-bill-signed/ (23 June 2017) — Accessed 2026-10-24.
3 July 2017 First MMTCs under the new law The five pre-Amendment 2 low-THC dispensing organisations became MMTCs under §381.986(8)(a)1. if they held an active, unrestricted licence under former §381.986 (2016) and met the new section (Run 1 Part 4). The 10 additional SB 8-A licences were to issue by October 2017; by November 2017 the Department had issued 13 MMTC licences, with 4 more to reach 17 (secondary, via Florida Bar-era reporting). Run 1 Part 4, §4.1.6 table — Accessed 2026-10-24 (carried forward; licence-issuance dates for the 2017 tranche [VERIFY] in Part 11's licence history if needed).
25 May 2018 (trial court) Smoking ban held unconstitutional (trial court) Judge Karen Gievers held SB 8-A's smoking ban unconstitutional as inconsistent with Amendment 2, which she read as giving patients the form of marijuana their physicians recommend, including smokable marijuana in private places. The Department appealed; the First District Court of Appeal kept a stay in place. This litigation is the direct cause of SB 182. The trial-court holding was never the final appellate word because the Legislature mooted it by statute — do not cite the 2018 trial decision as current law. Secondary litigation history in Run 1 Part 1 and Ballotpedia's Amendment 2 article (stay lifted 5 June 2018, First District stay re-imposed) — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary; First District disposition [VERIFY], Gap P9-07).
18 March 2019 Smokable flower legalised — SB 182, ch. 2019-1 Governor Ron DeSantis signed SB 182, "Medical Use of Marijuana" (ch. 2019-1), removing the smoking exclusion. The Governor's office stated on 18 March 2019: "Today, Governor Ron DeSantis signed SB 182 'Medical Use of Marijuana' into law (Ch. 2019-1 SB 182, Laws of Florida)." Source: http://www.flgov.com/eog/news/press/2019/governor-desantis-signs-medical-marijuana-bill-and-files-joint-motion-dismiss — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official Governor's office release). Senate 34–4 (7 March 2019), House 101–11 (13 March 2019) (secondary vote tallies). The same act made smokable-marijuana delivery devices exempt from sales tax even when bought outside an MMTC (DOR 2019 review, §9.1). Smoking certification remains subject to §381.986(4)(c) documentation for non-terminal patients and the minor regime in (4)(d) (Run 1 Part 1). Governor's release above; DOR review above — Accessed 2026-10-24.
25 June 2019 Hemp programme created — SB 1020 Governor DeSantis signed SB 1020, creating the State Hemp Program in §581.217, removing hemp from Florida's controlled-substance statutes consistently with the 2018 federal Farm Bill, and directing FDACS to develop rules (by 1 August 2019) and submit a plan to the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture within 30 days of final rule adoption, working with DOH and DBPR. FDACS's statement on signing: "Tonight's hemp bill signing marks a transformation in Florida, and a critical step on the journey to creating a green industrial revolution…" Source: https://southeastagnet.com/2019/05/03/commissioner-nikki-fried-florida-hemp-bill-passage/ (FDACS statement, 25 June 2019) — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official FDACS statement via trade press; direct FDACS release [VERIFY], Gap P9-08). Senate and House passed SB 1020 unanimously (secondary). FDACS statement above; https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=b582ebde-616c-4c6c-bb1a-2706c3e4e444 (SB 1020 summary) — Accessed 2026-10-24.

9.3 Ballot history, thresholds and Supreme Court rulings

9.3.1 The 60% rule and every cannabis vote

Florida requires 60% approval for a constitutional amendment. The rule is in Art. XI, §5(e), Fla. Const. (the 2006 amendment that raised the threshold from a simple majority to 60%; a new tax or fee amendment requires two-thirds, which does not apply to the cannabis measures as summarised). The practical consequence, visible in every row below, is that a cannabis measure can win a clear majority and still fail. The official constitutional text pinpoint for §5(e) was not re-opened verbatim in this Part — the threshold itself is not in doubt (it is stated in every official and secondary account of these votes), but a verbatim §5(e) quotation is [VERIFY] for the combined dossier (Gap P9-13).

Vote Measure Result Threshold consequence
4 Nov 2014 Amendment 2 — Use of Marijuana for Certain Medical Conditions (medical) Yes 3,370,761 (57.62%) / No 2,478,993 (42.38%); valid votes 5,849,754 FAILED — majority, but 2.38 points short of 60%. The low-THC programme under SB 1030 was unaffected.
8 Nov 2016 Amendment 2 — Medical Marijuana Legalization Measure (medical; Art. X, §29) Yes 6,518,919 (71.32%) / No 2,621,845 (28.68%) PASSED — cleared 60% by 11.32 points. Current medical programme's constitutional basis.
5 Nov 2024 Amendment 3 — Adult Personal Use of Marijuana (adult-use) Yes 5,950,589 (55.90%) / No 4,693,524 (44.10%); valid votes 10,644,113; invalid/blank 360,096; total votes cast on the measure 11,004,209 FAILED — majority, but 4.10 points short of 60%. See reconciliation in §9.0(1): the certified pair 5,950,589 / 4,693,524 is adopted; Run 1 Part 1's 5,934,139 / 4,685,443 pair is a pre-certification snapshot. None is law.

What Amendment 3 (2024) would have done (proposed only, never law): adults 21+ could possess up to 3 oz of marijuana (≤5 g concentrate), purchase and use marijuana products for non-medical personal consumption by smoking, ingestion or otherwise; MMTCs and "other state licensed entities" could acquire, cultivate, process, manufacture, sell and distribute marijuana products for personal use; the Legislature could license entities other than MMTCs. It contained no excise tax, no home-grow right, and no expungement provision in its operative summary (Run 1 Parts 1–2). Its ballot financial-impact statement projected only sales tax, "at least $195.6m annually" at full operation (Run 1 Part 2, proposed only).

9.3.2 Florida Supreme Court rulings on cannabis ballot language — verified holdings

The Court's review is narrow by design. In the 2024 opinion the Court states its role in terms that govern every case below: "Our role is narrow—we assess only whether the amendment conforms to the constitutionally mandated single-subject requirement, whether the ballot summary meets the statutory standard for clarity, and whether the amendment is facially invalid under the federal constitution. In light of those limited considerations, we approve the proposed amendment for placement on the ballot." Source: Advisory Opinion to the Attorney General re Adult Personal Use of Marijuana, No. SC2023-0682 (Fla. 1 Apr. 2024) (Grosshans, J.), reproduced at https://beardbrospharms.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Opinion-Disposition.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24 (opinion text via secondary host; Justia summary at https://law.justia.com/cases/florida/supreme-court/2024/sc2023-0682.html — Accessed 2026-10-24). The Court does not rule on the wisdom of legalisation, and approval for the ballot is not approval of the policy.

Case Date / vote / author Holding Why it matters / verbatim core
Advisory Opinion to the Attorney General re Use of Marijuana for Certain Medical Conditions (Medical Marijuana I), 132 So. 3d 786 27 Jan 2014; 4–3; per curiam APPROVED for the ballot (2014 Amendment 2). Single subject satisfied (medical use of marijuana); ballot title/summary not clearly and conclusively defective; financial impact statement compliant. The ballot summary stated the amendment "[a]pplie[d] only to Florida law" and "[did] not authorize violations of federal law" — language the Court later treated as the safe "roadmap" for federal-law disclosure. The Court held "the voters are given fair notice as to the chief purpose and scope of the proposed amendment, which is to allow a restricted use of marijuana for certain debilitating medical conditions." Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/florida/supreme-court/2014/sc13-2132.html (financial-impact companion, same date) — Accessed 2026-10-24. The 2014 measure then failed at the ballot (57.62%), so the approval did not produce law.
Advisory Opinion to the Attorney General re Use of Marijuana for Debilitating Medical Conditions (Medical Marijuana II), 181 So. 3d 471 17 Dec 2015; unanimous APPROVED for the ballot (2016 Amendment 2). Single subject; title/summary clear; financial impact statement compliant. The summary here stated the amendment "[a]pplie[d] only to Florida law" and "[did] not immunize violations of federal law" — clearer than in Medical Marijuana I. This is the opinion that put Art. X, §29 on the 2016 ballot. The Court's unanimity contrasts with the 4–3 split in 2014 and the 5–2 splits in 2021 and 2024. Source: case summary at https://bondcasebriefs.com/2016/01/06/cases/in-re-advisory-opinion-to-atty-gen-re-use-of-marijuana-for-debilitating-medical-conditions/?print=pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary summary of the opinion; opinion text pinpoint [VERIFY], Gap P9-14).
Advisory Opinion to the Attorney General re Adult Use of Marijuana (Make It Legal Florida; "Recreational Marijuana I"), 315 So. 3d 1176, No. SC19-2116 22 Apr 2021; 5–2 (per curiam); sponsor Make It Legal Florida STRUCK — ballot summary affirmatively misleading under §101.161(1); single-subject question not reached because the clarity defect was "clearly dispositive". The Attorney General had petitioned 19 December 2019; oral argument was held 6 May 2020. The proposed amendment would have added Art. X, §33, permitting adults 21+ to possess/use/purchase/display/transport up to 2.5 oz for personal use and permitting MMTCs to sell to adults, with liability removed only "under Florida law". The summary said the amendment "[p]ermits" those acts without qualification. Verbatim, from the opinion text as reproduced on FindLaw (opened in this run): "We conclude that the language in the ballot summary indicating that the proposed amendment unqualifiedly '[p]ermits' the use (and distribution) of recreational marijuana is affirmatively misleading. Because the proposed amendment fails to comply with section 101.161(1), Florida Statutes, we strike the proposed amendment." And: "A constitutional amendment cannot unequivocally 'permit' or authorize conduct that is criminalized under federal law. And a ballot summary suggesting otherwise is affirmatively misleading." Source: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/fl-supreme-court/2123470.html — Accessed 2026-10-24 (opinion text). Note for the fixed baseline: the opinion's federal-law premise (activities "criminal offenses under federal law", 21 U.S.C. §§801–904) remains true for adult-use marijuana, which is still Schedule I; it does not speak to the 2026 Schedule III medical move.
Advisory Opinion to the Attorney General re Regulate Marijuana in a Manner Similar to Alcohol to Establish Age, Licensing and Other Restrictions (Sensible Florida) 17 June 2021; 5–2 (Canady, C.J., and Polston, J., majority); sponsor Sensible Florida Inc. STRUCK — ballot summary affirmatively misleading under §101.161(1); "clearly and conclusively defective". The summary said the amendment would regulate marijuana "for limited use and growing by persons twenty-one years of age or older", but the amendment's text set no limit on personal use (consumption): its quantities were "minimum quantities, subject to increase by state, county, or municipal legislation, but not subject to decrease". The Attorney General had petitioned 11 September 2019. The initiative had only ~29,000 of the 891,589 signatures then required, so the ruling ended a measure that was already far from qualification. Verbatim, from the opinion as quoted in contemporaneous reporting of the opinion text: "The ballot summary plainly tells voters that the proposed amendment 'limit[s]' the personal use—i.e., consumption—of recreational marijuana by age-eligible persons. But the proposed amendment itself does not do so." And: "The Sponsor's inability to point to anything in the text of the measure that could credibly support the 'limited use' language in the summary leaves no doubt that the summary is affirmatively misleading." Sources: https://www.bressler.com/news-the-florida-supreme-court-rejects-recreational-marijuana-initiative ; https://www.ganjapreneur.com/florida-supreme-court-rules-proposal-cannabis-legalization-ballot-question-misleading/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary quotations of the opinion; So. 3d citation and opinion-text pinpoint [VERIFY], Gap P9-14). The proposal would also have allowed home grows (up to six mature plants per household member 21+) — a provision that never became law and must not be cited as a current Florida right.
Advisory Opinion to the Attorney General re Adult Personal Use of Marijuana, No. SC2023-0682 1 Apr 2024; 5–2 (Grosshans, J.); dissents by Sasso and Francis, JJ. (secondary) APPROVED for the ballot (2024 Amendment 3). Single subject satisfied: "Allowing businesses to distribute personal-use marijuana, and authorizing individuals to possess it, are logically and naturally related as part of a dominant plan or scheme. Legalization of marijuana presumes the product will be available for the consumer." Ballot summary clear: the "allow … other state licensed entities" language was read naturally as "subject to a state-licensing process", not as implying entities were already licensed; and the summary followed the Medical Marijuana federal-law roadmap by stating the amendment "[a]pplies to Florida law; does not change, or immunize violations of, federal law." Not facially invalid under the U.S. Constitution: the Court rejected the Supremacy Clause / CSA preemption argument. "No rehearing will be permitted." Verbatim holding language (from the opinion text): "We conclude that the ballot summary and amendment comply with the requirements imposed by article XI, section 3 of the Florida Constitution and section 101.161(1) of the Florida Statutes. We therefore approve the proposed amendment for placement on the ballot." Sources: opinion text https://beardbrospharms.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Opinion-Disposition.pdf ; Justia summary https://law.justia.com/cases/florida/supreme-court/2024/sc2023-0682.html — Accessed 2026-10-24. So. 3d citation for SC2023-0682 was not confirmed in this run [VERIFY] (Gap P9-14). The approval put Amendment 3 on the ballot; voters then defeated it (55.90%), so the approval produced no law.

Pattern the Court's cases establish. The Court has approved every medical initiative it reviewed (2014, 2015) and the 2024 adult-use initiative, and struck two adult-use initiatives in 2021 — both on ballot-summary clarity, not on single-subject grounds and not on the policy merits. The recurring trap is federal-law / limits language in the summary: a summary that says "permits" without the "under Florida law" qualifier, or that claims a "limited use" the text does not impose, is "affirmatively misleading" and "clearly and conclusively defective". The 2024 summary survived precisely because it copied the Medical Marijuana roadmap language. Future 2028 initiative drafters face the same test, and Supreme Court review is mandatory once the review threshold (25% of the full signature requirement, i.e. 220,016 on the Run 1 figures) is reached — that review has not been reported for Serials 26-01/26-03 in this run [VERIFY] (Gap P9-04).

9.3.3 Public opinion polling — what voters say vs what voters do

Polls in this section are secondary sources, used only for non-law facts, with pollster, field dates and sample size as required. Reading rule: a poll asking about "legalization in general" is not a ballot test. The 2024 experience proves the gap: UNF found 66% "yes" on the ballot question in October 2024 (see below) and the measure still received only 55.90%. General-support polls running at 66–67% do not predict clearing 60% on a specific amendment after an opposition campaign, and no poll in this table should be quoted as a forecast.

Ron DeSantis began heavily campaigning against the amendment, support soured enough to lead to its failure. This could happen again, though we won't find out in 2026, given enough signatures were rejected in legal challenges to keep the issue off the ballot." Sources: https://www.scribd.com/document/1007607002/UNF-PORL-Spring-2026 (methodology) and https://gmg-wjxt-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/news/politics/2026/03/04/unf-poll-likely-voters-in-florida-still-focused-on-affordability-most-support-eliminating-property-taxes/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary). Margin of error for this wave was not stated in the sources consulted [VERIFY]. A UNF subgroup finding also reported in 2026 coverage — only 40% of registered Republican voters supporting a 2026 legalization initiative vs 58% opposed — appears to be a different cut (Republican subsample / initiative-specific wording) from the 50% Republican figure in the Spring 2026 topline; the two Republican figures are NOT reconciled here and neither should be quoted without its question wording [VERIFY] (Gap P9-15).
(No medical-marijuana support poll relied on) — — — — Medical marijuana itself is settled law (Art. X, §29, 71.32% in 2016); no recent medical-only support poll was needed for this Part, and none is asserted. Historical Quinnipiac medical-support figures from 2014 (88% in July 2014, falling to 48% by October 2014 in one secondary account) are not relied on here because they predate the current programme and their methodology was not re-verified.

Polling conclusion. General support for adult-use legalization in Florida has run above 60% in independent university polls in 2024–2026 (UNF 64–67%, Spring 2026 66%), below 60% in the FAU August 2024 poll (56%) and in sponsor-affected polls (Cherry/Chamber 58%, Mason-Dixon memo 50%). The only ballot test, Amendment 3 in 2024, produced 55.90% — below every independent university poll's topline except FAU's. The gap between general support and ballot performance, and the 60% threshold, are the two facts that matter for 2028; neither a poll nor a petition filing predicts passage.
