10.1 Tribal cannabis and hemp

10.1.1 Bottom line — stated plainly

  • No verified tribal marijuana operation exists in Florida. Neither the Seminole Tribe of Florida nor the Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida was found, in this run, to operate a marijuana dispensary, a state-licensed MMTC, a tribal marijuana cultivation or processing facility, or a tribal marijuana ordinance open to the public. Searches were run for each tribe combined with "cannabis", "marijuana", "hemp", "ordinance" and "dispensary" (see §10.1.7 for method). What the searches return instead is gaming, tobacco smoke shops, and — for the Miccosukee only — a USDA-approved hemp production plan. A casino, a tobacco smoke shop, or a hotel is not a cannabis operation, and none is treated as one here.
  • The one verified tribal cannabis-related instrument in Florida is a hemp plan, not a marijuana programme: the Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida holds a USDA-approved tribal hemp production plan, approved 7 May 2020 and still listed as "Approved Plan (pdf)" on the USDA list updated 17 February 2026 (§10.1.3). Plan approval is authority to regulate hemp production under that plan; it is not evidence, on its own, of a currently operating hemp farm, brand, or retail business, and no such operating business was verified in this run (§10.1.5).
  • The Seminole Tribe of Florida holds no USDA tribal hemp plan on the USDA list (§10.1.3) and no tribal marijuana or hemp operation was verified for it (§10.1.4).
  • No gaming compact provision touching cannabis was found for either tribe (§10.1.6). The Seminole 2021 gaming compact, opened and searched in this run, contains no "cannabis" or "marijuana" provision. The Miccosukee Tribe has no Class III gaming compact at all (secondary reporting, §10.1.6).

10.1.2 Which tribes count in Florida — the BIA list, and the Poarch Creek trap

Official list used. The Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) publishes the authoritative list as "Indian Entities Recognized by and Eligible To Receive Services From the United States Bureau of Indian Affairs" in the Federal Register. The most recent list retrieved in this run is 89 FR 944 (8 January 2024), reproduced at:

  • Source: https://regulations.justia.com/regulations/fedreg/2024/01/08/2024-00109.html — Accessed 2026-10-24 (Federal Register reproduction; the Federal Register original itself was not separately re-opened — [VERIFY] for a post-2024 update, Gap P10-01).

That list contains, as Florida-headquartered tribes:

  • Miccosukee Tribe of Indians (listed without a Florida qualifier in the 2024 alphabetical list; listed elsewhere as "Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida").
  • Seminole Tribe of Florida.

State-by-state compilations derived from the BIA list agree that Florida has exactly these two:

  • Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_federally_recognized_tribes_by_state — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary compilation of the BIA list; used only to cross-check the count, not as the legal source). Under "Florida" it lists: "Miccosukee Tribe of Indians (previously listed as Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida)" and "Seminole Tribe of Florida — Big Cypress Reservation, Brighton Reservation, Hollywood Reservation, Tampa Reservation".
  • Source: https://disabilityrightsflorida.org/disability-topics/disability_topic_info/native_american_resources — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary): "Florida's 2 Federally Recognized* Tribes" — Seminole Tribe and Miccosukee Tribe.

The Poarch Creek trap — do not count a third Florida tribe. An older University of Florida publication states: "Today Florida has three federally recognized Native American tribes: the Seminole, the Miccosukee and the Poarch Creeks" (Source: https://research.ufl.edu/publications/explore/v03n2/indians.html — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary, undated in the extract and plainly written against 1990 census figures). That statement is not adopted here, for two reasons verified in this run:

  1. The Poarch Band of Creek Indians is a federally recognised tribe headquartered in Alabama (Atmore, Alabama); its reservation is in Alabama. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poarch_Creek_Indian_Reservation — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary).
  2. The Poarch Band does hold trust land in Florida as well as Alabama — a congressional hearing record states the Band's lands "in Alabama and Florida" were administratively placed into trust, and a 2014 secondary report describes "the one acre Poarch Creek site … in Nokomis, Florida" (Sarasota County), placed in trust in 1984. Sources: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-118hhrg56170/html/CHRG-118hhrg56170.htm and https://news.worldcasinodirectory.com/?p=4201 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (both secondary for this point; the hearing record is a federal publication but is not a BIA recognition list).

The same 2014 report is the only Poarch-cannabis item found: it says the Poarch Band "say they may use their trust land to grow marijuana" as leverage in gaming-compact talks, expressly adding "That's not to say they have made a decision". That is a 2014 negotiating threat reported secondarily, not a law, not an ordinance, and not an operation — and no follow-through was found in this run. It is recorded here only so that a later researcher does not mistake it for a Florida tribal cannabis programme. No current Poarch Band cannabis or hemp operation in Florida was verified [UNAVAILABLE]. Whether the Nokomis parcel remains in trust, and whether any Poarch hemp activity occurs on it, is Gap P10-02.

No other federally recognised tribe headquartered in Florida was found. State-recognised groups, unrecognised groups, and individual Native people living in Florida are not federally recognised tribes for the purposes of this Part and are not treated as holding tribal regulatory authority over cannabis or hemp.

10.1.3 USDA tribal hemp plans — Miccosukee approved, Seminole absent

The list, opened directly. The USDA Agricultural Marketing Service "List of USDA-approved Hemp Plans" was opened directly in this run:

  • Source: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review — Accessed 2026-10-24. Page header: "Updated February 17, 2026". It states: "Once a plan is approved by USDA, it remains in effect unless withdrawn by the State or Tribal government or revoked by USDA pursuant to the procedures described in the Final Rule."

Entries relevant to Florida on that page, verbatim:

  • States: "| Florida | FL Approved Plan (pdf) |" — confirming Run 1's state-plan finding.
  • Tribes: "| Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida | Approved Plan (pdf) |".
  • Tribes: "| Seminole Nation of Oklahoma | Approved Plan (pdf) |" — this is the Oklahoma Seminole Nation, not the Seminole Tribe of Florida. The two must not be conflated. No entry reading "Seminole Tribe of Florida" appears anywhere in the Tribes table on the page as opened.

Miccosukee approval date and scope (secondary, dated). USDA announced the approval on 7 May 2020, together with Massachusetts and four other tribes:

  • Source: https://www.marijuanamoment.net/usda-approves-hemp-plans-for-massachusetts-and-five-indian-tribes/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary, reporting a USDA announcement of 7 May 2020): "The Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida, the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska, Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes, Rosebud Sioux Tribe and the Pala Band of Mission Indians also had their plans newly accepted."
  • Source: https://www.bisnow.com/news/south-florida/economy/miccosukee-tribe-hemp-plan-104464 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary, 2020): "The Miccosukee Tribe of Indians, which controls more than 270,000 acres in and around the Florida Everglades, has won a key approval from the U.S. Department of Agriculture that opens the door to hemp production on tribal lands" and "On May 7, the USDA approved hemp production plans for five tribes, including the Miccosukee".

The Bisnow report further states (secondary, not the plan text itself) that the Tribe's application "signal[led] its 'formal intention to engage in the hemp business'", that "the tribe 'boasts a land mass sufficient for any proposed hemp endeavor'", and that "the application says the tribe would open certain lands within its jurisdiction for cultivation, processing and distribution of hemp and designate a hemp control officer to issue licenses and comply with laws." A further secondary summary of tribal plans states the Miccosukee plan "explicitly gives for functions [applications] by companies 'not owned by the Tribe or a Tribal member,' supplied they maintain an Indian trader license" and that the Miccosukee established "the place of hemp management officer (HCO)". Source: https://growstox.com/hemp-cbd-across-state-lines-tribal-plans/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary summary; the Miccosukee plan PDF itself was not opened in this run — [VERIFY], Gap P10-03). Those two details are therefore reported as secondary-plan-summary claims, not as quoted plan text, and must not be cited as the plan's operative language without opening the plan PDF linked from the USDA list.

What a tribal hemp plan does and does not do (federal framework). Under the 2018 Farm Act (Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018, Pub. L. 115-334, §10113, adding Subtitle G to the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946, 7 U.S.C. §§1639o–1639s) and USDA's final rule (7 CFR Part 990, effective 22 March 2021), a tribe with an approved plan has primary regulatory authority over hemp production in its territory. The final rule's territorial point is:

"a Tribe may exercise jurisdiction and therefore primary regulatory authority over all production of hemp in its Territory regardless of the extent of its inherent regulatory authority." — 7 CFR §990.4(b)(4), as summarised in secondary legal reporting: Source: https://Www.lippes.com/insights/usda-issues-final-rule-for-hemp-production-in-indian-country-1398 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary; the CFR text itself was not re-opened — [VERIFY] pinpoint, Gap P10-04).

Practical consequences, stated as analysis (not as quoted statute):

  • Hemp production on Miccosukee territory is governed by the Miccosukee tribal plan and USDA oversight, not by a FDACS cultivation licence under §581.217. A FDACS licence is the state-plan route; it is not the tribal-plan route.
  • That production authority does not by itself authorise marijuana production, and it does not by itself authorise the sale of hemp extract products in Florida outside tribal territory: a hemp extract product distributed or sold in the state must still meet §581.217(7) (COA, QR/barcode, batch, website, expiry, mg per serving — §10.2.4). Whether a tribal-plan producer selling off-territory is subject to FDACS food-establishment permitting in addition to the tribal plan is not resolved in any source opened in this run [VERIFY] (Gap P10-05). Do not assume either answer.
  • The Seminole Tribe of Florida, having no approved tribal plan on the USDA list, has no tribal-plan hemp production authority. If Seminole producers grew hemp, they would need a route under the Florida state plan (FDACS licence) or a USDA producer licence — and no such Seminole hemp licence was verified in this run either [UNAVAILABLE] (Gap P10-06). Note the contrast with the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma, which does hold an approved plan; that plan covers Oklahoma territory, not Florida.

Federal hemp-definition change and tribal plans. The fixed baseline (PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019, 12 November / 11 December 2026) changes the federal definition of hemp. A USDA-approved tribal plan does not insulate a producer from a changed federal definition: hemp that ceases to be federal hemp ceases to be producible under a Subtitle G plan. No USDA or Miccosukee statement on the 2026 federal hemp redefinition was located in this run [UNAVAILABLE] (Gap P10-07). This mirrors Run 1's finding for the state plan.

10.1.4 Seminole Tribe of Florida — gaming and tobacco, no verified cannabis

Who and where (general, secondary). The Seminole Tribe of Florida is a federally recognised tribe whose Florida reservations include Big Cypress, Brighton, Hollywood and Tampa (BIA-derived list, §10.1.2). It operates the Seminole Hard Rock casinos and hotels, including Seminole Hard Rock Hollywood and Seminole Hard Rock Tampa, and other casinos at Coconut Creek, Immokalee and Brighton (secondary casino reporting, §10.1.6). Those are gaming and hospitality businesses.

Marijuana: none verified. No Seminole tribal marijuana ordinance, tribal marijuana licence, tribal dispensary, or Seminole MMTC licence was located in this run. In particular:

  • The Seminole Tribe does not appear in the OMMU MMTC framework as a tribal licensee: §381.986 licences "medical marijuana treatment centers" through the Department of Health, with no tribal-licence category (Run 1, Part 4). No amendment creating one was found.
  • No Seminole cannabis brand, dispensary address, or tribal cannabis regulatory commission for Florida was verified. Search results for "Seminole Hard Rock cannabis dispensary" return unrelated businesses (a Tampa-area "Seminole Smoke Shop" — a tobacco shop — and dispensaries in Seminole, Oklahoma and Seminole, Texas), which are excluded here as same-name / out-of-state traps. The Tampa smoke shop result (Source: https://moovitapp.com/index/en/public_transit-Seminole_Smoke_Shop-TampaSt_Petersburg_FL-site_18165872-1345 — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary transit listing) evidences a tobacco smoke shop near the Seminole Hard Rock Tampa area; it does not evidence a cannabis dispensary, and no claim is made that it sells marijuana.
  • Tobacco smoking areas in Seminole casinos (designated casino-floor smoking areas) are tobacco policy, not cannabis policy. Secondary casino reporting states smoking is allowed in designated areas at Seminole Hard Rock Hollywood, Tampa, Coconut Creek, Classic Hollywood, Immokalee and Brighton. Source: https://www.casino.org/news/florida-tribal-casino-to-open-dedicated-smoking-room/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary). That reporting is about tobacco smoking privileges on sovereign land (Florida's Clean Air Act does not reach tribal enterprises in the same way); it says nothing about marijuana smoking, and marijuana smoking in a casino must not be inferred from it.

Hemp: none verified beyond the negative USDA finding. No Seminole hemp cultivation licence, hemp product, or hemp ordinance was verified. The Seminole Tribe's absence from the USDA tribal-plan list (§10.1.3) is the firmest fact; everything else about Seminole hemp is absence of evidence, reported as [UNAVAILABLE], not as proof that no Seminole member or Seminole-owned business anywhere sells a hemp product under the state regime (which would be indistinguishable in state records from any other FDACS permittee — see Gap P10-06).

10.1.5 Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida — hemp plan approved, no verified operating business

Who and where (general). The Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida is a federally recognised tribe based in the Everglades west of Miami. Its resort and casino are at 500 SW 177th Ave, Miami, FL 33194 (tribal casino's own public page, secondary for location only):

  • Source: https://miccosukee.com/about-us/ — Accessed 2026-10-24: "Miccosukee Casino & Resort … Located 17 miles west of Miami International Airport, on the edge of this scenic wetland ecosystem … 302 elegant guest rooms and suites … a high-stakes Bingo Hall, a 20-table Poker Room, over 1,800 slot machines". The same page states: "We remain a non-smoking facility. There will be designated smoking areas outside."

Marijuana: none verified. No Miccosukee tribal marijuana ordinance, dispensary, or MMTC licence was located. The Miccosukee casino's gaming offering is bingo-based (Class II) gaming — bingo hall, poker room, electronic bingo machines — plus a tobacco shop on the casino floor (secondary: https://www.casino.org/news/florida-tribal-casino-to-open-dedicated-smoking-room/ — Accessed 2026-10-24, which also reports a 2024 smoking room/bar and a Little Trail Casino at I-75 Exit 49 with electronic bingo machines, a gas station and convenience store). None of that is a cannabis operation. The casino's own non-smoking-facility statement above cuts against any inference of on-site marijuana consumption.

Hemp: plan yes, operating business not verified. The approved tribal plan (§10.1.3) is the only verified Miccosukee cannabis-related fact. Specifically not verified in this run:

  • No Miccosukee hemp farm, acreage, harvest, licence count, brand, product, or retail outlet was found in dated 2020–2026 reporting. The 2020 Bisnow report speaks of an "intention to engage in the hemp business" and land "sufficient for any proposed hemp endeavor" — prospective language, not an operating farm.
  • No Miccosukee hemp production figures appear in Run 1's FDACS/NASS hemp tables (Run 1, Part 6), which is expected: tribal-plan production would not be reported as FDACS state-plan production, and NASS state tables do not break out tribal-plan acres. Absence from those tables is therefore not evidence of zero production, and zero production is not asserted.
  • Whether the Miccosukee plan is still actively administered in 2026 (hemp control officer in post, licences issued, lots tested) is [UNAVAILABLE] (Gap P10-03). The USDA list shows the plan has not been withdrawn or revoked as of 17 February 2026, which is a weaker claim than "the Tribe is currently growing hemp" — and only the weaker claim is made here.

10.1.6 Legal framework between the tribes and the state, and gaming compacts

Florida Chapter 285 — Indian Affairs (official statute, opened via search extract). Florida Statutes Chapter 285, Part I (ss. 285.01–285.20) governs Indian affairs, including lands set aside, Seminole and Miccosukee reservation lands, and tribal councils as governing bodies. Source: https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2025/Chapter285/Part_I — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official Senate index page; individual sections below were confirmed from statute text as reproduced in search results — direct Online Sunshine re-open for §§285.16/285.165 is Gap P10-09, because the extracts used were from the 2003–2009 statute editions and a mirror).

The single most important provision for cannabis purposes is §285.16, quoted verbatim:

285.16 Civil and criminal jurisdiction; Indian reservation. — "(1) The State of Florida hereby assumes jurisdiction over criminal offenses committed by or against Indians or other persons within Indian reservations and over civil causes of actions between Indians or other persons or to which Indians or other persons are parties rising within Indian reservations. (2) The civil and criminal laws of Florida shall obtain on all Indian reservations in this state and shall be enforced in the same manner as elsewhere throughout the state. History. — ss. 1, 2, ch. 61-252."

Source: https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2003/285.16 (official Senate archive) and https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._285.16 (mirror, citing the 2024 statute page) — Accessed 2026-10-24. The provision dates to ch. 61-252 (1961); it is Florida's assumption of jurisdiction in the Public Law 280 mould. Its cannabis consequence, stated as analysis and flagged [VERIFY] for a cannabis-specific application (no Florida cannabis-on-reservation case was located, Gap P10-10):

  • On its face, §285.16(2) makes Florida's civil and criminal laws — including Chapter 893 (controlled substances) and §381.986's MMTC-only structure — applicable "on all Indian reservations in this state … in the same manner as elsewhere". That is a materially different starting point from states where the state has not assumed reservation jurisdiction. It means a tribe in Florida cannot simply be assumed to be outside state cannabis criminal law.
  • It does not follow that §285.16 alone decides every question: federal law (the CSA, the 2018 Farm Act's hemp framework, IGRA for gaming) still applies, tribal sovereignty and any applicable federal preemption still matter, and the Miccosukee tribal hemp plan is a federal approval that displaces the state plan for production in Miccosukee territory. The interaction of §285.16 with a USDA-approved tribal hemp plan, and with any hypothetical tribal marijuana ordinance, has not been litigated in any authority located in this run and is flagged [VERIFY], not resolved by assertion.

Other Chapter 285 provisions located, none touching cannabis:

  • §285.061 — transfer of state Indian reservation lands to the United States in trust for the Seminole and Miccosukee Tribes; subsection (3) reserves state civil and criminal jurisdiction "in accordance with ss. 285.16 and 285.165 and applicable federal law". Source: https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2001/285.061 — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • §285.165 — water rights compact with the Seminole Tribe (ratified, effective only on congressional approval; "the sole source of regulation of water use" on reservation and Tribal Trust lands once effective). This is a water compact. It is mentioned only to prevent confusion: Florida–Seminole "compacts" in Chapter 285 are not cannabis compacts.
  • §285.18 — tribal council as governing body; powers and duties. No cannabis power is stated in the section heading or in any extract located.

A failed attempt to carve Miccosukee out of §285.16 (proposed, not law). In 2003, SB 468 would have added a subsection (3) to §285.16 providing that subsections (1) and (2) "do not apply to Indian reservations of the Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida". Source: https://flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2003/468/BillText/Filed/PDF — Accessed 2026-10-24 (filed bill text, secondary for status). That bill did not become the current §285.16 text as reproduced above, and it is recorded here only as proposed history. It must not be cited as current law.

Seminole gaming compact 2021 — opened, searched, no cannabis provision. The Tribal-State Gaming Compact between the Seminole Tribe of Florida and the State of Florida (2021), as published by the BIA with the Department of the Interior's 11 August 2021 review letter, was opened directly in this run:

  • Source: https://www.bia.gov/sites/bia.gov/files/assets/as-ia/oig/pdf/508%20Compliant%202021.08.11%20Seminole%20Tribe%20Gaming%20Compact.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24 (BIA-hosted compact PDF, 4,234 lines as rendered).

Finds in that document:

  • The Interior letter (5 August 2021, 45th day) states the compact was "considered to have been approved by operation of law to the extent that it complies with IGRA and existing Federal law" after the Department took no action to approve or disapprove. IGRA is the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, 25 U.S.C. §2701 et seq.
  • "Covered Game" is defined (Compact Part III.F, as summarised in the Interior letter) as "slot machines, raffles and drawings, table games, fantasy sports contests, sports betting, and any new game authorized by Florida law for any person for any purpose." The letter's game list is: slot machines; raffles and drawings; banked card games (baccarat, chemin de fer, blackjack); plus new games craps, roulette, sports betting (including mobile), and fantasy sports contests if authorised by future legislation (Part III.F.3–5, L, FF, CC).
  • Text searches of the opened compact document for "cannabis" and for "marijuana" returned no matches. No cannabis, marijuana, hemp, MMTC, or medical-marijuana provision was located in the compact. The compact's subject is Class III gaming under IGRA; cannabis is not a "Covered Game" and no cannabis revenue-sharing, licensing, or exclusivity provision appears in it. (Caveat: the search was over the document as rendered by the text-fetch tool; a differently-rendered copy could in principle contain a scanned-image passage — Gap P10-11 — but no cannabis provision is asserted on that basis.)
  • The compact's exclusivity exceptions (Part XII.B) include, as exception (i), "Any Class III Gaming or other Casino-Style Gaming authorized by a compact between the State and any other federally recognized tribe under IGRA, provided that the Tribe has land in trust as of January 2, 2021" — a gaming provision that would in principle cover a future Miccosukee or Poarch Class III compact, but it says nothing about cannabis.

Miccosukee gaming compact — none. The Miccosukee Tribe has not entered into a revenue-sharing Class III gaming compact with Florida; it operates bingo-based (Class II) gaming and retains 100% of its gaming revenue. Source: https://www.casino.org/news/florida-tribal-casino-to-open-dedicated-smoking-room/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary). There is therefore no Miccosukee gaming compact that could contain a cannabis provision, and none was found. The Miccosukee's gaming position is sometimes described as operating without a compact; that description is secondary and its IGRA classification (Class II vs Class III) is [VERIFY] for legal purposes (Gap P10-12), but the negative cannabis finding does not turn on it: with no compact document, there is no compact cannabis clause to quote.

No tribal–state cannabis agreement of any kind was located. No Florida–Seminole or Florida–Miccosukee agreement, memorandum, or compact on marijuana cultivation, dispensing, taxation, or enforcement was found in this run [UNAVAILABLE]. That includes no tax-sharing agreement of the kind some states have struck with tribes for cannabis (none is asserted for Florida, and none should be inferred from the gaming revenue-sharing figures, which concern gaming Net Win, not cannabis).

Tribal sovereignty — what it does and does not mean here (framework, not a Florida holding). Tribes are sovereign governments within the U.S. federal system, and Indian lands held in trust are subject to a distinct federal framework (tribal self-government, federal trust responsibility, IGRA for gaming, Subtitle G for hemp production). Sovereignty does not, on its own, authorise conduct that federal law prohibits: adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I federally under the fixed baseline, and state-licensed medical marijuana's Schedule III status is defined by reference to state licensing. Whether a hypothetical tribal-licensed medical marijuana operation would fall within the federal Schedule III medical category — which the baseline describes as "state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana" — is not resolved in any authority located in this run and is flagged [VERIFY] (Gap P10-13). It must not be assumed that tribal medical marijuana automatically receives the same federal treatment as Florida MMTC medical marijuana, nor assumed that it does not. Likewise, whether a tribal marijuana ordinance would survive §285.16, federal CSA enforcement, or both, is unlitigated in Florida on the authorities found and is not answered here.

10.1.7 Method note for the negative findings

Negative findings ("no operation found") rest on: (a) directly opening the USDA plan list (§10.1.3) and confirming the presence/absence pattern; (b) opening the BIA Seminole compact PDF and searching it for "cannabis"/"marijuana"; (c) web searches for each tribe + cannabis/marijuana/hemp/ordinance/dispensary, and for each tribe's casino + cannabis/marijuana policy; (d) checking Run 1's MMTC and FDACS inventories, which contain no tribal licensee. A negative search result is not proof that no tribal document exists anywhere (tribal codes are not always published online, and neither tribe's code was located in this run — Gap P10-14). The correct reading of this section is: no verified tribal cannabis/marijuana operation, ordinance, or agreement was located through official and public sources in this run — not "the tribes have certified they have none".

10.2 Interstate issues

10.2.1 Hemp shipments — federal protection, Florida plant-material rules, and the destination-sale distinction

Federal rule, quoted verbatim. The 2018 Farm Act's interstate-commerce provision (§10114, adding §297D-type language; now reflected in 7 CFR §990.63) provides:

"No State or Indian Tribe may prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp lawfully produced under a State or Tribal plan approved under subpart B of this part, under a license issued under subpart C of this part, or under 7 U.S.C. 5940 through the State or territory of the Indian Tribe, as applicable."

Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/7/990.63 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (Cornell LII reproduction of 7 CFR §990.63). The Farm Act's own wording, as reproduced in the conference report, is to the same effect:

"No State or Indian Tribe shall prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp or hemp products produced in accordance with subtitle G of the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 (as added by section 10113) through the State or the territory of the Indian Tribe, as applicable."

Source: https://www.hemp.com/hemp-university/states-allowing-hemp-farming/2018-farm-bill-hemp-in-the-united-states/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary reproduction of the Farm Act text; the operative federal text for citation purposes is 7 CFR §990.63 above and 7 U.S.C. §1639o note).

Three limits on that protection, each important for Florida:

  1. It protects hemp "lawfully produced" under an approved plan / USDA licence / §5940 pilot. Hemp produced outside Subtitle G, hemp that tests over 0.3% total delta-9, and (after the baseline dates) hemp that ceases to be federal hemp under PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019, are outside the protection. A shipment's paperwork must therefore prove lawful production, not merely assert that the cargo "is hemp".
  2. It is a transportation / through-shipment protection, not a destination-sale licence. Nothing in §990.63 prohibits a destination state from applying its own product, labelling, food-safety, age, and retail rules to hemp products sold in that state. Florida's §581.217(7) distribution/sale rules (§10.2.4) are destination-sale rules, not a transportation ban, and are not displaced by §990.63 on any authority located.
  3. It does not cover marijuana. Marijuana (including adult-use marijuana, and hemp that has lost federal hemp status) has no §990.63 protection at all (§10.2.2).

Florida's own hemp-movement rules — Rule 5B-57.014, opened directly. Florida Administrative Code Rule 5B-57.014 (State Hemp Program) was opened directly in this run (Cornell LII reproduction of the Florida rule):

  • Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/florida/Fla-Admin-Code-Ann-R-5B-57-014 — Accessed 2026-10-24.

Operative provisions, quoted verbatim in substance (line breaks normalised):

  • General prohibition and retail-packaging carve-out — Rule 5B-57.014(3):

    "It is unlawful for any Person to introduce into this state or move through this state the propagative parts of hemp, live hemp plants, Processed hemp plant material, or Unprocessed hemp plant material unless introduced or moved in compliance with this rule. This prohibition does not apply to products containing Hemp extract purchased, sold, and transported in retail packaging."

Note the scope carefully: the prohibition covers plant material (propagative parts, live plants, processed and unprocessed plant material). Retail-packaged hemp extract products are carved out of this paragraph — but they remain subject to §581.217(7) when distributed or sold in Florida (§10.2.4). The carve-out is not a general exemption for bulk extract, biomass, or flower in non-retail packaging [VERIFY against the current flrules.org text — the Cornell reproduction is used here and its currency date is not stated on the page, Gap P10-15].

  • THC test — Rule 5B-57.014(2)(i): "'Total delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol concentration' means [delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol] + (0.877 x [tetrahydrocannabinolic acid])." And (2)(a): "'Acceptable THC level' means that the representative sample has a Total delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol concentration that does not exceed 0.3% on a dry-weight basis." This confirms Run 1's 0.877 factor and 0.3% test from the rule text itself.

  • Intrastate movement — Rule 5B-57.014(11)(a). Any person transporting propagative parts, live plants, processed or unprocessed plant material within Florida shall:

  • "Transport in a fully enclosed vehicle or container when being moved between noncontiguous locations."
  • "Have in their possession a bill of lading or proof of ownership, documentation showing the name, physical address, Lot designation number, and license number of the originating licensed cultivator, and the name and physical address of the recipient of the delivery when transporting between non-contiguous locations."

  • "Stop and submit for inspection while passing any official agricultural inspection station pursuant to Section 570.15, F.S."

  • Interstate movement INTO Florida — Rule 5B-57.014(11)(b). "Any Person outside the State of Florida who desires to ship into this state propagative parts of hemp, live hemp plants, Processed hemp plant material, and Unprocessed hemp plant material from any state, U.S. possession, territory, or district of the United States, or foreign jurisdiction, shall comply with the following regulations":

  • Propagative parts / live plants are prohibited unless: (a) "Maintained and shipped in a soilless growing media, sterile growing media, or sterile environment"; and (b) "Accompanied by proof of origin with hemp cultivation license number, or equivalent, from the jurisdiction of origin and an original phytosanitary certificate of inspection issued by a state or country plant protection governmental agency."
  • Unprocessed plant material is prohibited unless: (a) "Accompanied by proof of origin with a hemp cultivation license number, or equivalent, from the jurisdiction of origin"; (b) "Accompanied by a certificate of analysis showing that the Unprocessed hemp plant material has an Acceptable THC level"; and (c) "Transported frozen or dried."
  • Processed plant material is prohibited unless: (a) "The Processed hemp plant material has been rendered non-viable through processing"; (b) "Accompanied by proof of origin with a hemp cultivation license number, or equivalent, from the jurisdiction of origin"; and (c) "Accompanied by a certificate of analysis showing that the Processed hemp plant material has an Acceptable THC level."
  • On entry, intrastate rules apply: "Upon entry in the state, all Persons transporting propagative parts of hemp, live hemp plants, Processed hemp plant material, and Unprocessed hemp plant material must comply with the intrastate movement requirements outlined in this rule" (i.e. enclosed vehicle/container, bill of lading / proof of ownership with originator name, address, lot and licence number and recipient name/address, and agricultural inspection-station stops under §570.15).

No separate "interstate movement OUT OF Florida" paragraph appears in Rule 5B-57.014(11) as opened: paragraph (11)(b) governs shipment into Florida, and paragraph (11)(a) governs movement within Florida. A Florida licensee shipping plant material out of Florida must therefore comply with (a) while in Florida, with the destination state's import rules on arrival, and with the federal §990.63 through-shipment protection for the transit legs — and must not assume Florida's (11)(b) import conditions are the outbound conditions. The absence of an outbound paragraph is noted, not filled in [VERIFY against flrules.org current text, Gap P10-15].

  • What the rule does not require (on its face). Rule 5B-57.014(11) as opened does not impose a Florida "hemp transport licence" or a pre-notification filing for plant-material shipments beyond the documents listed (bill of lading / proof of ownership, proof of origin with licence number, phytosanitary certificate where required, COA where required, and inspection-station stops). Secondary practical guidance (e.g. "drivers should carry copies of the hemp license, bills of lading, cargo manifests, and lab test results") is consistent with the rule but is not the rule; it is not cited as a legal requirement here. Source for that secondary guidance only: https://legalclarity.org/florida-hemp-license-application-and-requirements/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary; not used for any legal proposition in this Part).

Practical shipment checklist (derived strictly from the authorities above — not a new rule):

Shipment Federal protection Florida documents / conditions on entry
Lawfully produced hemp plant material shipped through Florida to another state §990.63: Florida "may not prohibit" through-transport While in Florida, (11)(a) intrastate conditions apply on the Florida leg (enclosed vehicle/container between noncontiguous locations, bill of lading/proof of ownership, inspection-station stops) — the through-shipment protection is not a documentation waiver
Hemp plant material shipped into Florida for Florida use/sale §990.63 does not waive destination-state import rules (11)(b) category conditions above (phytosanitary certificate for live/propagative; COA + frozen/dried for unprocessed; non-viable + COA for processed), plus (11)(a) on entry
Retail-packaged hemp extract products shipped into Florida for sale §990.63 (hemp products) for transport; destination-sale rules still apply §581.217(7): COA, QR/barcode linked to COA, batch number, website, expiry, mg per serving; 21+ for ingestion/inhalation (Run 1); FDACS food-establishment permitting for the Florida seller/processor as applicable (Run 1, Part 7 topic — not decided here)
Hemp that tests >0.3% total delta-9, or that loses federal hemp status under PL 119-37/119-103 None — outside §990.63 Treated as cannabis/marijuana under Chapter 893 and §381.986 framework; see §10.2.2. Do not ship as "hemp".

10.2.2 What can legally be brought into Florida — marijuana: no; hemp: only if compliant

Marijuana — import is an offence, and MMTCs are the sole lawful source. FDLE's medical-marijuana enforcement guidance states the Florida position directly (official FDLE document):

"Medical marijuana treatment centers licensed by the Florida Department of Health (DOH) are the sole source for medical marijuana. Bringing medical or recreational marijuana from another state into Florida violates s. 893.13, F.S., and Florida has no reciprocity agreements with other states. So tourists, for example, authorized to possess and use medical marijuana in their home state, could be charged under section 893.13 for bringing it to Florida."

Source: https://www.fdle.state.fl.us/getContentAsset/dc941cd4-f649-4c61-99a8-337faeef1fa0/73aabf56-e6e5-4330-95a3-5f2a270a1d2b/TM-2019-03-MedicalMarijuanaUpdates-final3-signedPkt.pdf?language=en — Accessed 2026-10-24 (FDLE, "Medical Marijuana Updates", TM-2019-03; 2019 guidance, still the clearest official statement located — whether FDLE has reissued it for Schedule III is [VERIFY], Gap P10-16, but no contrary FDLE statement was found and the underlying statute has not gained a reciprocity or import provision).

The same guidance confirms the closed-system points that Run 1 states:

"Medical marijuana must be (1) authorized by a physician Certification and (2) acquired from a Department of Health licensed medical marijuana treatment center." "A person or entity that cultivates, processes, distributes, sells, or dispenses marijuana and is not licensed as a medical marijuana treatment center violates s. 893.13, F.S."

And, on possession of non-MMTC product:

"While possessing up to 4 ounces of marijuana for medical use is legal, possessing cannabis seeds or entire plants, whether growing or harvested, is still illegal under s. 893.13, F.S." and "Possession of a food item containing marijuana that didn't come from a treatment center is still illegal under s. 893.13, F.S." (the "4 ounces" figure is FDLE's 2019 summary of the then possession framework; Run 1's current supply framework — 70-day / 35-day dispensing caps and possession caps — governs over any summary figure and is not displaced by this quote).

Statutory import offence. Florida Statutes §893.13(5) prohibits bringing a controlled substance into Florida (secondary summaries of the section describe importation of cannabis without a state importation licence as a third-degree felony, up to 5 years / $5,000; the trafficking provision §893.135(1)(a) separately covers knowingly bringing into the state more than 25 lb of cannabis or 300+ plants as a first-degree trafficking felony). Sources (secondary summaries of the statutes, used only to locate the provisions — the statute text itself was not re-opened in this Part and its current pinpoint is [VERIFY], Gap P10-17):

  • https://theorlandocriminaldefense.com/drug-charges-in-florida/importation-smuggling-cannabis-marijuana/ — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • https://www.goldmanwetzel.com/blog/florida-marijuana-laws-and-penalties/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (quoting §893.135(1)(a) trafficking language).

Run 1's penalty table (§1.3) is the controlling statement of penalties in this dossier and is not repeated in full here; the import point adds only that crossing the state line with the product is itself within §893.13/§893.135, not merely possession after arrival.

Federal overlay. Marijuana remains federally controlled: adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I under the fixed baseline, and state-licensed medical marijuana's Schedule III status does not create a federal right to transport marijuana across state lines. No federal statute, regulation, or guidance located in this run authorises interstate marijuana commerce, interstate MMTC delivery, or a patient carrying marijuana between states — even between two medical states, and even for a Florida patient travelling out of Florida. A Florida patient's MMUR card has no legal force outside Florida; whether another state honours it is governed by that state's law, not Florida's, and no Florida agreement secures such honours (§10.2.6). Mailing marijuana is not a lawful workaround: it combines the state import/delivery offences with federal controlled-substance offences, and no lawful mail route for marijuana was located [UNAVAILABLE for any contrary authority — none is asserted].

Hemp — what may be brought in. The mirror image of the marijuana rule:

  • Hemp plant material meeting the federal definition and Florida's 0.3% total delta-9 test, with the Rule 5B-57.014(11)(b) documents for its category, may be shipped into Florida (§10.2.1).
  • Retail-packaged hemp extract products meeting §581.217(7) may be distributed and sold in Florida (§10.2.4).
  • Hemp that exceeds 0.3% total delta-9, hemp extract products without the §581.217(7) COA/labelling package, and — after the baseline dates — products that lose federal hemp status under PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019, may not be brought in as "hemp". The dual-compliance warning from Run 1 applies with full force at the border: a product lawful in its origin state (for example, a higher-THC hemp product lawful where made) is not thereby lawful in Florida, and a product meeting Florida's 0.3% test but failing the new federal test is federally unlawful even if Florida has not yet amended §581.217.

Seeds and plants — a specific trap. FDLE's guidance (above) treats possessing cannabis seeds or entire plants as illegal under §893.13 even for a medical patient, and Rule 5B-57.014(11)(b) separately gates hemp propagative parts and live plants behind sterile/soilless media, proof of origin with licence number, and a phytosanitary certificate. A traveller carrying seeds, clones, or live plants across the Florida line therefore faces two distinct regimes (marijuana prohibition; hemp plant-material import conditions) and satisfies neither by holding a medical card from another state. Do not advise that seeds or clones are a "personal" exception — none was located.

10.2.3 Out-of-state visitors and patients — no reciprocity, one narrow pathway

The rule (Run 1, restated, now with FDLE corroboration). Florida does not recognise out-of-state medical marijuana cards, certifications, or recommendations as authority to purchase from an MMTC, to possess marijuana in Florida, or to use marijuana in Florida. There is no temporary visitor card, no visitor registration, and no reciprocity agreement. FDLE states it in terms: "Florida has no reciprocity agreements with other states" (§10.2.2). Secondary summaries agree unanimously on this point (e.g. https://legalclarity.org/does-florida-accept-out-of-state-medical-cards/ — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary; https://www.mmtcfl.com/blog/does-florida-honor-other-states-medical-marijuana-cards/ — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary) — but the legal proposition rests on §381.986 itself (no reciprocity clause; "qualified patient" = Florida resident in the MMUR) and on FDLE, not on those summaries.

The seasonal-resident pathway — the only out-of-state route, and it is a Florida route. A person who is not a permanent Florida resident may still become a Florida qualified patient only if they meet the statutory "seasonal resident" test and then complete the full Florida process (Run 1, §§1.4.3, 1.4.5):

  • "Seasonal resident" means a person who temporarily resides in Florida for at least 31 consecutive days per calendar year, maintains a temporary residence, returns to the home jurisdiction at least once per calendar year, and is registered to vote or pays income tax elsewhere (§381.986(5)(b)3.).
  • Seasonal residents who cannot prove residency with a Florida driver licence or ID card may prove it with two documents from the statutory list (deed/mortgage/lease; co-resident proof + statement; utility hookup/work order within 60 days; utility bill ≤2 months old; financial-institution mail ≤2 months old; government-agency mail ≤2 months old; or other Department-rule documentation) (§381.986(5)(b)).
  • Even a qualifying seasonal resident must still: be seen in person by a Florida qualified physician for the initial certification (Run 1: initial exam must be in person; renewals by the same physician may be telehealth), be added to the MMUR, and hold a Florida MMUR ID card (Run 1: $75 fee as OMMU practice, not statute — [VERIFY] direct OMMU page, Run 1 Gap G-09, carried forward as P10-08).
  • A short visit, a vacation, a hotel stay under 31 consecutive days, or a home-state card plus a Florida address, does not meet the test. A seasonal resident who meets the test but has not yet completed the Florida process has no interim right to possess marijuana brought from home.

Consequences for a visitor who possesses marijuana in Florida without a Florida card. Run 1's penalty table applies in full: ≤20 g, 1st-degree misdemeanour (up to 1 year / $1,000); >20 g, 3rd-degree felony (up to 5 years / $5,000); trafficking thresholds above 25 lb / 300 plants; and local civil-citation ordinances (Run 1, Part 3) are discretionary, locality-specific, and do not create a defence under state law or a right to possess. An out-of-state card is not a defence in any of those proceedings on any authority located. Immigration consequences for non-citizen visitors are outside this Part's scope and are not addressed [UNAVAILABLE — no Florida-specific authority was sought on that point].

Florida patients travelling out of Florida. The converse is equally closed: a Florida MMUR card does not authorise purchase, possession, or use in another state unless that state's law says so, and it does not authorise transporting Florida MMTC marijuana across a state line (federal law and the destination state's law both stand in the way). No Florida statute purports to export Florida patient rights, and no interstate patient agreement was located (§10.2.6). A Florida patient who needs continuity of care while travelling must check the destination state's visitor/reciprocity rules in advance; in a no-reciprocity state, the lawful options are to qualify under that state's own process (if available to visitors) or to go without — carrying Florida product across the line is not one of them.

Schedule III does not create reciprocity. The fixed baseline's Schedule III move for state-licensed medical marijuana changes the federal scheduling and (generally) the §280E posture of state-licensed medical activity. It does not impose cross-state recognition of medical cards, does not amend §381.986's residency definition, and does not authorise interstate transport. No federal reciprocity statute or regulation was located in this run [UNAVAILABLE for any contrary authority — none is asserted]. This is stated expressly because it is the most likely misreading of the 2026 federal change in a travel context.

10.2.4 Hemp extract products shipped into Florida — destination-state rules

Hemp extract (as distinct from hemp plant material, §10.2.1) shipped into Florida for distribution or sale must meet §581.217(7), as summarised in Run 1 and confirmed in the statute extract opened in this run:

  • Source: https://flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2025/Chapter581/All — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official Senate chapter page, via search extract for §581.217(7); direct Online Sunshine re-open is Gap P10-18, as Run 1 also relied on extracts for parts of this section).

Under §581.217(7)(a), hemp extract may only be distributed and sold in the state if the product:

  1. Has a certificate of analysis prepared by an independent testing laboratory stating: (a) the extract is the product of a batch tested by that laboratory; (b) the batch contained a total delta-9-THC concentration that did not exceed 0.3 percent pursuant to testing of a random sample of the batch; (c) the batch does not contain contaminants unsafe for human consumption; and (d) the batch was processed in a facility holding a current and valid permit from a human-health or food-safety regulatory entity with authority over the facility, meeting that entity's sanitisation requirements, documented by a report from that entity confirming compliance; and
  2. Is distributed or sold in a container that includes: (a) a scannable barcode or QR code linked to the batch COA by an independent testing laboratory; (b) the batch number; (c) the internet address of a website where batch information may be obtained; (d) the expiration date; and (e) the number of milligrams of each marketed cannabinoid per serving.

Run 1's further hemp-product rules apply equally to shipped-in product once it is sold in Florida: 21+ for ingestion/inhalation products (2nd-degree misdemeanour, 1st on a repeat within 1 year — Run 1, Part 1), child-resistant / non-child-appealing packaging, and FDACS stop-sale enforcement for mislabelled or child-attractive product (Run 1, Part 1, §1.5). No per-serving or per-container mg cap exists in current Florida law (Run 1) — but that is a Florida statement, and after 11 December 2026 the federal 0.4 mg total THC per container cap will apply to federal hemp status (§10.2.5). A shipped-in product must therefore be checked against both regimes, not merely against the looser of the two.

No Florida hemp "import licence" for extract products was located. Rule 5B-57.014(11)(b)'s import conditions are written for plant material (propagative parts, live plants, processed/unprocessed plant material). No parallel FDACS import permit for retail-packaged hemp extract was located in this run [UNAVAILABLE] (Gap P10-19). The failed 2025 bill HB 7027 would have created out-of-state delivery permits for hemp — it died and is not law (Run 1, Part 1) — which confirms that no such permit regime currently exists to be complied with. Do not invent one.

10.2.5 The 11 December 2026 federal hemp change — interstate consequences

This is the highest-risk interstate item in this Part, and it restates Run 1's dual-compliance warning in interstate terms:

  • 12 November 2026: under PL 119-37 §781 as limited by PL 119-103 §2019, federal hemp status is lost first for products containing cannabinoids "not capable of being naturally produced" by the plant (final and intermediate products). Those products become federal marijuana on that date (per the Congressional Research Service summary reported secondarily in Run 1's research trail).
  • 11 December 2026: the balance of §781 takes effect — the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg combined total THC (and similarly acting cannabinoids) per container cap for final products, with a 0.3% limit for intermediate products.
  • Interstate consequence: after those dates, a hemp product that is lawful in its origin state but exceeds the federal cap, or contains a non-naturally-producible or out-of-plant-synthesised cannabinoid, loses §990.63 through-shipment protection (it is no longer "hemp lawfully produced" under Subtitle G) and cannot lawfully be shipped into or through Florida as hemp. Conversely, a product meeting the new federal cap but exceeding Florida's 0.3% total delta-9 test remains unlawful in Florida.
  • No Florida, Miccosukee, or Seminole response was located. No FDACS guidance, no Florida statute amendment, no Miccosukee plan amendment, and no Seminole position on PL 119-37 / PL 119-103 was found in this run [UNAVAILABLE] — the same gap Run 1 recorded for the state (Run 1 Gap G-04), now extended to the tribal plans. The USDA list (17 February 2026) predates the operative dates and says nothing about them. This Part therefore makes no prediction about post-December enforcement; it records only that the legal basis for shipping the affected products as "hemp" will have changed, and that shippers must re-check both the federal definition and §581.217 / Rule 5B-57.014 after 11 December 2026.

10.2.6 Interstate laws and agreements — marijuana: none; hemp: federal framework only

Marijuana interstate agreements: none found. No Florida law, interstate compact, memorandum of understanding, or reciprocity agreement authorising interstate marijuana commerce, interstate MMTC delivery, interstate patient recognition, or interstate licence recognition was located in this run [UNAVAILABLE for any such instrument — none is asserted]. This includes:

  • No Florida–other-state medical reciprocity agreement (FDLE: "Florida has no reciprocity agreements with other states").
  • No Florida interstate cannabis commerce law of the kind enacted (in trigger form) by some adult-use states, and no such law could operate in Florida in any event while Florida has no adult-use programme and adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I federally.
  • No tribal–state marijuana agreement (§10.1.6).
  • No MMTC delivery across a state line: Run 1's delivery rules are intra-Florida (patient delivery with seed-to-sale manifests, in-premises dispensing barred 9pm–7am, delivery allowed 24 hours — Run 1, Part 1). Nothing in §381.986 authorises delivery to a patient outside Florida, and the FDLE sole-source rule (§10.2.2) points the other way.

Secondary sources agree with the negative finding in general terms (e.g. https://www.stateregstoday.com/health/marijuana-legalization/cross-border-issues-in-florida — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary: "Currently, there are no known interstate agreements or compacts related to cannabis trade involving Florida. The state does not have any legal provisions for the import or export of cannabis products across state lines."), but the finding here rests on the absence of any such instrument in the Florida Statutes as researched in Run 1 and in this Part's searches, not on that summary alone.

Hemp interstate agreements: federal framework only, no Florida-specific instrument found. The operative interstate hemp framework is federal, not bilateral:

  • 2018 Farm Act §§10113–10114 (Subtitle G; interstate commerce / transportation protection);
  • 7 CFR Part 990, including §990.63 (interstate transportation) and the state/tribal plan approval system (Subpart B) / USDA producer licensing (Subpart C);
  • Florida's state plan (FDACS, §581.217, Rule 5B-57.014) and the Miccosukee tribal plan (USDA-approved) as the two Florida-territory production regimes;
  • Florida's Rule 5B-57.014(11) import conditions for plant material and §581.217(7) destination-sale conditions for extract.

No Florida-specific bilateral hemp agreement with another state, and no Florida–tribal hemp agreement beyond the federal plan-approval system itself, was located [UNAVAILABLE]. In particular, there is no Florida–Miccosukee hemp agreement to quote: the Miccosukee plan is an agreement with USDA (plan approval), not a compact with Florida. Likewise, no agreement governs hemp movement between Florida and the Seminole Tribe of Florida, because the Seminole Tribe holds no tribal hemp plan.

What a future agreement would need to address (forward-looking, not law). If Florida, another state, or a Florida tribe ever sought a lawful interstate marijuana arrangement, it would need, at minimum: a federal authorisation or a change in federal scheduling that permits interstate marijuana commerce (adult-use remains Schedule I under the baseline; medical Schedule III status is tied to state licensing and does not itself authorise interstate commerce); a Florida statute amending §381.986's closed MMTC system and residency rule; and, for tribal territory, a tribal ordinance plus a federal/tribal-state framework addressing §285.16. None of those exists as of 24 October 2026. This paragraph is analysis of what is missing, not a proposal, and no bill or initiative to that effect was located in this run.
