11.1.2 What must be tested — statute (verbatim core)

"Test the processed marijuana using a medical marijuana testing laboratory before it is dispensed. Results must be verified and signed by two medical marijuana treatment center employees. Before dispensing, the medical marijuana treatment center must determine that the test results indicate that low-THC cannabis meets the definition of low-THC cannabis, the concentration of tetrahydrocannabinol meets the potency requirements of this section, the labeling of the concentration of tetrahydrocannabinol and cannabidiol is accurate, and all marijuana is safe for human consumption and free from contaminants that are unsafe for human consumption. The department shall determine by rule which contaminants must be tested for and the maximum levels of each contaminant which are safe for human consumption." — §381.986(8)(e)11.d., Fla. Stat. Source: https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._381.986 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (mirror of the statute; Run 1 read the Online Sunshine text directly).

  • The Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services assists in developing the testing requirements for contaminants unsafe for human consumption in edibles (same paragraph). FDACS and the Department of Environmental Protection assist in developing the §381.988 certification standards (§381.988(3)).
  • Sample retention (statute-adjacent rule): the Rule 64-4.210 fine schedule penalises "Failure to reserve two processed samples from each marijuana batch and to retain such samples for at least nine (9) months" (§381.986(8)(e)11.d.) at $500–$1,000 per violation. Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/florida/64/64/chapter-64-4/section-64-4-210/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (Justia reproduction of the FAC rule; the 9-month figure is a rule-schedule statement, not a verbatim statute quote).
  • Testing panels (rule level, by product type). The former emergency Rule 64-4.016 (2019 draft, retained in the permanent-series structure as Rules 64-4.306/64-4.308) lists, for usable whole flower, derivative products and edibles, testing for: (a) microbiology; (b) mycotoxins; (c) residual solvents; (d) metals; (e) pesticides; (f) water activity; (g) moisture; (h) filth and foreign material; and (i) cannabinoid potency. Source: 2019 draft Rule 64-4.016 text via https://s27415.pcdn.co/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/DRAFT-2019-04-03-Rule-64-4.016-Marijuana-Testing-Laboratory-Certification-and-Renewal.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24. Caution: that panel list is from the 2019 draft; the current permanent Rule 64-4.308 panel list was not opened in full in this run, so the panel above is carried as the best-evidenced panel, not as a verbatim quote of the current rule [VERIFY — Gap P11-05].
  • 2026 panel changes (secondary summary of the March 2026 rule change, flagged). A laboratory compliance summary of the 2026 CMTL rule changes (ACS Laboratory, "What Florida MMTCs Need to Know for 2026", undated in the extract but describing the 2026 changes) reports three changes under Rule 64-4.308 (CMTL Sample Testing) and Rule 64-4.311 (CMTL Certificate of Analysis): (1) residual-solvent testing now applies to usable whole flower marijuana (including mechanically separated trichomes such as kief, bubble hash and pressed rosin), not only to derivative products; (2) heavy-metals testing expanded from four metals to six, adding nickel and tin to arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury, with CMTLs to report nickel and tin on regulatory compliance COAs within 60 days of the rule's effective date and add both to their ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation scope at the next renewal/scope update; (3) Listeria monocytogenes added to the required microbiological panel for usable whole-flower marijuana and edibles; and (4) regulatory compliance COAs must now carry an expiration date of one year or less from the sample date, unless a qualifying stability study under FDA Guidance for Industry Q1A(R2) supports a longer date. Source: https://www.acslab.com/compliance/what-florida-mmtcs-need-to-know-for-2026-compliance-testing-and-emerging-rules — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary, industry source; the COA-expiry point is corroborated by the 2 March 2026 FAR change notice extract for Rule 64-4.311, which states the same one-year-or-less rule — see the FAR document at https://flrules.org/Faw/FAWDocuments/FAWVOLUMEFOLDERS2026/5241/5241doc.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24). The nickel/tin and Listeria points rest on the secondary summary alone and are [VERIFY] against the adopted Rule 64-4.308 text. Numeric action limits (maximum levels) for each contaminant were not located in this run [UNAVAILABLE — Gap P11-05].

11.1.3 Sampling — who samples, what, and when

"An MMTC must contact a Certified Marijuana Testing Laboratory (CMTL) and arrange for the CMTL to select and collect a random and representative sample of Final Product from every Retail Batch for regulatory compliance testing from an MMTC's department-approved processing facility or department-approved fulfillment and storage facility." — Rule 64-4.212(2), F.A.C. (new 20 December 2021). "All Final Products must pass regulatory compliance testing as provided in the CMTL Sample Testing rule prior to being transported by an MMTC to a dispensing facility and prior to being dispensed to a qualified patient or caregiver." — Rule 64-4.212(3). Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/florida/64/64/chapter-64-4/section-64-4-212/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (Justia reproduction, "Current through Reg. 51, No. 122; June 24, 2025").

  • Key points: the CMTL, not the MMTC, selects and collects the sample; the sample must be random and representative; every Retail Batch is sampled; testing is a pre-transport and pre-dispensing gate, not a post-sale check.
  • An MMTC may also request testing at any point during cultivation or processing, but that does not exempt it from regulatory compliance testing before dispensing (Rule 64-4.212(7)). The MMTC bears the costs of resampling and retesting a previously failed Retail Batch (Rule 64-4.212(8)).
  • Chain of custody / rejection (former Rule 64-4.016 structure, carried forward in the permanent series as Rule 64-4.307, CMTL Submission for Product Testing): samples must be accompanied by a sample field log, chain-of-custody documentation and a travel manifest; a sample without them, with a forged/altered log or manifest, or not initially collected/acquired from an MMTC by a sampler, must be rejected; rejected samples are not returned to the MMTC, must be held at least three months before destruction, and are logged with the reason; a rejected sample is not treated as a failed test, and the originating MMTC may have the processed batch resampled and analysed. A CMTL may transfer a testing sample to another CMTL in Florida, subject to the §381.986(8)(g) transport requirements and the receiving lab's acceptance/rejection procedure. Source: former Rule 64-4.016 draft text — Accessed 2026-10-24 (draft; current Rule 64-4.307 text [VERIFY — Gap P11-05]).
  • Hemp testing contrast (do not conflate): hemp extract may only be distributed/sold in Florida if it has a certificate of analysis from an independent testing laboratory (no direct/indirect interest in the tested entity or in any hemp/marijuana cultivator/processor/distributor/dispenser/seller, and ISO/IEC 17025-accredited, §581.217(3)(g)) stating the batch's total delta-9-THC did not exceed 0.3% on a random sample and the batch contains no contaminants unsafe for human consumption (§581.217(7)(a), Run 1 §1.5). Hemp labs on the USDA DEA-registered list (AccuScience, ACS, ACT, Atlas Labs FL, Product Development Partners, US Pharma — Run 1 Part 5) are a different authorisation from OMMU CMTL certification, even where names overlap.

11.1.4 Failed tests, retesting, remediation, and disposal — the complete decision tree

Step 1 — the 14-day election (contaminant failures). Rule 64-4.212(4):

"Within 14 calendar days of receipt of a failed Certificate of Analysis from a CMTL due to Contaminants Unsafe for Human Consumption, an MMTC must: (a) Provide the department with a completed Notification of Resampling and Retesting form …; (b) Provide the department with a completed Notification of Remediation form as provided in Rule 64-4.213, F.A.C.; or (c) Provide notice to the department via email … indicating that the MMTC will dispose of the Retail Batch in accordance with Rule 64-4.207, F.A.C."

Step 2a — resampling and retesting (Rule 64-4.212(5)). Before resampling/retesting, the MMTC must give the Department the failed COA plus Form DH8024-OMMU-03/2021 (Notification of Resampling and Retesting), and must arrange the resampling/retesting within 30 calendar days of submitting that form; the retesting CMTL must have a copy of the failed COA. The failed batch must be quarantined, clearly marked "not for retail sale," and must not be transported to a dispensing facility or dispensed except as below. A previously failed Retail Batch must pass two complete regulatory compliance tests using two new samples to become eligible for dispensation, and may only be resampled and retested twice. If it passes the first retest, it may be retested again; if it passes the second, the MMTC must give the Department the two passing COAs before removing it from quarantine or transferring/dispensing it. If it fails either retest, the MMTC must dispose of it under Rule 64-4.207 or remediate it if permitted by Rule 64-4.213, with the appropriate notice. If a CMTL cannot complete testing after sampling, the MMTC may have the affected Retail Batch(es) resampled and tested as an initial Retail Batch sample (Rule 64-4.212(5)(e)).

Step 2b — remediation (Rule 64-4.213, verbatim core). An MMTC must give the Department the failed COA plus Form DH8025-OMMU-03/2021 (Notification of Remediation) and must remediate within 30 calendar days of submitting that form. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/florida/Fla-Admin-Code-Ann-R-64-4-213 — Accessed 2026-10-24.

Failed product Failure type Remediation permitted?
Usable whole flower marijuana Any (general) Yes — through processing to create Derivative Product (Rule 64-4.213(4))
Usable whole flower marijuana Water activity or moisture content Yes — also by additional drying or curing (Rule 64-4.213(4))
Derivative product (excluding edibles) Heavy metals or agricultural agents No — must be disposed of under Rule 64-4.207 (Rule 64-4.213(5))
Derivative product (excluding edibles) Residual solvents, microbes, or mycotoxins Yes — through further processing (Rule 64-4.213(5))
Edibles Any reason No — may not be remediated; must be disposed of under Rule 64-4.207 (Rule 64-4.213(6))
  • All remediated products must undergo and pass regulatory compliance testing as a new Retail Batch (Rule 64-4.213(7)). A remediated Retail Batch is not eligible for additional remediation (Rule 64-4.213(8)) — one remediation only.
  • Potency-label failures are not contaminant failures: if a Retail Batch fails because the labelled potency of total active THC, total active CBD, or any individual cannabinoid is wrong, the MMTC must correct the labelled potency to the CMTL-measured concentration before dispensing (Rule 64-4.212(6)) — relabelling, not destruction or remediation.

Step 3 — what "recall" means in Florida. No standalone Florida "recall" rule or OMMU recall procedure for already-dispensed MMTC product was located in this run [UNAVAILABLE — Gap P11-06]. The operative safeguards are preventive, not post-sale: (i) no Final Product may be transported to a dispensing facility or dispensed until it has passed testing; (ii) failed batches are quarantined and marked "not for retail sale"; (iii) the Department must inspect an MMTC on receiving a complaint or notice that it dispensed marijuana containing mold, bacteria or another contaminant that may cause or has caused an adverse effect (§381.986(10)(b)); (iv) the Department may fine, suspend, revoke or refuse to renew for the §381.986(10)(f) violations, including endangering a patient's health/safety/security (see §11.2.6). A product already dispensed that is later found contaminated therefore falls to complaint inspection and discipline, not to a codified recall-and-return procedure — that is a genuine gap in the codified rules, not an oversight in this report. - Scale (secondary reporting of OMMU testimony, 2025): OMMU's lab review team "examined over 400 certificates of analysis, 300 data packages and tracked 310 failed batches for retesting, remediation or destruction" in the 2024–25 fiscal period. Source: Citizen Portal summary of OMMU testimony to the Health Professions and Programs Subcommittee, https://citizenportal.ai/articles/7012350/Florida/2025-Legislature-FL/OMMU-tells-Florida-subcommittee-it-regulates-925000-patients-and-strengthens-seedtosale-oversight — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary summary of testimony; the underlying OMMU slides were not opened). Do not quote "310" as a current or annual figure — it is a single fiscal-period testimony figure.

11.1.5 Certified labs — certification, discipline, and the unresolved count/list

Statute (§381.988, history through ch. 2023-71; last amendment in the 2023 text: s. 3, ch. 2023-71). Source: https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2023/381.988 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official Senate text, opened directly).

"A person or entity seeking to be a certified marijuana testing laboratory must: (a) Not be owned or controlled by a medical marijuana treatment center. (b) Submit a completed application accompanied by an application fee, as established by department rule. (c) Submit proof of an accreditation or a certification approved by the department issued by an accreditation or a certification organization approved by the department. … (d) Require all employees, owners, and managers to submit to and pass a level 2 background screening pursuant to chapter 435." — §381.988(1) (verbatim core; the full disqualification language is in §11.8 below). "The department shall adopt rules … establishing a procedure for initial certification and biennial renewal, including initial application and biennial renewal fees sufficient to cover the costs of administering this certification program. The department shall renew the certification biennially if the laboratory meets the requirements of this section and pays the biennial renewal fee." — §381.988(2). "A marijuana testing laboratory may acquire marijuana only from a medical marijuana treatment center. A marijuana testing laboratory is prohibited from selling, distributing, or transferring marijuana received from a marijuana treatment center, except that a marijuana testing laboratory may transfer a sample to another marijuana testing laboratory in this state." — §381.988(4). "A marijuana testing laboratory must properly dispose of all samples it receives, unless transferred to another marijuana testing laboratory, after all necessary tests have been conducted and any required period of storage has elapsed, as established by department rule." — §381.988(5). "A marijuana testing laboratory shall use the computer software tracking system selected by the department under s. 381.986." — §381.988(6) (i.e. the Department STS system — BioTrack, per §11.2.5 — not a lab-chosen system).

  • Certification standards the rule must cover (§381.988(3)): security standards; minimum personnel standards; sample collection method/process standards; proficiency testing for THC potency, CBD concentration, and contaminants unsafe for human consumption as determined by rule; reporting content/format/frequency; audits and onsite inspections; quality assurance; equipment and methodology; chain of custody; and any other standard the Department deems necessary for public health/safety. FDACS and DEP assist in developing the rule.
  • Discipline (§381.988(7)–(8)): grounds include permitting unauthorised persons to perform technical procedures or issue reports; incompetence or consistent errors/erroneous reporting; testing/reporting for a person/entity not authorised to receive the services; failing to file a required report; reporting a result for a test not performed; failing to correct deficiencies in time; and violating or aiding/abetting a violation of §381.986, §381.988 or rules. The Department may refuse to issue or renew, or suspend or revoke, certification, and may impose fines on a rule-adopted schedule, weighing severity/probability of death or serious harm, corrective actions, previous violations, and financial benefit of the violation.
  • Permanent rule series (adopted 28 May 2026): Rule 64-4.300 (definitions), 64-4.301 (certification/application, incorporated form DH5062-OMMU-12/2025), 64-4.302 (renewal), 64-4.306 (testing methods, incorporating microbiological, residual-solvent, heavy-metals, agricultural-agent, and water-activity/moisture methods), 64-4.307 (submission for product testing, including vehicle notification), 64-4.308 (sample testing), 64-4.311 (certificate of analysis), 64-4.313 (waste management and disposal), 64-4.314 (background screening). Source: OMMU hearing-materials listing via https://knowthefactsmmj.com/feed/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (OMMU site listing of the rule package; individual rule texts beyond 64-4.301's history page not opened [VERIFY]).
  • Count and list — STILL NOT RESOLVED, do not quote a current list. The three dated figures are: 9 (December 2021 — Americanna became "only the ninth facility licensed by [OMMU]" on its approval; secondary, Cannabis News Florida, December 2021); 8 ("the office certifies eight marijuana testing laboratories" — OMMU Director testimony to the Health Professions and Programs Subcommittee, 2025, via Citizen Portal summary — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary); 6 (CannBus Q3 2026, secondary — Run 1). These are different years and different counting bases (a 2021 approval announcement, a 2025 testimony statement, and a 2026 secondary compilation); none is an official OMMU directory, and no OMMU CMTL directory URL was located in this run either (same result as Run 1 Part 5). Names evidenced in secondary sources (Run 1 §4.2.2, repeated here only as secondary-evidenced, NOT as a verified current list): ACS Laboratory (Sun City Center), Americanna Laboratories (Jacksonville), ACT Laboratories of Florida (Davie), AccuScience (Eustis), Atlas Labs FL (Lakeland). Any sixth, seventh or eighth current name, and any claim that a named lab is currently certified, is [VERIFY — Gap P11-01].

11.1.6 CMTL fees — now in conflict, not resolved

  • Catalyst BC (secondary, accessed 2026-10-24) states a "Certified testing laboratory application $78,000 per testing facility — Rule 64-4.301": https://catalyst-bc.com/florida-cannabis-licensing-opportunities/ — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • An older application-instruction summary states a [REMOVED as a current fee — Audit confirms $78,000; see Audit table] CMTL application fee: https://floridastatecannabis.org/licensing/testing — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary, undated, low weight).
  • Treatment: neither figure is adopted here. The $78,000 figure is the more recent and is tied to the current Rule 64-4.301 (effective 28 May 2026, incorporated form DH5062-OMMU-12/2025), but the rule text / incorporated form itself was not opened to confirm the dollar amount, and the older figure may reflect a superseded fee schedule. The CMTL application fee, renewal fee, and any per-facility vs per-entity distinction are [VERIFY — Gap P11-01]. Do not infer CMTL fees from MMTC fees.

11.2 Licence rules: transfers, ownership, renewal, caps, relocation, surrender, revocation, insurance/bonding

11.2.1 Transfers and sales of MMTC licences — the statute is the rule; Rule 64-4.018 was never adopted

"A licensed medical marijuana treatment center may transfer ownership to an individual or entity who meets the requirements of this section. A publicly traded corporation or publicly traded company that meets the requirements of this section is not precluded from ownership of a medical marijuana treatment center. To accommodate a change in ownership: a. The licensed medical marijuana treatment center shall notify the department in writing at least 60 days before the anticipated date of the change of ownership. b. The individual or entity applying for initial licensure due to a change of ownership must submit an application that must be received by the department at least 60 days before the date of change of ownership. c. Upon receipt of an application for a license, the department shall examine the application and, within 30 days after receipt, notify the applicant in writing of any apparent errors or omissions and request any additional information required. d. Requested information omitted from an application for licensure must be filed with the department within 21 days after the department's request for omitted information or the application shall be deemed incomplete and shall be withdrawn from further consideration and the fees shall be forfeited. Within 30 days after the receipt of a complete application, the department shall approve or deny the application." — §381.986(8)(e)1., Fla. Stat. (verbatim core, confirmed on the florida.public.law text — Accessed 2026-10-24).

  • Clock, in one line: seller notice ≥60 days before → buyer application ≥60 days before → Department error/omission notice within 30 days of receipt → applicant cure within 21 days or the application is withdrawn and fees forfeited → Department approve/deny within 30 days of receiving a complete application.
  • No implementing rule exists. Proposed Rule 64-4.018 ("Medical Marijuana Treatment Center Change of Ownership Application") was withdrawn in 2021 and never adopted; the Chapter 64-4 listing skips from 64-4.013 to 64-4.023, and OMMU still hosts a draft form captioned "Rule 64-4.018, F.A.C. Effective: ____" with the date blank. Source: Cannabis Industry Lawyer, "Florida MMTC License Transfer: 5 Critical Traps", 14 September 2026 (secondary law-firm analysis, but the FAC-listing fact it reports is checkable on flrules.org) — https://www.cannabisindustrylawyer.com/florida-mmtc-license-transfer/ — Accessed 2026-10-24. Practical consequence: a transfer runs on the statute plus OMMU's draft form and portal practice; there is no published change-of-ownership fee (the statute presupposes fees exist, since it provides for forfeiture, but no fee amount is published — [UNAVAILABLE — Gap P11-07]). Any memo citing Rule 64-4.018 as adopted law is wrong.
  • Buyer qualification trap (statute, not a holding period): because the buyer applies for initial licensure on a change of ownership, the buyer must meet every initial-licensure requirement, including §381.986(8)(b)1. — "for the 5 consecutive years before submitting the application, the applicant has been registered to do business in the state" — which the secondary analysis correctly identifies as expressly non-waivable and as a bar on a newly formed acquisition entity qualifying in its own right. The "five-year rule" is therefore a buyer-eligibility rule, not a rule that a licensee must hold the licence for five years before selling. No moratorium on transfers in 2026 was located (secondary analysis, September 2026, same source); OMMU publishes no transfer processing times or queue data, so no timeline beyond the statutory clock above is stated.
  • What a "sale" usually is in practice: because the licence itself is not separately assignable outside the §381.986(8)(e)1. process, market transactions are structured as equity/entity sales with the buyer going through initial licensure — Run 1's reported licence asking prices (~$3–4 million in September–October 2026, one $999,000 listing, secondary) are asking prices for the business/licence package, not a state transfer fee, and no completed sale price was verified in Run 1 or in this Part.

11.2.2 Renewal — biennial, conditional, and fee-by-formula

"The department shall renew the licensure of a medical marijuana treatment center biennially if the licensee meets the requirements of this section and pays the biennial renewal fee. However, the department may not renew the license of a medical marijuana treatment center that has not begun to cultivate, process, and dispense marijuana by the date that the medical marijuana treatment center is required to renew its license." — §381.986(8)(b), Fla. Stat.

  • What renewal requires beyond the fee: continued compliance with every licensure criterion and with the representations made in the initial application (see §11.2.4 on variances); a renewal applicant must show the effectiveness of its diversity plan by including (a) representation of minority persons and veterans in its workforce, (b) efforts to recruit minority persons and veterans, and (c) a record of contracts with minority and veteran business enterprises (§381.986(8)(b)10.). All owners, officers, board members and managers must have passed background screening (§381.986(8)(b)8., via subsection (9)); the MMTC must employ a medical director (§381.986(8)(b)9.).
  • Renewal fee — formula, not a fixed dollar amount in the statute. The statute requires "initial application and biennial renewal fees sufficient to cover the costs of implementing and administering this section, and … supplemental licensure fees for payment beginning May 1, 2018, sufficient to cover the costs of administering ss. 381.989 and 1004.4351" (§381.986(8)(b)). Secondary reporting (Catalyst BC, accessed 2026-10-24) states the formula as: the Department's programme spending over two fiscal years, less initial application fees received, divided by the number of licensed MMTCs; and states that Rule 64-4.215, which takes effect 6 October 2026 and replaces Emergency Rule 64ER25-1, sets that formula and requires renewal applications 120 to 150 days before the licence period ends (90 to 120 days under the emergency rule until then), with the fee for renewals due after 2026 not yet published. Source: https://catalyst-bc.com/florida-cannabis-licensing-opportunities/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary). Treatment: the $1,340,383.11 figure for renewals due 1 January 2025–31 December 2026 (Run 1, secondary) is consistent with that formula account, but the OMMU renewal-fee schedule itself was not opened directly in Run 1 or in this Part, so the figure remains [VERIFY — Gap P11-02]. The post-2026 renewal fee is [UNAVAILABLE].
  • Licence term evidenced for new licensees: OMMU's 14 September 2026 licensure letter to Alamanda Farms LLC (MMTC 2026-0030) states: "Your license is effective for a 2-year period measured from September 11, 2026, the date of your initial licensure." Source: https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/_documents/MMTC_Letters/Alamanda_Farms_LLC.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official OMMU letter). That 2-year term matches the biennial renewal cycle in the statute.
  • CMTL renewal: biennial, on meeting §381.988 and paying the biennial renewal fee (§381.988(2)); Rule 64-4.302 (renewal application requirements) is part of the 28 May 2026 permanent package. Dollar amount [VERIFY — Gap P11-01].

11.2.3 Ownership caps and other ownership rules

  • One licence per person/entity: "An individual or entity may not be awarded more than one license as a medical marijuana treatment center." (§381.986(8)(b)).
  • One application per individual: "An individual may not be an applicant, owner, officer, board member, or manager on more than one application for licensure as a medical marijuana treatment center." (§381.986(8)(b)).
  • 5% cross-ownership ban (verbatim core): "A medical marijuana treatment center, and any individual or entity who directly or indirectly owns, controls, or holds with power to vote 5 percent or more of the voting shares of a medical marijuana treatment center, may not acquire direct or indirect ownership or control of any voting shares or other form of ownership of any other medical marijuana treatment center." (§381.986(8)(e)2.). This is an attribution rule, not a transfer threshold: at 5% or more of one MMTC, a person is barred from any ownership of another.
  • No landlord profit-sharing: "A medical marijuana treatment center may not enter into any form of profit-sharing arrangement with the property owner or lessor of any of its facilities where cultivation, processing, storing, or dispensing of marijuana and marijuana delivery devices occurs." (§381.986(8)(e)3.).
  • No contracting-out of core functions: "A licensed medical marijuana treatment center must, at all times, maintain compliance with the criteria demonstrated and representations made in the initial application… A licensed medical marijuana treatment center shall cultivate, process, transport, and dispense marijuana for medical use. A licensed medical marijuana treatment center may not contract for services directly related to the cultivation, processing, and dispensing of marijuana or marijuana delivery devices, except that a medical marijuana treatment center licensed pursuant to subparagraph (a)1. may contract with a single entity for the cultivation, processing, transporting, and dispensing of marijuana and marijuana delivery devices." (§381.986(8)(d)–(e)).
  • No dispensary-count cap is stated as current law in this Part (see the consistency note and Gap P11-03). The patient-growth licence formula (4 additional MMTCs within 6 months after each additional 100,000 active patients, §381.986(8)(a)) is a licensing trigger, not an ownership cap.

11.2.4 Relocation, facility changes, and variances — no standalone relocation rule located

  • No standalone "relocation" statute or rule was located [UNAVAILABLE as a standalone procedure — Gap P11-08]. Relocation and other facility changes are handled through two mechanisms that were located:
  • Variance from application representations (§381.986(8)(e), Rule 64-4.023). "Upon request, the department may grant a medical marijuana treatment center a variance from the representations made in the initial application. Consideration of such a request shall be based upon the individual facts and circumstances… A variance may not be granted unless the requesting medical marijuana treatment center can demonstrate … a proposed alternative … which fulfills the same or a similar purpose … in a way that the department can reasonably determine will not be a lower standard than the specific representation in the application. A variance may not be granted from the requirements in subparagraph 2. and subparagraphs (b)1. and 2." (i.e. not from the citrus-preference/Pigford subparagraphs or the 5-year/ nursery-certificate requirements). Rule 64-4.023 (effective 10 January 2019) requires a variance request on Form DH8019-OMMU-11/2018 and provides: "A medical marijuana treatment center may not proceed with a proposed alternative until receipt of approval from the department." Changes to a medical director must be requested as a variance; an officer/board member/manager/employee may be added or removed by written notice with an updated organisational chart, but no person may be added before passing §381.986(9) background screening (Rule 64-4.023(5)). OMMU's September 2026 licensure letters confirm the practice: "Any changes from your initial application, including changes to the organizational structure and capitalization table, must be submitted through a variance request in compliance with Rule 64-4.023, F.A.C." (Alamanda Farms letter, 14 September 2026).
  • Facility authorisations for new licensees (Rule 64-4.216). An MMTC may not cultivate, process or dispense until it has Department authorisation for that activity at that facility. OMMU's September 2026 letters state the deadlines: cultivation authorisation request within 180 calendar days of licensure, processing within 270 calendar days, dispensing within 365 calendar days (licensure date 11 September 2026 for the 2026 cohort), with STS integration (see §11.2.5) completed before cultivation authorisation can issue. Secondary analysis (CannabisLAB, September 2026) adds that OMMU inspections for authorisation compare the completed facility and operations against the original application representations, with a corrective-action process for deficiencies. Source for the secondary point: https://www.joinclab.com/knowledge-center/florida-mmtc-authorization-rule-64-4-216 — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Local constraints on any relocation remain: the 500-foot school buffers (§381.986(11)(a) for cultivation/processing, (11)(c) for dispensing with the public-proceeding waiver), the local ban-or-pharmacy-parity rule (§381.986(11)(b)), and Building/Fire Code compliance (§381.986(11)(d)) all apply to a new site exactly as to an original site. A relocation that moves a dispensing facility into a banning jurisdiction, or within 500 feet of a school without the required local approval, is not cured by a state variance.

11.2.5 Seed-to-sale integration (operations detail — vendor correction)

  • Statute (Run 1 §1.7, restated): the Department "shall establish, maintain, and control a computer software tracking system that traces marijuana from seed to sale and allows real-time, 24-hour access by the department to data from all medical marijuana treatment centers and marijuana testing laboratories", covering at minimum planting, harvest/destruction, transport, sale, theft, diversion and loss; each MMTC must use the Department system or integrate its own with it; the Department may contract with a vendor, which may have no other §381.986 services contract with the Department and no direct/indirect financial interest in an MMTC or CMTL (§381.986(8)(d)).
  • Vendor — BioTrack (official OMMU document, resolving Run 1 Gap G-11): OMMU's 14 September 2026 licensure letter states: "Rule 64-4.221, F.A.C. requires that all MMTCs 'use an Internal Seed-to-Sale (STS) Tracking System that fully integrates with the Department STS Tracking System.' Prior to full integration, MMTCs must: (i) complete the three Department-approved training sessions (provided by the Department's STS System vendor, BioTrack); (ii) submit a written integration plan to the Department; (iii) receive Department approval of the integration plan; (iv) and complete BioTrack's validation process. These steps must occur before an MMTC may obtain cultivation authorization from the Department. For technical questions and guidance, contact BioTrack at flhelp@btgov.com. For any other questions regarding STS, please email OMMU_SeedToSale@flhealth.gov." Source: Alamanda Farms LLC letter — Accessed 2026-10-24. Metrc is NOT Florida's Department STS vendor on any official source found; do not assert it.
  • Operating detail (Emergency Rules 64ER24-1/64ER24-2, as carried into Rule 64-4.221 — permanent-rule text [VERIFY]): each MMTC operates an Internal STS Tracking System feeding the Department through an API using Form DH5059-OMMU-11/2023 (required data collection document); data retained 3 years; CSV production within 48 hours on Department request; only MMTC owners/officers/managers/employees, the MMTC's STS vendor, and the Department's STS vendor may access it; the Internal STS system must at all times accurately identify the specific location of marijuana within the facility; weight/count adjustments not resulting from a processing step, dispensation, wholesale purchase/distribution, or waste disposal must be justified in writing to ommu_seedtosale@flhealth.gov within 12 hours; failure to comply is disciplinable under Rule 64-4.210, including suspension and revocation. Sources: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/florida/Fla-Admin-Code-Ann-R-64ER24-1 and https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/florida/Fla-Admin-Code-Ann-R-64ER24-2 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (Cornell LII reproductions of the emergency rules; whether Rule 64-4.221 has replaced them in full is [VERIFY — Gap P11-04], but the September 2026 OMMU letters cite Rule 64-4.221 as the operative requirement).

11.2.6 Surrender, revocation, inspections, and fines

  • Inspections (verbatim core, §381.986(10)(a)–(c)): "The department shall conduct announced or unannounced inspections of medical marijuana treatment centers to determine compliance with this section or rules adopted pursuant to this section." "The department shall inspect a medical marijuana treatment center upon receiving a complaint or notice that the medical marijuana treatment center has dispensed marijuana containing mold, bacteria, or other contaminant that may cause or has caused an adverse effect to human health or the environment." "The department shall conduct at least a biennial inspection of each medical marijuana treatment center to evaluate the medical marijuana treatment center's records, personnel, equipment, processes, security measures, sanitation practices, and quality assurance practices."
  • Statutory fines and licence action (§381.986(10)(f)–(g)): "The department may impose reasonable fines not to exceed $10,000 on a medical marijuana treatment center for any of the following violations: Violating this section or department rule. Failing to maintain qualifications for approval. Endangering the health, safety, or security of a qualified patient. Improperly disclosing personal and confidential information of the qualified patient. Attempting to procure medical marijuana treatment center approval by bribery, fraudulent misrepresentation, or extortion. Being convicted or found guilty of, or entering a plea of guilty or nolo contendere to, regardless of adjudication, a crime in any jurisdiction which directly relates to the business of a medical marijuana treatment center. Making or filing a report or record that the medical marijuana treatment center knows to be false. Willfully failing to maintain a record required by this section or department rule. Willfully impeding or obstructing an employee or agent of the department in the furtherance of his or her official duties. Engaging in fraud or deceit, negligence, incompetence, or misconduct in the business practices of a medical marijuana treatment center. Making misleading, deceptive, or fraudulent representations in or related to the business practices of a medical marijuana treatment center. Having a license or the authority to engage in any regulated profession, occupation, or business that is related to the business practices of a medical marijuana treatment center suspended, revoked, or otherwise acted against by the licensing authority of any jurisdiction… for a violation that would constitute a violation under Florida law. Violating a lawful order of the department or an agency of the state, or failing to comply with a lawfully issued subpoena…" "The department may suspend, revoke, or refuse to renew a medical marijuana treatment center license if the medical marijuana treatment center commits any of the violations in paragraph (f)."
  • Rule fine schedule (Rule 64-4.210): per-violation fines run from $500–$1,000 for most operational violations (e.g. background-screening, cultivation, edibles, storage/display, security, and the testing violations at (nn)–(pp): dispensing when test results show low-THC non-compliance, THC potency failure, inaccurate THC/CBD labelling, or unsafe contaminants — $1,000–$2,000; failure to retain testing/sample records for at least 9 months — $1,000–$2,000; use of an uncertified laboratory when at least one certified laboratory exists — $1,000–$2,000). The statutory $10,000 ceiling in §381.986(10)(f) is the outer limit; the rule schedule sets the per-violation amounts actually imposed. Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/florida/64/64/chapter-64-4/section-64-4-210/ — Accessed 2026-10-24. Rule 64-4.210(2) adds the suspension/revocation factors: frequency/number of occurrences, potential for rehabilitation, prior violations, impact on the Department, potential/actual harm to a patient or the public, willfulness, severity and length of noncompliance, good-faith prevention efforts, and corrective action taken.
  • Enforcement scale (secondary reporting of OMMU testimony, 2025, fiscal 2024–25): 2,874 inspections of treatment centres and testing laboratories; 237 notices of violation, 124 of which resulted in fines; 11,060 background-screening requests, about 7% deemed ineligible. Source: Citizen Portal summary — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary; underlying OMMU slides not opened).
  • Surrender — no procedure located. No statute or rule section setting out a voluntary MMTC licence-surrender form, surrender effective date, or post-surrender inventory/wind-down procedure was located in this run [UNAVAILABLE — Gap P11-09]. The located endpoints of a licence are: non-renewal (including the bar on renewing an MMTC that has not begun to cultivate, process and dispense by its renewal date), suspension, revocation, and refusal to renew under §381.986(10)(g), plus the transfer process in §11.2.1. A surrendering licensee would still be bound by the waste-disposal (Rule 64-4.207), record-retention and STS requirements for its remaining inventory — but that wind-down sequence is an inference from those duties, not a located surrender rule, and is flagged as such. (For contrast, ID-card issuance/renewal/suspension/replacement/surrender/revocation procedures are provided for in §381.986(7) — but those are patient/caregiver cards, not MMTC licences.)

11.2.7 Insurance and bonding minimums

  • The only cannabis-specific financial-assurance minimum in §381.986 is the performance bond (not insurance): $5 million, or $2 million for an MMTC serving at least 1,000 qualified patients, issued by an authorised surety rated in one of the three highest categories by a nationally recognised rating service; or an irrevocable letter of credit payable to the Department, or cash deposited in the Grants and Donations Trust Fund on the same forfeiture conditions (interest on cash used for administration of the section) (§381.986(8)(b)7.). Rule 64-4.217 is the operative financial-assurance rule: OMMU's 14 September 2026 licensure letter states: "Pursuant to Rule 64-4.217, F.A.C., MMTCs must post a bond or provide an irrevocable letter of credit, payable to the Department, in the amount of $5 million. This financial assurance must be delivered to the Department within ten (10) business days after final approval for licensure as an MMTC. Accordingly, your financial assurance must be received by the Department by 5:00 p.m. EST on September 25, 2026." Source: Alamanda Farms letter — Accessed 2026-10-24. The reduced $2 million bond is available only once the MMTC is serving at least 1,000 patients — a new licensee therefore posts $5 million first; the reduction is not available at licensure.
  • No cannabis-specific general-liability, product-liability, property, cyber or commercial-auto insurance minimum was located in §381.986, §381.988 or Chapter 64-4 [UNAVAILABLE as a cannabis-specific minimum — Gap P11-10]. General Florida employer obligations (e.g. workers' compensation for employers with four or more employees under Chapter 440) apply to MMTCs as employers, not as cannabis licensees, and are noted here only to prevent the error of presenting the bond as "insurance": the bond is financial assurance to the Department, not liability coverage for patients or third parties. Secondary insurance-marketing sources list general liability, product liability, property, workers' compensation and commercial auto as recommended or generally required coverages, but none cites a cannabis-specific statutory minimum, and none is adopted here as a requirement.

11.3 Cultivation rules: indoor/outdoor/greenhouse, canopy, plant counts, approved facilities

  • Indoor only, in substance. "Must grow marijuana within an enclosed structure and in a room separate from any other plant." (§381.986(8)(e)6.b.). There is no outdoor-cultivation authorisation for MMTCs in the statute: "enclosed structure" plus a separate room per plant type excludes open-field cultivation. A greenhouse inside an enclosed structure that meets the separate-room requirement is not separately addressed in the statute [VERIFY — Gap P11-11]; do not describe greenhouse cultivation as either authorised or prohibited beyond the enclosed-structure/separate-room test.
  • No canopy limit and no plant-count limit in the statute was located. No square-footage canopy cap, plant-count cap, or tier system for MMTC cultivation appears in §381.986(8)(e)6. or in the rules opened in this run. Do not import another state's canopy tiers. Facility scale is instead controlled through: (i) the single vertically integrated licence (no separate cultivation licence to scale independently); (ii) Department-approved facilities and the Rule 64-4.216 authorisation sequence (no cultivation until cultivation authorisation issues for that facility); (iii) the enclosed-structure/separate-room requirement; (iv) STS tracking of planting, harvest and destruction; and (v) the licence itself being facility-specific through the application representations (changes via variance, §11.2.4).
  • Cultivation duties (verbatim core, §381.986(8)(e)6.): "May use pesticides determined by the department, after consultation with the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, to be safely applied to plants intended for human consumption, but may not use pesticides designated as restricted-use pesticides pursuant to s. 487.042." "Must inspect seeds and growing plants for plant pests that endanger or threaten the horticultural and agricultural interests of the state in accordance with chapter 581 and any rules adopted thereunder." "Must perform fumigation or treatment of plants, or remove and destroy infested or infected plants, in accordance with chapter 581 and any rules adopted thereunder." (See §11.6 for the pesticide rule.)
  • Processing facility rules (verbatim core, §381.986(8)(e)11.a.–c.): "Process the marijuana within an enclosed structure and in a room separate from other plants or products." "Comply with department rules when processing marijuana with hydrocarbon solvents or other solvents or gases exhibiting potential toxicity to humans. The department shall determine by rule the requirements for medical marijuana treatment centers to use such solvents or gases exhibiting potential toxicity to humans." "Comply with federal and state laws and regulations and department rules for solid and liquid wastes. The department shall determine by rule procedures for the storage, handling, transportation, management, and disposal of solid and liquid waste generated during marijuana production and processing. The Department of Environmental Protection shall assist the department in developing such rules." (See §§11.5–11.6.)
  • Edibles processing (additional facility duties, §381.986(8)(e)8.–9.): an MMTC producing edibles must hold a Chapter 500 food-establishment permit and comply with Chapter 500; within 12 months after licensure it must demonstrate that all its processing facilities have passed a Food Safety Good Manufacturing Practices inspection (e.g. Global Food Safety Initiative or equivalent) by a nationally accredited certifying body, and must immediately stop processing at any facility that fails until it demonstrates compliance. (Run 1 Part 4: FDACS food-establishment permit $650/year renewal, $325 July–December initial, $100 late, non-transferable, Chapter 5K-11 — restated, not re-verified in this Part.)
  • Approved facilities — how a facility becomes "approved": there is no separate facility licence. A facility is approved through (i) the MMTC licence application (which must demonstrate "an infrastructure reasonably located to dispense marijuana to registered qualified patients statewide or regionally as determined by the department" and "the ability to secure the premises, resources, and personnel necessary to operate"), (ii) Department inspection/approval of the facility for its designated use (express for solvent extraction areas — see §11.6), and (iii) for new licensees, the Rule 64-4.216 authorisation sequence (cultivation 180 days, processing 270 days, dispensing 365 days from licensure). A facility that has not received its activity authorisation may not hold marijuana for that activity. The 500-foot school buffers (§381.986(11)) are facility-location conditions, not facility licences.

11.4 Security: cameras, alarms, storage, transport/delivery vehicles

Statute — §381.986(8)(f) (verbatim core, restated consistently with Run 1 §1.6.3):

"To ensure the safety and security of premises where the cultivation, processing, storing, or dispensing of marijuana occurs, and to maintain adequate controls against the diversion, theft, and loss of marijuana or marijuana delivery devices, a medical marijuana treatment center shall: 1. a. Maintain a fully operational security alarm system that secures all entry points and perimeter windows and is equipped with motion detectors; pressure switches; and duress, panic, and hold-up alarms; and b. Maintain a video surveillance system that records continuously 24 hours a day and meets the following criteria: (I) Cameras are fixed in a place that allows for the clear identification of persons and activities in controlled areas of the premises. Controlled areas include grow rooms, processing rooms, storage rooms, disposal rooms or areas, and point-of-sale rooms. (II) Cameras are fixed in entrances and exits to the premises, which shall record from both indoor and outdoor, or ingress and egress, vantage points. (III) Recorded images must clearly and accurately display the time and date. (IV) Retain video surveillance recordings for at least 45 days or longer upon the request of a law enforcement agency. 2. Ensure that the medical marijuana treatment center's outdoor premises have sufficient lighting from dusk until dawn. 3. Ensure that the indoor premises where dispensing occurs includes a waiting area with sufficient space and seating to accommodate qualified patients and caregivers and at least one private consultation area that is isolated from the waiting area and area where dispensing occurs. A medical marijuana treatment center may not display products or dispense marijuana or marijuana delivery devices in the waiting area. 4. Not dispense from its premises marijuana or a marijuana delivery device between the hours of 9 p.m. and 7 a.m., but may perform all other operations and deliver marijuana to qualified patients 24 hours a day. 5. Store marijuana in a secured, locked room or a vault. 6. Require at least two of its employees, or two employees of a security agency with whom it contracts, to be on the premises at all times where cultivation, processing, or storing of marijuana occurs. 7. Require each employee or contractor to wear a photo identification badge at all times while on the premises. 8. Require each visitor to wear a visitor pass at all times while on the premises. 9. Implement an alcohol and drug-free workplace policy."

Source: https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._381.986 — Accessed 2026-10-24.

  • No camera-count, resolution, frame-rate, or off-site-monitoring minimum beyond the statute was located in this run [UNAVAILABLE — Gap P11-12]. Do not import another state's camera specifications. The 45-day retention figure is the statutory minimum for video surveillance recordings generally, and also the retention figure in the waste rule (see §11.5).
  • Transport and delivery vehicles — §381.986(8)(g) (verbatim core, restated consistently with Run 1 §1.6.3): every vehicle transporting marijuana must carry a manifest generated from the MMTC's seed-to-sale system stating departure date/time, originating MMTC name/address/licence number, recipient name/address, quantity/form, arrival date/estimated time, vehicle make/model/plate, and delivering employees' names/signatures; a copy goes to each recipient (signed receipt); the transporter must present the manifest and employee ID to law enforcement on request (failure/refusal: second-degree misdemeanour, §381.986(12)(h)); manifests retained at least 3 years. Vehicles must be in good working order; product locked in a separate compartment or container; transporter carries employee ID at all times; at least two persons per vehicle, at least one remaining in the vehicle during delivery; specific safety/security training for transport/delivery employees (§381.986(8)(g)2.–6.).
  • CMTL transport: CMTLs move samples under the same §381.986(8)(g) framework (Rule 64-4.307 includes a vehicle-notification requirement; detail [VERIFY]). CMTLs may transfer a sample to another CMTL in Florida (§381.988(4)) but may not sell, distribute or transfer marijuana received from an MMTC to anyone else.
  • Theft/loss/diversion reporting: the STS system must, at minimum, include notification of when marijuana is "transported, sold, stolen, diverted, or lost" (§381.986(8)(d)), and STS weight/count adjustments outside a processing step, dispensation, wholesale purchase/distribution, or waste disposal must be justified in writing within 12 hours (64ER24-2, see §11.2.5). No separate "report theft within X hours" statute section was located beyond that STS notification duty [VERIFY — Gap P11-12].

11.5 Waste disposal rules

11.5.1 MMTC waste — Rule 64-4.207 (Marijuana Waste Management and Disposal)

  • What counts as Marijuana Waste (Rule 64-4.207(1)): the rule's definition covers marijuana waste materials, excluding hazardous waste, universal waste (as defined in Rule 62-730.020, F.A.C.) and biomedical waste (as defined in §381.0098(1)(a)) — those streams are governed by their own regimes, not by Rule 64-4.207. (The parallel CMTL rule, 64-4.313, carries the same exclusion, confirmed in the 2 March 2026 FAR change extract.) Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/florida/Fla-Admin-Code-Ann-R-64-4-207 and https://flrules.org/Faw/FAWDocuments/FAWVOLUMEFOLDERS2026/5241/5241doc.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24.
  • Rendering unusable/unrecognisable or irretrievable (Rule 64-4.207(4), verbatim core): before disposal, Marijuana Waste must be: "(a) Rendered unusable and unrecognizable by grinding and mixing the compostable Marijuana Waste with at least an equal amount of other compostable materials (e.g., food waste, yard waste, vegetable-based grease or oils); (b) Rendered unusable and unrecognizable by grinding the Marijuana Waste with at least an equal amount of other compostable materials (e.g., food waste, yard waste, vegetable-based grease or oils) or non-compostable materials (e.g., paper waste, cardboard waste, plastic waste, or oil), or both; or (c) Rendered irretrievable by permanently altering the physical or chemical condition through irreversible means."
  • Storage before rendering (Rule 64-4.207(3)–(4)): until rendered, Marijuana Waste must be stored in a receptacle that is (1) a securely locked, enclosed container, (2) securely fastened to a permanent structure so that it cannot be removed, and (3) located in a secured area of the facility. At least two MMTC employees, one of whom must be a manager, must be present when rendering waste unusable/unrecognisable or irretrievable, and the steps must be conducted under video surveillance.
  • Disposal routes after rendering (Rule 64-4.207(5)): (a) delivered to an appropriate solid waste management facility (Chapter 62-701, F.A.C.); (b) delivered to a composting facility registered with or permitted by DEP under Chapter 62-709, F.A.C. (04/2021); or (c) composted onsite by the MMTC in accordance with Chapter 62-709, F.A.C.
  • Waste management plan (Rule 64-4.207(6)): every MMTC must maintain a current, up-to-date waste management plan covering, at minimum: (a) the identity of managers and employees with access to the waste storage area(s); (b) procedures for weighing, tracking and documenting waste out of the STS system; (c) procedures for rendering waste unusable/unrecognisable or irretrievable; (d) procedures for storing waste before rendering and for transporting it; (e) the manner of disposal after rendering; (f) record maintenance and retention procedures; and (g) employee training materials and exercises covering (b)–(f).
  • Records (Rule 64-4.207(7)–(8)): records must account for all waste-disposal activity, including the date, time and manner of rendering (with legible names and signatures of the persons who rendered it), the video recording of the rendering, the name of any collecting entity and evidence of subscription to its collection services, and the date, time and manner of disposal (solid-waste facility, composting facility, or onsite composting). Video surveillance recordings retained at least 45 days; all other Marijuana Waste records retained at least two years. An MMTC must give at least 72 hours' notice in the STS system before rendering waste unusable/unrecognisable or irretrievable, recording the weight to be rendered; at least two employees, one a manager, must be present when documenting waste out of the STS system.
  • Failed-batch disposal feeds into this rule: every "dispose of in accordance with Rule 64-4.207" direction in Rules 64-4.212/64-4.213 (see §11.1.4) means the failed batch goes through the rendering, 72-hour-notice, two-person, video-surveillance and record procedure above — failed product is not simply thrown away.

11.5.2 CMTL waste — Rule 64-4.313 and §381.988(5)

  • A CMTL must properly dispose of all samples it receives, unless transferred to another CMTL, after all necessary tests have been conducted and any required storage period has elapsed, as established by rule (§381.988(5)). Rule 64-4.313 (CMTL Waste Management and Disposal, part of the 28 May 2026 permanent package) mirrors Rule 64-4.207's structure: rendering, solid-waste-facility delivery, DEP-registered/permitted composting-facility delivery, or onsite composting under Chapter 62-709; video recordings retained at least 45 days, other waste records at least two years; chain-of-custody log must reflect sample disposal. Source: 2 March 2026 FAR change extract for Rule 64-4.313 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (extract only; full Rule 64-4.313 text [VERIFY — Gap P11-04]).
  • Old draft figure — do not use as current law: the 2019 draft Rule 64-4.016 provided that dry-flower nonlaboratory marijuana waste "must be ground and mixed with general waste to a 50:50 ratio" and liquid nonlaboratory waste "may be mixed with methylene chloride to a 50:50 ratio and disposed of as hazardous waste". That is a 2019 draft, superseded in structure by Rules 64-4.207/64-4.313 (equal-amount mixing, not a fixed 50:50 rule for MMTC waste). Do not quote the 50:50 draft figure as the current rule.

11.6 Environmental rules: water, pesticide limits, energy

  • Pesticides — statute and rule (the only cannabis-specific environmental rule located). Statute: only Department-approved pesticides (after FDACS consultation) may be used on plants intended for human consumption, and restricted-use pesticides under §487.042 may never be used (§381.986(8)(e)6.a.). Rule 64-4.013 (Pesticide Use on Medical Marijuana; adopted 23 July 2018, amended 10 January 2019 and 20 December 2021) permits a pesticide only if: (1) the label bears a U.S. EPA-approved logo and/or language indicating it is allowed for use in organic crop production safe for human consumption; (2) the active ingredient is exempt from tolerance requirements under 40 C.F.R. Part 180, Subpart D (07/01/2017), or does not require a tolerance exemption under Subpart E; (3) the label does not prohibit use within an enclosed structure for the site of application; (4) the label expressly has directions for use on unspecified crops or plants (the Cornell text gives both "unspecified crops or plants" and "crops or plants intended for human consumption" limbs — the full current text should be re-opened before quoting the label limbs verbatim [VERIFY — Gap P11-13]); and (5) the active ingredient(s) are allowed for use on tobacco by the U.S. EPA. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/florida/Fla-Admin-Code-Ann-R-64-4-013 — Accessed 2026-10-24. No Florida pesticide-residue action-limit table was located in this run [UNAVAILABLE — Gap P11-05]; residue limits are enforced through CMTL agricultural-agent testing (Rule 64-4.306 methods), not through a published limit table found here.
  • Solvent extraction — environmental and safety overlap. Processing with hydrocarbon solvents or other solvents/gases exhibiting potential toxicity to humans must comply with Department rules (§381.986(8)(e)11.b.). Emergency Rule 64ER21-13 (MMTC Solvent-Based Extraction) requires, in summary: solvent purity at least 99.5% with a manufacturer certificate of analysis; no odorants, bitterants or other additives; storage, handling and disposal per local, state and federal regulations; extraction only in a Department-approved, inspected Extraction Area of a Department-approved processing facility that has passed a Food Safety GMP inspection; hydrocarbon extraction only in a closed-loop system (sealed during operation, recovering all solvent through a feedback loop), with pressure vessels rated at least 125% of maximum operational pressure (not to exceed 10,000 psi), emergency pressure release vented outside, and certification by an independent engineer licensed under Chapter 471 that the system was commercially manufactured, is safe for its intended use, and is built to recognised good engineering practice; plus local fire-code inspection and Department written approval specifying the authorised solvent(s) before any solvent processing begins. Source: Emergency Rule 64ER21-13 summary via https://foxrothschild.gjassets.com/content/uploads/2021/08/Solvent-Rule-Florida.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary-hosted copy of the emergency rule; permanent Rule 64-4.209 status [VERIFY — Gap P11-04]).
  • Water — no cannabis-specific water rule located. No MMTC-specific water-use, irrigation, discharge, or water-quality rule was located in §381.986, Chapter 64-4, or the rules opened in this run [UNAVAILABLE — Gap P11-14]. MMTCs are instead caught by general law: solid and liquid waste must comply with "federal and state laws and regulations and department rules" (§381.986(8)(e)11.c., DEP assisting on the waste rules), and processing facilities must comply with the Florida Building Code and Florida Fire Prevention Code (§381.986(11)(d)). Do not assert a cannabis water-allocation, runoff, or discharge permit requirement for Florida MMTCs.
  • Energy — no cannabis-specific energy rule located. No MMTC energy-efficiency, lighting, HVAC, or carbon rule was located [UNAVAILABLE — Gap P11-14]. (Contrast: other states in this research series have energy rules — e.g. Vermont Rule 2.5 — but Florida's located rules do not include one, and none is imported here.)
  • Hemp environmental note: hemp cultivation is subject to FDACS licensing and inspection under §581.217 and to Chapter 581 plant-pest rules; no hemp-specific water/energy rule was located either (Part 7 topic, not expanded here).

11.7 Sampling, giveaways, discounts and promotions

  • Patient "sampling" does not exist as a right. The only "sampling" in the Florida medical regime is CMTL sampling for testing (§11.1.3): the CMTL selects and collects a random, representative sample of Final Product from every Retail Batch. There is no provision allowing an MMTC to give a patient a free sample outside a physician certification and registry order. Dispensing is lawful only to a qualified patient or caregiver for that patient's medical use, recorded in the registry with date, time, quantity, form, and patient/caregiver registry identification number (§381.986(8)(e)16.g., Run 1 §1.6.1); transfer to any other person is excluded from "medical use" (§381.986(1)(k)) and is a criminal offence for a patient who transfers (§381.986(12)). A "free sample" given to a non-patient, or above a patient's ordered supply, would therefore fall outside medical use — but no standalone "no giveaways" rule was located [UNAVAILABLE as a standalone prohibition — Gap P11-15]. Do not cite a giveaway ban that was not found.
  • Discounts are contemplated by statute and must be published. Every MMTC must publish on its website, for every product, the price for a 30-day, 50-day and 70-day supply at standard dose, each delivery-device price, and "any discount policies and eligibility criteria for such discounts" (§381.986(8)(e)9., Run 1 §1.6.1 — the "50-day" figure is as printed in the statute). Discounts are therefore lawful if they are published with their eligibility criteria; an unpublished or selectively applied discount policy would breach the publication duty, and any discount that takes a dispensation above a patient's ordered supply would breach the supply-limit rules. No discount percentage cap, loyalty-programme rule, or "buy-one-get-one" rule was located [UNAVAILABLE — Gap P11-15].
  • Promotions and advertising — statute in force, rule proposed. Statute (§381.986(8)(h), Run 1 §1.6.2): no advertising visible to the public from any street, sidewalk, park or other public place, except (1) a sign affixed to the outside or hanging in the window of the dispensing location identifying the dispensary by licensee business name, Department-approved trade name, or Department-approved logo (trade name/logo may not contain wording or images attractive to children or promoting recreational use), and (2) internet advertising/marketing only if Department-approved, with no child-attractive or recreational-promoting content, no unsolicited pop-ups, and an easy, permanent opt-out for opt-in marketing.
  • Proposed Rule 64-4.227 (MMTC Advertising and Marketing) — PROPOSED, NOT ADOPTED (as of this run). The FAR notice (Vol. 52, No. 164, 24 August 2026) proposes that an MMTC "may advertise and market only as follows: (a) Signage as set forth in subsection (4); (b) Inside the MMTC's dispensing facility as set forth in subsection (5); and (c) On the internet as set forth in subsection (6). No other advertisements or marketing are permitted." Proposed content bans include: false, misleading or deceptive content; content stating or implying a usable product cures any medical condition; and content stating or implying a usable product is intended for recreational use. Source: https://flrules.org/Faw/FAWDocuments/FAWVOLUMEFOLDERS2026/52164/52164doc.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24 (FAR proposed-rule document). Treatment: the proposed rule is consistent with, and narrower in channel terms than, the statute (inside-facility advertising is not in the statutory list), but until adopted it does not change the law. The statute's sign-plus-internet rule remains the operative law. Do not cite Rule 64-4.227 as adopted.
  • Usable-product and packaging approval (adjacent control on promotions): before processing or dispensing a proposed usable product, an MMTC must request Department approval of the product and its packaging; changes to an approved product/packaging that would alter the criteria demonstrated in the initial application or a prior variance also require prior approval (OMMU Request for Usable Product and Packaging form, citing Rule 64-4.023). Source: https://knowthefactsmmj.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Request-for-Usable-Product-and-Packaging.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official OMMU form).

11.8 Drug testing and background screening for licence holders and staff

11.8.1 Background screening — who, what standard, what disqualifies, what happens on arrest

MMTCs — §381.986(9) (verbatim core):

"An individual required to undergo a background screening pursuant to this section must pass a level 2 background screening as provided under chapter 435, which, in addition to the disqualifying offenses provided in s. 435.04, shall exclude an individual who has an arrest awaiting final disposition for, has been found guilty of, regardless of adjudication, or has entered a plea of nolo contendere or guilty to an offense under chapter 837, chapter 895, or chapter 896 or similar law of another jurisdiction. Exemptions from disqualification as provided under s. 435.07 do not apply to this subsection."

  • Fingerprints: a full set submitted to the Department or to a vendor/entity/agency authorised by §943.053(13), forwarded to FDLE for state processing and then to the FBI for national processing; fingerprint-processing and retention fees borne by the MMTC or caregiver as applicable (state cost per §943.053(3)(e)); fingerprints retained by FDLE per §943.05(2)(g)–(h) and, when FDLE participates, enrolled in the FBI's national retained-print arrest notification programme, with any arrest record reported to the Department (§381.986(9)(a)–(c)).
  • Who is screened: all MMTC owners, officers, board members and managers (licensure, §381.986(8)(b)8.); all MMTC employees — "All employees of a medical marijuana treatment center must be 21 years of age or older and have passed a background screening pursuant to subsection (9)" (§381.986(8)(e)4.); caregivers (unless the patient is a close relative, §381.986(6)(b), Run 1); and qualified physicians/medical directors are separately licensed under Chapters 458/459 (not §381.986(9) screening, but subject to their own licensing discipline).
  • Rule 64-4.208 (MMTC Background Screening, new 10 June 2020): MMTCs must give the Department written notice within 30 calendar days of the termination or separation of any employee, owner or manager so fingerprints may be removed from the FBI retained-print programme; employees/owners/managers whose fingerprints were submitted before 22 August 2018 had to be rescreened within 90 days of the rule's effective date. Continuing screening: after becoming aware of the arrest of any MMTC employee, owner or manager for a §435.04 disqualifying offence or a Chapter 837/895/896 offence (or similar law of another jurisdiction), the MMTC must give the Department written notice within 48 hours, including the individual's name, position/job title, and a copy of the arrest report if available; if the Department notifies the MMTC that the individual is thereby ineligible, the MMTC must ensure that person is no longer an employee, manager or owner within 24 hours of receiving the Department's written notice. Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/florida/64/64/chapter-64-4/section-64-4-208/ — Accessed 2026-10-24. A 2025 workshop draft of Rule 64-4.208 adds date of birth to the 48-hour notice contents — that draft is NOT adopted text and is not relied on here.
  • Scale (secondary, 2025 testimony): 11,060 background-screening requests in fiscal 2024–25, about 7% deemed ineligible (Citizen Portal summary — Accessed 2026-10-24).

CMTLs — §381.988(1)(d) (verbatim core, current 2023 text):

"Require all employees, owners, and managers to submit to and pass a level 2 background screening pursuant to chapter 435. The department shall deny certification if the person or entity seeking certification has a disqualifying offense as provided in s. 435.04 or has an arrest awaiting final disposition for, has been found guilty of, or has entered a plea of guilty or nolo contendere to, regardless of adjudication, any offense listed in chapter 837, chapter 895, or chapter 896 or similar law of another jurisdiction. Exemptions from disqualification as provided under s. 435.07 do not apply to this paragraph."

  • Note the scope difference from the older text: the 2022 text covered only "owners and managers"; the current text covers employees, owners, and managers, and defines "employee" as any person whose duties involve any aspect of regulatory compliance testing or R&D testing, whether or not compensated, and "manager" as any person with authority to exercise or contribute to operational control, direction or management. Fingerprint-processing and retention fees are borne by the CMTL. Rule 64-4.314 (CMTL Background Screening) is part of the 28 May 2026 permanent package.

11.8.2 Drug testing — staff, and patients (restated consistently with Run 1)

  • MMTC staff: the statute does not prescribe a drug-test panel, frequency, or cut-off for MMTC employees. What it does require is: "Implement an alcohol and drug-free workplace policy." (§381.986(8)(f)9.). That is a policy duty on the MMTC as employer; the content of the policy (which substances, which testing, what consequences) is left to the employer within general Florida employment law (Chapter 440, §112.0455 for public employers, §440.102 private drug-free-workplace provisions — Run 1 §1.8, texts not re-opened here). Do not describe Florida as mandating pre-employment or random drug testing of MMTC staff — no such mandate was located.
  • CMTL staff: the former Rule 64-4.016 draft required lab employees to be 21+, pass Level 2 screening, and hold at least a high-school diploma (or associate degree, or current Florida Board of Clinical Laboratory Personnel certification); samplers must meet the employee requirements plus specific sampling/security training, and an analyst who has not run a specific analysis within one calendar year must complete an initial demonstration of competency before running it again. Source: 2019 draft Rule 64-4.016 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (draft; current Rule 64-4.301/64-4.306 personnel provisions [VERIFY — Gap P11-05]). No drug-testing requirement for CMTL staff was located beyond the MMTC-style workplace-policy framework.
  • Patients: essentially no employment or drug-test protection, as in Run 1 §1.8: §381.986(15)(a)–(c) (verbatim in Run 1) imposes no limit on drug-free-workplace policies, no accommodation duty, and no wrongful-discharge/discrimination cause of action for medical use. The 2026 employer-immunity bills (SB 1702 / CS/HB 689) died 13 March 2026 (Run 1), so they did not change that position. A patient who tests positive therefore has no §381.986 protection against an employer's drug-free-workplace action; that is a Part 12 / employment-law point, restated here only because §11.8's scope includes drug testing.

11.9 Research and university cannabis licences

  • There is no separate "university cannabis licence" or "research licence" in Florida's located law. Universities do not hold MMTC licences to conduct research, and no research-only cultivation licence type was located [UNAVAILABLE as a licence type — Gap P11-16]. Research happens through three located mechanisms:
  • The Consortium for Medical Marijuana Clinical Outcomes Research (§1004.4351, the "Medical Marijuana Research Act"). "There is established within a state university designated by the Board of Governors the Consortium for Medical Marijuana Clinical Outcomes Research which shall consist of public and private universities. The purpose of the consortium is to conduct rigorous scientific research and disseminate such research." (§1004.4351(4)(a)). A Medical Marijuana Research Board, composed of members representing each participating university appointed by each university's president, directs the Consortium's operations (§1004.4351(4)(b)). Source: https://www.FLSenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2023/1004.4351 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official Senate text).
  • University of Florida as lead institution. The State University System Board of Governors selected the University of Florida to lead the Consortium (UF College of Pharmacy announcement, 14 June 2019), with $1.5 million in annual recurrent state funding at designation, to evaluate safety and effectiveness, dosing and routes of administration (including smoking vs other methods). Source: https://pharmacy.ufl.edu/2019/06/14/board-of-governors-selects-uf-to-lead-medical-marijuana-research-consortium/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (UF official announcement, 2019; current funding level [VERIFY — Gap P11-16]). The Consortium's programmes, as described by UF (May 2022), are: (i) a competitive grants programme funding researchers across participating universities; (ii) "Medical Marijuana and Me" (M3), tracking patients from first medical use for a year; and (iii) the Medical Marijuana Outcomes Research Repository (MEMORY), using de-identified Department of Health dispensing data to monitor health outcomes (the 2022 article cites ~700,000 registered patients at that time — a historical figure, not a current count). Source: https://news.ufl.edu/2022/05/florida-consortium-seeks-answers/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (UF official news, 2022).
  • Funding through MMTC supplemental fees and the ID-card fee. MMTC supplemental licensure fees, payable from 1 May 2018, must be "sufficient to cover the costs of administering ss. 381.989 and 1004.4351" (§381.986(8)(b)) — i.e. the public-education campaigns (§381.989) and the Consortium. Separately, §381.986(7)(d) requires the Department to "allocate $10 of the identification card fee to the Division of Research at Florida Agricultural and Mechanical University for the purpose of educating minorities about marijuana for medical use and the impact of the unlawful use of marijuana on minority communities" (Run 1 §1.4; the $75 card fee itself is OMMU practice, not statute). A Florida transparency record confirms the mechanism is still operating in FY 2025–26: Approved Budget Amendment B0901 (approved 26 May 2026) "Provides additional appropriation to the Department of Health, Office of Medical Marijuana, to fulfill its statutory obligation to the Division of Research at Florida Agricultural and Mechanical University (FAMU) to support research and education efforts focused on informing minority populations about medical marijuana use and the impacts of unlawful marijuana use on minority communities." Source: http://www.transparencyflorida.gov/arreports/arreport/60460 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (official transparency record). FAMU's role is therefore education/research funding via the $10 allocation, not a cultivation or dispensing licence.
  • Adjacent research-adjacent provisions (not licences): (i) a qualified physician must forward supporting documentation for a "comparable" qualifying condition to the applicable board within 14 days, and "the Department forwards it to the Consortium" (§381.986(4)(b), Run 1); (ii) teaching-nursing-home research participants are a caregiver-designation exception (§381.986(6)(c)–(d), Run 1), not a research licence; (iii) §381.989 requires the Department to run a statewide cannabis/marijuana education and illicit-use prevention campaign and the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles to run an impaired-driving education campaign, each with annual evaluations/reports to the Governor, Senate President and House Speaker by 31 January (source: https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2023/381.989 — Accessed 2026-10-24, opened directly); (iv) CMTLs may conduct R&D testing (the §381.988(1)(d) definition of "employee" expressly covers R&D testing personnel), but R&D testing is not a separate licence — it is activity within CMTL certification, and R&D results do not substitute for regulatory compliance testing (Rule 64-4.212(7) principle).
  • Federal overlay for university researchers (context, not Florida law): university research using marijuana still requires federal authorisation (DEA registration) outside Florida law; no Florida provision in this Part waives that. That point is stated as general context, not as a Florida-law finding.

12.1 Paraphernalia and smoke shops

12.1.1 What counts as "drug paraphernalia" — §893.145 and §893.146

Florida's paraphernalia law turns on use, intent, and design for use with a controlled substance in violation of Chapter 893 — not on the shape of the object alone. That is why the same pipe can be lawful tobacco merchandise in one shop and paraphernalia in another: the statute tells the fact-finder to weigh context.

  • §893.146 — "Determination of paraphernalia" (verbatim, operative sentence):
