    "In determining whether an object is drug paraphernalia, a court or other authority or jury shall consider, in addition to all other logically relevant factors, the following:" "(1) Statements by an owner or by anyone in control of the object concerning its use. (2) The proximity of the object, in time and space, to a direct violation of this act. (3) The proximity of the object to controlled substances. (4) The existence of any residue of controlled substances on the object. (5) Direct or circumstantial evidence of the intent of an owner, or of anyone in control of the object, to deliver it to persons who he or she knows, or should reasonably know, intend to use the object to facilitate a violation of this act. The innocence of an owner, or of anyone in control of the object, as to a direct violation of this act shall not prevent a finding that the object is intended for use, or designed for use, as drug paraphernalia. (6) Instructions, oral or written, provided with the object concerning its use. (7) Descriptive materials accompanying the object which explain or depict its use. (8) Any advertising concerning its use. (9) The manner in which the object is displayed for sale. (10) Whether the owner, or anyone in control of the object, is a legitimate supplier of like or related items to the community, such as a licensed distributor of or dealer in tobacco products. (11) Direct or circumstantial evidence of the ratio of sales of the object or objects to the total sales of the business enterprise. (12) The existence and scope of legitimate uses for the object in the community. (13) Expert testimony concerning its use." Source: §893.146, Florida Statutes — https://law.justia.com/codes/florida/2014/title-xlvi/chapter-893/section-893.146/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (2014 reproduction of the factor list; the factor list is unchanged in substance in later reproductions — current-year Online Sunshine re-open [VERIFY], Gap 12-01). The practical consequence, noted in secondary commentary on §893.146 (Rhoden Law, undated, accessed 2026-10-24 — https://rhodenlawbrevard.com/criminal-law/determination-of-paraphernalia/), is that shop signage, clerk statements, packaging, advertising, display, and sales mix are all evidence — which is why smoke shops post "for tobacco use only" signs. That sign is not a statutory safe harbour; it is one factor among thirteen, and residue, proximity to a controlled substance, or instructions to use the object with marijuana can outweigh it.

  • §893.145 — definition (summary; full itemised list not re-quoted here). "Drug paraphernalia" means equipment, products and materials of any kind used, intended for use, or designed for use in planting, propagating, cultivating, growing, harvesting, manufacturing, compounding, converting, producing, processing, preparing, testing, analysing, packaging, repackaging, storing, containing, concealing, transporting, injecting, ingesting, inhaling, or otherwise introducing into the human body a controlled substance in violation of Chapter 893 (or §877.111). The itemised list in §893.145(12) includes, among many other items, pipes (including water pipes), bongs, roach clips, miniature cocaine spoons, and related objects. Source: §893.145, Florida Statutes (via the Chapter 893 index — https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2002/Chapter893/All — Accessed 2026-10-24, 2002 chapter reproduction; current-year text [VERIFY], Gap 12-01). Do not quote the §893.145(12) list as current without that re-open: the list has been amended over time (notably the 2013 retail-sale provisions), and only the §893.146 factor list and §893.147 offences below were read in full in this run.

12.1.2 Offences — §893.147 (read in full, 2025 text)

"(1) USE OR POSSESSION OF DRUG PARAPHERNALIA.—It is unlawful for any person to use, or to possess with intent to use, drug paraphernalia: (a) To plant, propagate, cultivate, grow, harvest, manufacture, compound, convert, produce, process, prepare, test, analyze, pack, repack, store, contain, or conceal a controlled substance in violation of this chapter; or (b) To inject, ingest, inhale, or otherwise introduce into the human body a controlled substance in violation of this chapter. Any person who violates this subsection is guilty of a misdemeanor of the first degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082 or s. 775.083." "(2) MANUFACTURE OR DELIVERY OF DRUG PARAPHERNALIA.—It is unlawful for any person to deliver, possess with intent to deliver, or manufacture with intent to deliver drug paraphernalia, knowing, or under circumstances where one reasonably should know, that it will be used [for the purposes in (1)]. Any person who violates this subsection is guilty of a felony of the third degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084." "(3) DELIVERY OF DRUG PARAPHERNALIA TO A MINOR.—(a) Any person 18 years of age or over who violates subsection (2) by delivering drug paraphernalia to a person under 18 years of age is guilty of a felony of the second degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084. (b) It is unlawful for any person to sell or otherwise deliver hypodermic syringes, needles, or other objects which may be used, are intended for use, or are designed for use in parenterally injecting substances into the human body to any person under 18 years of age, except [by a licensed practitioner, parent, legal guardian, or pharmacist pursuant to a valid prescription]. Any person who violates [this paragraph] is guilty of a misdemeanor of the first degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082 or s. 775.083." "(4) TRANSPORTATION OF DRUG PARAPHERNALIA.—It is unlawful to use, possess with the intent to use, or manufacture with the intent to use drug paraphernalia, knowing or under circumstances in which one reasonably should know that it will be used to transport: (a) A controlled substance in violation of this chapter; or (b) Contraband as defined in s. 932.701(2)(a)1. Any person who violates this subsection commits a felony of the third degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084." "(5) ADVERTISEMENT OF DRUG PARAPHERNALIA.—It is unlawful for any person to place in any newspaper, magazine, handbill, or other publication any advertisement, knowing, or under circumstances where one reasonably should know, that the purpose of the advertisement, in whole or in part, is to promote the sale of objects designed or intended for use as drug paraphernalia. Any person who violates this subsection is guilty of a misdemeanor of the first degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082 or s. 775.083." "(6) RETAIL SALE OF DRUG PARAPHERNALIA.—(a) It is unlawful for a person to knowingly and willfully sell or offer for sale at retail any drug paraphernalia described in s. 893.145(12)(a)-(c) or (g)-(m), other than a pipe that is primarily made of briar, meerschaum, clay, or corn cob. (b) A person who violates paragraph (a) commits a misdemeanor of the first degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082 or s. 775.083, and, upon a second or subsequent violation, commits a felony of the third degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084." Source: §893.147, Florida Statutes (2025) — https://law.justia.com/codes/florida/title-xlvi/chapter-893/section-893-147/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (Justia reproduction; history through ch. 2018-13 shown on that page; Online Sunshine direct open [VERIFY], Gap 12-01).

Penalty summary table (§893.147):

Conduct Grade Maximum (per §§775.082/775.083, as Run 1 states)
Use / possession with intent to use paraphernalia (§893.147(1)) First-degree misdemeanour Up to 1 year / $1,000
Manufacture / delivery, or possession with intent to deliver (§893.147(2)) Third-degree felony Up to 5 years / $5,000
Delivery to a minor, age 18+ (§893.147(3)(a)) Second-degree felony Up to 15 years / $10,000
Sale/delivery of syringes/needles/injecting objects to a minor (§893.147(3)(b)) First-degree misdemeanour Up to 1 year / $1,000
Transportation use (§893.147(4)) Third-degree felony Up to 5 years / $5,000
Advertisement promoting sale (§893.147(5)) First-degree misdemeanour Up to 1 year / $1,000
Knowing/wilful retail sale of listed paraphernalia (§893.147(6)) First-degree misdemeanour; third-degree felony on second/subsequent violation Up to 1 year / $1,000, then up to 5 years / $5,000

Note on the retail-sale carve-out: §893.147(6)(a) expressly excepts "a pipe that is primarily made of briar, meerschaum, clay, or corn cob" from the retail-sale ban. That is a narrow material exception for traditional tobacco pipes — it does not legalise retail sale of glass/metal water pipes, bongs, or other listed items as "tobacco pipes" if the §893.146 factors show drug-paraphernalia intent. No Florida statute creates a "smoke shop licence" as a distinct licence type [UNAVAILABLE — no such licence was located in Chapter 893, §581.217, or Chapter 205 in this run].

12.1.3 How this applies to the three different kinds of shop — and to patients

  • MMTCs are not smoke shops. An MMTC may dispense only marijuana and marijuana delivery devices specified in a physician certification; it "may not dispense or sell any other type of cannabis, alcohol, or illicit drug-related product" (§381.986(8)(e)16.f., Run 1 Part 1), and pre-rolled cigarettes may not use tobacco or hemp wrapping paper (§381.986(8)(e)10., Run 1 Part 1). A "marijuana delivery device" under §381.986(1)(h) [current lettering; (1)(g) is now “Marijuana”] (as amended by ch. 2019-1, SB 182) is:

    "an object used, intended for use, or designed for use in preparing, storing, ingesting, inhaling, or otherwise introducing marijuana into the human body, and which is dispensed from a medical marijuana treatment center for medical use by a qualified patient, except that delivery devices intended for the medical use of marijuana by smoking need not be dispensed from a medical marijuana treatment center in order to qualify as marijuana delivery devices." Source: ch. 2019-1 (SB 182), §1 — https://sb.flleg.gov/nxt/gateway.dll/Laws/2019Laws/lf2019/general%20laws%20-%20regular%20session/chapters%202019-1%20-%202019-25/2019-001.htm — Accessed 2026-10-24 (session-law text; current §381.986(1)(h) [current lettering; (1)(g) is now “Marijuana”] lettering may have shifted with later amendments — [VERIFY] against the current Online Sunshine text, Gap 12-02). In practice: a patient using a device within a physician certification and the medical programme is not committing the §893.147(1) offence for that device, because the use is not "in violation of this chapter" — §381.986(14) excepts compliant medical use from Chapter 893. A non-patient using the same device with non-MMTC marijuana is within §893.147(1). The device does not launder the marijuana.

  • Hemp/CBD/smoke shops (non-MMTC retailers). There is no hemp-specific paraphernalia exemption in §581.217 and no hemp-specific local ban verified in Run 1 Part 3. A hemp/CBD shop therefore lives under the same §893.145/§893.146/§893.147 regime as any other retailer, plus general zoning, Chapter 205 business-tax receipts, and (for food establishments) FDACS permitting. Selling a pipe "for tobacco" while displaying it beside hemp flower, advertising it for smoking hemp, or telling a buyer how to smoke marijuana with it, is exactly the §893.146 evidence that converts merchandise into paraphernalia. Conversely, a genuinely tobacco-only shop with no drug-use statements, advertising, display, or residue is not automatically paraphernalia merely because it sells pipes — that is the point of the thirteen-factor test.
  • Hemp products themselves are not paraphernalia. Hemp and hemp extract within §581.217 (≤0.3% total delta-9, Run 1 Part 1) are not controlled substances under Chapter 893, so an object used with conforming hemp is not used with "a controlled substance in violation of this chapter." The risk arises where the product is over-limit, is a controlled substance (e.g. THC-O, treated as controlled under §893.03(1)(c)190 per Run 1 Part 1), or is marijuana: then the same object becomes paraphernalia. After 11 December 2026, under the fixed federal baseline, products that lose federal hemp status but remain lawful under Florida's unchanged §581.217 will sit in a federal/state split — the §893.147 analysis above is a Florida analysis and does not change by itself on that date [UNAVAILABLE — no FDACS or Florida Legislature response to PL 119-37/119-103 was found in Run 1 or in this run].
  • Age gates that do apply to shops. (i) §893.147(3): no delivery of paraphernalia to a person under 18 (second-degree felony for an adult deliverer under (3)(a); syringes/needles to under-18s a first-degree misdemeanour under (3)(b)). (ii) §581.217(7)(d) (Run 1 Part 1): hemp extract products intended for human ingestion or inhalation may not be sold to a person under 21 — second-degree misdemeanour, first-degree on a second/subsequent violation within 1 year. A shop that sells both paraphernalia and hemp extract must therefore apply two different age floors (18 for paraphernalia delivery, 21 for ingestible/inhalable hemp extract). (iii) Tobacco age rules (Chapter 569) are separate and are not treated here.
  • Proposed shop restrictions that are NOT law. HB 1409 (2026) and its Senate companion SB 1270 (2026) would have prohibited unpermitted business sales, street sales and festival sales of hemp extract, barred permitted hemp businesses within 500 feet of a school, daycare, motor-fuel retailer or another permitted hemp retailer, required locked/controlled storage and pre-approved advertising, and banned advertising using the terms "THC" or "medical card." HB 1409 died in the Industries & Professional Activities Subcommittee on 13 March 2026 (flsenate.gov bill page — https://flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026/1409 — Accessed 2026-10-24). None of those restrictions is current law and none is stated as law anywhere in this report. Secondary summaries that describe HB 1597 (2025) as banning festival sales or imposing school buffers from 1 October 2025 are not adopted here: Run 1 found HB 1597 among the bills that died in 2025, and the festival/buffer provisions in the 2026 bills died with them. Any source claiming those rules are in force should be treated as [VERIFY] until a chapter law is produced (Gap 12-03).

12.2 THC driving limits and impairment testing

12.2.1 There is NO per se THC limit in Florida — DUI is impairment-based

This is the single most important correction in Part 12. A secondary law-firm page found in this run claims Florida "has set a legal limit for THC in the bloodstream at 5 nanograms per milliliter (ng/mL)" (Musca Law, "Driving Under the Influence of Marijuana in Florida" — https://www.muscalaw.com/blog/driving-under-influence-marijuana-florida — Accessed 2026-10-24). That claim is wrong and is rejected here. No such ng/mL figure appears in §316.193, §316.1932, or §316.1939, and multiple other secondary sources correctly state the opposite. The 5 ng/mL figure is the per se limit in Colorado and Washington, not Florida. Do not quote it for Florida.

  • §316.193(1)(a) — the offence (verbatim):

    "A person is guilty of the offense of driving under the influence if the person is driving or in actual physical control of a vehicle within this state, and: (a) The person is under the influence of alcoholic beverages, any chemical substance set forth in s. 877.111, or any substance controlled under chapter 893, when affected to the extent that the person's normal faculties are impaired; or (b) The person has a blood-alcohol level of 0.08 or more grams of alcohol per 100 milliliters of blood or breath." Source: §316.193(1), Florida Statutes, as quoted in secondary reproductions — https://www.muscalaw.com/blog/can-prescription-medications-cause-dui-charge-florida and https://www.muscalaw.com/blog/can-i-be-arrested-dui-florida-even-if-i-passed-breath-test — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary reproductions; direct Online Sunshine open of §316.193 [VERIFY], Gap 12-04 — the (b) limb is alcohol-only and is the only per se limb in the statute).

  • What "normal faculties" means. The standard jury-instruction definition (secondary, from Florida Standard Jury Instructions as reproduced in case materials — https://static.case.law/fla-supp-2d/10/case-pdfs/0023-01.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24) is: "those faculties of a person, such as the ability to walk, talk, judge distances, drive an automobile, make judgments, act in emergencies and, in general, to normally perform the many mental and physical acts of our daily lives." The State must prove impairment of those faculties beyond a reasonable doubt; mere presence of a controlled substance in the body is legally insufficient. That proposition is stated in State v. Sabree (Fla. 4th DCA, discussed in Sabree v. State, FindLaw — https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/fl-district-court-of-appeal/1336947.html — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary case summary): "simply having cocaine in the system is legally insufficient to convict because the State is required to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Sabree was 'under the influence' of cocaine" — the same impairment element applies to cannabis under §316.193(1)(a).
  • Medical status is not a defence to DUI. §316.193(1)(a) contains no exception for lawfully prescribed or state-authorised substances, and §381.986 contains no driving defence. A qualified patient who drives while impaired by medical marijuana commits DUI on the same terms as any other driver. Conversely, a qualified patient who drives unimpaired — even with THC or metabolites detectable in blood or urine — has not committed DUI under (1)(a), because the element is impairment, not presence. Secondary defence commentary (The Law Office of William E. — https://www.thelawofwe.com/how-marijuana-use-impacts-driving/ — Accessed 2026-10-24) states this correctly: "the state has to prove impairment of normal faculties, not the presence of THC. A positive urine test showing a metabolite proves past use and nothing about the moment of driving."
  • Penalties (summary; full §316.193(2)–(4) table not re-quoted here). First DUI conviction: fine $500–$1,000 (higher with a minor in the vehicle — the §316.193(4) minor enhancement applies to a drug-only DUI as well — or with a high breath/blood alcohol level, which is alcohol-only and does not map onto a THC case) [Audit correction], imprisonment up to 6 months, licence revocation, DUI school, and related sanctions; penalties escalate with prior convictions, property damage, personal injury, and minors in the vehicle. Exact fine/imprisonment pinpoints for a drug-only DUI [VERIFY] against the current §316.193 text (Gap 12-04). A DUI conviction also interacts with record-clearing: see §12.3 — a DUI conviction (adjudication of guilt) cannot be sealed or expunged under §§943.0585/943.059.
  • Boating and other vehicles. §327.35 (boating under the influence; §316.1939 is refusal-to-submit penalties, not boating) and the parallel provisions for operating vessels follow the same impairment structure; the per se alcohol limb is again alcohol-only. No THC-specific boating limit was located [CORRECTED in Audit: boating is §327.35; Gap 12-04 resolved on citation only]. §381.986(1)(k)5.f. separately excludes from "medical use" any use in a school bus, vehicle, aircraft, or motorboat (except low-THC cannabis not in smoking form), and §381.986(12)(c) makes patient use in a vehicle/aircraft/boat a first-degree misdemeanour — that is a medical-programme offence distinct from DUI, and it applies even without proof of impaired driving.

12.2.2 How impairment is tested — and what tests cannot prove

  • No breath test for THC. There is no breathalyser for drugs in Florida law or practice. Breath tests measure alcohol only. A driver who "passes" a breath test at 0.00 can still be arrested for drug DUI on observations and other tests (secondary, Musca Law — https://www.muscalaw.com/blog/can-i-be-arrested-dui-florida-even-if-i-passed-breath-test — Accessed 2026-10-24).
  • Implied consent — §316.1932. A person who drives in Florida is deemed to have consented to approved chemical/physical tests (breath for alcohol; urine for chemical/controlled substances) when lawfully arrested on reasonable cause for DUI, and to a blood test for alcohol or controlled substances when the person appears for treatment at a hospital, clinic, or other medical facility (including an ambulance or other medical emergency vehicle) and breath/urine testing is impractical or impossible. Verbatim core (§316.1932(1)(c)):

    "Any person who accepts the privilege extended by the laws of this state of operating a motor vehicle within this state is, by operating such vehicle, deemed to have given his or her consent to submit to an approved blood test for the purpose of determining the alcoholic content of the blood or a blood test for the purpose of determining the presence of chemical substances or controlled substances as provided in this section if there is reasonable cause to believe the person was driving or in actual physical control of a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcoholic beverages or chemical or controlled substances and the person appears for treatment at a hospital, clinic, or other medical facility and the administration of a breath or urine test is impractical or impossible." Source: §316.1932(1)(c), Florida Statutes, as quoted by the Attorney General's office — https://www.myfloridalegal.com/ag-opinions/blood-draws-in-suspected-dui-cases-medical-facility — Accessed 2026-10-24 (AG opinion reproduction; current-year Online Sunshine open [VERIFY], Gap 12-04). Refusal consequences (licence suspension 1 year for a first refusal, 18 months if previously suspended for refusal; refusal admissible in evidence; refusal is a 2nd-degree misdemeanour for a first refusal and a 1st-degree misdemeanour for a second/subsequent refusal (§316.1939(1)) [Audit correction]) are stated in §316.1932 and are summarised here from the LawServer reproduction — https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/florida/statutes/florida_statutes_316-1932 — Accessed 2026-10-24.

  • What blood and urine results actually show. Blood can show active THC; urine typically shows inactive THC-COOH metabolite, which can persist for days to weeks after any impairing effect has worn off. Neither result, by itself, proves impairment at the time of driving, and Florida law "provides no statutory presumptions for a urine test" (secondary, Tampa DUI Lawyer — https://www.tampaflduilawyer.com/defenses/breath-test/presumptions-of-impairment/ — Accessed 2026-10-24, citing State v. Bodden, 877 So. 2d 680 (Fla. 2004)). The State's case therefore rests on the combination of driving pattern, officer observations (speech, coordination, pupils, admissions), standardised field sobriety exercises, and — where used — a Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) evaluation.
  • DRE evaluations [VERIFY — scope limited]. Secondary commentary (Arrieta Law — https://www.arrieta-law.com/blog-new-dui-law-florida.html — Accessed 2026-10-24) states that drug-DUI cases "typically" involve field sobriety exercises, officer observations, and often a DRE evaluation, and that "Florida's drug recognition standards don't perfectly align with the actual impairment window for THC, and DRE evaluations have been challenged in court." No Florida statute creating a DRE programme or prescribing a DRE protocol for cannabis was located in this run, and no Florida appellate holding on DRE admissibility for cannabis specifically was verified [VERIFY, Gap 12-05]. Do not present DRE as a statutory test or as a THC-impairment meter: it is an officer-opinion protocol whose weight is for the fact-finder, and its cannabis reliability is contested in the secondary literature.
  • Hemp/CBD and DUI. A driver impaired by a hemp product (including a hemp THC beverage) can commit DUI under §316.193(1)(a) if the impairing substance is a Chapter 893 controlled substance or a §877.111 chemical substance and normal faculties are impaired. Lawful hemp use that does not impair is not DUI. A positive test for hemp-derived THC, without impairment, is the same presence-without-impairment problem as for medical marijuana. No Florida statute creates a hemp-specific driving defence or a hemp-specific driving limit [UNAVAILABLE].

12.3 Expungement and sealing

12.3.1 The headline: Florida has NO general or automatic marijuana expungement

There is no automatic expungement of marijuana convictions in Florida, and no marijuana-specific expungement statute in force. Relief, where it exists at all, comes only from the general, petition-based sealing/expungement scheme in Chapter 943 — and that scheme is deliberately narrow. Secondary summaries state this plainly (Drug Policy Watch, Florida brief — http://drugpolicywatch.info/states/florida.html — Accessed 2026-10-24: "Florida has no automatic cannabis-record expungement. Sealing and expungement are petition-based and limited, generally to non-conviction outcomes or a single eligible record, and many drug convictions are excluded"; Marijuana Herald state survey, 2026 — https://themarijuanaherald.com/marijuana-expungement-laws-by-state/ — Accessed 2026-10-24: Florida "Generally no — Florida has no broad statutory process for expunging an adult conviction. Some non-conviction and withheld-adjudication records may be eligible, but an actual marijuana conviction generally cannot be expunged under existing law").

12.3.2 The two routes — and the outcome that decides everything

Route Statute When it is available What it does
Court-ordered expunction §943.0585 No charging document was ever filed, or the charge was dismissed, dropped/nolle prossed by the State, or ended in acquittal / verdict of not guilty; and the petitioner has never been adjudicated guilty of a criminal offence in Florida, has never had a record sealed or expunged before, and the offence is not on the §943.0584 ineligible list Record is destroyed (FDLE retains a confidential copy); the person may lawfully deny the arrest in most contexts
Court-ordered sealing §943.059 Adjudication was withheld (withhold of adjudication — the court accepted a plea or found guilt but did not adjudicate the person guilty); and the petitioner has never been adjudicated guilty of a criminal offence in Florida, was not adjudicated guilty of anything arising from the arrest being sealed, has never had a record sealed or expunged before, and the offence is not on the §943.0584 ineligible list Record is made confidential — hidden from the public and most employers, but still accessible to criminal-justice agencies, licensing bodies, schools, and DCF
Automatic sealing (no petition) §943.0595 (added 2019) No charging document was filed, charges were dismissed/dropped as to all counts, or a judge/jury returned a not-guilty verdict or judgment of acquittal FDLE must seal the record automatically. This is sealing, not expungement, and it does not consume the one court-ordered sealing/expungement a person is allowed. It does not apply where the charging document was for a forcible felony under §776.08 or a sexual offence listed in §943.0435(1)(h)1.a.(I)
Sealed → expunged §943.0585 [10-year-sealed rule; subparagraph pinpoint unresolved — (1)(h) vs (2)(h) — see Audit] A record that has been sealed for at least 10 years becomes eligible for expunction on petition The only path by which a withhold-of-adjudication record can eventually be expunged

Sources for the table: §§943.0585, 943.059, 943.0595, as summarised in secondary reproductions — https://www.thelawofwe.com/certain-florida-charges-cant-be-expunged/ and https://legalclarity.org/possession-of-a-controlled-substance-in-florida-laws-and-penalties/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary; direct Online Sunshine opens of §§943.0585/943.059/943.0595 [VERIFY], Gap 12-06). The FDLE process (Certificate of Eligibility, $75 FDLE processing fee as reported secondarily, certified disposition, fingerprint card, then petition to the circuit court) is described in secondary Orlando practice material — https://erasethecase.com/locations/orlando-expungement-lawyer/ — Accessed 2026-10-24; the $75 figure is a secondary-reported FDLE fee, not a statute quote [VERIFY against the FDLE Seal & Expunge page, Gap 12-06].

The decisive rule, stated three ways because it is the most commonly misunderstood point in this Part: 1. An adjudication of guilt closes both doors. §943.059(1)(b) requires that the petitioner "has never been adjudicated guilty in this state of a criminal offense," and §943.059(1)(c) requires that the petitioner "was not adjudicated guilty of anything arising from the arrest being sealed." A marijuana possession conviction therefore cannot be sealed and cannot be expunged under current law, however old or however small the amount. That is why a withhold of adjudication at plea/sentencing is outcome-determinative for a first-time possession defendant. 2. A withhold is sealable, not immediately expungeable. Withheld adjudication is not on the §943.0585(1) expunction list. It can be sealed under §943.059, and only after 10 years sealed can it be expunged under §943.0585 [10-year-sealed rule; subparagraph pinpoint unresolved — (1)(h) vs (2)(h) — see Audit]. 3. One lifetime limit. A person may obtain only one court-ordered sealing or expungement in their lifetime (subject to the narrow exceptions in the statutes, e.g. automatic sealing under §943.0595 does not count). A prior sealing/expungement — for any offence, not just a drug offence — bars a later one.

12.3.3 Which marijuana offences are categorically ineligible — §943.0584

Even a withhold of adjudication does not help if the offence is on the §943.0584(2) ineligible list. The drug-relevant entries are:

"(ff) Manufacturing a controlled substance in violation of chapter 893; (gg) Drug trafficking, as defined in s. 893.135;" Source: §943.0584(2)(ff)–(gg), Florida Statutes, as reproduced at https://syfert.com/florida/statutes/0943.0584.html — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary reproduction; history through ch. 2025-156 shown on that page; direct Online Sunshine open [VERIFY], Gap 12-06).

Consequences for cannabis offences: - Simple possession (≤20 g misdemeanour; >20 g felony possession, non-trafficking) is NOT on the §943.0584 list. It is therefore sealable on a withhold and expungeable on a non-conviction outcome, subject to all other criteria (no prior adjudication, no prior sealing/expungement, no open case, completion of supervision). This is the only marijuana category with a realistic Chapter 943 path. - Trafficking in cannabis (§893.135(1)(a) — >25 lb or 300+ plants, Run 1 Part 1) is categorically ineligible, even on a withhold, even on a dismissal? — careful: the §943.0584 bar applies to a finding of guilt or a guilty/no-contest plea to a listed offence; secondary commentary (Miami Criminal Lawyer — https://www.miami-criminal-lawyer.net/cases/state-crimes/seal-expunge-records.html — Accessed 2026-10-24) states: "The charge alone does not create this bar. If charges were never filed, were dismissed, or ended in an acquittal, you may still qualify if you meet the other requirements." That distinction is adopted here as secondary and flagged [VERIFY] against the current §943.0584 text (Gap 12-06). In practical terms: a trafficking charge that was dropped does not itself bar relief; a trafficking plea with withhold does. - Manufacturing a controlled substance (Chapter 893) is categorically ineligible on the same terms — which covers cultivation charged as manufacturing, not merely possession of a grown plant. Home-grow cultivation (prohibited for all persons in Florida, Run 1 Part 1) charged as manufacture therefore carries a permanent record-clearing bar that simple possession does not. - Sale / delivery / paraphernalia offences are not separately listed in §943.0584(2) (except as manufacturing/trafficking), so they follow the general rule: sealable on a withhold, expungeable on a non-conviction outcome, barred on an adjudication of guilt — subject to the full §943.0584 list (which includes, among many others, domestic violence, sexual offences, robbery, burglary of a dwelling, and aircraft piracy) and to the other §943.059 criteria. DUI is not on the §943.0584 list, but a DUI conviction is still barred by the adjudication-of-guilt rule in §943.059(1)(b); a DUI resolved by dismissal, diversion ending in dismissal, or withhold follows the general table above [VERIFY — diversion/withhold DUI practice varies by circuit and is secondary, Gap 12-06]. - Juvenile and human-trafficking-victim relief exist under separate statutes (§943.0583 for human-trafficking victims; juvenile provisions) and are not marijuana-specific; they are noted here only so they are not mistaken for a general marijuana amnesty. They were not researched in depth in this run [VERIFY if needed for a juvenile/victim case, Gap 12-06].

12.3.4 Bills that would have changed this — all dead, none is law

  • SB 1026 (2025) — "Expunction of Qualifying Marijuana Offenses" (Sen. Davis). Would have defined "qualifying marijuana offense," required FDLE to issue certificates of eligibility for expunction of qualifying marijuana offences, specified a petition procedure, and provided criminal penalties for false sworn statements. Last action: 16 June 2025 — Died in Criminal Justice (after being indefinitely postponed and withdrawn from consideration on 3 May 2025). Source: flsenate.gov bill page — https://flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2025/1026/?StartTab=Analyses — Accessed 2026-10-24. Not law. Do not describe it as an available procedure.
  • HB 747 (2026) — "Rec./Sealing of Criminal History Records." A public-records-exemption bill (expanding the exemption to sealed records of persons adjudicated guilty of certain nonviolent misdemeanours; it does not expand §943.059 sealing eligibility), not a marijuana-specific amnesty. It passed the Criminal Justice Subcommittee (15–2, 20 Jan 2026) and the Government Operations Subcommittee (14–0, 29 Jan 2026), then died in the Judiciary Committee on 13 March 2026. Source: LegiScan history — https://legiscan.com/FL/bill/H0747/2026 — Accessed 2026-10-24 (secondary tracker; flsenate.gov page https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026/747 — Accessed 2026-10-24). Not law.
  • No "Second Chance Act" marijuana expungement is in force in Florida. The District of Columbia's Second Chance Act dates that appear in other states' research must not be imported into Florida. If a future Florida bill uses that name, its chapter law — not its title — will decide its effect.

12.4 Consumption lounges and events

12.4.1 Marijuana consumption lounges: none authorised, and the law points the other way

No Florida statute authorises a marijuana consumption lounge, café, or on-site consumption facility, and no MMTC licence type includes on-site consumption. The position is established by the combination of four enacted rules, not by the absence of a single "no lounges" sentence:

  1. Medical use excludes public use. §381.986(1)(k)5. (Run 1 Part 1) excludes from "medical use" use/administration on public transportation, in a public place, at work (unless the employer permits it), in a correctional institution, on school grounds (except §1006.062), and in a school bus, vehicle, aircraft, or motorboat — except low-THC cannabis not in smoking form. A lounge open to the public is a "public place" for this purpose; patient use there is not medical use.
  2. Public use by a patient is a crime. §381.986(12)(c) (Run 1 Part 1): a qualified patient who uses marijuana (not low-THC cannabis) "in plain view of or in a place open to the general public" commits a first-degree misdemeanour. A lounge that invited patients to consume on its premises would be inviting the offence.
  3. MMTCs cannot sell anything else on site. §381.986(8)(e)16.f. (Run 1 Part 1): an MMTC "may not dispense or sell any other type of cannabis, alcohol, or illicit drug-related product" other than a certified delivery device. There is no "consumption endorsement," "lounge endorsement," or "social-use endorsement" in §381.986 or Chapter 64-4 [UNAVAILABLE — no such endorsement was located; cf. Run 1 Part 4, which found no separate edibles licence and only a FDACS food-establishment permit per location].
  4. Dispensing hours and premises rules do not create a consumption right. MMTCs may not dispense from their premises between 9 p.m. and 7 a.m. (but may deliver 24 hours a day) (§381.986(8)(f)4., Run 1 Part 1). That is a dispensing rule, not a consumption licence, and it does not authorise consumption on the premises at any hour.
  5. Smoking in enclosed indoor workplaces is separately excluded from medical use (§381.986(1)(k)6., Run 1 Part 1, citing §386.203(5)), and the Florida Clean Indoor Air Act (Chapter 386) prohibits smoking in enclosed indoor workplaces and public places generally. A 2026 proposal to extend Chapter 386 expressly to marijuana smoking/vaping in public places — SB 986 (2026) (Sen. Gruters), filed 19 December 2025, which would have defined "public place" to include streets, sidewalks, parks, beaches, and common areas of schools, hospitals, government buildings, apartment buildings, offices, lodging establishments, restaurants, transportation facilities and retail shops, and prohibited smoking/vaping a marijuana product in a customs smoking room at any time — was not enacted as of the Run 1 cutoff (its committee analysis is dated 16 January 2026 — https://www.flsenate.gov/Committees/DownloadMeetingDocument/8066 — Accessed 2026-10-24; final 2026 disposition now resolved in Audit: Died in Appropriations Committee on Agriculture, Environment, and General Government on 13 March 2026 — not law). It is cited here only to show the direction of travel: even the proposal was a ban, not a lounge authorisation. Do not cite SB 986 (2026) as law, and do not confuse it with SB 986 (2018), the dead school-marijuana bill in §12.9 — same number, different session, different subject.
  6. Private consumption by patients remains lawful only within the programme: in a private residence (subject to §12.6 landlord/HOA rules), in a form and amount consistent with the physician certification, within possession limits (70-day / greater-of-4-oz smoking possession cap, Run 1 Part 1), and not in any of the excluded locations in §381.986(1)(k)5. "Private" does not mean "a private club that sells admission to consume" — a members-only venue open to the public for consumption would still be a place open to the general public for §381.986(12)(c) purposes, and a venue that supplied marijuana to non-patients would commit unlicensed dispensing under §381.986(12)(j) and Chapter 893. No Florida case or rule creating a private-club exception was located [UNAVAILABLE].

12.4.2 Hemp events — a different, narrower picture

Hemp is not marijuana, so a hemp event is not automatically a marijuana lounge — but that does not make every hemp event lawful in every form:

  • Hemp product sale at events is currently governed by the general §581.217 regime, not by an event licence. There is no hemp "event licence" in §581.217 [UNAVAILABLE]. A business selling hemp extract at a festival must still comply with §581.217 labelling (batch, QR/website, expiry, mg-per-serving), child-appeal, and 21+ rules (Run 1 Part 1), and with any local event/temporary-vendor permitting that applies to any vendor at that venue. The festival-sale ban in HB 1409 / SB 1270 (2026) died (see §12.1.3) — festival sales are therefore not banned by that proposal, but neither are they specially authorised.
  • A dated, verified example — not a legal precedent. Cornbread Hemp was named "Official THC Beverage" sponsor of Rock the Ocean's Tortuga Music Festival, Fort Lauderdale Beach, 10–12 April 2026 (Business Wire, 9 April 2026 — https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260409660840/en/Cornbread-Hemp-Named-Official-THC-Beverage-of-Rock-the-Oceans-Tortuga-Music-Festival — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary press release). That shows hemp THC beverages being marketed at a major Florida festival in 2026. It does not show that on-site hemp consumption was authorised by any Florida statute, that the beverages were sold (as opposed to sampled/marketed) at the festival, or that any local ordinance permitted consumption on the beach — all [VERIFY] if a festival case is ever relied on. Fort Lauderdale Beach is a public place; a marijuana product consumed there would be public use under §381.986(12)(c) for a patient and a Chapter 893 offence for a non-patient, whatever the sponsor banner said.
  • Secondary claims about hemp public consumption are not adopted. A secondary hemp-retail page states flatly that "Public consumption of THC drinks is prohibited in Florida, including for registered medical marijuana patients" (GetSoul, undated — https://getsoul.com/blogs/cbd-education/are-thc-drinks-legal-in-florida — Accessed 2026-10-24). No Florida statute prohibiting hemp consumption in public was located in this run: the enacted public-use prohibition is the marijuana prohibition in §381.986(1)(k)5. and (12)(c). Whether a local ordinance (e.g. a beach or park alcohol-style open-container rule) prohibits hemp drinks in a specific public place is a local question [VERIFY jurisdiction by jurisdiction, Gap 12-07]. Do not state a statewide hemp public-consumption ban as law.
  • Industry/trade events (no consumption). Run 1 Part 6 verified 2026 trade events (Alternative Products Expo Miami, Florida Groves Orlando, FMCCE Orlando, CCORC Lake Nona, Florida CannFest Mt. Dora) as trade/education events. Nothing in this run changes their status, and nothing in their verified listings authorises on-site marijuana consumption. A trade show that allowed consumption would face the same §381.986(12)(c) / Chapter 893 problems as a lounge.

12.5 Cannabis tourism and visitor rules

  • Visitors cannot lawfully buy medical marijuana in Florida. Florida has no reciprocity and no visitor/temporary card. A "qualified patient" must be a Florida resident (or seasonal resident) added to the Medical Marijuana Use Registry by a Florida qualified physician and holding a Florida registry identification card (§381.986, Run 1 Part 1). Secondary summaries state this without qualification (LegalClarity — https://legalclarity.org/can-i-use-my-medical-card-in-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24: "Florida does not accept out-of-state medical marijuana cards. If you hold a card from another state, you cannot use it to buy cannabis at a Florida dispensary"; and https://legalclarity.org/does-florida-accept-out-of-state-medical-cards/ — Accessed 2026-10-24: "There is no reciprocity agreement, no visitor exception, and no workaround"). The seasonal-resident route is the only visitor-adjacent route, and it is not tourism: a seasonal resident who lives in Florida for at least 31 consecutive days per year and maintains a temporary residence can qualify through the same Florida-physician, in-person-initial-exam process as a permanent resident (Run 1 Part 1). A weekend or week-long visitor cannot meet that test, and a visitor who obtains a Florida card by misrepresenting residency risks revocation and fraud exposure [VERIFY — residency-fraud penalty pinpoint not opened in this run, Gap 12-08].
  • Bringing marijuana into Florida is a Florida offence, whatever the home state's law. Marijuana lawfully purchased in another state is still "cannabis" under §893.02(3) in Florida unless it was purchased from a Florida MMTC under a Florida certification. Possession by a non-patient is a first-degree misdemeanour (≤20 g) or third-degree felony (>20 g) (Run 1 Part 1), and bringing it into the state is within §893.13's "bringing into the state" language (Run 1 Part 1, §893.13 table). An out-of-state card is not a defence in a Florida court [secondary, LegalClarity — https://legalclarity.org/does-florida-accept-out-of-state-medical-cards/ — Accessed 2026-10-24; no Florida appellate case accepting an out-of-state card as a defence was located, Gap 12-08]. Transport across state lines also engages federal law (interstate transport of a controlled substance), which is outside this Part's Florida scope but is a further reason not to advise visitors to "bring their own."
  • What a visitor CAN lawfully buy and use. (i) Conforming hemp products (§581.217): a visitor aged 21+ may buy hemp extract products intended for ingestion/inhalation from a lawful Florida retailer on the same terms as a Floridian, subject to the same labelling and child-appeal rules; hemp is not limited to residents. After 11 December 2026, the federal hemp definition narrows (fixed baseline) while Florida's §581.217 does not change by itself — a visitor buying a product that is lawful in Florida but no longer federal hemp should not assume it is lawful to carry home to a state with a stricter hemp law, or to transport it interstate without advice. (ii) CBD-only / non-intoxicating hemp products on the same terms. (iii) Nothing else cannabis-related — no MMTC purchase, no patient transfer (transfer to anyone other than the patient or the patient's caregiver is expressly excluded from "medical use," §381.986(1)(k)4., Run 1 Part 1), no home grow, no "gifting" workaround (Florida has no adult-use gifting provision; a gift of marijuana to a non-patient is delivery under §893.13).
  • Florida patients travelling out of Florida. Whether another state honours a Florida card is that state's law, not Florida's, and is not determined here. A Florida patient who takes Florida marijuana out of state loses Florida's protection the moment the marijuana leaves the MMTC/patient chain and enters another jurisdiction's law — and federal interstate-transport exposure applies regardless of the destination state's reciprocity. Patients should not be advised that a Florida card "travels" (secondary reciprocity lists that name Arizona, Arkansas, Hawaii, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, New Hampshire, Oklahoma, Rhode Island, Utah and D.C. as honouring Florida cards — https://marijuanapackaging.com/blogs/resources/navigating-floridas-medical-marijuana-card-usage-reciprocity-and-regulations — Accessed 2026-10-24 — are not adopted here: each destination's current reciprocity rule [VERIFY] before any travel advice is given, Gap 12-08).
  • Cannabis tourism as a business. Because there is no adult-use market, no consumption lounge, and no visitor purchase right, there is no lawful "cannabis tourism" business model in Florida built on selling or serving marijuana to tourists. Lawful tourism-adjacent businesses are limited to: hemp retail (general retail rules), MMTC-adjacent services that do not dispense marijuana (e.g. physician clinics, which are regulated separately under §381.986(3)–(4)), and trade/education events without consumption (§12.4.2). Any marketing that invites tourists to "experience Florida cannabis" by consuming marijuana on site should be treated as inviting a §381.986(12)(c) / Chapter 893 offence unless a specific lawful basis is produced.

12.6 Landlord and tenant rules

12.6.1 No patient housing protection in Florida law

  • Chapter 83 (Landlord and Tenant) contains no marijuana-specific tenant protection. No section of Chapter 83 was located in this run that prohibits a landlord from refusing to rent to, or evicting, a medical marijuana patient, or that requires a landlord to permit medical marijuana use. The operative housing rules are therefore the lease, the general Chapter 83 termination provisions (§83.56 — notice to cure or terminate for lease violations; §83.56(2) for non-curable violations), and the private-property rule in §381.986(15)(d) (below). A landlord's right to enforce a lease term does not depend on Chapter 83 mentioning marijuana: if the lease prohibits smoking, drug use, or illegal activity, breach of that term is a lease violation on ordinary contract/Chapter 83 principles (secondary, Avvo landlord guide — https://www.avvo.com/legal-guides/ugc/what-landlords-should-know-about-marijuana-criminal-activity-and-lease-enforcement — Accessed 2026-10-24; secondary, not a statute quote).
  • §381.986(15)(d) — private property (verbatim, Run 1 Part 1):

    "This section does not impair the ability of any party to restrict or limit smoking or vaping marijuana on his or her private property." Source: §381.986(15)(d), Florida Statutes (Run 1 Part 1, Accessed 2026-10-24). "Any party" is not limited to landlords: it covers homeowners, HOAs/condominium associations, employers (as property owners), and any other private-property holder. A landlord or HOA that bans smoking/vaping marijuana on its property is exercising a right the medical-marijuana statute expressly preserves — it is not "overriding" the patient's card.

  • What the private-property rule does NOT say. It says "smoking or vaping." It does not, on its face, authorise a landlord to ban possession of marijuana, or non-smoking forms (tinctures, capsules, edibles, topicals) that produce no smoke or vapour. A 2025 adult-use bill (HB 1501, 2025 — https://legiscan.com/FL/text/H1501/id/3148020/Florida-2025-H1501-Introduced.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24) would have drawn exactly that line ("a landlord may not prevent his or her tenants from possessing or using marijuana by other means"), but HB 1501 was a proposed adult-use bill, not enacted, and its landlord sentence is not current law. Whether a lease that bans all marijuana possession/use (including non-smoking forms) is enforceable against a qualified patient is therefore a lease-construction question on which no Florida appellate holding was located in this run [VERIFY, Gap 12-09]. Practical advice in secondary sources (MMJ Health, 27 Aug 2026 — https://mmjhealth.com/medical-marijuana-lease-hoa-rules-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24) is consistent with this reading: "the question is never 'does my card cover this.' The question is 'what does this specific document say, and who signed it.'" Non-smoking forms are the patient's strongest practical position in a smoke-free building — but they are a negotiating position, not a statutory right, unless the lease or a court says otherwise.
  • Nursing homes, hospices, and assisted living facilities — facility policy controls. §381.986(15)(e) (Run 1 Part 1): the section "does not prohibit medical use (or caregiver assistance) in a licensed nursing home, hospice, or assisted living facility if the medical use of marijuana is not prohibited in the facility's policies." In other words, the facility may allow it or ban it; the statute does not compel either. A facility that bans it is not violating §381.986 by doing so.
  • Federally assisted / public housing — higher risk, and the old reasoning needs re-checking. Secondary sources state that HUD has taken the position that medical marijuana use is not a reasonable accommodation under the Fair Housing Act, §504 of the Rehabilitation Act, or the ADA, because federal law treats current users of illegal drugs as outside disability protection (JustAnswer/HUD summary — https://www.justanswer.com/fl-real-estate/nzuq5-1-downsides-sending-cease-desist.html — Accessed 2026-10-24; MMJ Health, 27 Aug 2026 — https://mmjhealth.com/medical-marijuana-lease-hoa-rules-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24). That reasoning was written when marijuana was Schedule I across the board. Under the fixed baseline, state-licensed medical marijuana is Schedule III from 28 April 2026. Whether HUD has updated its reasonable-accommodation position for Schedule III medical use, and whether a public housing authority may still deny admission or terminate for state-lawful medical use, was not verified in this run [VERIFY — HUD guidance post-April 2026, Gap 12-09]. Do not quote the old HUD Schedule I rationale as current without that check. What can be stated safely: (i) a Florida card does not override a federal housing rule; (ii) public-housing tenants face materially higher eviction/denial risk than private tenants, because the housing provider is bound by federal law; (iii) smoke-free public-housing policies (e.g. Orlando Housing Authority's policy prohibiting smoking, including marijuana, on all OHA property — https://www.orlandohousing.org/smoke-free-policy — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary/local policy) operate independently of the patient's card.
  • HOAs and condominiums. The same §381.986(15)(d) analysis applies: a declaration/bylaw that bans smoking/vaping is enforceable on its terms against a patient, subject to the declaration's own amendment and enforcement procedures. Secondary eviction-risk material (Law Firm Ocala, undated — https://www.lawfirmocala.com/blog/legal-information/medical-marijuana-eviction-risk-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24) notes the practical points that matter in a real case: the notice (7-day vs cure notice), the proof (odour alone is weaker after Williams v. State, Fla. 2d DCA, 1 Oct 2025, as reported secondarily — odour alone does not prove a crime, but can still support a no-smoking/nuisance lease claim), and the 5-business-day response deadline after service of an eviction complaint. Those are secondary practice points, not statute quotes, and the Williams holding [VERIFY] against the opinion itself (Gap 12-09).
  • No "medical marijuana" fair-housing claim under Florida law was located. Florida's Fair Housing Act (Chapter 760, Part II) prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, colour, national origin, sex, disability, familial status, and religion. No provision was located that treats qualified-patient status as a protected class or that requires a housing reasonable accommodation for marijuana use [UNAVAILABLE]. A patient whose underlying condition (e.g. PTSD, multiple sclerosis, cancer) is a disability may have a disability-accommodation claim for a non-marijuana accommodation (e.g. a parking space, a service animal, a structural modification) — but that is a disability claim, not a marijuana-use claim, and it does not compel a landlord to permit smoking/vaping.

12.7 Gun ownership conflicts for patients

Bottom line, stated honestly: there is no Florida safe harbour, the federal statute still says what it says, Schedule III does not by itself rewrite it, and the courts have narrowed — not removed — its application. A patient who buys or possesses a firearm on the assumption that "Schedule III fixed it" is taking a legal risk that no authority in this run supports.

12.7.1 The federal statute — 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3)

"It shall be unlawful for any person — … (3) who is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance (as defined in section 102 of the Controlled Substances Act (21 U.S.C. 802)) — … to ship or transport in interstate or foreign commerce, or possess in or affecting commerce, any firearm or ammunition; or to receive any firearm or ammunition which has been shipped or transported in interstate or foreign commerce." Source: 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3) (federal statute; quoted from the U.S. Code as reproduced in secondary Florida gun guides — https://legalclarity.org/can-you-own-a-firearm-with-a-medical-card-in-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24; direct U.S. Code open [VERIFY], Gap 12-10).

Two words do the work, and neither was changed by rescheduling: - "any controlled substance" — not "any Schedule I substance." Moving state-licensed medical marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III (fixed baseline, 28 April 2026) leaves it a controlled substance. Schedule III alone therefore does not remove a medical patient from the literal text of §922(g)(3). Secondary estate-planning commentary states this correctly (Florida Estate Planning Lawyer Blog, undated — https://www.floridaestateplanninglawyerblog.com/marijuana-rescheduling-and-gun-rights-what-florida-residents-need-to-know/ — Accessed 2026-10-24: "Rescheduling alone does not provide protection" and "Federal gun prohibitions remain in force" unless Congress changes the statute or courts invalidate it). - "unlawful user" — the contested word. The ATF's 2011 open letter to federal firearms licensees (Assistant Director Arthur Herbert, 2011, as quoted in secondary sources — https://www.cannamd.com/can-i-own-a-gun-in-florida-if-i-get-my-medical-marijuana-card/ — Accessed 2026-10-24) stated:

"[A]ny person who uses or is addicted to marijuana, regardless of whether his or her State has passed legislation authorizing marijuana use for medical purposes, is an unlawful user of a controlled substance and is prohibited by Federal law from possessing firearms or ammunition." That letter was written when all marijuana was Schedule I and federally unlawful for every purpose. Whether its reasoning survives for state-licensed medical marijuana now in Schedule III is the open question in §12.7.3 — it has not been answered by a new ATF rule or a Florida statute in this run.

12.7.2 The purchase point — ATF Form 4473

When buying from a federally licensed dealer (FFL), the buyer must complete ATF Form 4473 (Firearms Transaction Record). The form asks whether the buyer is an unlawful user of, or addicted to, marijuana or any other controlled substance, with a printed warning that the use or possession of marijuana remains unlawful under federal law regardless of state legalisation for medicinal or recreational purposes (secondary, LegalClarity — https://legalclarity.org/can-you-own-a-firearm-with-a-medical-card-in-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24; CannaMD — https://www.cannamd.com/can-i-own-a-gun-in-florida-if-i-get-my-medical-marijuana-card/ — Accessed 2026-10-24). The consequences at the counter are mechanical: - Answer "yes" → the dealer must deny the sale (§922(d)(3) prohibits selling to a person the dealer knows or has reasonable cause to believe is an unlawful user; ATF has instructed dealers that presentation of a medical marijuana card gives reasonable cause to believe the customer is a prohibited person — secondary, LegalClarity, same page). - Answer "no" while being a current medical marijuana user → exposure for making a false statement on a federal form (18 U.S.C. §924(a)(1)(A) / §1001; secondary sources variously state up to 5 years (false-statement) and up to 10 years (prohibited-possession) maxima — the exact charging theory and maximum [VERIFY] against the current U.S. Code, Gap 12-10; do not quote a single maximum as settled). - Private sales do not solve the problem. §922(g)(3) prohibits possession, not just dealer purchase. Acquiring a firearm by private sale, gift, or inheritance while being an "unlawful user" is still within the statute's text (secondary, LegalClarity, same page). Florida has no general private-sale background-check statute that would change this analysis, and none is asserted here. - A proposed Form 4473 revision is NOT law and is NOT a safe harbour. An opinion piece (Marijuana Moment, undated op-ed — https://www.marijuanamoment.net/new-changes-to-atf-gun-form-put-medical-marijuana-patients-on-the-path-to-restored-second-amendment-rights-op-ed/ — Accessed 2026-10-24) reports a proposed revision that would focus the warning on recreational marijuana and omit reference to state-authorised medical cannabis. A proposed form revision, reported in an op-ed, is not an adopted ATF rule, not a statute, and not a defence. It is noted here only so it is not mistaken for one. If ATF adopts a revised form, its text — not the op-ed's description — will decide what a patient may truthfully answer [VERIFY — ATF Federal Register / adopted Form 4473, Gap 12-10].

12.7.3 What the courts have actually done — narrowed, not removed

  • Eleventh Circuit — Florida Commissioner of Agriculture v. Attorney General (Florida medical-marijuana patients' challenge). The Eleventh Circuit (which covers Florida) vacated a district-court dismissal of an as-applied Second Amendment challenge to §§922(g)(3) and 922(d)(3), holding that at the pleading stage the federal government had failed to demonstrate that disarming state-law-compliant medical-marijuana users is consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearms regulation under Bruen/Rahimi (secondary, Snell & Wilmer via JD Supra — https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/medical-marijuana-and-the-second-1009075/ — Accessed 2026-10-24; plaintiffs included Florida patients Vera Cooper and Nicole Hansell, and prospective patient Neill Franklin). What this means: the challenge survived dismissal and was sent back for further proceedings. It did not hold that Florida patients may now lawfully buy or possess firearms, did not enjoin §922(g)(3), and did not create a Florida safe harbour. Secondary commentary states this correctly (Drug2Go — https://www.drug2go.com/blog/medical-marijuana-firearm-rights-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24: "Not automatically. Bruen set the framework… The Eleventh Circuit's ruling only means that the government must try harder to justify the law; it did not outright legalize firearm possession for patients").
  • United States v. Hemani, No. 24-1234 (U.S. Supreme Court, decided 18 June 2026, per the fixed federal baseline and Run 1's federal context). The Court held, as applied and narrowly, that a status-only §922(g)(3) prosecution of a regular marijuana user for in-home possession, with no danger showing, was inconsistent with the Second Amendment. That is a narrow, fact-specific holding: it does not hold that §922(g)(3) is facially unconstitutional, does not address dealer purchase (Form 4473), concealed carry, carrying in public, or possession combined with any danger-related fact, and — on the secondary Florida analysis found in this run (Dr. Green Relief, updated 2026 — https://www.drgreenrelief.com/blog/florida-guns-and-marijuana/ — Accessed 2026-10-24) — "Whether a Florida medical marijuana patient can truthfully make that certification after the Supreme Court's 2026 Hemani ruling is a legal question for a firearms lawyer." That is the correct posture for this report: Hemani is a defence argument for a specific prosecution, not a permission slip. No ATF safe harbour for medical patients was located in Run 1's federal research or in this run [VERIFY — ATF post-Hemani guidance, Gap 12-10].
  • Interaction with the fixed Schedule III baseline. Three distinct questions must not be collapsed: (1) Is state-licensed medical marijuana still a "controlled substance" for §922(g)(3)? Yes — Schedule III is still a schedule. (2) Is a state-licensed medical patient an "unlawful user"? Contested — the ATF 2011 letter says yes (on Schedule I reasoning); Hemani and the Eleventh Circuit remand say the government must justify disarmament historically and cannot rely on status alone in the narrow Hemani fact pattern; no binding holding in this run says a Florida patient is categorically not an unlawful user. (3) May a Florida patient truthfully answer "no" on Form 4473 today? Unresolved — that is the question the Dr. Green Relief analysis correctly leaves to a firearms lawyer. This report does not answer it.

12.7.4 Florida state law — no state ban, but no state override either

  • §381.986 does not mention firearms. There is no firearms provision in the medical-marijuana statute, and no Florida statute creates a patient firearms safe harbour [UNAVAILABLE].
  • Chapter 790 (Weapons and Firearms) does not list medical-marijuana patient status as a possession disqualifier. The state possession bans in §790.23 cover convicted felons and certain juvenile offenders, not controlled-substance users as such (secondary, LegalClarity — https://legalclarity.org/can-you-own-a-firearm-with-a-medical-card-in-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24). Possession under Florida law alone is therefore not barred by patient status — but that is a statement about Florida law only, and federal law applies concurrently. Under the Supremacy Clause, a state permission does not override a federal prohibition.
  • Concealed weapon/firearm licence — §790.06 — CONFLICTING secondary accounts, flagged. Secondary sources conflict on whether §790.06 incorporates the federal bar, and this report does not resolve the conflict:
  • One account (LegalClarity — https://legalclarity.org/do-you-lose-your-gun-rights-with-a-medical-card-in-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24) states §790.06 "does not mention medical marijuana cards directly," bars applicants found guilty of a Chapter 893 offence within the past 3 years and those who "chronically and habitually" use substances to the extent normal faculties are impaired, and that "simply holding a medical marijuana card does not trigger either of those bars," with FDACS (which processes concealed-weapon applications) not cross-referencing the OMMU registry.
  • Another account (The Gun Zone — https://thegunzone.com/can-you-have-concealed-carry-and-a-medical-card-in-florida/ — Accessed 2026-10-24) states §790.06(2)(e) "incorporates the restrictions imposed by federal law" and therefore "effectively prohibits" patients from obtaining or maintaining a licence — and a third (Dr. Green Relief — https://www.drgreenrelief.com/blog/florida-guns-and-marijuana/ — Accessed 2026-10-24) states §790.06 requires that "no Florida or federal law bars you from having a firearm," so "the question turns on federal law, which Florida's license statute adopts." Resolution: [VERIFY] against the current §790.06 text (Gap 12-10). Until that text is opened, do not state either that a patient can safely hold a concealed-weapon licence or that a licence will be revoked on patient status alone. What is safe to state: (i) Florida also has permitless carry for adults who are not otherwise prohibited — but "not otherwise prohibited" brings the federal question straight back in; (ii) a Florida concealed-weapon licence, even if issued, does not override §922(g)(3); (iii) the FDACS non-cross-referencing practice reported secondarily is an administrative practice, not a legal defence, and it can change without a statute changing.
  • Practical consequences for a patient who already owns firearms. This report gives no individual legal advice, but the risk map is: (a) federal prosecution for possession is rare as a standalone charge but is routinely added where guns and marijuana are found together; (b) a false Form 4473 answer is a separate federal offence from possession; (c) a state concealed-weapon licence does not cure (b) or (a); (d) Hemani helps only a defendant who can show the narrow Hemani facts (in-home possession, status-only prosecution, no danger showing) — it is not a pre-clearance. Any patient in this position needs a Florida firearms lawyer, not a dispensary's assurance.

12.8 Pet and veterinary products

12.8.1 There is no veterinary marijuana in Florida

  • Marijuana cannot be prescribed, dispensed, or administered for an animal under §381.986. The programme is for "qualified patients" — human patients with a qualifying condition diagnosed by a qualified physician (§381.986(2)–(4), Run 1 Part 1). A veterinarian is not a "qualified physician" under §381.986, an animal is not a "qualified patient," and no MMTC may dispense marijuana for veterinary use. Giving a pet marijuana (including a patient's own medical marijuana) is not "medical use" under §381.986(1)(k), and if the amount/form is outside the patient's own certification it is also a transfer/use outside the programme. No Florida veterinary-marijuana licence, rule, or Board of Veterinary Medicine position authorising veterinary marijuana was located [UNAVAILABLE].
  • Animal cruelty / poisoning exposure (not researched in depth). Knowingly giving an animal a substance that harms it can engage Chapter 828 (animal cruelty) and general veterinary-practice law. That exposure is noted here only as a risk flag; no Chapter 828 pinpoint was opened in this run [VERIFY if a poisoning case is ever advised on, Gap 12-11].

12.8.2 Hemp extract in pet food and treats — lawful, capped, and not a drug

  • Rule 5E-3.003(5), Florida Administrative Code — hemp extract in pet food/treats (verbatim core, via FAC reproduction):

    "(5) Hemp extract in pet food, pet treats, specialty pet food and specialty pet treats. (a) Hemp extract as defined in Section 581.217(3)(e), F.S. used in pet food, pet treats, specialty pet food and specialty pet treats must be tested and have a certificate of analysis prepared by an independent testing laboratory as required in Florida Statutes § 581.217(7). (b) Pet food, pet treats, specialty pet food and specialty pet treat products shall not contain more than 0.3% total delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol concentration on a dry weight basis. (c) [Products exceeding 0.3%] shall be detained pursuant to Florida Statutes § 580.111 [and] shall not be further subdivided or renumbered such that the integrity of the lot for identification is not maintained. The manufacturer or distributor shall not dispose of [them] in any manner until written permission is given by the Department or a court of competent jurisdiction." Source: Rule 5E-3.003(5), F.A.C. — http://flrules.elaws.us/fac/5e-3.003/ — Accessed 2026-10-24 (eLaws FAC reproduction; flrules.org direct open [VERIFY], Gap 12-11).

  • Labelling for pet hemp products (Rule 5E-3.005, via secondary draft/FAC summaries). Pet food/treats containing hemp extract must be labelled as required in §581.217(7) and must declare milligrams of CBD per serving, with the serving size defined on the label; the label must not contain claims indicating the product is intended for diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment, or prevention of disease — i.e. the product must not be a "drug" as defined in §580.031(9) (secondary, FVMA Advocate summary by legal advisor Ed Bayó, 2022 — https://embed-rech-01.dialog.cm/fvma_faep/docs/web_advocate_issue_1_2022/s/15840564 — Accessed 2026-10-24; Scribd draft of the FDACS hemp rules — https://www.scribd.com/document/413785160/FDACS-Hemp-Rules-Draft — Accessed 2026-10-24). The "not a drug" line is the whole regulatory distinction: a pet hemp product that claims to treat arthritis, anxiety, seizures, or any disease crosses from feed/treat into drug territory, where neither §581.217 nor Rule 5E-3 authorises it.
  • Veterinarians selling pet hemp products (secondary, flagged). The FVMA summary states veterinarians "may sell the above products without obtaining any additional licenses or permits," provided the products are not claimed to be drugs and the labels comply with §581.217 and Rule 5E-3.005, and that a veterinarian may explain that a product "helps" or provides "relief" for symptoms without claiming it cures or treats a condition (FVMA, 2022, same source). That is a 2022 secondary summary of a professional association, not a Board of Veterinary Medicine rule, and it is flagged [VERIFY] against the current Board/FDACS position (Gap 12-11). Do not present "vets may sell without a licence" as a current rule without that check. What is firmly established is the product rule (≤0.3% total delta-9, independent-lab COA, §581.217(7) labelling, no disease claims) — the seller rule for veterinarians is the unverified part.
  • Human hemp rules do not transfer to pets by analogy. The 21+ age rule in §581.217(7)(d) is for products "intended for human ingestion or inhalation" (Run 1 Part 1). It does not set a purchase age for pet treats (the purchaser is the human owner, and the product is not for human ingestion). Conversely, the pet-food cap (0.3% total delta-9, dry weight) is stricter in form than the human hemp-extract rule in one respect: for human hemp extract, §581.217 uses a wet-weight basis for extract (Run 1 Part 1), while Rule 5E-3.003(5)(b) uses a dry-weight basis for pet products. Do not conflate the two.
  • Post-11 December 2026 note. Under the fixed federal baseline, the federal hemp definition narrows to total THC and a 0.4 mg per-container cap. Rule 5E-3.003(5)(b) is a Florida rule keyed to 0.3% total delta-9; it does not change by itself on 11 December 2026, and no FDACS update to the pet rule was located [UNAVAILABLE — same gap as the general federal-response gap].

12.9 Medical marijuana in schools

12.9.1 The enacted law — §1006.062(8), not §381.9867

The task brief's reference to "§1002" is not adopted: the school provision is in Chapter 1006, and Run 1 cited it correctly. The enacted provision is short, and its brevity is the point: it mandates a district policy, not a statewide administration procedure.

  • §1006.062(8) — verbatim, opened directly on the official 2025 Florida Statutes chapter page in this run:

    "Each district school board shall adopt a policy and a procedure for allowing a student who is a qualified patient, as defined in s. 381.986, to use marijuana obtained pursuant to that section. Such policy and procedure shall ensure access by the qualified patient; identify how the marijuana will be received, accounted for, and stored; and establish processes to prevent access by other students and school personnel whose access would be unnecessary for the implementation of the policy." Source: §1006.062(8), Florida Statutes (2025), Chapter 1006 page — https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2025/Chapter1006/All — Accessed 2026-10-24 (direct official open; history: ss. 1, 13, ch. 2017-232; s. 89, ch. 2018-106; s. 39, ch. 2020-9).

  • Sunset note printed on the same page (verbatim):

    "Section 1, ch. 2017-232, provides that '[i]t is the intent of the Legislature to implement s. 29, Article X of the State Constitution by creating a unified regulatory structure. If s. 29, Article X of the State Constitution is amended or a constitutional amendment related to cannabis or marijuana is adopted, this act shall expire 6 months after the effective date of such amendment.' If such amendment or adoption takes place, subsection (8), as created by s. 13, ch. 2017-232, is repealed." Source: Note 1 to §1006.062, same page — Accessed 2026-10-24. Practical meaning: if a future constitutional amendment related to cannabis is adopted, §1006.062(8) is repealed 6 months after its effective date unless the Legislature re-enacts it. No such amendment has been adopted as of Run 1 (Amendment 3 failed in 2024; no 2026 measure qualified), so §1006.062(8) remains in force as of 24 October 2026 — but its conditional repeal is a live tripwire for any future adult-use amendment, and any Run 2 update after a future amendment must re-check it.

  • What §1006.062(8) does and does not do. It requires each district school board to adopt a policy and procedure. It does not prescribe the procedure: it does not say who administers, in what form, at what time, or in what location. Those details are left to the district policy — which is why district policies differ and why the "caregiver-only, designated-location, no-smoking" pattern below is district practice, not statute.

12.9.2 How districts actually implement it — practice, not statute (flagged as such)

The following pattern is drawn from district policies and Department of Education material, not from §1006.062(8) itself, and each element should be checked against the specific district's current policy before being relied on for a student:

  • Caregiver administration only. Secondary Department of Education / district material (Florida Department of Education, "Conversations on Cannabis," 22 Oct 2024 — https://myemail.constantcontact.com/52nd-Edition---Conversations-on-Cannabis---October-22--2024.html — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary) states: "only a caregiver can administer the drug, and that individual (usually a parent or guardian) must be registered with the Florida Department of Health. The medication also must be taken in a designated location and at a certain time. Smokeable products are not allowed." District policy examples are consistent: Volusia County Schools Policy 218 ("Zoe's Policy," via Florida DOE document server — https://info.fldoe.org/docushare/dsweb/Get/Rendition-22213/unknown — Accessed 2026-10-24) defines "designated location" as "a location identified, in his or her sole discretion, by the school principal for the administration of medical marijuana by an authorized caregiver," and states its exclusive purpose is to comply with §1006.062(8) and that "[n]othing in this policy shall be interpreted to extend any privilege beyond that mandated by section 1006.062(8)." Martin County's draft policy (BoardDocs — https://go.boarddocs.com/fl/martin/Board.nsf/files/BHGJJQ4CFA91/$file/TBD%20-%20%20Medical%20Marijuana%20-%20NEW%20For%20Review%20-%20V1.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-24) similarly limits administration to caregivers/designees, requires locked inventoried storage while the product is on campus, and includes a federal-funding contingency (suspension for up to 120 days on notice that the federal government is investigating whether the policy violates federal law or jeopardises federal funds).
  • No smoking, no self-administration, no storage on grounds — as district policy, not as §1006.062(8) text. The "no smokable products" and "designated location only" rules appear in district policies and DOE summaries, not in the statute's one paragraph. A district policy that permitted a different form or location would not violate §1006.062(8) on its face — but it would still have to satisfy §381.986 (physician certification, forms, possession limits) and federal law. Do not quote district-policy details as if they were statute.
  • School personnel are not required to administer. Nothing in §1006.062(8) requires a teacher, nurse, or administrator to administer marijuana, and district policies reviewed here expressly restrict administration to caregivers/designees. The 2019 DOE summary notes the compliance problem this creates: "not all school districts have implemented policies as required by state law. Some cite concerns that doing so would risk federal funding because marijuana is a Schedule 1 drug" (ReportWire republication of the DOE material — https://reportwire.org/marijuana-use-in-k-12-schools-presents-challenges-medical-marijuana-program-connection/ — Accessed 2026-10-24, secondary; the Schedule I reasoning in that 2019-era material is now stale under the Schedule III baseline for medical marijuana — whether any district has updated its federal-funding analysis [VERIFY], Gap 12-12). A district that has not adopted a §1006.062(8) policy is in breach of a statutory duty, but that breach does not itself create a student's right to self-administer on campus: self-administration by a student, and possession by a student on school grounds outside the district policy, remain within §381.986(12)(c)'s first-degree-misdemeanour provision (use on school grounds except as provided in §1006.062) and the district's student-discipline code.
  • Interaction with §381.986. Three §381.986 provisions frame the school position and are consistent with §1006.062(8): (i) §381.986(1)(k)5.e. excludes use on preschool/primary/secondary school grounds from "medical use" except as provided in §1006.062; (ii) §381.986(12)(c) criminalises patient use (or caregiver administration) on school grounds except as provided in §1006.062; (iii) for patients under 18, only a caregiver may purchase or administer marijuana (§381.986(6)(f), Run 1 Part 1) — which is why the school pattern is caregiver administration: a minor patient cannot self-administer at school even under a district policy, because the minor cannot purchase/administer at all under §381.986(6)(f). A district policy cannot override (iii).

12.9.3 The bills that would have created a detailed school scheme — all dead

§381.9867 ("Medical use of marijuana in schools") was proposed four times and enacted zero times.
